en: Preface to the Reprint of the Separate Commentary on the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*,
Spoken by the Greatly Extensive One.
Written with prostrations and reverence by Dao Kui of Xin’an.

The "Flower Garland" (Avataṃsaka) Sūtra refers to the fundamental Dharma-wheel of the Greatly Awakened Ones throughout the ten directions and three periods of time as the great causal matter inherent in every person.
It is solely because sentient beings obscure it that the Buddhas appear in the world to illuminate and establish it;
therein, they adapt to the times, the regions, the discourse, the understanding, and the conceptualizations of each individual to accord with them.

The fundamental desire to extensively expound the boundless distinctions of the wondrous Dharma reaches its ultimate limit; not even a hair’s breadth can be added or subtracted within the sphere of one's own realization.

Only those who have attained this awakening know that the Buddhas and Patriarchs have no Dharma to give to others, and that there is not a single moment, a single place, or a speck of dust or a sea of lands where this is not being proclaimed.
Even if one wished to use ink equal to the volume of the great ocean and a brush as large as Mount Sumeru, [it would still be insufficient].
Even a writing brush cannot express even a small fraction [of its meaning], let alone this present sutra.

Thus, when Nāgārjuna entered the palace of the Bhagavat, he saw that it was already recorded there in three versions; yet, as the mental capacity of those in Jambudvīpa is limited, he recited out one hundred thousand stanzas in forty-eight chapters.
It was propagated throughout the Five Indies and transmitted eastward to China, where it was first translated during the Jin dynasty.
The thirty-six thousand stanzas were translated into sixty fascicles during the Tang dynasty, while the forty-five thousand stanzas were translated into eighty fascicles.
Later, the latter portion of the Prajñāpāramitā, which had been offered by the kingdom of Oḍra, was retranslated by the Tripiṭaka Master together with National Teacher Qingliang into forty fascicles;
the final fascicle of this version is the present "Ten Great Vows King. Thus, it spans from the Jin to the Tang dynasties.

Although it is missing from the two major commentaries, because it fully encompasses the essential framework of the entire sutra, Qingliang [Zongmi] produced a ten-fascicle commentary outside of his *Great Commentary* (*Da shuchao*).
Later, after the [new] translation was made, he further composed a separate commentary in one fascicle.

Guifeng [Zongmi] then wrote a sub-commentary (*chao*) upon this, which is the most detailed of all; it exhausts the vast surges of the ocean of the Tripitaka and gathers them back into a single point.
The taste of honey from the center and edges of my fingertips is suddenly offered for you to taste; if you seek instruction, awakening, and entry [into the Dharma], there is no door other than this.

I have always lamented that of the six hundred fascicles of Qingliang’s writings, most have now been scattered and lost, and even the ten fascicles of his *Xùshū* (Continued Commentary) no longer survive.
Fortunately, this single fascicle of the *Shùchāo* (Commentary and Sub-commentary) is complete in the Zhaoking edition of the Tripitaka.
For reasons unknown, neither the Northern nor the Southern Tripitaka includes this work, and the same is true for the editions printed in Jiaxing.

I fear that as time passes and years accumulate, it may once again fall into oblivion. Now that Qiang Shilong desires to circulate this Great Dharma, I have instructed him to carve these blocks for wide distribution, so that all may plant the supreme causes of merit and wisdom, leading to inconceivable and most excellent spiritual benefits.

Virtue is like water in the palms of one’s hands, yet it can still rescue sentient beings; the merit of a single verse that ascends to heaven is such that one may turn back even upon reaching the gates of hell.
As described in detail in the accounts of translations and spiritual responses, the wondrousness of a single phrase encompasses all meanings without omission.

The merit of reciting, studying, contemplating, and practicing it is equal to that of the Buddha’s omniscience (*sarvajñā*). That the ancient masters have already spoken of this with certainty is for the person of today to contemplate deeply.
Through faith and practice, one ultimately attains full realization; only then does one know that the Buddhas and Patriarchs truly did not deceive us.
It was only because we deceived ourselves that we failed to respond to their vast compassion.

Deeply grieved by my own delusion, I shall guide all beings throughout the measure of infinite lands and for as long as the future kalpas endure, following in the noble footsteps of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva, as the sutras describe—that this is what every person ought to do.
This is merely that which one dares not fail to do.
*A Separate Commentary on the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices" from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*,
Volume One, together with the Preface.
In explaining the text of the commentary (*śāstra*), there are two major divisions: first, the explanation of the title of the commentary;

second, the actual explanation of the commentary's text. Within the first [division], there are two parts: first, clarifying the title of the commentary as it was composed; second, identifying the name of the author. Within the first of these, there are two sections:
first, clarifying the title of the sūtra being explained; second, clarifying the title of the commentary that explains it. Within the first of these...

The commentary on the general title explains that this is the common name for the entire great work, while the subsequent explanation of the chapter headings refers to the specific titles of the individual chapters.
Now, regarding the first passage: the question asks whether these seven characters comprising the general title are in the language of Tang (Chinese) or in Sanskrit. The answer is:
among them, the single character "Buddha" is in Sanskrit, while the remaining six characters are all in the language of Tang. The question continues: if...
If one asks how it is pronounced collectively according to the Sanskrit original, the answer is as follows:
If the old Sanskrit is *mahāvaipulyabuddhavaṃśaprabhāsa-sūtra*, this is a corruption and an abbreviation.
According to the correct form, it should be pronounced *mahā-vimokṣa-buddha-vaṃśa-nāma-sūtra*.
*Mahā* means "great"; *vaipulya* means "extensive" (*fangguǎng*); *buddha* means "awakened one" (*juézhě*); *gaṇḍa* means "various flowers" (*záhuā*);
*vyūha* means "ornamentation" (*yánshì*); *sūtra* means "discourse" (*qìjīng*).
Taken as a whole in the language of Táng, it should be rendered as "Great Extensive Awakened One’s Various Flower Ornamentation Discourse," totaling eleven characters. Now, [regarding this...]
Because following antiquity also gives rise to goodness, the two characters "awakened one" (覺者) were removed and the single character "Buddha" (佛) was retained;
furthermore, the three characters "miscellaneous adornments" (雜飾契) were removed and the three characters "Avataṃsaka Sūtra" (華嚴經) were retained.

Thus, from among these eleven characters, four were abbreviated away and seven were preserved to serve as the general title. Within this, the upper six characters are that which is explained (the signified).

Regarding the meaning of these terms: the single character "teaching" (*jiao*) refers to the means of expression; within that which is expressed, "Mahāvaipulya" (Great and Vast) refers to the Dharma realized, namely the pure *dharmadhātu* with its essence, characteristics, and functions.
"Buddhāvataṃsaka" (Flower Ornament) refers to the person who realizes it;

herein, "Ornament" (*avaṃsaka*) serves as the general characteristic, while the remaining parts refer to cause and effect. The single character "Sūtra" (*jing*) refers to the teaching as the means of expression, as explained below.
The second section of the commentary clarifies the title of the chapter:
it is the "Chapter on the Vows of Samantabhadra’s Conduct. In the Sanskrit language, it is called *Ardhyatathāgatotpattisambhavakṣetrasamantabhadracaryāpraṇidhāna*.
(1) *Ardhya*, (2) *tathāgata*, (3) *utpatti*, (4) *sambhava*, (5) *kṣetra*, (6) *samantabhadra*, (7) *caryā*, (8) *praṇidhāna*. *Pra*... [the text continues].
Rāvaśa (7) Balivata (8). It is said that *ajintiya* means "inconceivable" (*acintya*);
*vimukta* means "liberation" (*vimukti*); *viṣaya* means "sphere" (*viṣaya*);
*samantabhadra* means "Samantabhadra"; *caryā* means "conduct" (*caryā*); *pra*... [The text is incomplete].
*Nidāna* means "vow" (in Chinese); *praveśa* means "entry" (in Chinese); *vargga* means "chapter" (in Chinese).

This is the chapter on the entry into the inconceivable realm of liberation through the practices and vows of Samantabhadra. Following the conventions of this region [China], the character for "entry" (*ru*) is placed at the beginning.
In the commentary, the text is abbreviated; in full, it should read: "Entry into the Inconceivable Realm of Liberation."

The *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna* chapter of the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra*, which is inconceivable and so forth, is that which is entered (*praveśya*), while the *Bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna* itself is that by which one enters (*praveśaka*).
As for why the Master of the Commentary did not fully list both [the object and the subject of entry] in his title:

the answer is that when commenting on the text according to the sūtra, he did indeed list them both; therefore, the title of the commentary was abbreviated, listing only the "means of entry" (*praveśaka*). Thus it is.

This refers to the "Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra. The following text extensively discriminates [the meaning]; from here below, it clarifies the title of the commentary (*śāstra*).
This title consists of the one fascicle of the commentary together with the five characters for the preface. As for the term "commentary" (*shū*;

*shū* is pronounced in the departing tone, while *shū* in the level tone means "to resolve"), it carries the sense of "resolving and opening up. This is because the principles and meanings within the sutra are profound and subtle; if not...

Because there was no means by which [the meaning] could be resolved, clarified, or brought to awakening, it was further stated that according to the *Shuowen*, the meaning of "writing" (*shu*) is "to annotate" (*shu*).
Now, having compiled the profound meanings of the sūtras and śāstras and written them together in one place to explain the text of the sūtra, it is therefore called a "commentary" (*shu*).
As for the word "one" (*yi*), it refers to a number; "juan" (fascicle) refers to rolling up and unrolling; since this alone circulates independently, it is called "one juan," including the preface.
The term "zhe" (者) refers collectively to the inclusion [of the preface]; "xu" (序) means "orderly arrangement. The *Erya* states:

"Entering the gate and seeing the screen, it is called the 'xu' (preface/outer wall). This refers to the eastern and western walls; by seeing these walls, one distinguishes the depth of the residence, and by observing the "xu," one understands the intent of the author.
Furthermore, "xu" means "to narrate," that is, to describe; it refers to the narration of the scripture.
The general meaning is compiled at the beginning of the text so that students may immediately perceive its essential purport; hence it is called the "Preface.
△ Imperial Decree for the Great Chongfu Temple in Taiyuan Prefecture △ Śramaṇa Chengguan’s Separate Commentary.
Śramaṇa Zongmi of Guifeng Caotang Temple’s Sub-commentary on the Commentary.
From here below, the names of those capable of narrating [the history] are clarified. Regarding the edict concerning the Taiyuan Prefecture and other locations:

"Taiyuan Prefecture" refers collectively to that region, namely the Northern Capital among the Three Capitals. Geographically, it is situated within the jurisdiction of Hedong and Wei, corresponding to the ancient province of Bingzhou.
As for "Dachongfu Temple," this specifically indicates a distinct location; it is not the Kaiyuan Temple.
Examples include the Longxing Stone Chamber and others. In Sanskrit, this is called *vihāra*, correctly transcribed as *vihāra*, which means "place of practice.
It is so named because it is a place where those who have left the household life (renunciants) practice and reside.

The designation "monastery" (*si*) originated when Kāśyapa Mātanga first arrived in the Han land; he temporarily stayed with other guests at the Court of State Ceremonial (*Honglu*) before a *saṃghārāma* was subsequently established there.
The designation "White Horse" provides the name for the monastery. Regarding the phrase "śramaṇas and others," this specifically names those who can expound [the teachings].
*Śramaṇa* is a Sanskrit term; when written with one character above and two below (*shì luó mò ná*), it means "diligent and at rest.

Thus, a sutra states: "One whose mind is stilled reaches the fundamental source; therefore, he is called a śramaṇa. However, there are both ultimate meanings and conventional demonstrations of the path.
The differences regarding the defilement of the path are as described in the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*. The next two characters are the name of the Master of the Commentary (*śāstrakāra*).
Having passed through the holy eras of nine schools and served as the gate-teacher for seven emperors, he was granted the title "Qingliang.

As detailed extensively in his memorial stele, the term "commentary" (*shu*) is used by the Master himself as a mark of humility, implying that he did not compose it himself; the meaning is that he merely transmitted the ancient chapters without adding anything new.

Regarding the distinction between "transmitting" (*shu*) and "composing" (*zuo*): the one who transmits transmits rites and composes music. Thus, the *Lunyu* records: "The Master said: 'I transmit but do not compose;
I trust in and love antiquity, and I venture to compare myself to Lao Peng.

The Master meant that he merely transmitted and recounted the ancient chapters rather than creating new ones. The reason for this is that the composition of rites and music must necessarily accord with Heaven...
"Those of lower capacity practice it; because they possess virtue but lack rank, he 'transmits but does not create.

As for the phrase 'I venture to compare myself to our Old Peng,' 'venturing' (qie) means privately or modestly. 'Old Peng' refers to Pengzu; because he lived for eight hundred years, he is called Old Peng.
Furthermore, Wang Bi stated: "Lao refers to Lao Dan, and Peng refers to Pengzu. Old Peng was fond of..."
Regarding the narration of ancient matters, the Master [Confucius] said, "I have privately compared myself to Lao Peng"; this is likewise "narrating without creating.

To "trust and love antiquity" is the main intent of the commentary, which is also the same as this; therefore, it simply says "narrating. As for the term "edict" (*chì*), when a subordinate speaks of a command, they say "order" (*lìng*);
when a ruler issues an order, it is called an "edict" (*chì*). Thus, the author of the commentary was at that time receiving an imperial decree to translate the scriptures and compose this work.
Because this commentary circulated throughout the world, it says, "By imperial decree [it was promulgated] in Taiyuan and other regions.

How great is the True Realm! It is the source from which the myriad dharmas derive their beginning. Encompassing both emptiness and existence, it transcends all marks; entering into words and images, it leaves no trace.
Those who attain it through wondrous existence do not find it to be existent; those who attain it through true emptiness do not find it to be empty. It gives rise to all things.
When attained through cessation, it is true permanence; when attained through dependent origination, they mutually reflect one another.
From here begins the second section, the explanation of the commentary’s text, which is divided into four major parts: first, the general indication of the title and intent of the great work;
second, the homage, invocation, and request for empowerment; third, the opening of the chapters and the explanation of the text; and fourth, the expression of joy and dedication of merit. First:
Within this, there are four further sections: first, a general exposition on the Dharma-realm as the great foundation of the Buddha-dharma;
second, from "The Great Vaipulya Buddhāvataṃsaka Sūtra" onwards, a specific praise of this sūtra to clarify its essential purport;

third, from "Now, the profound relies upon the hundred thousand [verses]" onwards, the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching and the rare fortune of encountering it; fourth, from "Great Vaipulya" onwards, a brief [explanation].
This commentary on the general title serves to make known the essential framework. First, one might raise a hypothetical question:

"The commentaries composed by various schools generally begin by recounting how the Buddha manifested birth for the sake of sentient beings, appearing in formless or embodied manifestations as appropriate to teach the Dharma, starting with the Small Vehicle and proceeding to the Great Vehicle;
why does this work begin by first recounting the *dharmadhātu*? The answer should be: "Because this is the primary principle (*mūla*) of this sutra."
Furthermore, because it is the universal essence of all sutras, the universal basis of all dharmas, the fundamental source of delusion and enlightenment for all sentient beings,
the ultimate realization attained by all Buddhas, and the origin from which the practices of all Bodhisattvas arise,
this initial sudden teaching differs from the gradual approaches of other schools; that is to say, they differ in their provisional and ultimate aspects.
Because the schools differ, there are three parts within this passage: first, clarifying [the nature] by means of the Dharma; second, revealing it by means of persons, starting from "I, the Buddha";
and third, concluding with praise through both Dharma and analogy, starting from "To know. Within the first [section], there are two further parts:

the first line provides a general indication of the essential nature, while the subsequent part specifically clarifies its characteristics. Now, for the first: "How magnificent is the True Realm! This includes the following phrase, borrowing the term "pervasive" (zhōu).
Regarding the textual structure of the *Qian* hexagram in the *Yi*, the *Tuan* commentary states: "How great is the Great Primordial (Qianyuan)!
All things receive their beginning from it; it presides over Heaven. This means that the *Qian* hexagram possesses four virtues—namely, *yuan*, *heng*, *li*, and *zheng*.
Since *Qian* is the name of the hexagram and *yuan* is its primary virtue, they are mentioned together as "How great is the Great Primordial (*Qianyuan*). Thus, it is referred to in this manner.
The Yang energy is vast and great; the body of Heaven is expansive and far-reaching. Furthermore, because it initiates the Great Beginning (*yuan*) to give birth to the myriad things, it is said:

"How great! All things derive their beginning from it. The reason the *Qianyuan* (the Origin of Heaven) is designated as having the meaning of "vast and great" is that all phenomena of the ten thousand forms derive their life and beginning from the *Qianyuan*;
thus it may be called vast and great. As for its being "that which governs Heaven," it is because...
Its ultimate vigor serves as the beginning of all things; by means of this, it is able to preside over Heaven.
Heaven is a thing with form, and because its ultimate vigor can preside over all that has form, this is the virtue of the *Qianyuan* (the Primeval Purity of Qian).

Now, while these [first two lines] borrow the rhetorical momentum of that passage, what they take as their primary referent differs: that passage points to the *Qianyuan*, whereas this clarifies the *Zhen* (the True).
Regarding the term "realm" (*dhātu*), it refers to the myriad things as being nothing more than that which exists within heaven and earth;

this statement encompasses all phenomena (*dharma*) throughout both the mundane and supramundane worlds, and is thus distinct [from other usages]. The exclamation "How Great! (*dà zāi*) serves as an introductory phrase and a word of reverent praise.

As for the "True Realm," it is precisely the True Suchness Dharma-realm (*tathatā-dharmadhātu*); although there are many categories of dharma-realms, they are presented here in their unified totality.
However, the single true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is precisely the fundamentally pure mind that is the source of all Buddhas and sentient beings;
therefore, the thesis established below states: "The unified single true Dharma-realm is itself the one mind. Furthermore, the *Awakening of Faith* says:
"That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings; this mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane phenomena. Moreover, consider this in detail:

The *Xuánlù* states: "The realizations attained in the various assemblies of this sutra differ; when opened, they appear as ten thousand distinctions, yet when merged, they are but the one nature (*ekadhātu*).

When unfolded, it pervades and encompasses the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); when rolled up, it is subsumed within the single mind (*ekacitta*). Now, without departing from the single mind, it fully elucidates the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of the Dharma-realm.
What is called 'the single mind' is precisely the fundamental mind of sentient beings, which serves as [the basis] for the myriad dharmas."
From the *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* onwards, it is stated that "this dharma-realm is essentially one mind"; one should know that one's own mind is itself the fundamental essence of Buddhahood.

This meaning is clear when compared with the various preceding passages. It is evident that the provisional teachings take the eight consciousnesses as the "mind," which are exclusively conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and subject to arising and ceasing, and thus cannot serve as the ultimate essence.
Now, the "one dharma-realm mind" is clarified in accordance with the *Awakening of Faith*.

The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* opens two gates—True Suchness (*tathatā*) and arising-and-ceasing—within this single mind; this clarifies that the mind is the one true Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and thus it is designated here as the "essence-nature" (*svabhāva*).
The meaning of the mind according to these two schools will be explained extensively below. Having concluded the general designation of the essence-nature, the commentary [states]:

"The source from which the myriad dharmas derive their sustenance," and so forth, which constitutes the second section: the specific elucidation of the essence and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). Regarding this:

The middle three [points] are: first, clarifying that [the mind] is the root of all phenomena; second, clarifying its pervasive inclusion and freedom from conceptual attachment; third, clarifying the manifestation of its wondrous function in the present. Regarding the first, "provision" (*zī*) carries the meaning of relying upon or borrowing. There is not a single phenomenon that is not manifested by the fundamental mind; there is not a single phenomenon that is not the dependent origination of the true realm (*dharmadhātu*); there is not a single phenomenon that exists prior to the dharma-realm. Since even the subtle habitual tendencies are difficult to eliminate, yet all are completely purified, how much more so the seeds and active manifestations! The *Great Commentary* states: "To sweep away until not a speck of dust remains" is the meaning of severing the obstructions;

this is explained further below. Regarding the threefold grace: the *Sūtra Commentary* says, "From the profound stillness to the far-reaching illumination," illuminating the profound stillness within the myriad transformations.

Regarding "delimiting movement and function within a single void": the first phrase means functioning while remaining eternally quiescent; the second phrase means being quiescent while functioning eternally.

"Quiescence" (jì) means the absence of sound; "vast emptiness" (liáo) means the absence of form. "The myriad transformations" refers to all phenomena (dharmas), which arise provisionally from conditions like illusions and transformations.

To fuse the body and the lands so that they mutually contain one another means that the environment (*āśraya*) and its inhabitants (*adhiṣṭhita*) are without obstruction. However, regarding the principle of the mutual penetration of the environment and its inhabitants, there are six propositions:
First, the manifestation of the environment within the environment, meaning that dust motes contain worlds. As the *Xiangpin* (Chapter on Characteristics) states:
"The number of Buddha-lands equal to the atoms of a Buddha-field—such lands can all be manifested within a single thought-moment, each appearing within a single atom. Second... [text continues]

"The Tathāgata, within a single pore, has all the Buddhas as numerous as the atoms of all lands sitting amidst assemblies of Bodhisattvas, who together surround him as he expounds the supreme practices of Samantabhadra.
Regarding "correctly manifesting within based upon," this refers to the manifestation of lands within the pores, as stated in the *Gaṇanavyūha-parivarta*: "Within..."
Within a single subtle pore, unspeakable numbers of lands enter in succession; that pore can contain all those lands, yet those lands cannot pervade the entire pore.
This refers to the manifestation of the Buddhas within the four reliances (catvāri pratisaraṇāni).

Specifically, it means the manifestation of Buddhas within a speck of dust, as stated in the subsequent passage: "Within a single atom, there are Buddhas as numerous as atoms, each dwelling amidst assemblies of bodhisattvas, teaching the inexhaustible Dharma."
The same applies to the realms and particles; one should have deep faith that all Buddhas completely fill them. Fifth, the manifestation of the support and the supported within the internal [realms]:

this refers to the manifestation of the Buddha’s body and his lands within the particles. As a sutra says: "Within each and every particle, inexhaustible bodies appear, further manifesting various adorned lands.
Sixth, the manifestation of the support and the supported within the correct [body]: this refers to the manifestation of the entire Buddha-body and its lands within a single pore.
The Sūtra states: "Within a single pore are inconceivable lands as numerous as atoms;
in each of these dwellings, there is a World-Honored One of Universal Radiance preaching the Dharma amidst an assembly.

These two lines—fifth and sixth—fully manifest the mutual identity and mutual entry (*xiāngjí xiāngrù*) that constitute the fused body and land (*róngshēn jià*). As for "mutual containment" (*xiānghán*), because they accord with the nature of reality (*xìng*), whichever one is raised...
First, it must necessarily encompass all things entirely. The phrase "the stream of sound and light shines afar" refers precisely to the spreading light of the teachings and their proclamation;
thus, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* speaks of the "light of teaching" and the "light of wisdom.

Furthermore, since "sound" refers to the sound of the teachings and "light" refers to luminous radiance, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "The Buddha emits light that pervades the world, illuminating the ten [directions]."
Throughout all lands, he expounds the inconceivable and vast Dharma to forever shatter the darkness of sentient beings' ignorance and delusion.

"Far-reaching" (*xia*) means distant; "illuminating" (*chu*) means shining. Since the response to the spiritual capacity of those in the lands of the ten directions occurs immediately upon their invocation, it is not restricted to within the three thousandfold world system;
therefore, it is called "far-reaching illumination."

△ Our Sovereign attained this through spiritual discernment, reaching the ultimate void and preserving the great harmony. His sagely writings eclipse those of a hundred kings, and his pure influence blows upon the myriad nations.
He spreads the profound transformation to awaken the dreaming world, and transmits the Heavenly Truth for the sake of human nature and emotion.
Our Emperor attained the ultimate nature and sentiment; this second section summarizes what Wang Xian [said].

At that time, "the numinous discernment reaches the void and the Ultimate" means that his brilliant spirit was discerning and reached the Way of the Void and the Great Ultimate (*tài jí*). "Numinous discernment" refers to wisdom;
"the void and the Ultimate" refers to principle. "Knowing all phenomena and preserving the harmony of the Great Harmony" is from the *Book of Changes* (*Zhou Yī*).

The *Hexagram Commentary* on Qian states: "The Way of Qian undergoes transformation and change; each rectifies its nature and destiny, preserving and harmonizing the Great Harmony, which constitutes benefit and constancy.

This means that through non-action (*wuwei*), it transforms above in accordance with Heaven and unites below with humanity. Thus, the Sage has no private mind, taking the minds of the common people as his own.
Consequently, his virtue accords with Heaven and Earth, he responds appropriately to human relations, and he returns to simplicity and restores the primal purity.

The three powers (Heaven, Earth, and Humanity) are unified as one in Great Harmony; because harmony constitutes Great Joy, the *Book of Rites* states: "Great Music is in harmony with Heaven and Earth;
Great Ritual is in rhythm with Heaven and Earth. The *Analects* states: "To employ harmony is held as precious," which means employing ritual to provide regulation.
Thus, the perfection of both Ritual and Music is captured by this intent. That the sacred texts were eclipsed during the era of the Hundred Kings was due to the constraints of the times.
This treatise discusses virtues that surpass those of the three ancient eras: the Three Sovereigns of High Antiquity, the Five Emperors of Middle Antiquity, and the Three Kings of Late Antiquity.
"Wen" (Civility) refers to the weaving together of heaven and earth; thus, the *Book of Changes* says: "Observe the patterns of heaven (*tianwen*) to examine the changes of the seasons;

observe the patterns of humanity (*renwen*) to transform and perfect the world. The relationships between ruler and subject, father and son, and the distinctions of honor and subordination, high and low, are what constitute the patterns of humanity.
This is clearly manifest in the sagely brilliance of Emperor Dezong’s virtue. That the pure wind blows upon the myriad nations means that its pervasive influence extends across all lands;
it refers to the wind of simplicity and purity spreading throughout the ten thousand states, just as when a spring breeze rises once, the hundred flowers bloom in fragrance.
Thus, a poem says: "Only the spring wind knows no distinction between rich and poor; the peach of the humble home..."

Li Yecheng said: "To 'spread the profound transformation to awaken those in a dream' means to extensively expound the profound and wondrous Buddha-dharma, using its influence and teachings to alert sentient beings from the great dream of ignorance. Thus, the Great Sutra says:
'For example, a treasure in the darkness cannot be seen without a lamp; so too, if the Buddha-dharma is not spoken by someone, even the wise cannot comprehend it. Thereupon,"
To realize the true nature is to eternally sever ignorance. Regarding the statement that "heavenly truth is used as the basis for emotion and nature," the *Book of Rites* says:
"Human life is born tranquil; this is the nature of Heaven. To be moved by external things is the desire of nature. Desire is precisely emotional desire.
If one uses emotion to apply itself to nature, then nature becomes falsely active as emotion; if one uses nature to apply itself to emotion, [then emotion is truly grounded].

Sentiment is essentially true stillness, which constitutes one's nature; now, by extending the transformation of non-action, one causes the desires for deluded movement to cease, so that sentiment may harmonize with the true, celestial stillness of one's nature.
Thus we know: were there not the Great Void, how could boundless illumination be displayed? Were there not the True Realm, how could purity be equalized?
The mind of emptiness.

Regarding the concluding praise through the three dharmas and metaphors, the commentary states: "One knows that there is nothing; from the vast void up to the mind equal to space—this is the metaphor.

Within emptiness, the sun is absent and thus not manifest (just as when traveling at night during the dark fortnight, one does not dare take a step, yet upon the rising of the sun, one realizes it was originally empty). The sun is not..."

The sky does not spread [of its own accord]—if the sun is encountered while obstructed by something, the sun does not spread; it requires a sky free of clouds and obscurations for the sun to shine again. Thus, the sky and the sun are mutually dependent.
In reality, the illumination of the sun also has limits, but because human eyes cannot perceive beyond them, it is said to be "boundless.
A Great Sūtra says: "For example, in the month of midsummer, when the sky is clear and free of clouds and obscurations, the blazing sun..."
Radiating brilliance, there is nowhere throughout the ten directions that it does not illuminate. Within the Dharma, the true realm (*dharmadhātu*) is equal to emptiness, and the mind is likewise so.
If there were no true realm, how could the wisdom-mind unfold? If there were no wisdom-mind, how could one take the true realm as its object?
The *Samādhi Sūtra* says: "Equal to emptiness is the immovable wisdom."
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*, which is vast and expansive, exhaustively investigates this profound purport and fully traces its source and flow.
Therefore, it is broad and magnificent, encompassing the profound and subtle, such that it is beyond the reach of thought or speculation.

In the second section, "The Great Vaipulya," there is a specific eulogy of this sutra to express its underlying intent (*tātparya*). This section consists of three parts: first, the introduction of the eulogy;
second, the explanation of the eulogy; and third, the conclusion of the eulogy. Regarding the first: the term "this" (*si*) refers to the aforementioned intent of integration and fusion.
It is precisely because one has thoroughly realized this intent of integration and fusion that one attains a state that is vast, expansive, and far-reaching. "Vast" (*huai*) means broad and open.
"Kuo" (廓) means empty; "hong" (宏) means vast. Now, "hongyuan" (宏遠) signifies the meaning of pervasiveness, while "baona" (包納) signifies the meaning of inclusion.

This corresponds precisely to the third contemplation within the *Dharmadhātu-Contemplation*, namely the Contemplation of Pervasive Inclusion. "Chong" (沖) refers to its profound depth, and "shen" (邃) refers to its remote subtlety;
thus, both the gate of pervasive inclusion and the gate of containment are termed the profound depth of principle, which is difficult to perceive. It must not be [misunderstood otherwise].
That which can be attained and contemplated is called "inconceivable" because its principle is profound and its phenomena are vast; how much more so when the one and the many enter into each other!

Thus, words fail and thought ceases. For this reason, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna classified the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* as the *Svalpa-acintya-sūtra* (the Sutra of Minor Inconceivability)—as in "a mustard seed containing Mount Sumeru" or "a hair swallowing the great ocean"—and designated the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as the *Mahā-acintya-sūtra* (the Sutra of Great Inconceivability)—as in "a single mote of dust containing the Dharma-realm" or "a single thought encompassing all."
*Saṃghāṭa-sūtra*): These four meanings shall be explained in detail later in the commentary on the title of the chapter.

△ It points to the source. △ The objects of the mind and sensory dusts are encompassed by the ocean of wisdom; there is nothing outside it. △ Delusive confusion is not grasped, yet the profound mystery is not empty.
△ The fire of the four propositions cannot burn it; the gateway of the myriad dharmas all enter therein. △ It darkly unifies the two limits.
Yet it does not move as one, though its thousand transformations are not many. △ Phenomena and principle penetrate each other and both are simultaneously absent.
△ By means of nature, phenomena are fused and become inexhaustible. △ It is like the mutual reflection in the Qin mirror, or like imperial pearls containing one another;
their layered lights intermingle, appearing clearly and all at once.
This points to its source. Second, in the explanation of the passage of praise, there are six parts: 1) the source is profound and subtle; 2) the benefit achieved is immediate transcendence;
3) the expressed meaning is perfectly integrated; 4) the mode of exposition is profound and abstruse; 5) clarifying that it is not for those who lack the capacity, as they cannot fathom it;

6) citing examples to reveal that the benefit for those with the appropriate capacity is even deeper. Within the first [of these six], there are three sections: the first is the heading pointing to its source.
I. Source; II. Proper Elucidation of the Profound and Subtle; III. Conclusion by Way of Similes on the Inconceivability. Now, for the first [section]:
because one wishes to clarify the functional efficacy, one first sets forth the source. Second, the proper elucidation of the profound and subtle contains six parts:

1. Harmonizing Emotion and Wisdom; 2. Harmonizing Reality and Delusion; 3. Revealing the Four Propositions and Hundred Negations; 4. Sublating the True and the Conventional, and the One and the Many; 5. Harmonizing and Erasing Phenomena and Principle.

Sixth, the integration of phenomena through mutual permeation (*liú róng shè shì xiàng*). First, regarding the relationship between the sense objects (*jìng*) and the sense faculties (*qíng*): there is a scripture that states the ocean of wisdom has no exterior. This scripture has two meanings: first, by way of analogy; second, by way of the Dharma.
The analogy is that the sense objects contain scrolls as vast as the great chiliocosm, just as the thoughts of the sense faculties contain the perfectly luminous great wisdom.

The text is found in the "Appearance" chapter (*chūxiàn pǐn*), as will be fully cited below. In the *Huan yuan guan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source), the commentary explains: "The sense objects..."
That is to say, the deluded thoughts of sentient beings are themselves the Sūtra;

because the essence of the perfectly enlightened Great Wisdom is boundless, it is said that its measure is equal to the thousand worlds. Second, regarding the Dharma: the Sūtra has the meaning of "constancy.

Thus, the *Xiaojing* says, "The Sūtra of Heaven and Earth, and people take it as their model," with the commentary stating, "Sūtra means constancy. My present intention is to clarify the objects of the senses (*viṣaya*).
Because the essence of the thought-moment of arising and ceasing is, when investigated by wisdom, precisely the true and eternal, the next line states: "The ocean of wisdom has nothing outside it.
If the objects of the emotional faculties were not eternal, then the ocean of wisdom would have something outside it;
since there are no external emotional objects, one knows that emotion itself is eternal. However, delusion and awakening further depend upon the mutual relativity of the true and the false. If...

Seeking the truth while discarding delusion is like laboring to cast off a shadow by straining one's body; if one realizes that delusion is itself truth, it is like a shadow vanishing when one enters the shade.
Second, regarding the fusion of truth and delusion: delusive confusion is not something to be grasped, for in the profound mystery, it is not empty.

Yet "confusion" and "grasping" are essentially one and the same meaning. As the *Treatise by Sengzhao* states: "The cognition of confusion and grasping"—for indeed, delusive confusion is conjoined with this grasping and attachment.
Regarding the meaning of this: since it is now described as being in accord with the nature (*dharmatā*) and thus harmoniously pervasive, delusion is not something to be grasped;

hence the section is titled "Fusing the True and the False. As for "the profound mystery is not empty," this follows the stylistic usage of the *Laozi*. The *Laozi* states, "The mysterious within the mysterious," hence it is called "the profound mystery" (*chongxuan*).
Its intent takes "voidness and spontaneity" (*xuwu ziran*) as the ultimate mystery; fearing that people might become attached to this state, he [the author] has here swept away all traces.

Furthermore, it is said that "the profound is again profound. If, within the meaning of the Buddha-dharma, one takes emptiness-emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) as the profound profundity, this means that even the "sickness of emptiness" is itself empty.
The present intent, however, states that within emptiness-emptiness itself, the functions and virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are fully present;

therefore, it is called "not empty. The *Great Commentary* says: "The myriad virtues exist yet are not existent; their single source is emptiness and non-emptiness, like the ocean facing the clarity of heaven and earth."
"In the same color, this is the intermingling of emptiness and existence. (3) Regarding the "Exposition of the Four Phrases and Hundred Negations":

the fire of the four phrases cannot burn them, for the gateways of all phenomena enter into these four phrases—namely, existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence.
Since various schools fall into these, they incur the four types of slander; thus, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* says: "Prajñā..."

If the *pāramitās* were like a great mass of fire, they could not be grasped from any of the four directions; to grasp them would be to be burned, and to fall into such a view would constitute slander.
Therefore, one must distance oneself from them. Within the teaching of distancing oneself from these, the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) are now clarified:

according to the school of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), all dharmas are primordially free from faults, and by turning toward them, they become virtues. Since all four are themselves gateways to the Dharma, they are called "the fire of the four propositions."
"Do not burn it; otherwise, you will create slander and create a gate. Why is there a difference between these four phrases if they are not distinct?

It is because if one clings to one of the four phrases while rejecting the rest, then every phrase becomes a flaw (as when four people each cling to one phrase, or as when a single person sequentially traverses the meanings of the four phrases).
If the four phrases are free from the obstruction of either existence or cessation, then every phrase is a gate (as when a single person perceives all four phrases simultaneously). Question:

In response to the question of which dharmas serve as the basis for explaining the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), it is said: the basis upon which they rely consists of the relative establishment of the ultimate and conventional truths.
Thus, every dharma possesses all four [propositions]. Regarding the elucidation of the four propositions based on the two truths, the ultimate and the conventional:

first, because the ultimate follows conditions, there is "existence"; second, because conditions lack intrinsic nature, there is "non-existence"; third, because the former two propositions coexist, there is "both existence and non-existence."

Furthermore, because the four alternatives are mutually negated and all are extinguished, it is neither existent nor non-existent; moreover, since this "neither existence nor non-existence" is the true nature (*dharmatā*), it is so designated.
Furthermore, regarding the classification by teaching: when explaining *saṃsāra*, it is conventionally existent and truly non-existent;

when explaining *nirvāṇa*, it is conventionally non-existent and truly existent. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "That which is empty is called *saṃsāra*; that which is not empty is called Great Nirvāṇa."

The above discussion regarding "being" and "non-being" was still explained in terms of various phenomena (*dharmas*). If one examines the true nature (*tathatā*) itself, there are likewise four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
1. Nature is existent, because it possesses awareness and is not obscure. 2. Nature is non-existent, because it is without characteristics (*animitta*) and without names (*anāman*). 3.

Nature is neither existent nor non-existent, because it cannot be found when sought across the three time periods (past, future, and present) or within the three locations (internal, external, and intermediate). 4. Nature is both existent and non-existent, as indicated by the preceding two propositions.
Because they are simultaneous, the four natures are neither existent nor non-existent. This has two meanings:

first, because the two aforementioned [natures] mutually negate one another due to their simultaneity, both are simultaneously extinguished; second, it directly points to the true nature (*dharmatā*), which is neither existence nor non-existence, but is simply the true nature itself.
Regarding the statement that "the gates of the myriad dharmas all enter," this reveals the myriad dharmas. "Myriad" refers to—

In its total enumeration, this actually encompasses all things; yet, since all phenomena do not transcend the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*), and because various schools regard these four propositions as slanderous, they maintain that everything is "not so.
Thus, whenever the sublime principle is discussed, it is said to be "beyond the four propositions and transcending the hundred negations," meaning it is free from such slander.
Now, since the four propositions have been established as virtues, all phenomena are likewise [so].
Master Miaomen Xiaogong said: "If one loses the meaning, then all that is spoken is false; if one attains the meaning, then all that is spoken is true.

Just as when seeing a single speck of dust, if one examines it in accordance with principle, one immediately awakens to the entire substance of the emptiness of nature and thus perceives the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, this single speck of dust is precisely the gate for entering the Dharma-realm; all things are likewise so. This is the fourth: the True Reality of the Fourfold Extinction.
The mundane and the ultimate are neither one nor many; they are quiescent at their two limits yet undergo a thousand transformations without being many.

To speak of these "two limits" refers to the two truths of the ultimate and the mundane, as well as birth-and-death and nirvana, and even all phenomena of mutual dependence such as Buddhas and sentient beings—all of these constitute the two limits.
For now, let us clarify this by means of the two truths: when the ultimate follows conditions, it is the mundane.
Because the mundane lacks intrinsic nature and is thus identical to the Real, it is called "dark" (*ming*). Since these two are darkly united, they ought to be one;

for, through their mutual negation, they transcend names and numbers, and thus are also not one. A Great Sūtra says: "In non-existence there is no duality, and in non-duality there is likewise nothing;
the three periods of time are all empty—this is the Dharma of all Buddhas. The *Renwang Jing* says: "Regarding..."

Understanding that the permanent is always one (this dispels duality), and that the truths are always two (this dispels unity); furthermore, the two truths are neither a simultaneous pair nor eternally separate, yet they never exist as solitary individuals.
Like a lone wild goose soaring high across the earth, or a pair of mandarin ducks standing alone by the pond—though their movements manifest a thousand transformations, they are not many;
this is the merging of one and many, referring to the shifting and differentiating aspects of phenomena.
The Dharma is entirely identical to true nature (*dharmatā*); because this nature has no boundaries, it is not manifold.

Yet, it is also not one, as "not one" was already established in the preceding phrase; thus, by citing only "not manifold," both one and many are actually extinguished. Furthermore, these two phrases together establish the identity of the ultimate and the conventional:
being one with the two limits is the ultimate, while non-identity is the extinction of the ultimate. This moves through a thousand [manifestations].

"Transformation is the conventional, while 'not many' is the obliteration of the conventional. Furthermore, "mystically merging two limits is one," where saying "one" does not mean one, which is the obliteration of one.
"Moving through a thousand transformations is many," where saying "many" does not mean many, which is the obliteration of many.

Based on this latter meaning, the True is taken as one and the Conventional as many; this differs from the Ten Profound Gates (Shixuanmen), wherein both one and many are taken as phenomena (*dharma*).
Because of the Dharma, the five [aspects] are fused; they sweep away both phenomena and principle.
When phenomena and principle interpenetrate and both vanish, "interpenetration" is precisely fusion, and "both vanishing" is precisely sweeping away.

That which is explained by this sutra is necessarily a phenomenon that is entirely principle, and that which is explained as principle is necessarily a principle that is entirely phenomenon; therefore, it is said they "interpenetrate. Because this interpenetration occurs simultaneously, they mutually...

When principle and phenomena are mutually subsumed, both vanish; for principle is identical to phenomena, so when principle is dissolved, phenomena vanish as well. When phenomena are identical to principle, phenomena likewise vanish.

These six aspects of mutual fusion subsume phenomenal characteristics. In the *Sūtra Commentary*, it is said that "nature fuses with characteristics such that they are inexhaustible," meaning that each and every phenomenal characteristic subsumes the nature of reality.
Because nature fuses with them, it is able to encompass all and pervade all.
The phrase "layer upon layer, inexhaustible" indicates that the nature (*dharmatā*) fuses with phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*); this clarifies the reason why there are such layers.
This is the meaning of the fourth gate among the ten gates of the *myriad mysteries* (*daśa-guhya-dvāra*), namely, the Gate of the Interfusion of the Dharma-nature.

It means that if one considers only the principle (*li*), all things are of a single flavor and lack distinct characteristics for mutual inclusion; yet if one considers only phenomena (*shi*), they obstruct one another.
They cannot mutually enter one another; however, because phenomena and principle are now seen as interfused, this unimpeded state is possible.

That is to say, when a single phenomenon that is not distinct from principle fully encompasses the nature of principle, it causes all the many phenomena—which likewise are not distinct from principle—to appear within that one, each according to the principle upon which they depend.
If a single phenomenon were to encompass the principle incompletely, then the principle would be [fragmented].

Regarding the loss of delimitation: if a single phenomenon were to encompass the principle exhaustively while multiple phenomena did not manifest in accordance with that principle, then those phenomena would exist outside the principle.
Since a single phenomenon now fully encompasses the nature of the principle, how could multiple phenomena not manifest within that one?
Thus, the Sūtra says: "Within every single atom of all the Flower Treasury Worlds, one perceives the Dharma-realm" (referring to the four Dharma-realms).
The Buddhas of Jewel Light appear like gathering clouds; this is the Tathāgata’s mastery over his buddha-field.
The phrase "inexhaustible" precisely distinguishes the mutual non-obstruction of phenomena and phenomena (*shishi wuai*), which is infinitely layered and permeates the ten mysteries (*shi xuanyuan*).

Thus, within this single sentence, the four characters clarify the reason, while the three characters precisely distinguish the infinite layering. As the Preface to the Great Commentary states: "Principle conforms to the transformations of phenomena."
Thus, when the boundless phenomena of the dependent origination of the one and the many attain the harmony of principle, the myriad differences interpenetrate without obstruction.
Since both pairs [of terms] clarify the preceding phrase, the subsequent phrase correctly elucidates the inexhaustibility of phenomena within phenomena (*shishi wujin*).
This concludes the meaning explained through the perspective of "neither identical nor different. Furthermore, within the contemplation of "pervasive inclusion and fusion" (*zhoubian hanrong guan*):

Regarding each of the four propositions—within one there is one, within one there is all, within all there is one, and within all there is all—the three metaphors for resolving the difficulty are inconceivable.
According to the *Sūtra*, if the Qin mirror reflects everything up to the Qi state, the metaphor of the mirror encompasses the meaning of the mutual penetration of the various preceding gates;
it is like two mirrors facing each other, which corresponds to the two gates of phenomena (*dharma*) and principle (*tattva*).
Taking up characteristics and entering into mutual interpenetration to form a multiplicity is likewise a metaphor for the non-obstruction of phenomena with phenomena (*shishi wuai*).

As for the analogy of the pearl, it serves solely as a metaphor for infinite integration and inclusion. Regarding the "Qin mirror," because there was a mirror in the Qin dynasty that could reflect the hearts of men, Zhu Huang’s poem says:
"In the western lands there is the Qin mirror; its radiance is rare in the world. It reflects people so they see their own livers and gallbladders, and it examines [the innermost]."
Things are profound and subtle; now, my intention is to take up the literary expressions that reach back to antiquity and to capture their ultimate clarity.
Thus, it is said of the "Mirror of Qin" (Qin-jing): two mirrors face each other with a lamp placed between them, so that their reflections intersect and merge without obstruction.
As for the "Imperial Jewel" (Di-zhu), it refers to the jewels in the netting of Śakra’s palace; they are so bright and pure that one enters into many, and many enter into one.
Within this, there is a layer upon layer of inexhaustibility.

△ Within the minds of all Buddhas dwell sentient beings who newly and continuously attain Buddhahood; within the minds of these sentient beings dwell all Buddhas, who in every thought-moment realize the Truth.
Therefore, one attains the second [stage] of "accomplishing benefit," which suddenly transcends the middle two [stages]. First, regarding the transcendence of time and place:
the first phrase refers to time and the second phrase refers to place. Within the discussion of time, it says:
"Therefore, one attains perfection within a single moment. This is because, as described above, the objective realm is fused and subsumed with subtle refinement.
Having attained faith, understanding, and realization, there is this sudden realization. The *Brahmacaryā-varga* states:

"If bodhisattvas can accord with such contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-yoga*), they do not give rise to dualistic interpretations regarding all phenomena; all Buddha-dharmas will swiftly manifest before them.
At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment (*prathama-cittotpāda*), they realize *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. It is known thus.
All phenomena are the very nature of mind, perfected as the body of wisdom; they are not realized through another, but are attained in the mere instant of speech.
This is to be understood by contrast with the various teachings regarding time and kalpas. To "see the Buddha-realm within a speck of dust" means to transcend spatial locations.
By analogy with the examples concerning time, one may also say: if one accords with such contemplative practice, there is no need to seek it above.
When Maitreya traveled west to visit Amitābha, every single speck of dust and every single hair was immediately seen as the realm of the Buddha;
such passages are found throughout the great scriptures. If one wishes to see them, they are the very texts cited within the previous six lines concerning the "fusion of body and land.
Second, regarding the transcendence of cause and effect: the commentary states, "Within the minds of all Buddhas... until realizing the truth," for indeed, cause and effect [are transcended].
The meaning of mutual penetration consists of four propositions: first, because sentient beings are entirely within the Buddha’s mind;
second, because the phenomena of the fruit-gate encompass all things without exception. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, "Chapter on the Appearance of the World," states:

"When the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he universally beheld all sentient beings within his own body attaining perfect enlightenment, and even universally beheld all sentient beings entering parinirvāṇa."
Furthermore, the second chapter of the *Foxing lun* (Treatise on the Buddha-nature), the "Tathāgatagarbha" section, states:
"Because all sentient beings are entirely within the wisdom of the Tathāgata, they are called a 'garbha' (store). Thus it is said that sentient beings within the mind of the Buddhas become Buddhas.

Since the two Buddhas [the cause and the fruit] are fully present within the hearts of sentient beings, the causal gate encompasses all phenomena without exception; this is why it is called the "Appearance Chapter" (*Chuxian pin*).
It is said that a bodhisattva should know that their own mind is constantly and at every moment the place where Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment. Why is this?
Because all Tathāgatas do not depart from this mind when they attain perfect enlightenment. Just as it is with one's own mind, so it is with the minds of all sentient beings;
within them all, there is likewise the attainment of equal and perfect enlightenment by the Tathāgata. This is the third [point], arising from the mutual [relationship] of Buddhas in previous lives.
When the two aspects exist, each is truly real and not false; thus, cause and effect interpenetrate. If Buddhahood is realized through one aspect, it is entirely contained within both minds.
Fourth, if birth is entirely contained within Buddhahood, then birth is identical to Buddha; if Buddhahood is entirely contained within birth, then Buddha is identical to birth.
When these two aspects mutually negate one another and the two positions are simultaneously fused, there is neither the attainment of Buddhahood nor the non-attainment of Buddhahood. Therefore...
The "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "For example, just as space neither increases nor decreases whether all worlds are forming or disintegrating—why?
Because space is without arising or ceasing—so it is with the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas:
whether they attain perfect enlightenment or do not attain perfect enlightenment, there is neither increase nor decrease. Why? Because bodhi is without marks."

Because they are devoid of characteristics, O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were someone who could emanate as many minds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, and from each single mind, again emanate as many Buddhas as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River—all of whom are formless and without characteristics—and continue doing so for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River without ceasing.
Son of the Buddha, what do you think? Those emanated minds—

"How many emanations of the Tathāgata are there? The Bodhisattva Wondrous Virtue of the Arising of the Tathāgata-nature replied, "As I understand the meaning of what you have said, emanation and non-emanation are equal and without difference. Why then do you ask how many there are?
The Bodhisattva Samantabhadra said, "Excellent, excellent, Son of the Buddha! It is as you have said. [The text continues: "Even if..."
All sentient beings, within a single thought-moment, are entirely equal—whether they have attained perfect enlightenment or not—in that there is no difference between them.
Why is this? Because *bodhi* (enlightenment) is without marks (*animitta*). If there are no marks, then there is neither increase nor decrease.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should know that the attainment of perfect enlightenment is identical to *bodhi*.
Regarding the explanation of "marks" (*lakṣaṇa*) and "marklessness" (*alakṣaṇa*): what has been stated above consists of four propositions based on mutual opposition;
however, its great purport does not exceed the thorough interpenetration of cause and effect, which may also be seen according to the text.

Yet, the meaning of sentient beings attaining Buddhahood is difficult to accept within the mind; therefore, I shall briefly provide questions and answers. Herein, the attainment of Buddhahood is discussed in terms of...
Whether established according to phenomena (*dharma*) or established according to principle (*li*): if established according to phenomena, how can they be of the same nature?
If established according to principle, how can there be the attainment of perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and entry into *nirvāṇa*? Answer: This is a major theme of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*;

it is difficult to gain understanding unless one contrasts it with the various schools (*nikāya*). Now, we shall distinguish their relative depth and shallowness by means of the five vehicles and the five teachings. However, all...
If one examines sentient beings within the teachings of humans and devas, they are endowed with both the self of persons and the self of phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-ātman*).
If one examines them within the teachings of the Hīnayāna, they are merely the real dharmas of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which are fundamentally without self.

In the Mahāyāna, the initial teaching of the *Lakṣaṇa* school states that all is what is manifested by consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). The *Nirākāra* school, however, states that it is illusory existence (*māyopama-sat*). Thus...

In the emptiness where both person and phenomena are simultaneously discarded, according to the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao) of the Mahāyāna, because the Tathāgatagarbha alone possesses nature-endowed virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, sentient beings are the Dharmakāya while still enmeshed in afflictions;
the meanings of "Dharmakāya" and "sentient beings" are one in substance but differ only in name, being spoken of thus based on principle.
However, in the Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao) of the Mahāyāna, characteristics are fundamentally exhausted and nature is fundamentally manifest, such that it cannot be described in words.
Regarding whether one attains Buddhahood or not, according to this school, the Buddha has already attained perfect enlightenment and entered parinirvāṇa since time immemorial;
it is not a matter of a separate entity, for this attainment is precisely that [primordial] attainment. Objection:

If this is so, why is it that sentient beings currently existing are not themselves Buddhas? Answer: If one examines them from the standpoint of their status as sentient beings, they are not even perceived [as such].

Mind-only is itself emptiness; how could one see the phenomena within the Perfect Teaching otherwise? It is like a person who is deluded, mistaking east for west because they are firmly grasping it as west.
If all delusions are suddenly shattered, the Dharma-realm manifests perfectly, with nothing remaining unaccomplished—just as that awakened person realizes that what was west is entirely east.
Furthermore, if this were so, why do the Buddhas still engage in further teaching? The answer is: sentient beings are not yet [awakened].
Thus we know that the necessity for transformation lies in such transformation as being ultimate transformation;
because such transformation is never a time of non-transformation, the conclusion below states: "Great Compassion continues in succession to rescue and deliver sentient beings.
The differences among the five teachings are all authoritative words of the Sages (*āptavāda*); one must not interpret these teachings according to ordinary emotional consciousness.

△ Regarding the Dharma-gate of a Single Syllable: even if one were to write with ink as vast as the ocean, it would not exhaust a single hair’s breadth of its goodness; even if the realm of empty space were exhausted, it would remain infinite.

The threefold explanation of this principle is perfectly integrated. In the commentary on the "Dharma-gate of a Single Syllable" leading to the infinite, the first phrase explains the words and the second phrase explains the meaning.
"Explanation" refers to what the third spiritual friend encountered by Sudhana, the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha, said: "I have [come from...]"
That Buddha attained this Universal Eye Dharma-gate; having received, upheld, recited, memorized, and contemplated it,

suppose there were someone who used ink equal in volume to the great ocean and pens as numerous as the Mount Sumerus to write down even a single chapter within this Inexhaustible Vast Ocean-Treasury Universal Eye Dharma-gate,
a single gate within that chapter, a single dharma within that gate, and a single meaning within that dharma.
In this meaning, not even a single phrase or a mere fraction can be found, let alone the ability to write it down in its entirety.

The commentary explains: "Not even a mere fraction" refers to a single character (*akṣara*). This is because a single character that expresses (*vācaka*) is in its totality identical to the *dharmadhātu* which is expressed (*vācya*).
Thus, it is inexhaustible; it differs from the various schools for whom the expressing term is certainly not identical to the expressed reality.

If even a single hair’s breadth of goodness is inexhaustible until the limits of space are reached, then all ten types of vows and practices conclude by stating that they are "as inexhaustible as the realm of empty space," and so forth.
This is as seen in the first practice of prostrating to the Buddhas, where the conclusion states:
"Because the realm of empty space is inexhaustible, my prostrations here shall never come to an end. The remaining nine practices follow this same pattern.
△ Regarding its meditative concentration: it is darkly one with the mindless, such that amidst ten thousand movements, there is eternal stillness.
△ The ocean is serene; the light of true wisdom contains the emptiness of nature. △ Stars are arrayed as the reflections of the Dharma-body, their shadows falling upon the water of the mind.

△ The perfect sound unfolds eternally without being struck; the ocean of fruition transcends thought and is transmitted through the mind. △ The myriad practices are cultivated simultaneously, beyond the duality of illumination and non-illumination, encompassing both gradual and sudden approaches.
Entering both [realms] without obstruction.

Regarding the fourfold explanation of the profound ritual, there are five sections within the text: first, clarifying the ultimate concentration; second, clarifying wondrous wisdom; third, clarifying the true body;
fourth, clarifying the basis of the teaching; and fifth, clarifying cultivation and realization. Now, for the first, the Commentary says: as for that concentration... "To" (zhì).

The *Hengji* (Section on Constant Quiescence) states: "As for 'reaching concentration,' this is the concentration of wisdom (*prajñā*). Now, there are many kinds of concentration—some erroneous, some correct;

belonging to the Mahāyāna or Hīnayāna; with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*); and accompanied by wisdom or devoid of wisdom. For now, I shall explain according to what is essential. In general, there are two types:
first, that of phenomena (*vastu*), and second, that of principle (*tattva*). As the *Śāriputra-dharmapada-sūtra* says: 'To restrain [the mind] in one place, there is no [distraction]...'"
When affairs are not accomplished, this is precisely the concentration of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-samādhi*); as the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states:

"To contemplate the nature of the mind and accord with principle without wavering is the concentration of principle (*tattva-sthiti-samādhi*). Consequently, within various sūtras and śāstras, some speak exclusively of the concentration of phenomena while others emphasize the concentration of principle;
students who cling to a single passage may cite it as evidence to mutually refute one another. In this school, however, both must be present without obstruction.

Furthermore, it is essential that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) are simultaneous; for without concentration, there is no means to exhaustively fathom its stillness, and without wisdom, there is no means to deepen its illumination.
As the Seventh Patriarch of the Chan school said: "The function of the essence is self-knowing; the essence of knowing is itself still.
Therefore, following this, true wisdom is now elucidated. When we speak of "mysteriously merging with the One Suchness," this ability to merge is wisdom, which is non-mindful.
This samādhi is the very convergence with the original source; there is nothing that can be converged upon, whether in phenomena or principle.
It is a mind free from discrimination, yet it is not indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). It does not calculate existence or non-existence, nor emptiness or non-emptiness.
All things are ungraspable, and even "ungraspability" is ungraspable. This very statement is not accepted; it is utterly extinguished and has no locus, amidst the ten thousand kinds of confusion.
The fundamental nature of movement is inherently quiescent. Why is this? Because all phenomena arise from the arising of the mind;

if the mind does not arise, phenomena are fundamentally quiescent. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "All phenomena, from their very origin, are eternally characterized by quiescence and extinction.
It is like seeing hundreds of thousands of people in a dream; upon awakening, they are seen to be originally empty and quiescent.
Thus, we know that the arising and ceasing of phenomena arise from the arising and ceasing of the mind. As the *Awakening of Faith* says: "When the mind arises, all manner of phenomena arise;
when the mind ceases, all manner of phenomena cease. The present intent clarifies that while the mind does not arise, its essence is likewise not subject to cessation;

therefore, although the myriad movements [of phenomena] exist, they are fundamentally quiescent from the beginning, devoid of arising or ceasing. Second, the explanation of wondrous wisdom (from the Commentary).

The ocean is profound, and the light of true wisdom contains the emptiness of nature; because this is the wisdom that is identical with meditative concentration (*samādhi*), it is called "wondrous. The *Great Commentary* states:
"The clear ripples of the profound ocean of wisdom contain all phenomena within their voidness," which is largely the same as this [text], yet there are two differences:

first, that [passage] refers to the gate of meditative concentration (*samādhimukha*), whereas this refers to the gate of wisdom (*jñānamukha*); second, that [passage] contains all phenomena, whereas this contains the emptiness of nature.

Because this concentration is the Sea-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*), it contains the myriad phenomena; the myriad phenomena are the seal-prints manifested within the sea. This may be understood through the correspondence of dharmas:
the gate of wisdom is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which accords with true nature (*tathatā*);

therefore, it contains the emptiness of nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). Emptiness of nature is the principle that is realized; this principle is the objective realm (*viṣaya*). Because the realm is subsumed within wisdom, it is said to "contain."
In this passage, both sentences contain both a dharma (the subject) and a metaphor. Like the waves of the ocean, which are limpid, still, and unmoving;
like space, which is free from clouds and is vast, clear, and empty: the great ocean has no boundless shores and is of one color with the sky;

space penetrates to the bottom of the sea, and the sea contains the sky and the heavens. Because the ocean is void and luminous, it contains space; because space is bright and clear, [it is contained by the ocean].
Entering the ocean serves as a metaphor for true wisdom: mindfulness does not arise, it is tranquil and unmoving; its nature is free from sensory objects, vast and empty stillness.
Great wisdom extends boundlessly, containing the single flavor of the fundamental nature. The nature penetrates the essence of wisdom, and wisdom contains the nature of emptiness.
Because wisdom is pure and luminous, it contains the nature; because the nature is empty and still, it enters into wisdom. Thus, the Dharma and the metaphor are one.
The mutual correspondence between these two is clearly visible, as stated in the *Zhao lun* (Treatise by Sengzhao).
An ancient master said: "To have no mind toward the myriad things, yet the myriad things have never been absent. This means that when the mind is pure, things remain; things cannot enter the mind.

It is like clouds and mist in the sky—the sky cannot enter the clouds—or like [the sky] in relation to the sea. Therefore, Master Zhao judged: "The failure lies with the objects, not with the emptiness [of the mind]. This is the third point of illumination.
Regarding the phrase "The true body’s stars spread like a net; the Dharma-body’s reflection falls upon the water of the mind":
because the aforementioned principle and wisdom are in profound union, one attains the realization that all phenomena are none other than the Dharma-body.

Thus, for sentient beings throughout the worlds of the ten directions who have resolved to attain Bodhicitta and whose mental consciousness is pure, the Buddha manifests before them to preach the Dharma without exception—just as when the autumn sky is clear and bright, the stars are spread out like a net.
The array of stars and myriad vessels across the hundred rivers are distributed throughout the clear sky without distinction;

the constellations serve as a metaphor for the *dharmakāya*, while the pure water and tranquil rivers serve as metaphors for the responsive capacity of sentient beings. When the metaphors are matched with their principles, the correspondence is manifest. Thus, the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states:
"The cool moon of the Bodhisattva travels through ultimate emptiness; when the water of the sentient beings' minds is pure, the reflection of Bodhi appears."
In the present context, the moon is used as a metaphor for the Bodhisattva, while the stars serve as a metaphor for the Dharmakāya; the remaining meanings are the same.

Furthermore, regarding the correspondence between the response and the stimulus, there are four permutations: first, one star entering the water in a single vessel, which is like one Buddha responding to one sentient being;
second, one star entering the water in all vessels, which is like one Buddha responding to all sentient beings... [and so forth].
1. All sentient beings enter into a single vessel of water; 2. all stars enter into the waters of all vessels.
From these two phrases, the numerical relationship between one and many regarding the correspondence of sentient beings and Buddhas can be understood. As the subsequent text states:
"Before a single Buddha, one sees bodies as numerous as the atoms of unspeakable numbers, and before each body, one prostrates to bodies as numerous as the atoms of unspeakable numbers."

Regarding the "numerous Buddhas," this refers to the second and third phrases. The Great Commentary (*Dàshū*) states: "The full moon of the luminous emptiness of nature suddenly reflects in a hundred rivers.
However, if one obtains only the first two phrases while omitting the third and fourth, it is because the moon is singular.

If one takes the analogy of the stars, then the meaning is complete. Regarding Siming’s explanation of the "root," the Commentary says: "The perfect sound is not dependent on being struck... [and so forth].

That which is transmitted by the mind is the "perfect sound" (*paripūrṇa-svara*). Within a single sound, all sounds are contained; all sounds are themselves a single sound, or a single sound responds to all sounds—all are the manifestation of the perfect sound.
In the "Chapter on the Manifestation of the Perfect Sound," there are ten similes that illustrate the Tathāgata’s perfect sound.
Regarding these ten similes, the first is the simile of the sound of a cry at the end of an eon, which illustrates that sound has no master, as described in that sutra.
It is said that, for example, when the world is destroyed, though there is no master and no agent, four kinds of sounds naturally emerge.

Just as such sounds emerge in the desire realm, you should know that they likewise emerge in the first dhyāna, which is peaceful and blissful, free from all desires and evils, and transcends the beings of the desire realm.
Upon hearing them, those beings spontaneously achieve the first dhyāna and abandon desire.
Beings born in the Brahma-heaven up to the fourth dhyāna hear such a sound emerging from the third dhyāna.
Having heard it, those in the fourth dhyāna—who are more tranquil than the Śubhakṛtsna devas—spontaneously achieve rebirth there.
All of this arises from the roots of goodness of sentient beings; likewise, the voice of the Buddha has no owner and no agent, yet it emerges from the merits of the Buddha.

The four kinds of sounds refer to those that instruct sentient beings to practice the conduct of humans and devas, up to the fourth kind, which transcends the two vehicles and teaches the Unsurpassed Way;
yet because there is no presiding master, they are called "perfect sounds.
Regarding the "echoing sound," it follows conditions as a metaphor to illustrate that sound has no master. As the Sūtra says: "It is like an echo, which arises from a valley and from vocal sounds."
Its arising has no shape and it cannot be seen; it merely accords with conditions. The voice of the Buddha is also like this:
