it merely emerges according to the inclinations and understandings of sentient beings as conditions, yet its nature is ultimately without words, without demonstration, and cannot be proclaimed.

The analogy of the celestial drum awakening others illustrates that it is without a master, without an agent, and without interruption, universally entering all things. This is taught in the sutras as a parable.
Just as the gods possess a great Dharma drum named "Awakening," which is without owner, without agent, without arising, and without cessation;
when the gods become heedless, a voice issues from the air proclaiming: "Know that all things are impermanent, false, and subject to decay;
do not give rise to attachment. If you are heedless, it will be too late for regret. Having heard this, all the gods...
Those who, out of anxiety and fear, request the Dharma and practice the Path all attain peace and happiness. The Buddha’s voice is likewise:
it does not abide in any location and is beyond verbal expression, yet it can produce effortless sounds that pervade the entire Dharma-realm, awakening all sentient beings.

It is like the celestial maiden Sudarśanā, whose exquisite voice serves as a metaphor; according to the sutras, she follows the sound with faith and understanding, just like the celestial maiden Supriyā.
When a single wondrous sound issues forth, it corresponds with hundreds of thousands of kinds of music; each of these, in turn, possesses hundreds of thousands of tones.
The Buddha’s voice is likewise: from within a single sound, he produces immeasurable voices that accord with the inclinations of sentient beings, each giving rise to its own understanding.
He employs the five Brahma-voices and various metaphors to transform and guide them without missing the proper time. As the Sūtra says, it is like a great...
When Brahmā dwells in the Brahma-palace and utters the voice of Brahmā, the entire assembly of Brahmās hears it and each thinks, "It is my own voice," yet it does not issue from outside the assembly.
The Buddha’s voice is likewise: the entire assembly hears it and each thinks, "It is my own voice," yet it is not heard by those whose faculties are not yet matured.
This is illustrated by the analogy of the single taste of water; it serves as a metaphor for the absence of crookedness in the Sūtra.
It is said that, for example, all waters are of one and the same taste, yet they appear different according to the vessels;

the water has no thought or conceptual discrimination, and the Buddha’s voice is likewise of one flavor of liberation, yet it rains down in seven ways according to the differences in the faculties to nourish and flourish them.
This is illustrated by the analogy of the dragon king Anavatapta as taught in the sutras.

A great cloud of Dharma arises, pervading Jambudvīpa and pouring down sweet rain everywhere; all the various grains and crops grow and flourish, and all rivers, springs, and ponds become completely full.
Although this water does not issue from the bodies or minds of dragons, it is able to provide manifold benefits to sentient beings.
The Buddha’s voice is likewise: it raises the cloud of compassion to pervade everywhere and rains down the Dharma of ambrosia.
The assembly rejoices as wholesome dharmas increase; they fulfill all vehicles, neither coming nor going, benefiting all beings.

Through the eight gradual stages of descent and maturation, there is no delay or haste. As the Sūtra says: "For example, when the Nāga King Manasvin intends to send down rain, he does not do so immediately;
first, he raises a great cloud that completely covers the void and remains suspended for seven days."
Just as the sun waits for the labors of all sentient beings to be completed before gradually descending to universally moisten the great earth, so too does the Buddha’s voice:
first it raises the clouds of Dharma to mature sentient beings, and once their faculties have ripened, it then descends universally to satisfy them with the supreme flavor of the Dharma.
These nine showers are illustrated by inconceivable metaphors; though the metaphors differ, they are one in essence.

By nature, as the Sūtra says, it is like the Great Adornment Dragon King in the great ocean, who sends down hundreds of thousands of kinds of adorned rain, yet there is no differentiation in the water;
through the inconceivable power of the dragon, these adornments [appear].
So too is the Buddha’s voice: it makes no distinctions, whether by means of ten sounds, a hundred sounds, a thousand sounds, or eighty-four thousand.
The Buddhas such as Anantaghosa each preach the Dharma individually, causing all according to their faculties to rejoice;
they manifest ten kinds of universal descent through various metaphors. As the Sūtras state:

for example, when the Dragon King Sāgara wishes to manifest his sovereign power to benefit sentient beings and cause them all to rejoice, he raises clouds that completely cover [the sky] in many different forms and appearances.
Whether white or red, various differences arise as flashes of lightning from the midst of the four continents, raining down all kinds of rain.
The mind of the dragon is impartial, without distinction between self and other; yet there are differences according to the diversity of roots of goodness.
The Buddha’s voice is likewise: wishing to transform beings through the Dharma, he first spreads clouds of his body to pervade the entire Dharma-realm, according to their inclinations and desires.

To manifest these ten meanings—such as appearing in diverse forms, shaking the great Dharma-thunder, and raining down the various rains of the Dharma—it is called the "Perfect Sound" (*pariṣphuṭa-svara*).
To say that it does not wait for a strike before unfolding long is to mean that it is ever-present and universal, requiring no request from sentient beings.

As explained in the first of the ten causes for the arising of the teaching, within the section on "the nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā*), it is stated that the ocean of fruition is beyond conceptual thought.

That which is transmitted by mind is the ocean of fruition where thought is transcended; thus, it is not something to be understood through ordinary consciousness. Since such understanding is severed, it cannot be reached by words.
One must abandon words to grasp the meaning, and grasping the meaning is precisely what constitutes transmission by mind. Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* circulated separately states:
"I now speak of one part," and its commentary explains: "The Ten Grounds have two parts: first, the causal part (*hetubhāga*); second, [the resultant part]."

Regarding the "fruit-portion" (*phalāṃśa*): because the fruit-portion cannot be described directly, it is explained by relying upon the cause-portion (*hetvaṃśa*); therefore, it is called "one portion.

What is now termed "mind-transmission" refers to that which the oral transmission cannot reach; this is the fruit-portion. It is also what is called the "Patriarchal Transmission" (*zongshuo*) within the two types of transmission taught in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*.
The meaning of these two transmissions will be analyzed below in the section establishing the school's tenets. This is also the Dharma [of Bodhidharma].

Taking mindfulness as the fundamental principle and transmitting mind through mind without relying on words or letters is the meaning [of this teaching]. Thus, the Preface to the *Dhyāna-sūtra* states:

"The gateway of dhyāna-concentration—this was personally received from the imperial instructions by Ānanda. If one encounters an unworthy person, the profound barrier cannot be opened and its courtyard remains rarely glimpsed;
yet if one attains the meaning and forgets the words, it is as if it were bestowed upon them even while on the road."
Thus, in every phrase and every word there is speaking yet no speaking; in every thought and every moment there is wisdom that accords yet no accords.

That which is without speaking and without accord is constant speaking and constant accord. Regarding the cultivation and realization of the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*): "The myriad practices are forgotten and illumination is lost, reaching the twofold entry.

The upper phrase refers to cultivation and the lower phrase to realization. As for the phrase "forgotten and lost," it carries two meanings: first, "forgetting" means that all [practices] are completely stilled.

Taking conditions as the object constitutes concentration (*samādhi*); illuminating them is the illumination of the true, while awakening to the delusory is wisdom (*prajñā*). This accords with the ancient masters' teaching of "unconditioned" (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) precept, concentration, and wisdom.
They say that the absence of a deluded mind is concentration; knowing there is no deluded mind is wisdom; and the non-arising of the deluded mind is the precept.
This is also identical to Master Jin Chan of Shu’s statement: "Non-recollection is the precept; non-thought is concentration."
"Do not forget this wisdom"—what is now called "perishing" (wan) is precisely that precept and concentration which is without recollection or thought;

what is now called "illumination" (zhao) is precisely that wisdom which does not forget. However, these are all merely skillful means of counteraction and do not yet constitute cultivation that accords with the true nature (xing).
In the second case, both illumination and perishing are not to be grasped by the mind; this is "perishing-illumination. Even illumination must still...
How much less so for consciousness and thought? Nevertheless, because its fundamental nature is numinous awareness that is never obscured, it is not subject to annihilation.
This is precisely the meaning of Master Heze’s teaching that "emptiness-quiescence-illumination" constitutes the self-nature of precept, concentration, and wisdom.

Thus, when the Master of the Commentary (Zongmi) answered Emperor Shunzong regarding the Essentials of the Mind, he said: "If one is without mind regarding extinction and illumination, then the myriad concerns are all discarded; let [the mind] be as it is."
When one employs tranquil awareness, all practices arise; one is expansive and free, allowing them to come and go as they may. Through still observation, one perceives their source and flow;

whether speaking or remaining silent, one never loses the profound mystery. Whether in motion or stillness, everything accords with the *dharmadhātu*. This is the intent of practicing the myriad practices in equal measure through the transcendence of both illumination and non-illumination.
It is also the same as the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*’s teaching that there is no stinginess in the nature, for practice follows the original nature.

The practice of the *dāna-pāramitā* up to the inherent departure from ignorance and the subsequent cultivation of *prajñā* and the other perfections—this is what is meant by "gradual and sudden being unimpeded and entering both simultaneously.
First, there is a general explanation of the gradual, sudden, partial, and perfect; subsequently, there is the formal commentary on the meaning.
Regarding the first: the Dharma-character school (*Faxiang zong*) states that entering the Great Vehicle from the Small is "gradual," whereas setting out directly from the Great Vehicle is "sudden."

The mind is characterized by suddenness, but this is not the case here; rather, according to the Dharma-lakṣaṇa school, one subdues afflictions prior to the stages (*bhūmi*) and eradicates them upon entering the stages, thereby partially realizing *tathatā*.

This process continues until the final thought-moment of the Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), at which point, through the Diamond-like Samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*) on the Path of Liberation, one finally attains the perfect clarity of Wondrous Enlightenment—this constitutes the gradual approach.
The School of Non-appearance (*animitta-yāna*) does not speak of stages at all.
The positions are as stated in the fourth fascicle of the four-fascicle *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, where it says: "The ten stages are such that the first stage is actually the eighth;
the ninth is the seventh, and the seventh is likewise the eighth;
the second is the third, and the fourth is the fifth; the third is the sixth. Since there is nothing [ultimately] existent, what order can there be? All of the above is thus.
The text of that sutra is thus; its underlying intent reveals that the practice of perfect interfusion does not rely on the sequential stages of gradual progression (*xingbu*).
Furthermore, the Chan school’s method of contemplating purity and sweeping away dust, as well as the various schools’ methods for subduing the mind, are all considered gradual.

Alternatively, the teaching that greed and anger are themselves the Way, that every movement is nothing other than the Buddha, and that there is neither realization nor cultivation, constitutes the sudden (*dun*).
However, the passages cited above each represent the intent of a single gate; they do not constitute the perfect realization and perfect cultivation that accords with the nature (*dharmatā*).

Since this present teaching of the Perfect School speaks directly of the True Realm, it is neither gradual nor sudden. When one cultivates and realizes in accordance with conditions, it encompasses both the gradual and the sudden.
As the sutra says: "At the very moment of first generating the mind of enlightenment, one immediately attains Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi," yet only then does one begin [the formal practice].

From the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) and ten practices (*daśacaryā*) up to the stages of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*vibuddha*), because the stages of practice are not destroyed, they possess both the gradual and the sudden.
In the Chan school, awakening is instantaneous, whereby one ascends to Sublime Enlightenment;

after this single awakening, every thought-moment is in accord with it, such that habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) become merely subtle and fundamental wisdom (*mūlaprajñā*) becomes purely radiant—thus it possesses both the gradual and the sudden. Therefore, the Great Master Heze revealed this.

The sudden awakening followed by gradual cultivation constitutes the perfect and subtle [teaching]. The subsequent intent of the commentary is as follows: because it is taught according to conditions that there are ordinary beings and sages, delusion and awakening, the terms "gradual" and "sudden" are used.
Since dependent origination lacks inherent nature and its entire substance is nothing but the true source, it is said that the gradual and the sudden are unimpeded.
It is precisely through this non-obstruction that the gradual and the sudden are darkly in accord with the ultimate subtlety; therefore, it is said that they "enter both."
Question: Based on what has been said above, one first attains sudden awakening and subsequently practices gradually;

how can this constitute "simultaneous entry into both" (sudden awakening and gradual cultivation)? Answer: At the very moment of sudden awakening, one is already free from defiled attachment, which is itself the practice of cultivation.
Once awakened, that awakening endures forever until the end of the future, without interruption; likewise, cultivation corresponds to every thought-moment. Thus, they are simultaneous.
Because there is no rest, the beginning and end encompass one another, and both are termed "double entry. Furthermore, it was asked: "This phrase is a realization;
for what reason is it explained as being cultivated concurrently? The answer is: The preceding phrase is the cultivation of realization, hence it is called "extinction and illumination";

this phrase is the realization of cultivation, hence it is called "gradual and sudden. Moreover, because unimpeded and signless cultivation and realization are both wondrous, they are termed "double."
Entering [the stages] is precisely how one attains Buddhahood in each and every one of the forty-two positions.

△ Although the four minds encompass the eight difficult conditions and transcend them instantaneously, △ the single ultimate teaching is so exalted that it is beyond the hearing of those of the Two Vehicles.

Fifth, clarifying those who are not suitable vessels by way of their capacity: although the Commentary states that "the four minds extend widely even to those beyond hearing," the first two phrases concern the capacity of the vessel.
The first phrase corresponds to the second phrase; to express this, it says "the four minds extend widely.

These four minds are the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), also called the four equal minds, namely: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

That which has a broad and manifold range of objects is called "immeasurable" (*apramāṇa*). The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* (29) states that it is so named because immeasurable sentient beings serve as its object.
Furthermore, there are two meanings for it being termed "immeasurable": first, because it draws forth immeasurable merit; second, because it brings about immeasurable fruits.
According to the *Prakaraṇapāda*, there are two types: the great and the small. The great [immeasurables]...
Regarding "measure" (*mātra*): that which is attained solely by the Buddha is the essence of subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), which is the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*);

therefore, it is exclusively untainted (*anāsrava*). Regarding the two minor immeasurables (*apramāṇa*): compassion (*karuṇā*) is non-hatred (*avyāpāda*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*) is the feeling of joy (*saumanasya*). Equanimity (*upekṣā*) has non-attachment (*alobha*) as its nature;
this is the same as in the *Abhidharmakośa*. As that verse states: "Compassion and pity have non-hatred as their nature; sympathetic joy and equanimity have non-attachment as their nature. If...
According to the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra*, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna take wisdom as their essential nature; thus that treatise states:

"The mind of wisdom, the mind of benefiting others, the pure and unclouded mind—these are called loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).

Furthermore, because these four mental states are practiced equally without partiality, they are termed the "four equalities. Moreover, these four mental states all possess three conditions, namely: sentient beings...

Regarding the objects of focus—those with conditions (*sālambana*) and those without conditions (*anālambana*)—I shall now briefly clarify the three types of loving-kindness (*maitrī-citta*); the remaining two may be understood by analogy.
Herein are three interpretations. First, the interpretation based directly on the benefit of transformation, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*:

"To take all sentient beings as one's object and desire to bestow happiness upon them is called 'sentient-being-focused' (*sattvālambana*). To take the various necessities required by sentient beings as one's object and bestow them upon them is called..."
Taking the Dharma as the object-condition for the Tathāgata is called "objectless" (anālambana).

Second, transforming and benefiting others by contemplating and entering into the analysis of conditions while intending to grant happiness to all sentient beings is called "sentient-being-object" (sattvālambana).

Taking all the dharmas used to transform sentient beings as the object is called "dharma-object" (dharmālambana)—these two constitute the transformative benefits. Taking the emptiness and quiescence of dharmas as the object is called "objectless"—this constitutes the first contemplative entry. Third.

Returning to the contemplation of transformative benefit (*parārtha*), one enters into analytical understanding (*vibhaṅga*) of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). To contemplate [beings] with a sense of compassion and designate them as "sentient beings" is called the object-condition of sentient beings (*sattvālambana*; this is the first transformative benefit).

To contemplate that sentient beings are without self and are merely the numerical categories of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) arising from causes and conditions is called the object-condition of phenomena (*dharmālambana*).

To contemplate those aggregates as empty is called the objectless condition (*anālambana*; these are the two contemplative entries). Furthermore, there is another interpretation: the first is the object-condition of sentient beings, which takes sentient beings as its object.
It is like parents, wives, children, and relatives; these two types of conditions condition sentient beings, yet they are merely conditions for arising.

Third, there is the absence of conditions, wherein one does not dwell in the characteristics of dharmas or the characteristics of sentient beings. Fourth, the mind possesses all three of these [characteristics].

This is explained in detail in the "Chapter on Brahma-conduct" (*Brahmacarya-parivarta*) of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Regarding the phrase "suddenly transcending the eight difficulties," it refers to having previously heard of the perfect realization of the Golden [Light].
Those of the adamantine lineage, having heard this teaching again in this life, will certainly be able to enter it regardless of whether they are ordinary beings or sages;

for, compared to those of the two lower vehicles who have not heard this Dharma for many kalpas and have not yet given rise to this mind, even though they practice and realize the fruits of their cultivation, they cannot enter it.
If one follows various other explanations, the eight difficulties obstruct the holy path; here, however, it is clarified that by the power of the Perfect Teaching (Vimalakīrti), [one overcomes them].
If even ordinary people amidst obstacles and difficulties can enter [the path], how much more so those without such difficulties? How much more so the sages and saints?

Thus, the efficacy of this sutra surpasses that of all other teachings, as is clearly evident. Regarding the "eight difficulties" (aṣṭāv akṣaṇāḥ), they are: first, the hells; second, the hungry ghosts; third, the animals;
fourth, the northern continent (Uttarakuru); fifth, being blind, deaf, or mute; sixth, living before or after a Buddha. This...

Regarding these ancient explanations, the new translations by the Tang Tripiṭaka Master state that among "those before the Dharma" (*dharmapūrva*) and "those after the Dharma" (*dharmapaścāt*), the latter are superior in understanding.
The seventh [obstacle] is being "wise and eloquent" (*jñānavijñā-pratibhāna*). The eighth is being born in the "long-lived heavens" (*dīrghāyuṣka-deva*). As the *Śāstra* states:

"Among the three miserable realms and the long-lived [heavens], those who are wise and eloquent [are hindered] by their faculties. These eight are called "difficulties" because they are incapable of receiving the teaching and thus difficult to enter into the Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, according to the teachings, there are methods for subduing the eight difficulties (*aṣṭāvakṣaṇa*) so that one may give rise to right vows and not fall into those states.
It is said that there are four wheels capable of subduing the eight difficulties. First is the wheel of being born in a central land (*madhyadeśa*), which can subdue five of the difficulties.
If one maintains the precepts according to the Dharma and applies the mind with the sincere aspiration to be born in a central land, once such birth is attained, one will immediately transcend them.

This excludes those in the hells, the hungry ghosts, the animals, the northern continent (Uttarakuru), and the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*). Second, the vow to encounter virtuous friends:
if one meets a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) and receives their instruction to hear the True Dharma, this constitutes the destruction of obstacles both preceding and following the Dharma.
This applies to all who understand the Buddha-Dharma, from the Buddhas above down to ordinary beings below.
All those who are beneficial to me are collectively termed "virtuous friends. Third, the wheel that can give rise to right aspirations and crushes the obstacle of worldly wisdom and eloquence:

this means that if one conceives deep faith and joy toward the Triple Gem and constantly gives rise to right aspirations that continue from lifetime to lifetime, one will be able to crush the obstacle of worldly wisdom and eloquence. Fourth, planting all roots of goodness.
The wheel can destroy the hardships of being born blind, deaf, or otherwise deficient in the sense faculties.
If one relies upon the Buddha’s true Dharma to practice with a focused mind, one will in the future attain a physical form with all sense faculties complete;

this is precisely what it means to destroy the hardships of sensory deficiency. Therefore, a verse says: "Skillfully destroying the first five [difficulties] by virtue, one plants the remaining three through aspiration."
This refers to the four wheels that can destroy the eight difficulties (*aṣṭākṣaṇa*). Sentient beings within these eight difficulties are unable to enter into the Buddha-dharma;

there is no sūtra or śāstra that does not state this. However, by the power of the *Avataṃsaka* Perfect Teaching (*pūrṇa-yāna*), one may also enter the Buddha-dharma to advance in practice and realize the fruits [of the path].
Therefore, the "Chapter on the Minor Marks" (*Anuvyañjana-parivarta*) speaks of the celestial son from hell.
Having attained birth in Tuṣita, one suddenly realizes the ten stages (*bhūmi*), thereby knowing that sentient beings in the hells do not constitute an obstacle. Thus, the Sūtra says:

"O Son of the Buddha, when I was a bodhisattva in the Tuṣita Heaven palace, I emitted a great light called 'King of Light-Pennants' (*Prabhāketurāja*), which illuminated worlds as numerous as the atoms within ten buddha-fields. The sentient beings in the hells of those worlds encountered [this light]..."
This light causes the cessation of all suffering and the attainment of the ten kinds of pure faculties of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind;
it is likewise so for all others, who all give rise to joy, leap for gladness, and offer praise. When their lives there come to an end, they are reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven.
In that heaven, there is a drum named "Exceedingly Delightful"; once those beings are born there, this drum emits a sound for them.

In the discourse on the Dharma, it is said that at that time, when the sons of the gods heard this teaching on the vast and expansive dedication of Samantabhadra, they immediately attained the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
From this, one knows that even the hells do not constitute an obstacle. Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Ten Stages" states:

"Even if one dwells amidst the waters of the ocean or within the fires of the kalpa, if one is capable of receiving this Dharma, one will certainly hear its words. Regarding the phrase "dwelling amidst the waters of the ocean," this refers to beings such as nāgas.

As for the claim that those who dwell there are not difficult to find even amidst the kalpa-fire of the animal realm: if one speaks according to the general course of things, there are no sentient beings within the kalpa-fire;

however, if one speaks from the perspective of the Buddha’s sphere—wherein he maintains all through his power, performs transformations and deeds, and exerts the majestic authority of the Dharma—one may indeed find them.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "Sentient beings see the end of the kalpa... and so forth.
"When burned by fire, this land of mine remains secure, always filled with devas and humans, and likewise always present on Vulture Peak and other dwelling places.
This is mostly a "difficulty regarding what precedes and follows the Dharma," meaning that it would be illogical for sentient beings to encounter a Buddha amidst the kalpa-ending fires;
how then could they possibly hear the Dharma? Yet now, they have indeed attained both sight and hearing of it.

This is precisely resolving what would otherwise be a difficulty within a difficulty. Now, in this *Avataṃsaka*, it is taught that even those in the realms of hell and animals can hear the Dharma and attain realization of the holy fruits;
how much more so for other classes of beings, whether ordinary or noble! Thus it is said: "The four minds are universally applied, and the eight difficulties are instantly transcended.
Furthermore, the *Great Commentary* states: "To see or hear [the Dharma] serves as the seed; the eight difficulties are transcended at the level of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*)."
The *Jiading ji* (Record of Determination) states: "If one possesses the seed of the Vajra, even if subject to the eight difficulties, hearing this sutra is in every way the same as this.
As the *Shuxian pin* (Chapter on Manifestation) says: 'For example, it is like a man who eats a small amount of vajra;
it will never be digested, but must pierce through his body and emerge outside. Why? Because the vajra does not mix with the fleshly body.'"

Because one dwells together with what is defiled, even if one plants a small root of goodness in the presence of the Tathāgata, it is likewise essential that this root pierce through the body of afflictions of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and reach the state of ultimate unconditioned wisdom (*asaṃskṛta-jñāna*). Why is this?
It is because this small root of goodness does not coexist with conditioned formations or afflictions.
Because the nature of these minor roots of goodness is ultimately consummate, this teaching speaks of practicing even a small amount of wholesome dharmas in accordance with that nature.

The commentary states that those who "sing at the highest pitch" while the Two Vehicles remain beyond hearing are not yet vessels for it; they cannot fathom it. "The ultimate pinnacle" refers to the most supreme teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
It is like worldly songs: when the melody is sung at a high pitch, those who can harmonize with it are few. Furthermore, it is as [difficult as] the *bā* [scale].
When one song is sung, hundreds or thousands respond; when "Yangchun" (The Spring) or "Bai xue" (The Snowy White) are sung, only one or two respond.

It is said that those of the Two Vehicles cannot hear this. Thus, at the beginning of this chapter, when the World-Honored One entered the Lion-Stretching Samādhi, the assembly of bodhisattvas in the gathering all saw the Jetavana Grove, the palace, and the void—these three places—all adorned with various kinds of ornaments.
Furthermore, regarding matters such as the Buddha’s realm and the hearing of inconceivable dharmas,
because the great śrāvakas neither see nor hear them, the Sūtra says: "At that time, the preeminent great śrāvakas— the great wisdom Śāriputra, the supernormal powers Maudgalyāyana,
Mahākāśyapa, and so forth, listing all ten great disciples— were all in the Jeta Grove, yet none of them saw [it], just as before."

They do not see the miraculous powers of the Tathāgatas, the adornments of the Tathāgatas, the realms of the Tathāgatas, the playful manifestations of the Tathāgatas, or even the supernatural transformations of the Tathāgatas;
they do not even see such inconceivable matters as the spheres of the Bodhisattvas. Why is this?
Because their roots of goodness are not identical; in the past, they did not cultivate the practice of beholding the various miracles of all Buddhas.

Because they have thoroughly mastered the roots of goodness that lead to the sublime, and because it is said that they have never, throughout the cycle of birth and death, failed to resolve their minds upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, all such various qualities constitute the sphere of Samantabhadra’s eye of wisdom;
they are not shared with any of the followers of the two vehicles. For these reasons, those eminent leaders...
Virtuous śrāvakas are unable to hear it, unable to see it, unable to believe it, and unable to know it. Furthermore, it is said:

"O Son of the Buddha, suppose there were hundreds of thousands of billions of immeasurable hungry ghosts on the banks of the Ganges River—naked, famished, parched, and with their entire bodies scorched by heat—as crows, vultures, jackals, and wolves compete to peck and claw at them; driven by thirst, they seek to drink water."
Although they dwell by the river, they do not see it; even if they were to see it, they would see it as parched.
Why is this? Because they are shrouded by profound karmic obstructions. Those great śrāvakas are likewise:
although they reside within the Jeta Grove, they do not perceive the Tathāgata’s vast and great supernormal powers, nor do they abandon their ignorance regarding omniscience.
Because their eyes are shrouded by cataracts and they have never planted the roots of goodness on the ground of *sarvajñatā* (all-knowledge), the *Shu* (Commentary) states:
"The Two Vehicles are cut off from hearing [the Dharma]. Furthermore, the *Da Shu* (Great Commentary) states:

"If it is so high that it cannot be looked up to, then the Bodhisattvas who have accumulated practices are like fish gasping for air at the Dragon Gate; if it is so deep that it cannot be peered into, then the Śrāvakas of superior virtue [are like those trapped in the abyss]."

To block sight and hearing at a grand assembly is a method that simultaneously employs both provisional and ultimate teachings; even Bodhisattvas practicing the six perfections likewise sever their hearing. Thus, an ancient eulogy states:
"When the Original Buddha entered the Samādhi of Right Reception, he was named Siṃha-vijṛmbhita (Lion’s Stretch).

The great assembly gazed up with longing and gave rise to doubts. The King of All Dharmas opened his discourse, and the Tathāgata manifested signs to answer them. This reveals the meaning of the Buddha’s virtuous function.
When human beings and dharmas are indistinguishable in their boundlessness, how can cause and effect be divided? All are equally returned to the assembly of the Dharma-realm.

Within this gathering, five hundred bhikṣus—representing śrāvakas of the provisional small fruits—are situated together in the Jeta Grove; yet they do not behold the Tathāgata’s sublime assembly. This is for four reasons:
first, because the Dharma-gate is profound and far-reaching; second, because their causes were not rooted in a great mind; third, because their self-interest lacked compassion; and fourth...

To remedy the loss [of the true path] and seek the supreme fruit, this work now skillfully manifests the Buddha’s virtues. Its profound intent is difficult for those of the Two Vehicles with their shallow wisdom to comprehend;

it reveals that the Perfect Teaching is rarely encountered and is a unique scripture not shared with others. It is not merely that those of the Small Vehicle fail to understand or cling to provisional means while loftily claiming superiority;
rather, it clarifies that this is the realm of the Universal Eye, which cannot be fathomed by inferior views.
△ When he was a vessel of great capacity, he sought out friends across a hundred cities; when he settled his spirit in the Way, he dwelt alone. △ Mingzheng was the southernmost limit of the South;
Yiji was my friend, and all others were likewise my friends.
Regarding the phrase "fitting the vessel," six finger-widths below [the navel] serves as an illustration; it reveals that the benefit for the practitioner is profound.

Within this passage, there are four sections: first, revealing the benefit by way of the person; second, revealing the benefit by way of the Dharma; third, revealing the benefit through the mutual penetration of beginning and end;
and fourth, revealing the benefit through the contrast of gain and loss. Now, for the first: "fitting the vessel" refers to the youth Sudhana.
This serves as an illustration; according to the teachings, all cases are likewise so. Thus, Maitreya said: "If one possesses a heart of reverent admiration, one should also train in this manner.
As for the phrase "inquiring of friends in a hundred cities," this merely cites a round number; in reality, he inquired after virtuous friends in one hundred and ten cities.
Therefore, at the beginning of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, it says: "At that time, the youth Sudhana, relying on Maitreya..."
The Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, teaching and practicing in gradual succession, traveled through one hundred and ten cities until he reached the country of Samantamukha.
There, he contemplated and observed with single-minded resolve, wishing to see Mañjuśrī;

these one hundred and ten [cities] symbolize the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), for each and every one is fully endowed with the merits of all the stages, or perhaps they are not so divided.
"Awakening" (覺) indicates the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*), while "advancing and retreating" (進退) both represent one hundred and ten.

Because the characteristics of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-vidyā*) in this school do not differ from those of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), they are not represented separately—namely, the first dwelling, the first practice, the first dedication, and the first stage.
This applies likewise for the second through the tenth dwellings and stages; such is the explanation according to the *Great Commentary* (*Dàshù*).
"One Path for the Dwelling of the Spirit" refers to the entrusting of the mind and spirit to a single path. This "One Path" has three meanings: first, it is exclusively directed toward the South;

second, it is characterized by a single cause and a single fruit; third, the myriad sages and thousands of worthies all cultivate the myriad practices without any alternative route—these three constitute the meaning of the One Path.
To clarify that "South" signifies correctness means that from the time Sudhana first resolved his mind upon awakening, his merit...
Upon seeing Mañjuśrī to the east of the city, he proceeded gradually and successively, traveling directly south through various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*).
He did so because the south presides over fire, which is yang and luminous, while the north presides over water, which is yin and dark;

and because the "correct" path does not abide in the two extremes of east and west (the east being left and the west being right, thus constituting the two extremes), but rather seeks the Dharma upon the central path between the north and south.

Because one turns one's back to darkness and faces toward light, departing from extremes and abiding in the correct [Middle Way], it is called "Bright and Correct" (*prabhāsvara-samyak*). Furthermore, there are three additional meanings:

first, since there are already many companions in this direction, the same applies to other directions; second, the south presides over growth and development, signifying that those who seek the Dharma cause the roots of goodness to grow;
third, the dwellings of the people in the Western Regions mostly face east, following the movement of the sun and moon, which signifies... [the alignment with] the [Dharma].

Because Sudhana follows the principles of persons and dharmas, the old commentary states: "Sudhana’s seeking of friends symbolizes compliance; by traveling south, he exhausts the direction of the South.
'Direction' is a provisional dharma with no fixed essence; East, West, South, and North are established names based on mutual relativity.
One merely takes the meaning of clarity and correctness: wherever one's aim is directed to its ultimate end, it is called the South. Only in this way does one truly attain enlightenment."
Because he enters the Dharma-realm, Sudhana visits friends who represent the ten stages (*bhūmi*);

these are mostly located at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), and since it is not said that he turns back toward the north, we know that if one faces toward the light and the correct direction, everything is indeed south.

Regarding the statement, "He benefits me as a friend; I take all as my friends," there are two meanings: first, the explanation according to phenomenal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); second, the explanation according to the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
Regarding the explanation according to specific characteristics: this means that upon seeing the virtuous, one gives rise to the thought of being unable to equal them;

upon seeing the wicked, one develops the wisdom to avoid them like touching hot water. Since three people traveling together must surely have someone who can serve as a teacher, how much more so when there are many?
If one can simply choose to follow what is good and reform what is not good, then everything encountered will be a teacher. Furthermore, upon seeing the worthy, one reflects...
To rectify oneself is itself a form of benefit; even seeing those who are not virtuous and reflecting inwardly upon oneself is likewise a form of benefit.
Furthermore, Laozi said: "The good person is the teacher of the not-good person, and the not-good person is the resource of the good person.
These are all ways in which they benefit me, according to the principle of friendship; therefore, everyone takes them as friends. As for the two [aspects] explained in terms of nature: the Dharma...
In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), all categories of phenomena constitute the Dharma; by generating understanding through these very phenomena, they are immediately named "Teachers.

Just as when one examines a single atom and perceives its possession of infinite virtues, that atom itself is the Teacher, so it is that after Sudhana’s wisdom-illumination reached non-duality upon his second encounter with Mañjuśrī, he subsequently met spiritual friends and teachers numbering as many as the atoms in three thousandfold world-systems.
The meaning lies herein.

△ Encountering the three poisons, the three virtues are perfected; entering a single speck of dust, the one mind is purified. △ Through a thousand transformations, his contemplation remains unchanged;
through ten thousand objects, he accords with and penetrates the Way.
Second, regarding the manifestation of benefits through the Dharma: when one encounters the three poisons, the three virtues become perfectly realized.

For those who accord with and penetrate the Way, the three poisons become the three virtues. This has both a general and a specific sense. Generally, the three poisons are fundamentally empty and are originally the three virtues;
it is only through deluded attachment that one takes virtue for poison. Now, upon awakening, greed lacks the characteristic of greed and is originally precept (*śīla*).
Furthermore, when anger neither arises nor ceases, being fundamentally quiescent from the beginning, this is inherently samādhi.
Thus, the *Dharmapada-sūtra* states: "The nature of precepts is like empty space. It further says: "A mind of anger is like a mirage; the absence of the mark of delusion is wisdom.
Moreover, the *Cittarāja-sūtra* explains the Three Pitakas as follows: "The non-arising of the mark of greed is the Precept Pitaka (Śīlaskandha); the non-arising of the mark of anger..."
Arising is the characteristic of delusion, the treasury of fixed views; non-arising is the treasury of wisdom.
The *Dharmāparyāya-sūtra* states: "Lust is itself the Way; anger and delusion are likewise so. Within these three matters lie immeasurable Buddha-dharmas.
This means that delusion constitutes the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction, while awakening achieves the eighty-four thousand waves [of merit].
Although the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the *pāramitās* are numerous, their root does not exceed the three poisons; although the *pāramitās* are many, their root is simply the three virtues.
As for the distinctions, these correspond to the various types of spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) encountered by Sudhana:
they represent the fact that within every category there exists a Dharma-gate, so that later students do not observe the specific lineage (*gotra*) of a person.
Because the Dharma is characterized by neither grasping nor abandoning, the woman Vasumitrā manifested the signs of lustful desire;
thus, when her neighbors became suspicious and seized her to kiss her, they all obtained merit. The dharma-gate she attained is called the "Liberation Gate of the Limit Beyond Lust.
King Anala manifested the signs of anger, killing and slaughtering immeasurable sentient beings.
The dharma-door he attained is named the Gate of Liberation Like an Illusion.
Within a mass of fire on four sides at the site of the Brahmin Śroṇakoṭīviṃśa, there was a mountain of blades where he was made to cast himself down;

furthermore, he manifested the practice of the five fires, scorching his body while facing upward toward the sun, displaying the appearance of the deluded and false views of non-Buddhist practitioners. When Sudhana saw this, the dharma-door he attained is named Prajñāpāramitā.
If even the characteristics of the three poisons possess gates of liberation through the universal adornment of the *pāramitās*, how much more so for other categories?
Thus we know that one who accords with the perfect teaching of the *Avataṃsaka* is not drowned by the waters of desire, not burned by the fire of aversion, and not invaded by the heat of wrong views.
It is said that entering a single atom is to enter the one mind.
"Purity" has two meanings: first, because emotional thoughts are "dust-thoughts" (rajas-citta), they are pure by virtue of being non-existent;

second, because the substance of even a minute particle accords with the nature (dharmatā), it is pure. Since this is true for a single particle and a single thought, it is likewise so for a thousand minds and myriad objects;

therefore, it is said next that "the thousand transformations do not alter their deliberation. (Thus, the *Xinyao* says: "Mind after mind becomes Buddha; there is not a single mind that is not the Buddha-mind.")
The myriad realms accord with and flow through the Way (that is, the Way is realized everywhere, such that not a single speck of dust is not a Buddha-land).
△ To realize Mañjuśrī’s wondrous wisdom is precisely the original mind. △ To enter Samantabhadra’s profound gate has never been a separate entity.
Third, the beginning and end interpenetrate to manifest the benefit. This section has two parts: first, the beginning and end; second, the root and the branches. Now, for the first:

in accordance with the text, he accords with Mañjuśrī’s wondrous wisdom. That is to say, when Sudhana encounters Mañjuśrī again after passing through various spiritual friends, his wisdom-illumination accords with the non-dual aspect, harmonizing with his fundamental mind and transcending the characteristics of subject and object. Therefore, he does not see [Mañjuśrī’s] body, but only perceives him from afar.
Extending his right hand, he strokes [the crown of] the head; the attainment of the meaning of the Dharma is explained within the subsequent five phases.

This is precisely the beginning for a novice, wherein one first beholds Mañjuśrī in the eastern part of Puṇyavatī to signify the wisdom of faith (*śraddhā-jñāna*). Now, beholding Mañjuśrī again signifies the wisdom of realization (*adhigama-jñāna*).
The intent is that although faith and realization are spoken of as having a beginning and an end, the essence of wisdom (*jñāna-svabhāva*) has from the outset never been distinct. Therefore—

All of these are the teachings of Mañjuśrī; just as the twentieth assembly on Faith was preached in the Hall of Universal Radiance (*Samantaprabhā*), so too this seventh assembly on the Perfection of Causes and Fulfillment of Results is a re-convening at the Hall of Universal Radiance to signify that the realization of the ultimate does not depart from the initial resolve—it is precisely the same as this.

Therefore, the *Great Commentary* states: "The illumination initiated in the Eastern Temple [of the initial resolve] reaches the fulfillment of wisdom without differing from the initial resolve. Thus, the two aspects of beginning and end are one.

The Commentary states that entering the profound gate of Samantabhadra involves no separate entity whatsoever. When Sudhana sought his spiritual friends, he finally arrived at the abode of Bodhisattva Samantabhadra;
there, he minutely observed the body of Samantabhadra and saw within every single pore an unspeakably unspeakable number of oceans of Buddha-fields, and so forth, up to the Buddhas seen by Sudhana.
If one were to approach and attend upon as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in a buddha-field to accumulate wisdom,
it would not equal even a hundredth part of the境界 (state) attained by Samantabhadra from merely seeing him for a moment— not even a fraction approaching an *upaniṣad*.
This applies to all that was [attained] by Sudhana from his first generation of the mind until [the stage of] Samantabhadra, throughout that interval.

Entering the oceans of lands in an uninterrupted succession, what is now entered within a single pore of Samantabhadra in a single thought-moment exceeds the former by unspeakably unspeakable multiples;
as it is with one pore, so it is with all pores, with each mark and sign, and with every limb and joint—all are likewise thus. Thus did Sudhana enter into the lands within the pores of Samantabhadra.
If one were to walk for a single step, reaching as many worlds as there are atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields,
and continued in this manner until the end of all future eons, one would still be unable to know even a single pore;
such oceans of various world-systems, oceans of various Buddhas, and oceans of various assemblies of Bodhisattvas— all such oceans would remain utterly unknown.

Because it is the ultimate limit, it is called the "Mysterious Gate" (*xuánmén*). Yet, as it does not depart from the single mind, the single nature, a single hair, or a single speck of dust, it is next stated that "it has never had a separate essence.
Furthermore, at the conclusion of the sutra, it is summarized: "Then Sudhana attained the ocean of Samantabhadra’s practices and vows;
he became equal to Samantabhadra and equal to all Buddhas; his single body filled [all things], and Perfect Enlightenment manifested before him."

From these stages up to the inconceivable liberation and mastery, all are entirely equal. Since they are equal in terms of both temporal sequence (before and after) and spatial extension (horizontal and vertical), how could there be any distinct entity?
Thus, the Great Commentary states: "By means of the provisional stations, one seeks the perfection of causes;
yet this does not exceed the confines of a single pore."
△ To lose its essential meaning is to labor in vain through kalpas of cultivation. △ To find its gateway is to become equal to all Buddhas in a single morning.
Regarding the four pairs of gains and losses that manifest benefit, the commentary states: "To lose its essential meaning" refers to reaching [the goal] in a single morning.

Regarding these two meanings, from the perspective of their common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), because the objects of this sutra completely encompass the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) within every single thought-moment (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*) and every single atom (*paramāṇu*), if one loses even a single thought-moment, one entirely deviates from it and all cultivation over vast eons becomes fruitless; yet if one attains even a single thought-moment, one is entirely in accord with it, realizing it in an instant without omission.
If one points specifically to the text of the sutra, the intent of the "Appearance" chapter (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) is to distinguish the provisional from the ultimate.

The teaching that bodhisattvas who have not practiced the six perfections are not vessels for this [teaching] and are barred from hearing it before those of the two vehicles is like the intent of the saying that a bodhisattva who has accumulated practices is "exposing its gills and scales at the Dragon Gate. As the Sūtra says:

"Suppose there were a bodhisattva who, for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of kalpas, fully practiced the six pāramitās and cultivated various factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharma)."
If one has not heard this Dharma-gate of the inconceivable great majestic power of the Tathāgata, or if having heard it at some time, one does not believe it, does not understand it,
does not accord with it, and does not enter into it, such a person cannot be called a true Bodhisattva,

because they are unable to be born into the family of the Tathāgata (as the preceding phrase says, "they cultivate causes in vain"). If, however, upon hearing this Dharma, one believes, accords with, awakens to, and enters into it, one should know that this person—

Born into the Tathāgata’s family and fully endowed with all the dharmas of a bodhisattva, one remains far removed from all worldly dharmas and enters deeply into the immeasurable realm of the Tathāgata (which the subsequent phrase describes as "equaling the Buddhas"). Therefore, the Great Commentary states:

"For it is because practice involving effort, even over many kalpas, ultimately results in decay and destruction (referring to the preceding phrase), whereas when the essence of the mindless state reaches its ultimate limit, in a single thought-moment..."
Since one accords with the Buddha’s house (this refers to the latter phrase), it is known that taking non-thought as the fundamental principle is truly wondrous.
That attaining the meaning and failing to attain the meaning are vastly different clearly demonstrates the great benefit of this sutra.
△ Profound! Sublime! Vast! Great! △ Truly, it exhausts the spiritual treasury of all Buddhas and extracts the subtle essence from the depths of the mysterious root.

It raises the sun of wisdom to broaden the delusions and fans the breeze of compassion to perpetuate the spring. It encompasses the surging tides of both nature (svabhāva) and characteristics (lakṣaṇa), eclipsing the brilliance of all other scriptures.
How could it be merely that its clarity surpasses the "transparency at dawn" and its stillness exceeds the "passing away while seated"?

The threefold concluding eulogy consists of: first, a eulogy by means of the names of the four virtues; second, a eulogy by means of the meanings of the six virtues; and finally, a conclusion that integrates the external form with the internal meaning.
Regarding the first, the commentary states: "Profound! Sublime! Vast! Great! "Profound" refers to the meaning of the subtle and wondrous marks of virtue;
"vast" refers to the activity and function; and "great" refers to the essential nature. Next, the commentary provides a eulogy by means of the meanings of the six virtues, stating: "It is real."
This is the capital where the spiritual wonders of all Buddhas converge, like a treasury where thousands of treasures and myriad jewels are gathered;
it is only this sutra that exhausts them completely, leaving nothing hidden or concealed.
Second, it is as if names obscure profound principles, like roots buried in the earth; it is only this sutra that causes these profound and wondrous teachings to be revealed.
1. It is like the clearing of clouds: when three suns emerge, the clouds and mist disperse; when wisdom arises, delusive thoughts are eliminated. 2.
When the warm Yang energy shines upon things, both near and far flourish together; withered trees do not sprout once the season has passed. 3.

The Buddha’s compassion benefits living beings with impartiality and universal salvation, even for icchantikas, continuing without end until the future is exhausted. Furthermore, that which is nurtured by the Yang energy will subsequently [flourish].

In the end, even those who wither and fall away are ultimately brought to *nirvāṇa* by the Buddha’s compassion; because there are these two layers of meaning, it is said that [this teaching] is "eternally flourishing" (*changchun*).
Fifth, like the gentle and surging currents, there is no stream that the great ocean does not receive.

Whether in terms of essence (*svabhāva*) or characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), there is no principle that this Great Sūtra does not elucidate. The Great Commentary states: "The thousand gates flow secretly together, serving as a source for all other scriptures."
The source of the flood returns all myriad virtues; it gathers the various sutras as its retinue.

The sixfold morning sun shines resplendent in the sky, eclipsing the brilliance of the multitude of constellations (the "multitude of constellations" refers to the moon and the stars). The Perfect Teaching is spread throughout the world, obscuring the luster of the various sutras (the "various sutras" refers to the provisional teachings and the Two Vehicles).

Later, he manifested the external meaning by composing commentaries; how could his clarity alone not surpass the "transparency at dawn" mentioned in the *Zhuangzi*? (This refers to an episode in the *Zhuangzi*).
This has two meanings. The general meaning is that it surpasses all other scriptures, let alone external treatises.
Regarding the term "penetrating the dawn" (*zhāochè*), in the third chapter of the *Zhuangzi*, Nanbo Qikui asks Nüyu: "Your years are advanced, yet your complexion is like that of a child;
why is this? He replied, "I have heard the Dao. Qikui asked, "Can it be learned?"
Yangzi said: "To hate what is evil is permissible, but you, my son, are not the right person for this.
Fu Liangyi possesses the talent of a sage but lacks the Way of a sage. I possess the Way of a sage but lack the talent of a sage;
I wish to teach him, hoping that he might truly become a sage. (The note says: "Possessing the talent of a sage" means he has the wisdom of a sage.)

The Way of this is said to possess the Real; by teaching with the Real, one can accomplish that Way. I maintained this for three days and was thereafter able to cast off the world (meaning the affairs of the world).
Having cast off the world, I maintained it again for seven days and was thereafter able to cast off things (things meaning all objective phenomena).
Having cast off things, I maintained it again for nine days and was thereafter able to cast off life (not seeing [the self]...).

[This body] has already been cast off, and only then can one achieve "dawn-penetration" (*zhāochè*). (Not having the myriad things, only the True alone remains; like the rising sun, it is luminous, penetrating, and unobstructed.

All people possess this, yet they cannot know it themselves. Having achieved dawn-penetration, one can then perceive the "Solitary" (*jiàn dú*). Having perceived the Solitary, one can then transcend past and present.
Having transcended past and present, one can then enter the state of neither birth nor death. That which is called "perishing while seated" (*zuò wáng*) is also from Zhuangzi.
Fifth, Yan Hui addressed the Master with words concerning his realization of the Dao, saying, "Hui is making progress. Zhongni asked, "What do you mean?
He replied, "Hui has lost benevolence and righteousness" (benevolence being excessive and righteousness falling short). The Master said, "It is acceptable, yet not yet sufficient.
On another day, he saw him again and said, "Hui is making progress. The Master asked, "What do you mean? He replied, "Hui has lost ritual and music" (ritual being excessive...).

[Zi Gong] said, "When one is troubled, the mind is agitated; when one is joyful, the mind is moved. [The Master] said, "It is acceptable, yet not yet sufficient. On another day, [Zi Gong] saw him again and said, "Hui has progressed further.
[The Master] asked, "What do you mean? He replied, "Hui sits and becomes non-existent. Zhongni looked startled and asked, "What do you mean by 'sitting and becoming non-existent'?

He replied, "Hui has cast off his limbs and discarded his intelligence; he has detached from form and abandoned knowledge, merging with the Great Pervasion. This is what is called 'sitting and becoming non-existent. (To have the mind still is to sit.)"
"Things being empty is what constitutes 'perishing'. Zhongni said, "Hui is indeed the most virtuous; I follow him from behind.

Now, the intention of this commentary is to say that, according to the principles elucidated by all the teachings, the wisdom of discernment and the principle of quiescent extinction have long surpassed the clarity of "transcending at dawn" and the stillness of "perishing while seated.
If one considers the purport of the perfect illumination of the *Avataṃsaka*, it not only transcends those [other teachings], but...
Since this already encompasses all provisional teachings and even transcends the Hīnayāna, how could it be merely that?
This is the meaning of the phrase "how could it be merely...?
△ However, of the hundreds of thousands of profound gates in the mysterious scriptures, half remain closed.

Now, regarding the third section of the "Preface to the Hundred Thousand Profound Scriptures," which explains the causes and conditions for the arising of the teachings and the joy of encountering these rare wonders, there are two parts:
first, clarifying that previous translations were incomplete; second, clarifying that the current translation is largely complete. As for the first:
when Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna reached the Dragon Palace, he beheld the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in three versions; the "lower version" consisted of one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters.
The middle version consists of 498,800 verses and 1,200 chapters;
the upper version consists of as many verses as there are atoms in thirteen thousand great chiliocosms and as many chapters as there are atoms in one four-continent world-system.

Because the physical strength of the people of Jambudvīpa was inferior, they were unable to uphold either the upper or the middle versions. Thus, the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna [preserved the lower version].
He then took the original text and circulated it throughout India. As for the term "mysterious records" (*xuánjí*), they refer to the profound and wondrous scriptures.
The phrase "one hundred thousand" refers to the one hundred thousand *gāthās* of the original text translated below.

Regarding the expression "the dark portal half-shut," this means that while the Jin translation consisted of thirty-six thousand *gāthās*, the Tang version added nine thousand *gāthās* to reach forty-five thousand; thus, the scripture had not yet arrived [in its entirety].
Consequently, the teachings on the subtle and profound key points remained half-concealed.

△ Now, as our Sovereign rules the realm, his virtue harmonizes with Heaven and Earth; his enlightened dominion extends to the myriad regions, and tribute arrives from lands whose names require double translation.

△ As the east wind enters the seasonal order, the Western Heavens offer sincerity that crosses the seas; from South India come imperial calligraphies, and the northern passes present the reverence of tributary submission.
△ A special edict was issued to re-translate the True Sūtras, illuminating the Great Way and enhancing the brilliance of the new principles.

△ I, Chengguan, have enjoyed great good fortune; with deep reverence for this glorious reign, I have received the imperial decree at the translation hall to assist in the profound exegesis according to the instructions.

△ With trembling joy and reverent trepidation, I have thrice reflected upon my task, exhausting my meager wisdom. May these drops of dew merge with the flavor of the hundred rivers in the celestial pond, and may this dust of toil contribute to the heightening of Mount Hua.
Increasing its height by ten thousand *ren*.
Second, it clarifies that the current translation largely incorporates commentaries;

under the reign of our Emperor, the twenty-one fascicles of the *Dharmadhātu-parivarta* were expanded into forty fascicles, yet even this was not entirely complete—thus it is said to "largely incorporate. Within the text, there are three points that clarify this.

First, the virtue of our Sacred Court has spread far and wide, serving as the condition for this translation; second, foreign lands have presented Sanskrit manuscripts from afar, serving as the cause for this translation;
third, the imperial decree is formally explained, describing the circumstances of the translation and its praise. Regarding the first point, the commentary states:

"Our Emperor reigns over the realm, his virtue harmonizing with Heaven and Earth" means that he presides over the domain, and his virtue accords with Heaven (*qian*) and Earth (*kun*). Heaven is *qian* and Earth is *kun*.

Regarding the phrase "illuminating and dwelling over the myriad regions," the *Shangshu*, in the chapter "The Canon of Yao" (*Yao Dian*), states: "In the past, Emperor Yao was intelligent, wise, and reflective;
he illuminated and dwelt throughout the world. Kong An-guo’s commentary explains this as meaning that the influence of his sage-like virtue was far-reaching.
My current interpretation, however, is that his "wind" (influence) and "light" reached afar, taking the world as his dwelling place. Now, our Emperor Dezong’s virtue extends beyond [his own borders].
Therefore, that [text] was offered as a tribute in its original *Avataṃsaka* Sanskrit version. Regarding those offerings brought via successive translations:
when foreign tributes pass through several countries, they undergo translation from one land to another until they finally reach this [land];
hence it is called "successive translation" (*chóngyì*). This is like the white pheasant offered here after having passed through nine stages of translation. Second, explaining foreign lands.

The distant offering of the Sanskrit original is the cause for this translation. Regarding the phrase "the east wind enters the musical laws" (*dōfū nyūritsu*) leading to the expression of "respectful submission to the court" (*chōshū no kei*):

as for "the east wind entering the musical laws," the *Ten Shū Ki* (Record of the Ten Continents) of Emperor Wu of the Han states that an envoy from the Western Hu Yue-zhi kingdom sent three kinds of items as a distant tribute:
namely, a small lion, string-glue, and soul-returning incense. After half a year had passed...
The Emperor did not inquire about this matter, so the envoy followed him into the garden to shoot.

When the string of the Emperor’s bow snapped, the envoy asked, "Why do you not take some glue for joining strings to mend it? He then took a vessel of glue and joined it; indeed, it was just as he had said.
The Emperor said, "That ruler possesses such things—why does he send them from afar as tribute? The envoy replied, "Your servant’s country is thirty thousand *li* from here."

There was a regular diviner who observed that an east wind had entered the *lǜ* (musical pitch-pipe) and did not cease for ten decades; azure clouds reached up to the *lǚ* (or, according to another reading, were viewed by it).

Peng Kang’s poem says: "Auspicious radiance ascends to the *lǚ*, dense and profuse once more; it distantly manifests the transformation of non-action (*wúwéi*) and shall clarify the Most Honored One of the Ultimate Way.
Its momentum congeals as the thousand *qī* (li) become still; its color returns from the nine heavens, divided. We have already seen the dragon ascending."
The mind wonders how it could know that the patterns on the stone were touched by smoke, which dispersed in extraordinary profusion; for over a month, the vapors remained dense and swirling.
This caused the guests from the kingdom of Linbi to gaze westward in reverence at the auspicious clouds, which did not disperse for a whole month.

The diviners declared, "To the east, there is a ruler who follows the Way," and thus they sent this distant tribute. As for those in the Western Heaven who have crossed the seas with such sincerity, it is because the Emperor’s virtuous influence has reached them.

Furthermore, because he was from the Western Heaven (India), he offered his loyalty by crossing the sea to present the original texts of the scriptures, just as in the case of the three items [offered] in the past.

As for "Southern India," this refers generally to the land of India; specifically, it is the region to the west of this country, comprising the Five Regions of India, which constitutes Southern India.
Regarding the "imperial manuscript," the inscription on that scroll states: "Written by my own hand. Great!

The "Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra," in which fifty-five holy beings enter the realm of inconceivable liberation through the conduct of approaching and serving spiritual friends as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field,
as taught in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* in One Hundred Thousand Verses; this is respectfully presented to the Northern Palace for the imperial audience.

Regarding the veneration of the Founder [the Buddha]: just as the hundred rivers flow toward the sea as their ultimate destination, so too do the myriad nations look toward our Great Tang as their sovereign.

Therefore, in presenting this scripture, I have expressed my profound reverence; specifically, I have requested that Your Majesty’s illustrious decree be returned to me, so that I may clarify the circumstances of the translation and the composition of the hymn of praise.
This section consists of three parts: first, the Sage issues the imperial decree; second, the joy of receiving the decree; and third, the translation and the hymn of praise.
The first point here is that this work merely unfolds the "Entering the Dharma Realm" chapter of the old sutra;

thus it is said to "illuminate the Great Way" and "augment its brilliance. "Way" (*yōu*) refers to the "Noble Way," meaning excellent and beautiful virtue. Second, regarding the reception of the imperial decree to compose the commentary:

Chengguan reflects that he possesses great good fortune in reaching this point, and as for the term "profound assistance," he looks back and sees that he himself has been blessed with such natural fortune.
Having encountered this era of great brilliance, I have received the imperial decree to translate the sutras and compose commentaries.
Regarding the three translations of the *Praise of the Mutual Commentary*, "bàn" (抃) refers to dancing with the hands and "yuè" (躍) refers to leaping with the feet;

"jīng" (兢) means being cautious and fearful, while "tì" (惕) means being alarmed and apprehensive. "Sānfù jiéyú" (三復竭愚) means to repeatedly review [the text] three times, exhausting one's own foolish intellect.
I do not dare to speak recklessly; out of humility, I call myself ignorant.

As for my words being "repeated three times," this refers to what is said in the *Analects* regarding Nanrong [Zhongni] repeating the lines of the *Odes*: "The flaw in a white jade disc may yet be polished away, but the flaw in these words cannot be remedied.
The meaning is that while a flaw in a jade disc can be ground and repaired, once an excessive word has been uttered, it cannot be undone.

Four horses could not overtake him as he fled; when Nanrong reached this passage in his recitation of the *Shi*, he repeated it two or three times to manifest his sincerity and exercise caution regarding his speech.
Now, employing this same intent, "drops falling into the Celestial Pond" refers to the *Jizhu lun* (Treatise on the Wisdom Degrees), which identifies the ocean as the "Celestial Pond.
The meaning is that in composing commentaries and translating scriptures, every word and every principle must accord with the Buddha’s mind.
Regarding the phrases "like a drop of dew in the ocean" and "like dust piled up," these refer to the words spoken by Zi Gong in praise of the Master to Duke Ai of Lu.
It is said that when Duke Ai asked Zi Gong, "Is your teacher virtuous? he replied, "He is virtuous. The Duke asked, "Being virtuous, what else is he like?
He answered, "I do not know. The Duke asked again, "Why do you not know? Zi Gong replied, "In my..."
"Those under the Master's gate are like people who, though wearing the sky all day long, do not know its height; though treading upon the earth all day long, do not know its thickness;
they drink from the sea until satisfied, yet how could they know its depth? Duke Ai asked, "Is this praising the Master too much?
Zi Gong replied, "If one were to take up soil and pile it to nourish a mountain, would it not be beneficial? [The term] *ren* (one *ren* being seven feet) is entirely a word of humility."

△ *Mahāvaipulya* refers to the Dharma realized; the *Buddhāvataṃsaka* refers to the person who realizes it. △ It is "Great" (*mahā*) because its substance, which can be measured against the limits of space, is boundless;
it is "Extensive" (*vaipulya*) because its Dharma-gates, which can be drunk from like the depths of the vast ocean, are inexhaustible;

it is "Vast" (*vipula*) because even if one were to count every atom within all lands, its utility remains unfathomable; it is "Broad" (*vaipulya*) because it transcends both the perceiver and the perceived, illuminating the myriad dharmas.

"Profound and remote" refers to the Buddha; "fragrant and spreading" refers to the myriad practices; "radiant and glorious" refers to the manifold virtues; "flower" refers to the perfection of these practices and virtues;

"adornment" refers to the embellishment of the ten bodies; and "sutra" refers to the threading together and encompassing of the profound and mysterious, thereby manifesting the splendor of true radiance.
△ If one takes these seven characters as the grand framework of this entire work, then more than half of the inexhaustible Dharma gates will have been contemplated.

Regarding "Mahāvaipulya" (The Great Vaipulya), the fourth section below provides a brief explanation of the general title so that its essential framework may be understood. This section consists of three parts: first, the designation of the name;
second, the explanation of the name; and third, the concluding praise. The first part [the designation] is self-evident. Second, regarding the explanation of the name:

the passage from the commentary beginning with "Exceeding the limits of space" up to the end of the sutra refers to these three phrases—"exceeding the limits of space," etc.—which are the verses of Samantabhadra praising the Buddha’s virtues and concluding the homage.
The *Anantamukha-sūtra* states: "The atoms within a buddha-field and the thoughts of the mind may be counted;
the waters within the great ocean may be drunk dry; space may be measured and the wind may be bound. Yet no one can fully describe the merits of the Buddha.

Here, "space" explains the essence (*svabhāva*), "the waters of the great ocean" explain the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and "the great atoms and fields" explain the functions (*karman*). The term "mind-thoughts" and "wind" are not taken up here.
"Shattering the lands as numerous as motes of dust" means that lands as numerous as motes of dust are all reduced to atoms. Regarding "transcending awakening and so forth":
the subject that awakens is *bodhi*, and the object awakened to is *nirvāṇa*. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "There is no nirvāṇa for anything;

there is no Buddha who possesses nirvāṇa, nor is there nirvāṇa apart from the Buddha. Since both wisdom (*jñāna*) and principle (*tattva*) are transcended once the subject and object of awakening have been left behind, [this state is realized].
When subject and object are obliterated and both vanish, such that the beginning and the end are non-dual, this is ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*).
Thus, although it is equally free from [duality], it brilliantly illuminates all phenomena without omission; it is not entirely the same as the *Laṅkāvatāra*.

That which causes the myriad practices to flourish is like the flowers of plants and trees bearing fruit; that which brings glory to the multitude of virtues is like plants and trees possessing both jade and gold in their adornment.
Regarding "the flowers are round": these flowers of practice and virtue adorn those ten bodies; that is, the two flowers and two virtues together adorn the Buddha-body.
Regarding "pervading and encompassing" and so forth: they penetrate and sustain the profound and wondrous gates of meaning, with each gate shining brilliantly.
If one seeks out these immeasurable and boundless gates, each and every one reaches through to the Buddha-wisdom, just as if seeking a reflection.
Because it returns to the source, the Great Sūtra says: "Just as by the light of the sun one sees the solar disk, so too by the light of wisdom does one penetrate the Buddha-wisdom;
the essence of Buddha-wisdom is like the solar disk, expounding immeasurable meanings like the sunlight.
Regarding the three concluding praises, the Commentary [on the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*] summarizes these seven characters and so forth, citing the *Book of Documents*: "As if a net were in..."
"The main ropes have their strands and are not disordered; 'disordered' means chaos. Master Kong’s preface states:
"To present its grand framework and encompass its essential points—this would amount to more than half [the understanding].

This refers to the phrasing of the *Appended Statements* of the *Book of Changes*, where Confucius says that by examining its *tuan* (hexagram judgments), the student thereby exhausts more than half of his contemplation. My current intention is to explain these seven characters.
The meaning of this constitutes more than half the merit of the entire work.
