Above is the second section, the "Correct Explanation of the Text of the Commentary," which consists of four parts. The first part is the "General Exposition of the Meaning of the Text," followed by the "Homage."
Please add the third chapter, "Explanation of the Text," consisting of four sections: (1) Praise and Dedication. The first section, the general summary of the meaning of the text, is now complete.
From here on is the second section, the extensive explanation of the homage, praise, and request for additions.
△ I bow my head in refuge. △ To the True Dharma-realm. △ To all Tathāgatas whose radiance shines everywhere.
△ To Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and the honored ones of the ocean-like assembly. △ May I receive secret sustenance and assist in the profound and wondrous.

The second section, "Taking Refuge, Paying Homage, and Requesting Blessings," is divided into two parts. The first part, consisting of the initial three lines, concerns taking refuge and paying homage;

the latter part, consisting of one line, concerns requesting blessings. Within the former, there are again two sub-sections. First, there are four characters representing the "three karmas" (body, speech, and mind) that perform the act of bowing the head in refuge.
Following this, there are seventeen characters representing the "Three Jewels" to which one takes refuge—the True Dharmadhātu. [End of] the current section. Commentary: "Ji" (稽).

"Taking refuge with the head" (*śīrṣa-praṇāma*): "To bow" (*kī*) means to bend down or to arrive at [the ground]. "Head" (*śīrṣa*) refers to the crown of the head. "To take refuge" (*praṇāma*) carries the meaning of turning toward and following;
"to rely" (*ni*) conveys the sense of entrusting oneself. The commentator, wishing to compose this treatise, first gives rise to reverence through the three karmas:
he bends his head and crown until it reaches the earth, his mind merges with the realm of the Buddha, and his mouth recites these words to analyze [the truth].
This analysis is a sincere prayer for the bestowal of protection. Question: For what reason does one first pay homage to the Triple Gem?
Answer: Briefly, there are seven reasons: First, to manifest auspiciousness; Second, to give rise to faith;

Third, to cause one to recognize their kindness and virtue; Fourth, because it is appropriate according to ritual protocol; Fifth, to indicate that there is someone from whom one has received instruction; Sixth, for the purpose of seeking protection.

Therefore, in order to follow the former sages, and because the merit of the Three Jewels is the foremost auspiciousness, the author first manifests auspiciousness by offering initial homage at the very beginning;
this is done so that the work he has composed may circulate for a long time and bring about the auspiciousness of the twofold benefit.
Thus, the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* states: "The Three Jewels are the most auspicious."

Regarding the statement that "I first speak of two [jewels] in order to generate faith": this is intended so that future generations, upon hearing this scripture, will not give rise to doubt but will instead develop faith;

thus, at the very outset, the Three Jewels are praised so that, having first produced compliant faith toward the Three Jewels, one will subsequently refrain from doubting or slandering the true teaching.
Thirdly, it is to make known their debt of gratitude and their sublime virtues.
This means that the Buddha has the grace of preaching the Dharma, the Dharma has the grace of generating understanding, and the Saṃgha has the grace of transmitting the teachings.
If there were no Buddha Jewel, there would be no one to preach the Dharma; if there were no Dharma Jewel, there would be no basis for generating understanding;

if there were no Saṃgha Jewel, there would be no one to transmit the teachings. Therefore, it is through the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma, through the Dharma’s generation of understanding, and through the Saṃgha’s transmission [that these graces exist].
The teaching enables one to hear [the Dharma], and it is through these three kinds of grace that wisdom and awakening are perfected; thus, one comes to recognize their debt of gratitude.

Therefore, the commentary first clarifies that the four ritual protocols must be observed as they ought to be. For in the world, whenever a subject or a son has anything to do, they first inform their sovereign or father, which alone accords with proper ritual.
Since the grace and virtue of the Triple Gem exceed those of a sovereign or a father, what [could compare] to the intention of the Great Master?
Not only this, but since a minister or son who intends to propagate the True Teaching must first pay homage to the Triple Gem according to ritual protocol, he offers this reverence.
Furthermore, the phrase "having received instruction" is used to manifest that what is being described is not merely the product of his own imagination, but is entirely based upon the Holy Teachings;
having fully received the scriptures and been certified by what has been taught by the Three Jewels, he has composed this commentary.
Sixth, regarding the purpose of seeking protection: in this age of the Dharma’s semblance (*pratirūpaka*), obstacles to the transmission of the teachings are ever numerous;
therefore, one first pays homage to the Triple Gem to seek their supreme protection. Seventh, regarding the purpose of following the precedents of past sages:
the assemblies of holy beings in the Western Heaven—the Bodhisattvas of the Saṃgha—who composed treatises to explain the sūtras, all first offered homage.
In order to follow the former sages, I pay homage to the Triple Gem; as my reverent intention is so vast, I cannot describe it in exhaustive detail.
Regarding the section on the Three Jewels to which one takes refuge, there are two parts: first, the presentation of the meaning of the Three Jewels, and second, the formal commentary on the text.

Now, for the first part, the meaning of the Three Jewels is the great framework of the Buddha-dharma, which students must know; it cannot be left unexplained. Briefly, I shall divide this into five sections.

There are four sections: first, the etymological explanation; second, the determination of the essence; third, the establishment [of the categories]; and fourth, the detailed analysis through questions and answers. Regarding the first section, there are two parts:
first, the general name, and second, the specific names. As for the general name: "three" is the meaning of the number, and "jewel" (*ratna*) is a name derived from a metaphor.
According to the *Ratnagotravibhāga*, there are six meanings: first, it is rare, like the gold and jade of the world.
The Three Jewels, which are difficult for the world to encounter, are likewise so; throughout hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas, sentient beings find it hard to meet them.

Second, their clarity and purity are like those of worldly gold and jade: the essential nature of gold and jade is clear and pure, and the Three Jewels are likewise so, being free from defilement and stainless, which is why they are clear and pure.
Third, their power and influence are like those of worldly gold and jade: they possess majestic power and influence, and the Three Jewels are likewise so when seen.
1. Adorned with the power of the Path, supernatural faculties, and majestic authority, just as gold and jade adorn the world;
the Three Jewels are likewise adorned by concentration and wisdom, for they are the supramundane Dharma. 2. Most supreme, just as gold and jade are the most supreme in the world;
the Three Jewels are likewise so, being the most honored and supreme in the cultivation of the supramundane path. 3. Unchanging, just as...
The gold and jade of the world cannot be altered; even after being smelted a hundred times, it does not become light, and though buried for a long time, it does not decay.
The Three Jewels are likewise: they are not altered by worldly dharmas. Because they possess these six characteristics, they are called "jewels" (*ratna*);

their name is derived from both their numerical count and their metaphorical analogy. As for their individual names—namely Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha—the term *buddha* (梵云佛陀) is translated as follows:

Regarding "Awakened One" (*buddha*), the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "One who is able to eliminate the two obstacles regarding all objects of cognition—like awakening from sleep or like a lotus flower opening—is called a Buddha because their self-awakening and awakening of others, as well as their practice of awakening, are perfected. Awakening itself is the very essence of a Buddha.
In Sanskrit this is called *dharma*, which here means "Dharma"; it refers to the nature of the teachings, principles, practices, and fruits, serving as the track for self-nature.
Holding the name constitutes the dharma-vehicle; "holding" is the dharma itself, which serves as the name. In Sanskrit it is called *saṃgha*, which here means "harmonious assembly.

The noble ones of the three vehicles are harmonious in both principle and phenomena, their essence being free from conflict. "Harmony" refers to this function, and "assembly" is a provisional designation for this harmonious gathering;
thus the name is derived by dependent designation (*tatpuruṣa*). Second, regarding the determination of its essential nature (*svabhāva*): therein—
There are two [parts]: first, distinguishing the differences; second, clarifying their essential nature. The first section has three parts: 1) the *saṃgha* as the sustaining support (*pratipatti*);

2) the distinct characteristics (*pṛthak-lakṣaṇa*) of the Three Jewels; and 3) the identical essence (*tulya-svabhāva*). All of these are fields for generating merit through the preciousness of rebirth. Regarding the first, the "sustaining support":

the Buddha refers to the physical image, the Dharma refers to the teaching, and the Saṃgha refers to the fivefold assembly. Second, the Three Jewels of distinct characteristics (according to Great Master Xianshou’s five [categories]...).

The Teaching is clarified by dividing it into five parts: first, the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) teaching, which consists of three sections: Buddha, Dharma, and Saṅgha. First, the Buddha Jewel, which has three sections: 1. The *dharmakāya* (Dharma-body), which is the fivefold [qualities]:

precepts, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation; 2. The *saṃbhogakāya* (Reward-body), which is the sixteen-foot body; 3. The *nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation-body), meaning the transformation bodies that appear according to the various classes of beings.

Second, the Dharma Jewel, which has four sections: 1. The Dharma of Teaching (the verbal teaching, i.e., the sound of the doctrine); 2. The Dharma of Principle (the principle of the emptiness of persons); 3. [The Dharma of Practice]; 4. The Dharma of Fruition.

The Dharmas of Practice (referring to the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment: the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path);

the Dharmas of the Four Fruits (referring to analytical cessation, which is nirvana); the Three Jewels of the Sangha (namely, those on the four fruits and the four paths). Furthermore, the first of the two Mahayana teachings (the Initial Teaching) is also threefold:

first, the Jewel of the Buddha, which is threefold: 1. the Dharma-body (referring to pure *tathatā*); 2. the Reward-body (referring to the two kinds of enjoyment, for oneself and others); 3. the Transformation-body (the Great Transformation-body, the thousand [buddhas]).

1. The *zhàngxiǎo huàshēn* (the one-chang small transformation body) and the *zhàngliù suílèi huàshēn* (the one-chang-six-foot transformation body according to type). 2. The Dharma Jewel (*fǎbǎo*), with four sections: A. The Dharma of Teaching (*jiàofǎ*)—referring to the original essence and its reflected image; B. The Dharma of Principle (*lǐfǎ*)—referring to the true principle of the two emptinesses (*èrkōng zhēnlǐ*); C.

The Dharma of Practice (*xíngfǎ*)—referring to the myriad practices of the six perfections (*liùdù wànháng*); D. The Dharma of Fruition (*guǒfǎ*)—Bodhi and Nirvana. 3. The Sangha Jewel (*sēngbǎo*)—namely the three stages of worthiness (*sānxián*) and the ten stages of sagehood (*shíshèng*).

3. The Final Teaching of the Mahayana (*dàchéng zhōnjiào*), also consisting of three parts: A. The Buddha Jewel (*fóbǎo*), with two sections: i. The True Body (*zhēnshēn*)—referring to the Dharma-body (*fǎshēn*) and the self-enjoyment body (*zìshòuyòng shēn*). [Note: The text fragment ends here.]
2) The two types of *saṃbhogakāya* (namely, the *parasaṃbhogakāya* and the *nirmāṇakāya*). 2) The Jewel of the Dharma, in four parts: (1) The Dharma of Teaching (the images of mind-only);

(2) The Dharma of Principle (the true reality of the two kinds of emptiness); (3) The Dharma of Practice (the myriad practices of the six pāramitās); (4) The Dharma of Fruition (the union of initial awakening with original awakening).

3) The Jewel of the Saṃgha (referring to the three stages of worthiness and the ten stages of sagehood). 4) According to the Sudden Teaching of the Mahāyāna, there is only true nature and no other dharmas; even if...

Even in strong arguments, it does not depart from the single nature, which is threefold: first, the Buddha Jewel (in the sense of awakening and knowing); second, the Dharma Jewel (in the sense of guiding and upholding); third, the Sangha Jewel (in the sense of non-contradiction).
The five sections of the Mahāyāna Perfect Teaching Text: 1. The Text on the Buddha Jewel, Part One:

The Fusion of the Three Worlds into the Ten Bodies (*daśakāya*)—namely, the sentient-being world (*sattva-loka*), the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*), and the world of the perfectly awakened wisdom (*vidyā-sambuddha-loka*). 2. The Buddha Himself Possesses the Ten Bodies (the bodies of enlightenment, vows, and transformation).

[The Dharma Jewel of] Power-Adorned Majestic Authority, Mind-Born Merit, and Dharma-Wisdom consists of four parts: first, the Dharma of Teaching (referring to the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle); second, the Dharma of Principle (referring to the Dharma-realm and the ten mysteries);

third, the Dharma of Practice (referring to the sequential and the perfect-and-fused); and fourth, the Dharma of Fruition (referring to the non-obstruction between the environment and its inhabitants).

Third, the Sangha Jewel (referring to the Bodhisattvas of the oceanic assembly). Regarding the "identity in essence" (*samavāya*), there are three explanations: first, speaking from the perspective of original nature, it is the inherent spiritual awakening of that nature.
The Buddha is the nature that is fundamentally quiescent; the Dharma is the nature that is fundamentally endowed with virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

These functions are mutually non-contradictory and do not conflict, being of one flavor and pure in their essential substance—this is the Sangha. Second, speaking in terms of contemplative practice: the Buddha is the observing wisdom.
Because it observes, it is free from consciousness and can serve as a standard for upholding the Dharma. Within this contemplation, all phenomena are already [transcended].
The perfect, moment-to-moment state is itself free from discord; this is the Sangha. Third, speaking in terms of pervasive integration:

all differentiated phenomena of the mundane and supramundane realms rely entirely upon the perfectly luminous Great Enlightenment to manifest provisionally. Each and every one lacks an intrinsic nature;
its very substance is Perfect Enlightenment, and thus everything is the Buddha. It is like images appearing in a mirror; the images are all nothing but the mirror itself.
The dharmas manifested in the present are each and every one quiescent; yet, though quiescent, they do not destroy their characteristics, for characteristic and nature are not distinct.
Each characteristic conforms to its nature and pervades the dharma-realm; the nature follows the characteristics and manifests a thousandfold differentiation.

Extending to the end of the future, nature and characteristics are unimpeded, and ultimately all are dharmas that can be taken as models and upheld. Since each and every characteristic conforms to its nature...
When obstructed, one enters all and all enter one; the whole encompasses the individual and the individual encompasses the whole.

Interpenetrating and interfusing in this manner, they are in harmonious union without conflict; this is true for every ordinary and sagely being alike—this is the Sangha. Second, to clarify the essential nature, there are three points.
First, regarding the Three Jewels of Sustenance (*saṃghāra-sarva-ratna*): as for the Buddha Jewel, it does not refer merely to gold, jade, paintings, or clay sculptures.
Furthermore, the Dharma Jewel, whether it be paper, silk, bamboo, or cloth, takes the four sense-objects (*catvāraḥ viṣayāḥ*) as its substance.
As for the Sangha Jewel, if it refers to the Sangha of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), it takes the five contaminated aggregates (*pañca sāsravaskandhāḥ*) as its substance;
if it refers to images of the Sangha, these likewise take the four sense-objects as their substance. These supports of the teachings ensure that the power of the true Triple Gem remains intact.

"Severance" refers to maintenance; thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "To perpetuate the Three Jewels so that they may not be interrupted. Second, regarding the distinct characteristics of the Three Jewels:

the Dharma Jewel, as the Dharmakāya, takes stainless *tathatā* (suchness) as its essence; the Self-Enjoyment Body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) takes the actual, untainted five aggregates (*skandha*) as its essence;
and the Other-Enjoyment Body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*) takes the marks manifested by the Wisdom of Equality (*samatājñāna*) as its essence.
The transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) has as its essence portions that resemble the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*). There are three types of transformation bodies: 1.

The Great Transformation Body has as its essence the subtle aspects of form and mind manifested within the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), which resemble the five untainted aggregates.
2. The Small Transformation Body has as its essence the aspects of form and mind—both coarse and subtle—that are manifested within the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done.

Its essence consists of the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*). Alternatively, when manifesting as a transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) according to the capacities of beings, its essence consists of the subtle mental and physical aspects (*nimitta-bhāga*) appearing within the wisdom of accomplishing what is to be done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), which resemble the five untainted aggregates. Regarding the Jewel of the Dharma (*dharmaratna*), there are four types:

first, the teaching (*deśanā*), which refers to names, phrases, and phonemes; second, the principle (*tattva*), which refers to the true suchness of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā-tathatā*); third, the practice (*pratipatti*), which refers to the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*).
The ten thousand practices and the four fruits refer to the supreme fruits of bodhi and nirvāṇa; these four dharmas collectively constitute the essence of the Dharma Jewel.
The Saṃgha Jewel takes the untainted five aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*) of the noble ones of the three vehicles as its essence.

These three jewels of identical essence all take True Suchness (*tathatā*) as their essence: that which possesses the meaning of "awakening" is named the Buddha Jewel, and that which possesses the meaning of "guiding and maintaining" [the teachings] is named the Dharma Jewel.
"Principle" (yì) is called the Jewel of the Dharma; that which is endowed with reason and harmony is called the Jewel of the Sangha. Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"If one can contemplate the Three Jewels as eternally abiding and identical to the True Truth (*tattva*), and so forth. Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra* states: "The Buddha is the Dharma, and the Dharma is the Saṃgha;
these Three Jewels all possess the characteristic of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and are equal to empty space. Moreover, the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* states:
In right view, one does not even perceive the Dharma-body, let alone its physical form;

because it is empty and detached, one does not even perceive the Dharma, let alone its verbal expression; because it is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one does not even perceive the Saṅgha, let alone a community of harmonious assembly.
Regarding the third [section], the establishment [of the refutation], there are four parts. First, the overturning of false refuges: regarding those external sects, there are three [points]. First...
The three types of false objects of refuge—false Buddhas, false teachings, and false persons—are established as the opposites of those three [true refuges].
Having taken refuge in the Buddha, one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever take refuge in Maheśvara or other such deities.

Having taken refuge in the Dharma, one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever take refuge in the scriptures of non-Buddhist paths. Having taken refuge in the Saṃgha, one would rather sacrifice body and life than ever... [take refuge in others].
Not taking refuge in the heterodox and false assemblies is established as the Three Jewels because there are three things to be overturned, as explained at length in the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*.
Second, regarding the faculties: for those of superior faculties, one teaches the Buddha Jewel so they may aspire toward the Bodhi of the Buddha;

for those of middling faculties, one teaches so that they may seek natural wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) and the law of causes and conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda-dharma*), thereby being able to enter the Path.

Regarding the Jewel of the Dharma: for those of inferior faculties, one is able to enter the Path only when learning from a teacher in accordance with both principle and phenomena without contradiction.
Regarding the Jewel of the Saṅgha, there are three points concerning analogies: (1) the Buddha is like a skilled physician; (2) the Dharma is like excellent medicine;
and (3) the Jewel of the Saṅgha is like a nurse. Regarding the four reliances as causes: (1) relying on the Tathāgata as the cause; and (2) relying on the True Dharma as the cause.
Third, regarding the reliance on my disciples as the cause: all sentient beings must attain the bliss of nirvāṇa through three causes, as stated in the *Daśacakrakṣitigarbha-sūtra*.
Possessing the aforementioned four meanings, neither more nor less, it speaks only of the Three Jewels.
Fourth, the analysis of the sequence has three parts: first, regarding the sequence of application, there is no error in the way one teaches and transforms sentient beings.
Regarding the Buddha, the Jewel of the Buddha is explained first; because there is a Buddha, the teachings of the Three Vehicles are proclaimed, and thus next the Jewel of the Dharma is explained.

Because there is the Buddha-Dharma that transforms the assemblies of the Three Vehicles, the Jewel of the Saṅgha is explained last. Second, according to the sequence of practice, all noble ones take the Dharma as their foundation;
therefore, the Jewel of the Dharma is explained first, for it is only by virtue of the existence of the Dharma that [the others] come to exist.

In the sequence of practice, it is first explained that the Jewel of the Sangha exists because through the Dharma and the Sangha one shall attain the fruit of Buddhahood; subsequently, the Jewel of the Buddha is explained.
Regarding these three, the order of their superiority and inferiority is as follows: within the Three Jewels of identical essence (*sārabhūta-triratna*), the Jewel of the Dharma is supreme.
Thus, the Sūtra says: "That which all Buddhas take as their teacher is the Dharma. Because the Dharma is eternal, the Buddhas are also eternal; therefore, the Jewel of the Dharma is supreme.

Among the Three Jewels distinguished by their individual characteristics (*pṛthag-lakṣaṇa*), the Jewel of the Buddha is supreme; thus a verse in a sutra says: "In the heavens above and the earth below, there is none equal to the Buddha;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is likewise no peer. Having seen all that exists within these worlds, I find that none at all is like the Buddha.

Therefore, the Jewel of the Buddha is supreme. Among the Three Jewels as they are maintained in the world (*saṃdhāraṇa*), the Jewel of the Saṅgha is supreme, because it is through human beings [that the Dharma is preserved].
It is the Dharma that can propagate the Way; it is not the Way that propagates people. When people exist, the Dharma exists; when people perish, the Dharma perishes.

Therefore, the Jewel of the Sangha is supreme. Fifth, the analysis through question and answer: Question: It was stated previously that the holy ones of the three vehicles are all the Jewel of the Sangha.
While the multitude of Śrāvakas may be called the Sangha, a Pratyekabuddha appears alone; how, then, can they constitute a Sangha? Answer: [They do so] by virtue of their conditions...
There are two types of Pratyekabuddhas: first, those who appear in an age without a Buddha and attain realization through solitary contemplation in quietude;
since they lack a community and are deficient in the harmony of ritual action, they practice the Dharma alone and do not constitute the Sangha Jewel.

Second, there are those who appear as a community, including immeasurable numbers of Mahāpratyekabuddhas who possess both the harmony of principle and the harmony of ritual action; thus they form the Sangha. Here, we refer to the latter group.

The *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) states: "At that time, there were eight hundred trillion great seers and pratyekabuddhas who had fully accomplished the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, which are neither annihilated nor eternal. Question: A renunciant bodhisattva possesses both types of harmony [physical and doctrinal] and may thus be called a *saṃgha*. A lay bodhisattva possesses only the harmony of principle; does this not mean they cannot constitute a *saṃgha*? Answer: [They do constitute a *saṃgha*]. This is because the *Mahāyāna-abhidharma-samuccaya-śāstra* states: "In the Mahāyāna, even a single person can be called a *saṃgha*. Furthermore, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* says: "The *saṃgha* of the Bodhisattvas is the true *saṃgha*; it is the foremost among the three jewels. Therefore, one should know that both the lay and the renunciant bodhisattvas are capable of constituting a *saṃgha*. As for the distinction between the two types of harmony, the harmony of principle is established through the realization of the truth, while the harmony of physical assembly is established through the gathering of persons. Since the former is superior to the latter, it is said that the harmony of principle alone suffices to constitute a *saṃgha*. Thus, it is established that both the lay and the renunciant bodhisattvas possess the nature of the *saṃgha*. This concludes the section on the *saṃgha*. 10. The Section on the Precepts. 1. Although a lay bodhisattva lacks formal ritual concord (*karmārha-sāmagrī*), they possess concord in principle (*dharmasāmagrī*) and, being free from discord and contention, they constitute a *saṃgha*.
This differs from the śrāvakas, who require both types of concord. Question: How many individuals are there within the bodhisattva *saṃgha*?

Answer: According to the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sūtra) and the *Yingluo jing* (Garuḍa-Necklace Sūtra), there are forty-two classes of noble beings (*ārya-pudgala*), namely those prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).

The three stages of worthiness (*śaikṣa*), the ten stages of sages (*ārya*) above the ground, as well as the stages of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Sublime Enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*), are as explained at length therein.
The reason the stage of the Ten Faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*) is not included is that it belongs to the rank of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Among these forty-two stages, forty-one are subsumed within the Jewel of the Saṅgha, while the single stage of Sublime Enlightenment is subsumed within the Jewel of the Buddha. Thus, the five distinct sections above have been briefly elucidated.
The exposition on the meaning of the Three Jewels is concluded. Following this, the commentary (*shu*) is separately explained: "The True Dharma-realm" refers to the Jewel of the Dharma;
it encompasses all the distinctions of phenomena, yet they ultimately return to the True Realm. The reason for first indicating the Dharma is that it is the teacher of all Buddhas.
Regarding the phrase "the light shines everywhere" and so forth, this refers to the Jewel of the Buddha. In Sanskrit, *Vairocana*; in Chinese, this means "light."
"Universally Illuminating" (*Pianzhao*) is a translation based on the new Sanskrit terminology;

if one follows the old Sanskrit terminology, *Vairocana* is translated as "pervading all places" (*bian yiqie chu*), which pertains to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), while *Rocana* is translated as "light universally illuminating" (*guangming bianzhao*), which pertains to the Reward-body (*saṃbhogakāya*).
According to the Sanskrit texts themselves, it is not actually like this; these two types of Sanskrit names are merely the result of the new and old translations.
Because there is a distinction between the *dharmakāya* (the dharma-body) and its fruition (*vipāka*), the old translations of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* generally name it Vairocana;
however, in the Tang translations of the sūtras, it is always called Vairocana—meaning that the three bodies and ten bodies are collectively termed Vairocana.
Herein, the term used refers to both the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) and the fruition, which is the most correct interpretation, especially within this school’s doctrine of the Dharma.

The retribution [of the three bodies] is without difference or distinction; they are a single source. It is not the case that various teachings differentiate between the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Furthermore, according to this Great Sūtra and the *Ekākṣaroṣṇīṣacakravartin-sūtra*, Śākyamuni, Vairocana, and Sarvārthasiddha are all merely alternative names.
Thus, one knows that the three bodies have no further distinct appellations; they are simply designations established by the interpretations of ancient masters.

Therefore, it should be known that there is no error in the application [of these terms] herein. As for the phrase "the light shines universally," it means that the *dharmadhātu* of eternal quiescence (*nitya-śānti-prabhā*) pervades all phenomena;

just as the clarity of a mirror pervades every image reflected therein, so too does this light pervade all. Regarding the phrase "all Tathāgatas," this refers to the mutual inclusion of the principal and the retinue (*pramukha-parivāra*).
Taking one as the principal, all others are the retinue; the retinue is not separate from the principal. —From the *Puxian* (Samantabhadra) chapter.
The Venerable [Śāriputra] of the Ocean-like Assembly is the Honored Jewel among the Saṅgha; the Two Sages are the Honored Ones among the Bodhisattvas of the Ocean-like Assembly.
Furthermore, looking toward those who are able to take refuge, it is indicated that the Bodhisattvas of the Ocean-like Assembly are one's own Honored Ones.

Later, when the two sages and the number of bodhisattvas—exceeding the dust motes of the lands—are correlated, there are several hundred whose names are recorded in the sutras; [the text] specifically refers to them.
There is indeed a profound reason for the two sages; the two sages and the Honored One together constitute the Three Sages, entrusted to symbolize the Dharma, not in vain.
Now, based on the contemplation of the perfect fusion of the Three Sages, I shall briefly manifest two gates: first, clarifying the symbolism through mutual correspondence;

second, revealing the perfection through mutual integration. Regarding the first, there are two parts: the two sages represent the cause, while Vairocana represents the fruit. The fruit transcends words.
Now, let us briefly discuss two causes; if one awakens to the profound subtlety of these two causes, one will perceive the deep and wondrous ocean of fruition.
The two sages provide three brief pairs: first, the pair of the "one who can believe" and the "object of belief.

To speak of the one who can believe and the object of belief as being within the cause refers to Samantabhadra representing the object of belief—the Dharma-realm, which is the Tathāgatagarbha while still entangled in defilements—therefore, it is the *Tattvārtha-sūtra*.

If it is said that all sentient beings are the Tathāgatagarbha because the self-substance of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva pervades everywhere, then the intent behind [the statement] that at the first assembly he immediately entered the *Tathāgatagarbha-samādhi* lies herein. Mañjuśrī represents the mind capable of faith;
as the *Buddhanāma-sūtra* states, "All Buddhas have resolved their minds toward enlightenment because of Mañjuśrī. Thus, when Sudhana first...
Because one sees the arousal of the great resolve (*mahācitta*), the Sūtra says: "It gives birth to all bodhisattvas without rest.
Second, regarding the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-caryā*) in contrast to Samantabhadra: this represents the myriad practices that have been initiated.

Since the five cycles of cause and effect throughout the preceding and following sūtra texts are all the practices of Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī is the understanding that initiates them, while Maitreya says: "You have now been able to see all spiritual friends."

Hearing that the entry into the gates of liberation through the bodhisattva practices is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of Mañjuśrī, and that he is the constant teacher of all bodhisattvas;

and that the three wisdoms and the principle correspond to Samantabhadra as the representation of the realized *dharmadhātu*, which is the *tathāgatagarbha* free from entanglements, such that Sudhana enters his body;
and that a single hair-pore is vast and immeasurable—this is [the teaching of] non-duality.
Regarding the "limit" (anta), it is so called because it refers to the *dharmatā*. Thus, a sutra says: "The physical marks of Samantabhadra are like empty space.
Furthermore, the statement that one attains the *jñānapāramitā* upon seeing Samantabhadra clarifies that wisdom is generated based on principle (*tattva*).

Mañjuśrī symbolizes the great wisdom that realizes [this], while the Buddha whom he serves is named Acalajñāna (Immovable Wisdom). This is because [Mañjuśrī] is eternally the mother of immeasurable Buddhas.
Because the teachings on the Dharma in the various sūtras predominantly manifest the essential intent of Prajñā, Sudhana only encounters Samantabhadra after having seen Mañjuśrī twice;
this demonstrates that only one who possesses wisdom is able to realize the principle.

For this reason, the ancient masters inscribed the verse following [the encounter with] Mañjuśrī as "Wisdom-illumination is the non-dual aspect. As for "not attending to the body," it is because both mind and objects have perished.
Mañjuśrī’s wisdom of provisional and ultimate reality realizes the principle of Samantabhadra’s essence and function.

Regarding this single gate, the ancient masters personally questioned the Tripiṭaka Master, who replied that although there are scriptural explanations for it, they have not yet been transmitted to this land.

Furthermore, this gate also symbolizes the principle of meditative concentration and wisdom, for the principle is fundamentally quiescent; thus, wisdom is itself insight. It also symbolizes the essence and function, wherein the principle of Samantabhadra is quiescent.

Because the essence of the mind is taken as Mañjuśrī and the illumination of wisdom is taken as the Great Function, these two aspects are fused and revealed. Regarding the "Perfect" (*yuan*), there are also two parts:
first, clarifying that the Dharma-gates of the two sages are each individually perfect and fused; second, clarifying that the Dharma-gates of the two sages are mutually perfect and fused.
In the first part, it is said that Mañjuśrī must rely upon faith (*śraddhā*) before he can achieve understanding (*prajñā*); if there is understanding but no faith, [understanding cannot arise].

Because false views increase, there is faith without understanding; because ignorance grows, even when faith and understanding are genuine, one only then realizes the original source and achieves ultimate wisdom.
When reflecting back, it is no different from the initial mind; at the very moment the first aspiration is made, one attains perfect enlightenment.
Furthermore, because the wisdom of the preceding skillful means does not depart from the essence, the subsequent Mañjuśrī is named "Wisdom" that illuminates the non-dual nature.
Because illumination and faith are not different from wisdom, one extends the right hand from the formless body. Thus, the three matters of Mañjuśrī are interpenetrating;
following this, the three matters of Samantabhadra are mutually integrated within their own characteristics.

If principle were without practice, principle would ultimately never be manifested. Practice arises based on the essence, and practice must accord with the essence; through practice one realizes principle, yet principle is without practice.

The external reason is that because practice is manifested through principle and there is no practice outside of principle, according to the principle realized, there is no aspect of practice that is not fully possessed;
thus, realizing one thing is to realize all things.

Furthermore, the dharma-gate attained by Samantabhadra within a single pore exceeds what was previously described by unspeakably many times, and because this is the function of the very essence itself, it is the dharma within a pore.

The gate of dependent origination is inexhaustible; thus, the three matters of Samantabhadra interpenetrate one another in infinite layers. Second, as for the mutual integration of the dharma-gates of the two sages:

this means that one must rely upon faith to know the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). If there is no faith, the dharma-realm cannot be known; if there is faith, yet it is not true faith, then it is false.
Therefore, subject and object are non-dual. Without faith, one’s own mind is already the Tathāgata.

Because the treasury [of the Dharma] is not for those who are not bodhisattvas, one must rely on understanding (*jñāna*) in order to be able to give rise to practice; thus it is called "giving rise to practice through understanding.
When practice does not differ from understanding, then understanding and practice are not two.

Furthermore, because wisdom is the function of principle and principle is the essence that constitutes wisdom, when wisdom returns to illuminate principle and wisdom merges with principle, it is then called "true wisdom" (*bhūta-jñāna*). Thus, principle and wisdom are non-dual. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
There is no suchness outside of wisdom that can realize suchness, nor is there a suchness outside of wisdom that can be entered by wisdom.

Furthermore, the quiescence of the dharma-realm is called *śamatha* (calm abiding); its constant illumination within that quiescence is called *vipaśyanā* (insight). When insight reaches its ultimate limit and perfectly accords with quiescence, then concentration and wisdom are non-dual.
Moreover, the function of the essence itself is called wisdom, and the essence of that very function is called principle (*li*).
Since essence and function are non-dual, the three matters of Mañjuśrī are interpenetrating and profound, while the three matters of Samantabhadra are mutually inclusive and multilayered.
Only when these two are neither identical nor different can they be called the conduct of Samantabhadra’s Indra-net.

Therefore, the "Chapter on the Conduct of Samantabhadra" and the preceding and following scriptural passages extensively reveal the perfect fusion of phenomena and principle as the conduct of Samantabhadra.
Practicing deeds that are not solitary is called the conduct of Samantabhadra; it is as stated in the Mañjuśrī-sahasrabhojana-sūtra:

"At that time, among the assembly, all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas and all sentient beings together practiced the vows and conduct of Samantabhadra and Mañjuśrī, and realized entry into the ten great compassionate Buddha-minds of Vairocana Tathāgata. This also represents the two sages.
Question: Since the two sages are mutually integrated, why is this not called the practice of Mañjuśrī?
Answer: Because wisdom is subsumed under principle, which is the single True Dharma-realm; thus, by citing one, the whole is fully encompassed. Second, as for Vairocana being the fruit:
since the dharma-gates of the two sages are integrated, Samantabhadra’s causes are perfected; being free from marks and transcending words, he merges into the fruit.
The ocean is called Vairocana because its light shines everywhere through the realization of exclusive correspondence;
therefore, the verses praising the Buddha’s virtues following the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra at the end of the "Dharmadhātu-parivarta" manifest the characteristics of the fruit (*phala-lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, at the beginning of the chapter, the Tathāgata himself enters samādhi and manifests signs without speaking, signifying that the realized state transcends words, while Samantabhadra then opens [the teaching].
The emission of light to cause awakening signifies that the capacity for realization transcends words; it is precisely this meaning that Mañjuśrī elucidates.

Nevertheless, the aforementioned principles, such as the principle of wisdom (*li*), are not separate from the mind; there is no distinction among mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are non-dual.

If one can understand this within the mind, then in every thought-moment the cause is perfected and in every thought-moment the fruit is fulfilled. As the "Chapter on Manifestation" states: "O Bodhi..."
The practitioner should know that because the Buddha always attains perfect enlightenment within every moment of one’s own mind, there is no distinction between the one and the many;
do not look outward, and do not be obstructed by verbal expressions.

If one can accord with this contemplative practice, then upon touching objects and facing phenomena, one will constantly see the Three Sages and all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions; for the one is identical to the all, and thus the mind [is realized].
Because the objective realm is non-dual, by practicing in reliance upon this, one may not achieve success in a single lifetime, but it will certainly be perfected within three lifetimes.
