That which is accomplished through virtuous conduct is also the fruit of the gate of "attaining the fruit without abandoning the cause"; it is the functional utility of that fruit.
Furthermore, this marks the ultimate conclusion of the forty-fascicle [text], comprehensively encompassing all profound and subtle mysteries.
Regarding the subsequent section on the Western Regions (*Xiyu*), the following provides a brief summary that encompasses the broad details of the text, which is divided into three parts:

First, it cites verses from the Western Regions tradition concerning this sutra as the "Praise of Vows and Conduct" (*Xingyuan Zan*); thus, it is not a mere hymn of praise (*zanybai*), though previous translations, being unaware that it was a sutra, referred to it as a "laudatory text.
Second, starting with "Now," the reasoning is detailed and confirmed. Finally, starting with "Furthermore, one sutra," the meaning is explained.

The reason why it is said that the master of this single sutra is Samantabhadra is that Samantabhadra is the essence of the Dharma-realm (the meaning of which is explained in the section on "Homage").
Since the sutra exclusively elucidates the Dharma-realm, regarding the first assembly and so forth: the first assembly is the Bodhimanda;
it has three names in total. In terms of its location, it is called the "Bodhimanda Assembly"; in terms of the person, it is the "Samantabhadra Bodhisattva [Assembly]."
The Assembly on the Names of the Dharma-agreements for What is Trusted as Cause and Effect, with Samantabhadra as the Principal:

This assembly brings forth Vairocana’s cultivation of causes throughout vast eons to purify the ocean of lands, so that sentient beings may believe and accept it, knowing that all possess the capacity and that practice will necessarily accord with reality;
thus it represents what the Buddha has taught as being exactly as he realized, and it is spoken at the place where enlightenment was attained.
The Sūtra states that only through the practice of Samantabhadra can one realize and enter [this state]; therefore, in this assembly, Samantabhadra is the principal figure.

The Commentary states that "reaching the ultimate" is also equivalent [to this], meaning that when Sudhana sought spiritual friends and traversed all stages, reaching finally the "Gate of the Perfection of Causes," it was likewise taught by Samantabhadra.
The Commentary’s mention of the "five cycles" and so forth clarifies the Great Sūtra.

The first part consists of five cycles of cause and effect. In the first assembly, there are six chapters and eleven fascicles of sutra titled *The Cause and Effect of What is Trusted*, comprising the "Chapter on the Formation of the World," the "Chapter on the Flower Treasury World," and the "Chapter on Vairocana.
These clarify the excellence of the fruition; because they clarify the causal practices of the past, they constitute that which is trusted. The second [part] begins from the second assembly.
From the seventh assembly, the "Chapter on the Merits of the Light of the Minor Marks," there are twenty-nine chapters in thirty-seven fascicles.
Twenty-six chapters are titled "Discriminating the Causes and Effects"; the final three chapters of the "Chapter on the Buddha’s Inconceivable Dharmas" clarify the effects.
Because the causes are not fully encompassed throughout the six assemblies, it is named "Discriminating Causes and Effects. First...

The third is the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Conduct," the latter part of which consists of two chapters in four fascicles titled "Equality of Cause and Effect" and "Manifestation of Samantabhadra’s Conduct.
The former is the cause, and the latter is the fruit; this cause is the cause that does not abandon the attainment of the fruit.

This cause-and-fruit relationship is the fruit of the Great Function of Nature-Arising (xingqi). Because the fruit encompasses the ocean of causes and the fruit penetrates to the source of the causes, it is called "equality. Fourthly... [end of fragment].
The eighth assembly, the first chapter, consists of seven fascicles of scripture titled *The Causes and Effects of Accomplishing Practice*.
It encompasses the five stages of practice collectively termed "causes," while the manifestation of the eight phases of appearance is termed the "fruit.

Because it causes those stages to subside and suddenly reveals the dharmas of practice, its two hundred questions flow like a rushing river and its two thousand responses are written like pouring from a vessel; both clarify the universally integrated practices of Samantabhadra.

Therefore, it is named "The Fifth: Accomplishing Practice. Because the ninth assembly contains one chapter consisting of twenty-one fascicles—namely, the present forty-fascicle work—the general title is *Zhengru Yin-guo* (Entering into Cause and Effect).
It first clarifies the great function of the Buddha-fruit, which is the entry into the fruit;
subsequently, it clarifies the benefits obtained by Bodhisattvas, which is the entry into the cause. Whether gradual or sudden, whether cause or fruit, [it is all contained herein].
Because all have realized and entered [this state], it is now said that the causes are all the practices of Samantabhadra and the fruits are all accomplished by the practices of Samantabhadra;
this clarifies the mutual inclusion of cause and fruit, referring both to the stage prior to the position and to the position itself.

The commentary states, "attaining the fruit without abandoning [the cause]," etc., which clarifies the cause within the fruit—that is, the Samantabhadra of the stage subsequent to the position. The statement, "furthermore, these are the forty," etc., [is as follows].
This means that while the preceding section generally indicated the entire great treatise across five cycles, this subsequent portion refers only to the present chapter.
△ Second, regarding the translators: from ancient times to the present, there have been three translations in total.

△ The first was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Buddhabhadra (whose name means "Awakened Wisdom" in the language of Tang) during the Jin dynasty; he produced a single fascicle in which five characters form a verse.
The second part, the translation of the text, has three sections: first, a general indication of the three translations; second, a reconciliation of the ancient and the present;
third, a specific explanation of the present sutra. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, a general indication, followed by a specific listing.
Regarding the phrase "First, the Jin Dynasty," this refers to the period of the Eastern Jin. "Buddhabhadra" means "Jue Xian" (Awakened Virtue) in Chinese. Ancient... [text fragment ends].
It is said that the Buddha-bhadra was a native of Northern India who became an orphan at the age of five. He entered the monastic order at seventeen;

in a single day of recitation and study, he could match what others took a month to achieve. After receiving full ordination, he applied himself with diligent effort to his practice, becoming widely learned in the various sūtras and attaining mastery in many areas.
His deportment was simple and unadorned, differing from Chinese customs, yet his refined resonance was pure and far-reaching.
Possessing profound insight, he frequently engaged in discussions on the principles of the Dharma with Dharma Master Kumārajīva,
illuminating the subtle threads of the mysteries and offering many wondrous insights. Later, Meng Yi, the Interior Governor of Ying Commandery, and Chu Shudu, the Right Guard General,
along with over one hundred people including the śramaṇas Huiyan and Huiyi, requested that he translate the texts brought by Zhi Falin.
Among the twelve scriptures such as the *Avataṃsaka* that Xuanzang obtained, this scripture was translated into five-character verse;
therefore, it says "during the Jin dynasty," and so forth.
△ Second, during the reign of Emperor Daizong of the Great Tang, the Tripitaka Master of Great Eloquence and Orthodoxy translated one version in seven characters.
This completes the verse.
Regarding "the second, the Tang Emperor Daizong" and so forth: Daizong was the eighth emperor of the Tang dynasty.

"Great Debater of Correctness" (Dàbiànzhèng) is the title of this Tripiṭaka Master; Amoghavajra (Āmùqiéjiā)—translated here as "Not Empty" (Bùkōng)—served during the reigns of Emperors Xuanzong and Suzong.
Master Kongzong was an imperial preceptor for the three emperors. His original name was Zhizang; he was of the Brahmin caste from Northern India.
As his father passed away early, he was raised by his maternal uncle and thus followed his mother’s surname, Kang. At the age of ten, he accompanied his uncle to Wuwei and Taiyuan.
At thirteen, he entered the service of the National Preceptor Da Hongjiao, and at fifteen, he received the tonsure.

At twenty, he received full ordination; well-versed in all aspects of the Sarvāstivāda school and possessing profound mastery of the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*), he subsequently traveled throughout the Five Indias to study extensively both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings.
In the fifth year of the Tianbao era, he returned to the capital, where he propagated the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings on a vast scale.

Three emperors submitted with sincere devotion and personally received empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) from him. On the first day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Yongtai era of Emperor Daizong, by imperial decree, he was conferred the title of Great... [Dharmamitra].

The Master was specially promoted to the office of Minister of the Court of State Ceremonial (Honglu Qing) and titled the Great Master of Vast Wisdom (Da Guangzhi Sanzang). His imperial favors during the three reigns were many times greater than those of his peers.
The number of those he initiated through the *guanding* (consecration) rite exceeded hundreds of millions.

On the eleventh day of the sixth month in the ninth year of the Dali era, an imperial edict was issued appointing him to the rank of Kai-fu Yitong Sansi (Peer of the Court with the Rank of a Commandery Governor) and conferring upon him the title of Duke of Su, with a fief of three thousand households.
A disciple of the household, having observed that the Great Master was displeased by his congratulations, informed him, saying:

"The assembly of noble ones stands solemnly, extending their hands to offer consolation. The white moon is full; how can it be that at the time of my departure, you would further usurp titles and positions?

I have submitted a memorial earnestly requesting your resignation, but you did not comply. Consequently, I have submitted another memorial to decline the honor of 'Saint' (Sheng). For this reason, you now manifest illness, sitting with your legs crossed."
In his final years, he had reached seventy years of age and fifty-one years of *śrāmaṇera* ordination (*bhikṣu-lakṣa*).

Later, on the sixteenth day of the seventh month, the rites for cremation were performed at the stūpa site, with hundreds of millions of people participating in the act of sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).

The Master Gō saw that the original text contained verses numbering as many as the atoms in ten sets of three-thousand-great-thousandfold world-systems and chapters numbering as many as the atoms in one set of four-continent world-systems.
He asked: "Since these are names for things that have an end, why is it said here that they are inexhaustible?
Answer: According to the *Great Sutra Commentary* (*Dai-kyō-so*), there are ten categories in total, ranging from the narrowest to the broadest. The first is the abbreviated version (*ryaku-hon*).
The Sūtra consists of four versions: first, the present version in eighty fascicles and so forth, which is the "smaller" (xia) edition containing one hundred thousand verses and forty-eight chapters;
second, the "medium" (zhong) edition containing four hundred and ninety-eight thousand eight hundred verses and one thousand two hundred chapters;
third, the "larger" (shang) edition containing as many verses as there are atoms in ten trichiliocosms.
The *Five Chapters on the Universal Eye Sūtra*, equal in number to the atoms within one set of four continents, was upheld by Sāgaramegha;

even if one were to use ink in the volume of the great ocean and pens as numerous as Mount Sumeru, one could not record a single chapter of this Universal Eye Dharma-gate, nor a single gate within that chapter, nor a single dharma within that gate, nor a single meaning within that dharma, nor a single phrase within that meaning. Furthermore, within each phrase, it cannot be fully grasped.
How much less could one exhaustively describe even a small portion? It can only be sustained by the power of the dhāraṇīs of Bodhisattvas who have deeply entered the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This is as stated in the *Ṣaḍpāramitā-samādhi-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Sixfold Recitation):

"A world-system shaped like Mount Sumeru, pervading all of space yet contained within the tip of a hair, may be described through speech and sound without end, just as in the 'Inconceivable Dharma' chapter."
It is as if a single Buddha-body, by means of its supernormal powers, turns such various wheels of Dharma in all worlds;

no phenomenon can serve as a metaphor for this. Thus, throughout the entirety of the realm of empty space—in every location the size of a single hair-tip, and even in each and every emanated body—it is spoken in this same way, with every sound, syllable, phrase, and meaning.
The *Saptabuddhaka-sūtra* and other scriptures speak of seven different types of world-systems, such as those shaped like trees.

Since these world-systems differ, the faculties and categories of sentient beings within them also vary. Consequently, the Tathāgata manifests his body and establishes his teachings differently in each;
thus, it is impossible to definitively determine whether these manifestations are material or immaterial, verbal or non-verbal, and so forth—their varieties being immeasurable.

The eighth is the Sūtra on Principal and Retinue (*pramukha-parivāra-sūtra*). This refers to the teaching that although Vairocana’s speech pervades the entire Dharma-realm, he acts as both principal and retinue in relation to one another with all Buddhas.
The ninth is the Sūtra on the Retinue (*parivāra-sūtra*). Because the capacities of other vessels are each different, they cannot hear this universal discourse;
therefore, according to their respective teachings, they are led to enter this gate. These are all the superior skillful means (*upāya*) of this sūtra.
The *Nāma-gaṇa-sūtra* and the *Daśa-paripūrṇa-sūtra* refer to the total integration of all these aforementioned versions into a single, inexhaustible ocean of Mahāsūtras.
Within this, every single assembly, chapter, phrase, and word encompasses everything without limitation.
Nevertheless, while these ten categories constitute the *Avataṃsaka*, when compared to the preceding four categories, they are finite.
The phrase "limitless, universal vision, etc. refers to the inexhaustible; thus, it is called "inexhaustible, etc. as a collective name. Regarding the term *sūtra*:
in Sanskrit it is also called *sūtrānta*, *sūtra*, or *sūtraka*. In ancient translations, it was rendered as "Sutra of Accordance" (*qijing*).
"Accordance" (*qi*) means to accord with principle and to accord with the capacities of sentient beings; "sutra" (*jing*) means to string together, penetrate, and gather in for transformation.
A sūtra is that which accords with both the faculties [of sentient beings] and the principle; if it accords with the principle but does not accord with the faculties, it is not a sūtra.
Alternatively, even if the teaching is skillful and moves the hearts of people, if it does not accord with the ultimate truth, it is also not called a sūtra.

It must accord with the ultimate truth and harmonize with the hearts of people to be rightly called a "sūtra. As for the literal translation of the name, *sūtra* means "thread," for a thread is able to string together flowers.

Because it can sustain [the teachings], this region does not value the term for "thread" (*sūtra*) and thus retains the name for "warp" (*taṃtu*). In India, however, both the "warp" and the "loom-cloth" (*taṃtuka*) are called *sūtra*;

furthermore, the rope used for weaving and the sacred teachings are both termed *sūtra*, which refers specifically to the sūtras themselves. Since they belong to the category of the "loom-cloth," they should properly be called "sacred teachings" (*āgama*).
This is why the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) translated by the Liang dynasty renders it as "sacred teaching. As that treatise states: "There is the Abhidharma... [and so forth].
The Dharma is not itself the holy teaching; rather, it is established as the holy teaching through its identity with the term *sūtra*.
Furthermore, because the ancients observed that both the Confucians and the Mohists of this land refer to their own texts as "classics" (*jing*), they borrowed that name for the holy teaching.

Thus, the term encompasses both meanings and accords with both traditions. By borrowing the meaning to assist the name, the character "Qie" (契) was added to distinguish it from the "Classics" used for secular seats.

This is most appropriate; although a single name is used to refer to four substances, the author of the *Vyākhyā* (the *Śāstra*) also harmonizes the four names with the five meanings of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
The "fountainhead" (*yǒngquán*) gives rise to meanings similar to those of the "well-rope" (*jǐngsuò*), for it possesses the sense of drawing up and leading forth.

Thus, it reveals a single meaning that properly belongs to the Holy Teaching (*āgama*), as it manifests both phenomena and principle (*dharmatā*). Furthermore, it serves as a "plumb line" (*shéngmò*) to demarcate and determine what is correct and what is erroneous.

The warp of a cord is able to hold the woof; the meaning is the same as that of the warp of a mat. A string for binding a garland is like a thread: the thread is able to pierce through flowers to form a garland.
Therefore, according to the Sanskrit intention, it simply clarifies that the "thread-warp" has the function of piercing and gathering.

Taken in its essential nature, it is called "thread"; taken by its functional application, it is translated as "warp. Apart from the thread, there is no separate entity of piercing and gathering; the piercer is the thread itself, which pierces through.
The warp is called the "sūtra" because it is the union of the subject and the object; thus it is termed a "sūtra.

Regarding the phrase "the chapter titles are that which is taken as the primary principle," this chapter signifies the intent of cultivation and realization to return to the source; therefore, "entering inconceivable liberation" and so forth constitute that which is taken as the primary principle.
Regarding the phrase "the general encompasses the particular," since these seven characters encompass both the extensive and the abbreviated, they are likewise present within the abbreviated version.
The meanings of these characters are preserved for this reason. △ The commentary [shū] summarizes the seven characters into four sections:
first, a general explanation of how the title is named; second, a comparative analysis of their opening and closing; third, a full elucidation of their categories of meaning;

fourth, the inconceivable nature of their expansion and contraction. △ Now, for the first section: the seven characters of the sutra’s title constitute seven primary meanings, which serve as its essential substance and formal characteristics.

"Extensive application" refers to the fruit of Buddhahood; "adornment" refers to the cause; "ornamentation" refers to the general characteristic; and the "sūtra" is that which provides the definitive expression.

Thus, both person and dharma are titled together, and both the metaphor and the reality are presented simultaneously; essence and function are unimpeded, and cause and effect are complete and perfect.
Therefore, no inexhaustible dharma-gate lies outside this inclusion. *Commentary:* First, regarding the seven characters of the sūtra title up to the phrase "does not lie outside this inclusion":
This collectively reveals the origin of the name. In Sanskrit, it is called *Mahāvaipulya-buddha* (or *Buddha*, which means "the Awakened One";

"Great" (*mahat*) is so called because its essence is vast and transcends all functions; it merely clarifies that the "greatness of arising characteristics" (*utpatti-lakṣaṇa-mahat*) is precisely the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) of the Dharma, and thus it specifically receives this designation.

Its meaning is "guiding and upholding" (*naya-dhāraṇa*): it simultaneously upholds both nature (*svabhāva*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) such that they are forever without diminution or loss; it guides the production of understanding in beings, and when established through illumination, wisdom becomes perfect. It is named "broad" (*vistīrṇa*) according to its function, with the meaning of "encompassing and pervasive" (*saṃgraha-vyāpti*):

"encompassing" means wide containment, and "pervasive" means wide extension. "Buddha" is named according to the fruition, with the meaning of "awakening and illuminating" (*bodhana-avabhāsana*): "awakening" refers to realizing the deep darkness of the great night, and "illumination" refers to...
"Lang" (Luminous) is named for its profound depth of all phenomena. "Hua" (Flower) is named by way of metaphor; its meaning is that it brings about the fruition [of practice] and adorns the body.

(As for bringing about fruition, the myriad practices are perfected; as for adorning the body, the multitude of virtues are complete within the person. "Yan" (Adornment) is named for its function. (The Commentary states: regarding the general characteristic, both that which can adorn and that which is adorned are called "adornment.

Its meaning is to provide the resources for the vast essence and function, and to embellish the Buddha-bodies of Truth and Response. "Jing" (Sutra) is named for its capacity to express; its meaning is to encompass and maintain. (It maintains the nature...)

The meaning of "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*) encompasses sentient beings and returns them to the source, as explained in detail elsewhere. Therefore, the phrase "the human and the Dharma reach equality" clarifies that the names of the seven characters are perfectly complete.

As for the various ways titles are established in the various sutras—whether they are named after a person or after a teaching—there are distinctions such as being requested by a person or expounded by one.

(1) Some derive their names from the person who requested [the teaching], such as the *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* (The Questions of the Brahma Heaven Suvikrāntavikramī). (2) Others derive their names from the person who expounds [the teaching].

There are four ways in which names are established: (1) by way of the name [of the teaching] itself, such as the *Akṣayamati-nirdeśa-sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*; (2) by way of the person for whom it was taught, such as the *Sudāna-sūtra* and the *Rājñaḥ-utpanna-sūtra*; (3) by way of the person who spoke it, such as the *Suvarṇavarṇa-avadāna*;

and (4) by way of the distinction between the Dharma, the dharmas, and similes—wherein "simile" refers to works such as the *Mahāmegha-sūtra* and the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra*, while "Dharma" has many varieties which will be explained below. Furthermore, there are those named by way of essence (*tattva*), such as the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;

by way of function (*vṛtti*), such as the [sūtras on] supernormal powers; by way of fruit (*phala*), such as the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*; or by way of cause (*hetu*), where "causal practice" includes the *Samyak-gaurava-sūtra* and "the stage of the cause" includes the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*.
They alternate between being combined and single, their categories being numerous and extensive. The single [teachings] can be understood directly; the combined [teachings] consist of four pairs:
first, dharma and parable, such as the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*; second, person and dharma, such as the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*;
third, essence and function, such as the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-saṃgraha-sūtra*; and fourth, cause and fruit, such as the *Anupūrva-sarvajña-jñāna-guṇa-saṃbhāra-sūtra*.

Regarding the *sūtras* and so forth, even if there were names that were not entirely missing, they would not exceed a single pair; however, since this present *sūtra* fully possesses all such [elements] as mentioned above, it is complete and exhaustive.
As for the statement that "person and dharma are titled together," "Great, Vast, and Broad" refers to the Dharma, while "Buddha-Flower-Adornment" refers to the person.
When the metaphor and the dharma are raised together, "Flower" is the metaphor, and all the rest are the dharma. This is the essence.

"Utilizing the unimpeded" refers to the Great Body (Mahākāya); "vast application" refers to its function. "The perfection of cause and fruit" refers to the Buddha-fruit; "flowers" refer to the causes.
Therefore, it concludes by stating that the inexhaustible Dharma-gate is not apart from this subsumption.

△ The second section of the Commentary, "Discriminating the Openings and Closings," consists of ten matters in five pairs. △ First, the Sūtra is the means of expression (*vyañjana*), while the preceding six [categories] are the expressed objects (*artha*).

1. "Explanation" (*vyākhyā*) refers to the pair of teaching (*śāsana*) and meaning (*artha*); 2. "Two Adornments" (*dvaya-vyūha*) refers to the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), while the aforementioned five [points] refer to the specific characteristics (*viśeṣa-lakṹ�aṇa*);

this constitutes the pair of the general and the specific; 3. "Flower" (*puṣpa*) refers to the adornment (*vyūha*), while the aforementioned four [points] refer to that which is adorned (*vyūhya*); this constitutes the pair of the adorning agent and the object adorned; 4.

"Buddha" refers to the person who realizes (*pramātṛ-pudgala*), while "Mahāvaipulya" refers to the dharma realized (*prameya-dharma*); this constitutes the pair of the person and the dharma; 5. As for "Vaipulya" (Extensive):...

"Function (*yòng*) is the manifestation, while the Great Square (*dàfāng*) is the essence; thus, essence and function are one. The character 'Square' (*fāng*) has two functions. △ Third, "Fully Manifesting the Categories of Meaning":
Each of the seven characters possesses ten meanings. ○ Regarding the *Commentary* (Chāo): "Third, 'Fully Manifesting the Categories of Meaning':
each of the seven characters has ten meanings" means that the Great (*Dà*) has ten meanings, the Square (*Fāng*) has ten meanings, and so forth; furthermore, regarding the seven characters—
Within each [of these], there are seven characters each, which signify: "Great" (大) means that all seven characters are great; "Square" (方) means that all seven characters are square;
and the seven characters constitute seven sections of explanation. The Commentary (Sū): First, the ten meanings of the character "Great" (大): 1. The Greatness of Essence (體大):
Whether as nature (性) or as characteristic (相), it is identical to the true nature (真性) and is eternally pervasive. 2. The Greatness of Characteristic (相大).

1. The Greatness of Essential Virtues (*svabhāva-guṇa*): Because the virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges pervade the essence. 2. The Greatness of Activity (*karma*): Because the three functions and great deeds are universally pervasive, just as the essence encompasses all. 3. The Greatness of Fruition (*phala*):
Because wisdom and the severance of afflictions encompass both the primary and secondary realms throughout the entire *dharmadhātu*.

4. The Greatness of Causes (*hetu*): Because the cultivation of virtues that accord with the nature proceeds without fail. 5. The Greatness of Wisdom (*jñāna*): This refers to great wisdom acting as the sovereign, directing the myriad practices to adorn the *dharmakāya*.
Therefore, the seventh is the greatness of the teaching, for every single word and phrase connects to the ten directions and accords with the *dharmatā*.

The eighth is the greatness of the principle, for the seven aforementioned [greatnesses] correspond in sequence to these seven characters, and no phenomenon is not elucidated as it exhausts the source of all phenomena.

The ninth is the greatness of the object, for all inexhaustible sentient beings serve as the objective conditions (*ālambana*). The tenth is the greatness of activity, for it extends through the three periods of time.
Because this Dharma is constantly used to benefit all sentient beings, the seven characters above are all termed "Great" (大). [From] *The Commentary* (鈔):

Regarding the first of the ten meanings of "Great," the single character "Great" refers to the title of the Sūtra. As for "Greatness of Essence" (一體大), whether in terms of characteristics (相) or nature (性), they are all identical to the true nature (眞性) and are eternally pervasive.
In the phrase above, the character "nature" (性) refers to the nature of the lack of nature (無性) of all dharmas. Below...

The phrase "the nature of words is the nature of original enlightenment" means that while the preceding phrase [relates to] the relative opposition between nature (*dharmatā*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), thereby clarifying the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional, the subsequent phrase identifies true nature as the supreme truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Therefore, it subsumes both nature and characteristics entirely within true nature, which is eternal and pervasive. This is like a mirror reflecting images or empty space being identical to luminosity; thus, it is explained by way of its eternity and pervasiveness.

Regarding "Great and Constant" (*mahānitya*), the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "That which is called 'Great' is termed 'Constant'. This clarifies that the essence of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is immutable;
it is called "Great" because it is the most preeminent among all things, just as one is called "great" for being the eldest.

There is not a single dharma that precedes it; only this [Dharma-realm] is prior to all dharmas. Thus, in the explanation of its name and meaning, it says: "As for 'Constant,' it is vertically without beginning; as for 'Pervasive'..."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* further states that its nature is as vast and expansive as empty space; this clarifies that because its substance (*tī*) is all-pervasive, it is called "Great" (*mahat*).
In the explanation of the meaning of the name, it is said that "pervasive" means it extends horizontally across all things without exception.

Regarding the second [of the two meanings], the character "constant" (*heng*) refers to the fact that the nature-virtues (*xingde*), as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, pervade the substance. As for the former [meaning], it does not speak of the existence or destruction of the characteristics (*xiang*) of those virtues.
When [the attributes] are merged and indistinguishable, they are entirely identical to the essence and pervade it;
this does not destroy the characteristic of being boundless, as they are distributed throughout the essence, and thus differs from the former case. Therefore, the Seventh Patriarch said:

"The essence inherently possesses merits as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, just as pure gold inherently possesses a thousand kinds of vessels, and just as a *maṇi* jewel inherently possesses a thousand varieties."

The myriad forms that are not of the nature of form are not established by being produced, nor are they identical when confronted, because at the time of their formation, not a single atom of a dharma enters from without.
Among the three [aspects], this refers to the character "Guang" (廣), meaning "universal," "all-pervasive," and "encompassing.
This is precisely the aforementioned characteristic of being boundless; because it pervades the substance such that each and every instance is identical to the substance, it is thus established.
The great function is such that each and every one can encompass and pervade: entering all from within one constitutes pervasion; entering one from within all constitutes encompassment.
These interpenetrate and intersect, mutually unobstructed, in layers upon layers without end. "Zhou" (周) means pervasive; "Pu" (普) means universally encompassing.
Within these four [meanings], the character "Fo" (佛) arises because one attains the three greatnesses (*trisāra*); thus, one is named a Buddha. [This concludes the section on] afflictions.
The wisdom of fundamental emptiness fundamentally reveals that both self and other are thus, pervading the entire dharma-realm; therefore, one attains perfect enlightenment.

Seeing that others have all attained it is as the verse says: "Bodhi and the severance of [delusion] are both called bodhi; the teaching of wisdom and the locus of wisdom—both are called prajñā. This carries the same meaning.
However, because it has not yet encompassed both self and other, as well as the support (the body) and the supported (the environment), [it is not yet complete].

This refers to what was clarified in the six phrases concerning the non-obstruction between body and lands in the preceding introduction. Within the fifth [phrase], the character "Flower" (*hua*) signifies conformity with the nature;
thus, one practice is all practices, as explained in the sixth section, "Proclaiming the Supreme Practices," within the "Causes and Conditions for the Arising of the Teaching.
Within the sixth [phrase], the character "Adornment" (*yan*): if there were no great wisdom, even if one were to cultivate ten thousand...
When practicing, one dwells in the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each practice; because they cannot be integrated [on their own], one must rely on wisdom to adorn the *dharmakāya*.
Adorning the *dharmakāya* is likened to applying colors to a painting: the myriad practices are the colors, and great wisdom is the painter.
As the "Chapter on the Inquiry into Wisdom" states: "Within the Buddha-dharma, wisdom is the foremost"; thus, wisdom is the true path. Furthermore—

Because conduct assists the Way, it is said to be the "master. Among the seven [aspects], the word "text" (*vyañjana*) refers to the various schools' means of expression, as these are not the expressed meaning itself;
thus, the text has limitations. In this school, however, the teaching is identical to the meaning; therefore, being the same as the Dharma-realm, each and every part is boundless.
Consequently, whenever a single assembly or a single stage concludes its exposition of the meaning, it is always universally extended by stating, "In the ten directions..."

It is likewise stated that because of this, there is a teaching so vast that even if one were to write it with ink as deep as the ocean, a single phrase would never be exhausted (the seven characters above are the title of the sutra).
In the eighth [section], it says that "there is no dharma that is not explained," meaning that its layered and inexhaustible nature certainly cannot be fully expressed in words;

yet within the gate of following appearances (*suxiangmen*), the teachings on the profound and the shallow are also explained in meticulous detail. In the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmiḥ*), the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*) are extensively elucidated.

The ten wholesome paths encompass the vehicles of humans and devas; the fourfold truths in the "Chapter on the Four Truths" and the ten stages of the fourfold truths in the fifth stage encompass the Śrāvaka vehicle;
the ten stages of the twelve links of dependent origination in the sixth stage encompass the Pratyekabuddha vehicle;
and the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* do not exceed the three types of verses, as seen in the "Appearance Chapter" of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
The two gates have thus fully explained these matters, which cannot be recounted in detail.

Among the nine meanings, the meaning of "the cause for the arising of the teaching" (教起因緣) extensively clarifies the capacities of those to be converted (*vineya*) who respond to the stimulus. The eighth is the meaning of the sutra’s "pervasive threading" (貫穿), and the ninth is the meaning of its "comprehensive sustaining" (攝持).
Regarding the tenth meaning, it is also like the ten causes: first, the nature of things (*dharmatā*); second, retribution; [and so forth].
This is explained in detail within the "Ten Benefits. △ The second section of the *Shu* (Commentary) explains the ten meanings of the character *fang* (method/standard).

Regarding "method" (*fang*): it means "Dharma" (*fa*). That is to say, the aforementioned ten great [principles] are the very essence of the standard and the sustainer; they are thus the ten Dharmas. ○ The second explanation of the ten meanings of the character *fang* in the *Chao* (Sub-commentary) states:
"Method" (*fang*) means "Dharma" (*fa*). As in the expression 'medical prescription' (*yaofang*), which refers to the method of medicine, one should say 'essence' (*ti*)."

Regarding the statement that the dharmas of characteristics, the dharmas of application, the dharmas of fruit, and even the dharmas of karma "take as their substance, norm, and sustenance," this means that all ten possess these two qualities.
The commentary explains the ten meanings of the character "vast" (*guang*) as follows: 1. The meaning of being vast and transcendent:
because it cannot be known through the deliberations of the mind-consciousness. 2. The meaning of being vast and surpassing: because there are no other dharmas capable of comparing with it.
1. It is "vast" in terms of its category (*jāti*), because it universally encompasses all phenomena of infinite diverse types; 2.

It is "vast" in terms of its meaning of knowledge (*jñāna*), because it is endowed with the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*) and destroys false views; 3. It is "vast" in terms of its meaning of destruction (*bhaṅga*), because it destroys all obstacles without exception; 4.

It is "vast" in terms of its meaning of remedy (*pratipakṣa*), because it fully comprises the boundless remedial dharmas; 5. It is "vast" in terms of its meaning of production (*utpāda*), because it can produce the [unconditioned] without limit.
1. Because the measure is vast; 2. Because it possesses the meaning of the eight broad virtues; 3. Because it is endowed with the two adornments and all meritorious qualities; 4.
Because it has the meaning of being a vast basis, as the verbal teachings are profuse and extensive to serve as a basis for sentient beings; 5.

Because it has the meaning of extensive exposition, proclaiming the vast and profound Dharma—thus, all seven characters are "vast. (This concludes the third section of the Commentary: the general characteristics of the ten meanings of the character "vast.")

To say that "extensive" (*viśāla*) means "much" is because it involves much and arises in great abundance, encompassing everything without exception. Thus, the ten preceding [stages] are all "much" in that they pervade all;
being "one" while encompassing all constitutes "great," and being "one" within that constitutes "extensive.

If one merely severs deluded conceptualization and the wisdom of the lower stages, this is not yet considered extensive; it must reach the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) for its illumination to be truly extensive.
Because even the wisdom of tranquil subtlety does not accord with the emotional mind, it is said to be "vastly severed.
Since the fundamental nature illuminates the essence as standing alone, it cannot be known by wisdom nor cognized by consciousness; thus, any conceptualization of the mind immediately errs.

Therefore, within the two [aspects], there is the character "fang" (square/direction). Although the characteristics of the boundless qualities of the nature are not separate from worldly phenomena, they nonetheless remain distinct from the world.
Regarding the statement that "there is not a single dharma capable of being compared to its vastness and transcendence," there are two intended meanings:

first, that the dharmas of the marks of virtue (de zhi xiang) surpass all worldly dharmas, and thus are "vast"; second, that the dharmas of the marks of virtue themselves all transcend the world, and thus are "vast.
What was referred to above as "dharmas" are the worldly dharmas that are surpassed; what is referred to below as "dharmas" are the virtues that perform the surpassing.
The objects manifested by a mani jewel are such that no external thing can compare with them;

as the Śrīmālā-sūtra says, "The wondrous form-body of the Tathāgata has nothing in the world equal to it. This refers to the physical marks (rūpa-lakṣaṇa) being unequaled in the world, which shares the same meaning as the above.
Among the three [aspects], this corresponds precisely to the "broad" character, just like the Buddha-realm in the various schools.
Within the realms (*dhātu*), there would otherwise be no sentient beings; furthermore, such points as "the cause does not encompass the fruit" have not yet been fully explained.
Now, by citing one [case], everything is necessarily encompassed, for all similar and dissimilar categories are completely subsumed; thus, it is "extensive.

Among these four, the word "Buddha" itself encompasses them through wisdom, because everything is wisdom. Therefore, the *Samantabhadracaryā-prasthāna-parivarta* (Chapter on the Manifestation) clarifies that the Buddha’s wisdom pervades all things.
Furthermore, when one attains Buddhahood within the bodies of sentient beings and perceives that those beings likewise attain it, this is called being fully endowed with wisdom.

Beyond this, nothing further is seen as "erroneous," which is termed the "shattering of false views. This means that by means of the wisdom of the totality of phenomena (*dharmas*), one knows the phenomena of total wisdom;
therefore, it is called "vast knowledge" (*prabhūtajñāna*). The five, six, and seven [stages] all share the meaning of the character "flower" (*puṣpa*), for they are three.
All are due to the five original [afflictions]; however, the Dharma of this school must encompass both the vertical and the horizontal.
The vertical refers to awakening to the fact that afflictions from time immemorial are fundamentally bodhi, thereby breaking the barrier of the past;

it means that this bodhi, from this day forward until the end of the future, will never again give rise to afflictions, thereby breaking the barriers of the present and the future. The horizontal refers to the ten directions and the six realms of existence.
The four modes of birth are fundamentally pure. Regarding this, the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* provides an analogy:
suppose there is a man who goes to a skilled physician and studies medicine for many years until his craft is perfected;

wishing to depart, the teacher says, "First, find for me a herb that is not a medicine, and once you have found it, you may go. This man searches throughout the world for a year, examining everything he sees.

All such grasses are capable of serving as medicine; thus, when [the student] failed to find what he sought, he returned and informed his teacher. The teacher said, "Your medical skill has been perfected; therefore, I tested you.

If one truly understands medicine, there is no herb that is not medicinal. Thus we know that if one truly understands the application of remedies to sever hindrances, there is no single state of mind that is not wisdom.
Therefore, it is said that [wisdom] encompasses all boundless [qualities]. Among the seven [types of wisdom], this is the appropriate one.
Knowing that [the first] eight are the "ornament" (*vyūha*) characters and the [remaining] ninety are the "sutra" (*sūtra*) characters, their meanings are likewise all easy to understand.

Furthermore, the ten from the beginning, the two in the middle, and the five, nine, and ten correspond to the four meanings in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, while the remaining six correspond to the six meanings in the *Mahāyānāvatāra-śāstra*.
Since that latter treatise explains the "Vaipulya" section among the twelve divisions of the scriptures, these words [of the commentary] appear here. △ Commentary.

The fourfold explanation of the ten meanings of the word "Buddha" consists of the ten Buddhas: first, the Buddha of the Dharma-realm; second, the Buddha of Original Nature; third, the Buddha of Nirvana;
fourth, the Buddha of Accordance with Desires; fifth, the Buddha of Attaining Perfect Enlightenment;

sixth, the Buddha of Vows; seventh, the Buddha of Samādhi; eighth, the Buddha of Karmic Retribution; ninth, the Buddha of Sustenance; and tenth, the Buddha of Mind. Thus, all seven characters [of the name] are "Buddha. (Commentary)
Fourth, the explanation of the ten meanings of the word "Buddha" (Fo) is now applied to the seven characters and further correlated with the Buddha-body itself.
There are naturally ten bodies; by distinguishing yet integrating them, the ten bodies of the three worlds are explained through their mutual participation.

Thus, the ten virtues of the Buddha-body are of one essence, eternally true and constant, and are named the Dharma-realm Buddha. That is to say, whether mind or environment, every dharma is the Buddha. This is it.
1. The Dharma-body (dharmakāya) corresponds to the character "Dà" (大). Because its fundamental nature is that of a Buddha, it is the body of wisdom;

as its profound and far-reaching insight is deep and remote, it is the Buddha of the sentient beings' original enlightenment (mūlapratibhāsa), the Buddha of the mind-nature of wisdom, which corresponds to the character "Fāng" (方).

2. The Nirvana-Buddha is the Transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya). Because its transformative functions are sovereign and free, and because it returns to quiescence once the transformation is complete, it is called the Nirvana-Buddha; this refers to the Response-body (nirmāṇakāya).

1. The Buddha of Transformation-Nirvāṇa: This refers to the four types of bodies that accord with the inclinations [of beings]; because they respond to stimuli and bring about realization, these two [categories] both correspond to the character "broad" (guǎng).
2. The Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment: This is the Bodhi-body; because enlightenment was achieved at the tree of the path, it corresponds to the character "Buddha" (fó).
3. The Buddha of Vow: This is the body of vows; because the vows pervade the entire Dharma-realm, it corresponds to the character "vow" (yuàn). 4. The Buddha of Samādhi.
This is the Body of Merit; merit is concentration, for by relying on the Great Samādhi, accumulated merit becomes perfected.
Thus, these two are both represented by the character "Hua" (Flower). Ninth, the Buddha of Karmic Retribution is the Body of Adornment;

the retributive merits of the marks and signs are subtle, wondrous, and inconceivable, serving to adorn the Dharma-body because they all arise from virtuous karma—this corresponds to the character "Yan" (Adornment). Tenth, the Buddha of Sustenance is...
Because the power sustains the body and its benefits flow forth without end, this corresponds to the "Ten Minds" (十心) of the *Sūtra of the Ten Stages*.

The Buddha is the Body of Majestic Power (*vibhūti-kāya*); all phenomena revolve according to the mind. This majestic power and dignified countenance outshine and surpass all else; thus, these seven characters collectively signify that the ten Buddhas are fused as one, serving as the Teacher for this assembly.
To show that all beings equally possess the realization that must be profound and identical [to the Buddha]. △ Commentary 5: Explanation.
The ten meanings of the character "flower" (*puṣpa*) are as follows: first, the meaning of containing the fruit, because it signifies that the Dharma-realm contains the inherent virtues;

second, the meaning of luminous purity, because fundamental wisdom is manifest and illuminates all things without exception; third, the meaning of subtlety and wonder, because each and every conditioned phenomenon is identical to the Dharma-realm;
fourth, the meaning of appropriateness and joy, because it accords with the capacities of sentient beings and causes them to rejoice; fifth, the meaning of inducing the fruit... [and so forth].

1. The meaning of being the cause for birth, because it gives rise to perfect enlightenment; 2. The meaning of being upright conduct, because the six forms of upright conduct are complete and lack nothing when conjoined with vows;

3. The meaning of being untainted, because each and every door of practice is conjoined with samādhi; 4. The meaning of skillful accomplishment, because the meritorious deeds one cultivates are accomplished through skillful means;
5. The meaning of fragrance, because the various virtues one upholds and maintains spread their scent far and wide.
Therefore, the ten meanings of "blooming" (kaifu) refer to the flourishing of various practices that cause the mind to open;

thus, these ten flowers correspond respectively to the preceding ten causes of the Buddhas, and they likewise do not depart from the seven characters within the title. In the fifth section of the *Chao*, the ten meanings of the character "flower" (hua) are explained.
There are two kinds of flowers: first, the flowers of plants and trees, which serve as a metaphor for the myriad practices (*sahasracaryā*) that evoke their fruits, or [the fruit itself]. Or with...
If the fruit is simultaneous with [the flower], it is metaphorically illustrated as being "perfectly integrated" (*yuanrong*), like the lotus flower and so forth;

if the fruit is not simultaneous with it, it is metaphorically illustrated as being "gradual and sequential" (*xingbu*), like the flowers of the peach or plum tree. The two metaphors of the golden and jade flowers illustrate the myriad virtues adorning the body, which are invariably simultaneous with the fruit.
These ten meanings correspond respectively to the preceding ten Buddhas to explain the seven characters. The first contains the reality (*shi*).

"Equality" (等) refers to the essence containing reality; "name containing real meaning" (名含實義) corresponds to the character *da* (大), which represents the Buddha of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and the purity of the two lights.
"Purity of light" (光淨) refers to the wisdom-light being pure; this corresponds to the character *fang* (方), representing the aforementioned Buddha of Original Nature (*prakṛti-buddha*).
"Subtlety" (微妙) refers to the subtle and wondrous outshining [of all things]; this is the meaning of "subtle and wondrous. It corresponds to... [the character] *wei* (微).

Regarding "the four kinds of joy, etc., toward the Buddha of Prior Nirvāṇa": this refers to the mind that takes joy in the objects of joy; it signifies "joy" (prāmodya) and corresponds to the aforementioned "Buddha who accords with pleasure.

These two [terms] correspond to the five characters beginning with "Extensive" (*viśāla*). Regarding "the six kinds of drawing forth the fruit, etc.": this refers to drawing forth the fruit as a recompense for the cause;

it signifies "drawing forth the fruit" (phalākṣepa) and corresponds to the character "Buddha. This corresponds to the aforementioned "Buddha who has attained Perfect Enlightenment. Sixth, "Elegant Features."
"Equal" (*sama*) means "exquisite and worthy of being beheld," which is the meaning of "handsome" (*sudarśana*).

In contrast to the aforementioned "Buddha of Vows," "sevenfold non-defilement" (*vimala*) means "untainted by dust or water," which is the meaning of "non-defiled. In contrast to the three preceding [types of] Buddhas, these two correspond to the character "Flower" (*puṣpa*).
"Eightfold skillful accomplishment" (*siddhi*) means "the skillful fulfillment of vows," which is the meaning of "skillful accomplishment"; this corresponds to "Adornment" (*alaṃkāra*).
Regarding "the character *fenfu* (fragrant) corresponds to the Buddha of Past Karmic Retribution": *fenfu liuxing* (flowing fragrance) is named *fenfu*;
this meaning corresponds to the character in the present sutra. Regarding "the character *kaifu* (blooming) corresponds to the Buddha of Sustaining Power":
*kaifu hantan* (the blooming calyx) is named *kaifu*; this corresponds to the Buddha of Mind above. That is to say, these seven characters above are collectively one among the ten flowers.

The five, nine, and ten [lotuses] are restricted to grasses and trees; the remainder apply to both types of flowers. △ Regarding the sixth section, the commentary explains the ten meanings of the character "ornament" (yán):
△ These ten flowers collectively adorn a single Buddha, and the fact that their modes of adornment differ constitutes the ten meanings.
Furthermore, these ten flowers respectively adorn the ten preceding Buddhas, which likewise constitutes the ten meanings. △ Therefore, the flowers are taken as the agents of adornment.

Because the ten Buddhas are accomplished through the adornment of the preceding Dharma-realm, "adornment" (*yan*) serves as the general characteristic. [From] the *Commentary* (Chao), section six, the explanation of the character "adornment" (*yan*) in its ten meanings is divided into three parts:

first, the heading; second, the explanation; and third, the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are two interpretations. The first interpretation concerns the ten *Avataṃsaka* [sūtras] as pertaining to a single Buddha;

the second interpretation concerns the ten *Avataṃsaka* [sūtras] as pertaining to the ten Buddhas. Regarding the first, the *Sub-commentary* (Shu) states: "This refers to the aforementioned ten *Avataṃsaka* [sūtras] being identical..."

"Excellence" (*śobhā*) and so forth refer as follows: first, the ten flowers are the ten perfections; second, "containing fruit" (*phalavat*) corresponds to the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*);

third, "radiant purity" (*vimalaprabhā*) corresponds to the perfection of knowledge (*jñāna-pāramitā*); fourth, "subtlety" (*sūkṣma*) corresponds to the perfection of skillful means (*upāya-pāramitā*); fifth, "delight" (*pramoda*) corresponds to the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*);

sixth, "inducing fruit" (*phalāvahā*) corresponds to the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*); seventh, "loveliness" (*abhirūpa*) corresponds to the perfection of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-pāramitā*); eighth, "stainlessness" (*nirmala*) corresponds to the perfection of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-pāramitā*); ninth, "skillfulness" (*kauśalya*)...

"Attainment" refers to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*); "fragrance" refers to the perfection of power (*bala-pāramitā*); and "blooming" refers to the perfection of diligence (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
These ten perfections collectively adorn a single Buddha; the same applies to the remaining nine. Furthermore, since the causes are perfected, the fruit is also perfectly realized.

How are they perfected? Through the dual flow of concentration and wisdom: in stillness there is no lack of illumination, and in movement one does not depart from tranquility—within a single thought-moment.
Because the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) are fulfilled through their mutual correspondence, the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:

"The arousal of the thought [of enlightenment] and its dedication is generosity; the extinction of delusions is morality; non-harming is patience; seeking the good without weariness is diligence; being immovable in the Path is meditation;

enduring the non-arising [of phenomena] is named wisdom (*prajñā*); dedication is skillful means (*upāya*); the aspiration for what is sought is power (*bala*); and that which cannot be crushed is resolve (*praṇidhāna*)."

Because the wisdom that thoroughly understands all these things is fully perfected, and because all virtues are suddenly adorned in a single thought-moment, there is no virtue that is not completely prepared upon reaching the stage of fruition.
Next, regarding the ten flowers adorning the ten Buddhas in sequence:

as mentioned above, these ten flowers correspond to the ten perfections (*pāramitās*). That is to say, through wealth, Dharma, and fearlessness, they gladden and delight sentient beings, thereby accomplishing adornment.

1. Adorning the body is the Buddha of Karmic Retribution; through the purity of the two types of precepts, one universally pervades all things and, by departing from faults according to the mind, accomplishes the Mind-born Body, which is the Buddha of Accordance with Joy.
2. Enduring and affirming the principles of truth accomplishes the Bodhi-body, which is the Buddha of Perfect Enlightenment.
3. Exerting oneself in the myriad practices accomplishes the Body of Majestic Power, which is the Buddha of Prior Resolve. 4. Concentration draws forth merits, accomplishing the Body of Blessedness.

Wisdom discerns principle and perfects the wisdom-body, which is the Buddha of original nature. The ten flowers successively adorn the aforementioned ten bodies;

these general and specific aspects are mutually unimpeded. Furthermore, there are ten meanings: first, adorning the fruit with the cause, thereby forming the person, for this Flower Adornment fruit is attained through causes;
second, adorning the cause with the fruit, so as to manifest its excellence after the fruit has been realized.
Because each and every causal practice is made boundless, this refers to the three characters "Buddha," "Flower," and "Adornment" (Fó Huá Yán).
Third, by using the person to adorn the Dharma to manifest its function: this means that the Buddha cultivated causes over vast eons in order to manifest the essence and function of the Dharma.
Fourth, by using the Dharma to adorn the person to manifest perfection: if one does not attain the essence and function of the Dharma, cause and effect cannot be perfectly wondrous.

Therefore, summarizing the above: first, the six characters [of *Mahāvaipulya*] are used to adorn the essence (*tattva*) so that its function may be all-pervasive; this is because function cannot be all-pervasive if it does not obtain the essence.
Second, the six characters are used to adorn the essence so that one may know the source;

for if there were no great function, the vastness of the essence’s source would not be manifested. Thus, the three characters *Mahāvaipulya* [are explained]. Seventh, the essence is used to adorn the marks (*lakṣaṇa*) so that their wondrousness may be known; as for the marks...
9. If there were a substantial entity (*tattva*), it would immediately enter into a state of mutual interpenetration;

thus, the eighth [point] uses characteristics to adorn the substance, for through the manifestation of the profound signlessness, the depth and mystery of the substance are revealed—this refers to the two characters "Great" (*da*) and "Square" (*fang*). 10. The ninth uses meaning to adorn the teaching, for it transcends words and thought;
this is because the referent (*vācya*) is inconceivable and the designating words (*vācaka*) are detached from them. 10. All functions mutually adorn one another through their harmonious integration.

Just as there is no way to exhaustively fathom stillness without dhyāna, and no way to deepen illumination without wisdom, so too within this mutual adornment (*parasparālaṃkāra*), there are four permutations (*catuṣkoṭi*) involving mutual support and mutual identity;
fearing prolixity, they are not set forth here. As stated in the aforementioned commentary, there are only three permutations:
namely, ten *puṣpavyūha* (flower-adornments) for one Buddha, ten *puṣpavyūha* successively adorning ten Buddhas, and ten Buddhas adorning ten *puṣpavyūha*.
Furthermore, ten Buddhas are mutually adorned within the first phrase; it is also possible for a single flower to adorn ten Buddhas to complete the four phrases, thereby forming the inexhaustible.
Thus, the phrase "using flowers as [the means]" is the conclusion.

As for the statement that they "adorn the prior dharma-realm," this means that while the dharma-realm inherently contains Buddha-wisdom, it is only through the adornment of practice and virtue that it becomes manifest.
The function of the Buddha. △ The commentary (*shū*) provides seven explanations for the ten meanings of the character *jīng* (經):
first, a gushing spring; second, giving birth; third, manifesting; fourth, a carpenter’s line; fifth, threading together;
sixth, upholding; seventh, constancy; eighth, the Dharma; ninth, a classic; tenth, a path. ○ The sub-commentary (*chāo*) provides seven explanations.
Within the ten meanings of the word "sūtra" (*sūtra*), there are two parts: first, the presentation; second, the explanation. Regarding the explanation of these ten meanings:
1. **Fountainhead**: It flows forth without ever being exhausted. 2. **Source of Birth**: It provides successive support for many. 3. **Manifestation**:

It reveals both phenomena and principle. 4. **Plumb Line**: It demarcates the correct from the deviant; just as wood becomes straight by following the line, so too does the mind become upright by following the teaching.
"Leaving behind the five perversions" means to penetrate the meaning of the nature and characteristics as they are taught;

"the six modes of gathering" means to gather those beings to be transformed back to the original source, preventing them from clinging to the six sense objects and wandering through the five realms of rebirth.
These two [meanings] are the explanations of the word *sūtra* (貫穿) found in the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*; thus, that treatise’s first fascicle states: "It is able to penetrate..."

It is called a *sūtra* because it is able to collect [the teachings]; for the holy teaching of the Buddha pierces through and gathers together the meanings that ought to be explained for the sake of those to be converted.
Alternatively, "piercing through" and "gathering together" apply both to what is spoken and to those to be converted:

piercing through the characteristics of the Dharma and gathering together those to be converted is the meaning here; or, piercing through those to be converted and gathering together what is spoken is the sense of "piercing through."
That "Mind-Flower" (*citta-puṣpa*) encompasses this essential meaning. Seventh, "Constant" (*nitya*) refers to the eternal norm of ten thousand ages;
eighth, "Dharma" (*dharma*) refers to the true track of a thousand petals. These two were expounded by Prince Zhaoming of the Liang Dynasty.
Master Gan interpreted these two meanings—"Dharma" and "Constant"—as the guiding lines for the gushing spring of truth; thus he said: "In the Dharma, one promotes the upright."

Using the straightening of a warped line against the carpenter’s square as a metaphor for the constant, and comparing it to drawing from a spring that never runs dry—this also constitutes a distinct intention.
As for the "nine canons," they signify correct principles free from deviation; as for the "ten paths," they are the paths for escaping death.
Within the ten [paths], the first four correspond to the four among the five meanings in the *Saṃyuktābhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra*, while the remaining ones are the residual knots.
The "Garland" (Mālā) [commentary] likewise explains the integration of five and six as being based on the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*;

the latter four [categories] rely on the etymological interpretation of this [text] to complete the ten meanings. △ Regarding the fourth section of the Commentary, "The Unfolding and Rolling Up are Inconceivable":
△ This means that, based upon the pure *dharmadhātu*, one first opens the two gates of principle (*li*) and wisdom (*zhi*). △ Next, principle opens into essence (*ti*) and function (*yong*).
The seven characters of the title of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—the Great Vaipulya Wisdom—which distinguish cause and effect, are first explained as the six "identities" (ji).

△ Next, these seven characters are further expanded to signify the Dharma-realm realized by this entire scripture as the "Great Vaipulya," and the universal conduct and vows that realize it as the "Buddha-Flower Adornment.
△ If one were to expand this even further, it constitutes the entirety of this one section.
Thus, the five cycles of cause and effect are all realized through the cause and effect of the *Buddhāvataṃsaka*, and all that is "Great Vaipulya" (Mahāvaipulya) arises from this.

△ Even to the point of being inexhaustible, it all originates from here. ○ In the fourth section of the *Commentary* (*Chao*), titled "The Inconceivable Nature of Unfolding and Rolling Up," there are four parts:
first, unfolding; second, rolling up; third, the unimpeded nature of both unfolding and rolling up; and fourth, concluding by returning to the title of the Sūtra. Part One: Unfolding.

Section Five: Unfolding [the Text]. First, unfolding the true realm (*dharmadhātu*) to reach the principle-intelligence (*prajñā*). Second, unfolding the principle to open up and unfold the intelligence down to the general title.
Third, unfolding this [section] below; unfolding the general title down to this fascicle. Fourth, if one further unfolds this fascicle down to the entire treatise.
Fifth, even further, unfolding the entire treatise down to the inexhaustible. △ The Commentary (*Sūtra*) encompasses the inexhaustible.
The Dharma-realm constitutes the nine assemblies. △ Furthermore, these nine assemblies are subsumed into this single scripture.
△ Furthermore, this scripture is subsumed to form the general title. △ Furthermore, the general title is subsumed to become the principle-wisdom (*prajñā-jñāna*).

Eighteen hundred plus two hundred and ten makes two thousand one hundred. These two thousand one hundred serve as antidotes for four types of sentient beings:

Those with excessive greed produce much defiled attachment toward objects; those with excessive hatred produce much resentment and anger toward objects; and those with excessive delusion produce much [ignorance] toward objects.

When sentient beings give rise to an upper-upper grade of greed toward an inferior or lower-grade object, it is called "excessive greed" (*bahurāga*);
when they give rise to a middle-grade greed toward a middle-grade object, it is called "equal-parted" (*sama-bhāga*);

and when they give rise to a lower-grade greed toward an upper-upper grade object, it is called "thin dust" (*tanu-rajas*). Hatred and delusion should be understood according to this same principle; thus, there are these four categories.
Each of the mental states consists of two thousand one hundred, totaling eight thousand four hundred.

namely, one hundred thousand is one *lakṣa*; one hundred *lakṣas* is one *koṭi*; and one *koṭi* times one *koṭi*... [is a *niyuta*].
One *ayuta* is the starting point; from here, the number doubles successively until it reaches one hundred and twenty names, at which point it is called an *aprameya-parivarta*.
One hundred and twenty *aprameya-parivartas* is called one *anabhilāpya-anabhilāpya-anabhilāpya*.
One hundred and twenty *anabhilāpya-parivartas* is called one *anabhilāpya-anabhilāpya-parivarta*. One hundred and twenty *anabhilāpya-anabhilāpya-parivartas* is called one *akṣaya*.
That which is called "unspeakable" (anabhilāpya) is itself multiplied by this same factor to constitute one "unspeakable-unspeakable" (anabhilāpyānabhilāpya).
What is here termed "unspeakable-unspeakable" corresponds to the one hundred and twenty-third numerical category;
in reality, it is simply a number that transcends verbal expression, and is thus named "unspeakable-unspeakable."
Regarding the term "kalpa" (劫), in Sanskrit it is called *kalpa*, which here means "differentiation of time. There are many types:

from a single year, month, day, or hour, they are collectively termed a kalpa; furthermore, five years with two intercalary months constitute one "pair," and reaching up to an infinite number of these is also called a kalpa;
likewise, one period of increase followed by one period of decrease is also called a kalpa, and twenty such periods of increase and decrease are also termed a kalpa.
A *kalpa* is also defined as twenty cycles each of formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness; this is called a fire-disaster *kalpa*.
Furthermore, seven fire-disasters followed by one water-disaster is also called a *kalpa*, and when seven water-disasters have occurred, it is called a wind-disaster *kalpa*.
Moreover, the three great *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* of a Bodhisattva’s practice are also called *kalpas*, specifically referred to as "rubbing stones."
Kalpas such as those defined by the shedding of a single drop of tears or the destruction of a mustard-seed city are all termed "kalpas. Here, citing a large number merely indicates a vast duration;
it is not fixed as to which specific type of kalpa is meant, for even if one were to pass through great kalpas, they could never be exhausted, as the world has no end.

△ Commentary 3: The Characteristics of the One Who Pays Homage (2-1 General Explanation).
All [acts] are performed with the pure karma of body, speech, and mind, constantly practicing reverence.
This means that the three karmas are all pervasive, constant, and uninterrupted. ○ Sub-commentary: Within the section on the characteristics of the one who pays homage, the Sūtra says "all."
Regarding "pure and so forth": "all" (*xi*) means every, universally, and completely; "by" (*yi*) means by means of. "Pure threefold action" (*qingjing san ye*) distinguishes it from defiled action;
that is, because the body is free from the three evils, speech is detached from the four transgressions, and the three mental actions are pure, it is called "pure and so forth.
Because of defiled action, one revolves through the evil realms; now, by means of this [pure action], it becomes the cause for attaining Buddhahood.

One must rely upon pure karma. Regarding those who revere the three types of action (*trikarma*), there is that which they represent; the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna differ in their respective representations.
As for the Mahāyāna’s reverence through the three types of action, it represents that the Buddha possesses three kinds of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

First, to manifest that the Great Teacher possesses the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣur-abhijñā*), because he can be seen through reverence by means of the body (*kāyakarma*). Second, to manifest that the Great Teacher possesses the supernormal power of the divine ear (*divyaśrotra-abhijñā*)... [text continues]

Regarding verbal action (*vākkarman*), it is because [the teacher] can be heard with respect; thus, three [actions] are for the purpose of manifesting that the Great Master possesses the supernormal power of knowing others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), since mental action (*manaskarman*) can be known through respect.
Second, in the *Kṣaṇika-śāstra* of the Hīnayāna, it is said that the teacher’s three actions are respected:

first, when one is in light and at a distance, bodily action (*kāyakarman*) is required for respect, as he is visible; second, when one is in darkness and nearby, verbal action is required for respect, as he... [can be heard].
Because they are heard, three [of the faculties] remain in darkness and are further distant; thus, one must rely on the mental action of reverence.

Since they are neither seen nor heard, the reverence of the three actions serves as the cause for attaining the three wheels within the fruit: the body attains the wheel of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-cakra*), speech attains the wheel of instruction (*anuśāsanī-cakra*), and the mind attains the wheel of telepathy (*cetaḥparyāya-cakra*).
△ Commentary 2: Specific Manifestation.
Before each and every Buddha, he manifests bodies as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields;
that is to say, he suddenly manifests many bodies before a single Buddha. ○ Sub-commentary: Before a single Buddha, he suddenly manifests many bodies.
The term "and so forth" refers to the fact that by relying on the two aforementioned powers, one is able to perceive many Buddhas within a single object and manifest many bodies within oneself.
At first glance, the scriptural text might suggest that if one manifests many bodies before each individual Buddha, then there appear to be many bodies and few Buddhas;
whereas if one pays homage to many Buddhas with each individual body, it would seem as though there are few bodies and many Buddhas.
According to its underlying principle, the *Śarīrabuddhasamatā-sūtra* intends to clarify the non-obstruction between the one and the many;

therefore, it alternately cites "body" and "Buddha" in terms of the one and the many. If we were to arrange these meanings in a systematic correspondence, there should be four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):

first, bowing with a single body to many Buddhas, which corresponds to the latter part of the sūtra’s text; second, bowing with many bodies to a single Buddha, which corresponds to the former part of the sūtra’s text; third, [bowing] with a single body...

Worshiping one Buddha is as described in the third of the ten successive modes of worship mentioned previously; worshiping many Buddhas with many bodies is as described in the tenth mode, the "Imperial Net" (Indra’s Net) worship.
Regarding the first and third phrases, other schools may also accommodate them, but the second and fourth phrases are elucidated exclusively in this *Avataṃsaka* [Sūtra].
As for the statement that the number of bodies and Buddhas is identical, the "Appearance of the Tathāgata" chapter (*Prādurbhāva-parivarta*) says: "Just as..."
When he comes to achieve perfect enlightenment, he enters the *samādhi* of the Wisdom of Excellent Awakening (*sujñāna*) by means of the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇopāya*).
Because awakening does not stagnate in quiescence, it is called "Excellent Awakening"; because that [awakening] is a single characteristic, it is employed as the means.

Having entered, within his single body of great perfect enlightenment, he manifests bodies equal in number to all sentient beings, abiding within those bodies. (Since the single characteristic is used as the means, every thing is a single characteristic; therefore, the one manifests as the many.)
Therefore, you should know that the body manifested by the Tathāgata is immeasurable;
because it is immeasurable, the body of the Tathāgata is said to be an immeasurable realm equal to the realm of all sentient beings. Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas should know this:
within a single pore of the Tathāgata’s body, there are as many bodies of Buddhas as there are sentient beings. Why is this?
For this reason, because the Tathāgata’s body of perfect enlightenment is ultimately without arising or ceasing, as it is in a single pore, so it is in all pores throughout the entire Dharma-realm;
one should know that there is not even the slightest place empty of the Buddha-body.
Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should know that in every thought-moment of their own minds, the Buddha is always present in his perfected state.
Why is it called Perfect Enlightenment? Because all Buddhas and Tathāgatas attain perfect enlightenment without departing from this mind.
Just as it is with one's own mind, so it is with the minds of all sentient beings; in them all, there is a Tathāgata who has attained equal and perfect enlightenment. The commentary states:

By citing that the Buddha-bodies are equal in number to the count of sentient beings, it serves as proof for the preceding point—that the body which performs the prostration is itself the object of worship.
Furthermore, since the Buddhas are equal in number to the total count of sentient beings, and since these Buddhas— possessing bodies equal in number to the beings dwelling within the realm of birth—
abide within the minds of those beings, and since a Buddha attains perfect enlightenment in every moment of thought, we know that before each Buddha there were originally many bodies,
and before each body there were originally many Buddhas. It is only because one clings to objects and deludes the mind that one fails to see them at all.
To perceive [the Buddha] through the Samādhi of Good Enlightenment is entry by way of the fruit;
to perceive him now through the contemplative practice of Samantabhadra is entry by way of the cause. Although the characteristics of cause and fruit differ, the realm entered is without distinction;
thus, the cause encompasses the ocean of the fruit, and the fruit reaches the source of the cause.
