Regarding "eloquence" (*pratibhāna*), there are four types in total: first, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), because one has thorough mastery over all phenomena;

second, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), because there is no obstruction regarding the principles that are explained; third, the unimpeded analytical knowledge of language (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*)...
By the power of wisdom, one universally accords with the differences in the mental activities of all sentient beings;
this is the unimpeded analytical knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*). This, moreover, has seven aspects:

first, instantaneous eloquence (*kṣipra-pratibhāna*), which means that within a single moment, one is able to universally accord with the faculties, natures, and inclinations—whether they prefer the extensive or the concise—of all sentient beings across the three vehicles and five vehicles. Second, swift eloquence (*tvara-pratibhāna*), which means...
1. Speech that is swift and fluent, without any hesitation or stammering; 2. Sublime eloquence like a cascading torrent, like pouring water from a high vessel; 3.
Eloquence free from error, meaning that every word and phrase accords with principle and suits the capacity of the listener, without the fault of negligence or mistake; 4.
Eloquence that is inexhaustible, because one can preach the sutras for a long duration without interruption; 5. Eloquence rich in flavor, such that all that is spoken...
The eloquent exposition of abundant meaning and flavor possesses five characteristics: first, it is profound like thunder; second, it is clear and heard from afar;
third, it is precise and easy to understand; fourth, it inspires reverence and affection in people's hearts; fifth, listeners never grow weary of it.
Seventh, it is the most supreme and wondrous eloquence in all the world, with nothing superior to it. Taken together, these seven qualities are termed "unimpeded eloquence."
The analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), or these seven types of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), are also derived from within the first three [of the four analytical knowledges].
However, when various sūtras and śāstras state that there are many kinds of eloquence, these are all successive elaborations based on specific meanings;

fundamentally, they do not exceed the four analytical knowledges. A Bodhisattva in the ninth stage fully attains these four analytical knowledges, though they may be attained to some degree prior to that.

This is not supreme. Only those who exhaustively investigate principles and fully comprehend all phenomena, illuminating them clearly without omission—such as the Buddha and Samantabhadra—may truly be called "exhaustively perfected in eloquence.
As for what the sutras call the "subtle and wondrous faculty of the tongue," it is as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*:

a tongue that eloquently articulates inexhaustible diction and eloquence; a tongue that elucidates the Mahāyāna aids to the Path;

a tongue that completely covers the empty space of the ten directions; a tongue that universally illumines all Buddha-lands; a tongue that causes all sentient beings to awaken to understanding; a tongue that causes all...
The Buddha’s tongue of joy subdues all tongues of demons and externalists;

it extinguishes all afflictions of birth and death and leads one to nirvana. If bodhisattvas accomplish this dharma, they shall attain the Tathāgata’s mark of a tongue that universally covers all lands.

If a karma is fixed or its retribution is not yet fixed but can be altered by encountering conditions, it may then be eliminated.

For example, if one has committed a grave evil that is certain to be experienced as retribution in this very life, yet that retribution is still alterable, then through repentance, the karma of superior goodness will certainly bring about a good retribution in this life as well.
However, because the power of the wholesome karma is strong, it supersedes the evil; thus, one does not undergo the evil retribution, precisely because the timing [of the retribution] was fixed.

Because they belong to the same moment, they can mutually exclude one another; since retribution is not fixed, a single lapse may lead to permanent deviation, resulting in never again receiving [the fruit].

Furthermore, in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong), repentance must be complete in both principle and phenomena, thereby attaining purity in a single moment. Moreover, there are three types of repentance for karma:

One does not enter the evil realms; one undergoes the three types of cessation to repent for and expiate karmic offenses, just as a lamp dispels darkness in a dark room—darkness cannot resist a lamp simply because it has existed for a long time. This refers to two or three matters; the third is the principle.

Furthermore, the repentance that eliminates offenses and the wisdom that severs afflictions differ in their categories of counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*); that is, repentance and offenses mutually suppress one another.
One must necessarily have an equal opponent in order to eliminate [defilements];

if an inferior wholesome mind confronts a superior unwholesome mind, they do not constitute an equal opponent because the stronger force first draws one away. Therefore, it is essential that a superior wholesome mind eliminates a superior unwholesome mind;

the same applies to the intermediate and inferior grades relative to each other. This is not the case when wisdom eradicates delusions; for instance, inferior wisdom can eradicate superior delusions, and superior [wisdom] [can eradicate inferior ones].
Wisdom abandons lower-level afflictions because coarse afflictions obstruct a shallow principle; thus, wisdom that reflects upon a shallow principle is used to eliminate them.

Subtle afflictions obstruct a profound principle, and there is no way to dispel or sever them except through superior wisdom. If one considers the prevention of unarisen transgressions, it is analogous to the abandonment of afflictions:
a lower-grade wholesome mind can prevent a higher-grade grave transgression, just as a lower-grade evil [mind] [can produce a grave one].
These are subtle and difficult to guard against; they require a superior degree of wholesome mind. Regarding the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*), the *Buddhanāmasūtra* states:
"Although the characteristics of these transgressions are immeasurably great, when described briefly, they do not exceed three:

Since these are the most excellent and wondrous matters for humans and devas, the sutras designate them as the "three obstacles.

Therefore, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas teach that one should perform repentance; once these three are extinguished, the six sense faculties, the ten unwholesome actions, and even the eighty-four thousand afflictions will all become completely pure.
Furthermore, it is said that these three obstacles rely upon one another, arising from the causes of mental affliction.
Because of afflictions (*kleśa*), one gives rise to evil karma; due to the causes and conditions of that evil karma, one obtains bitter fruits. Therefore, today I first repent of the afflictions.
These afflictions are censured in various ways by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble ones who have entered into the principle of reality.
I record these afflictions as my enemies, for they are able to sever the life-root of wisdom in sentient beings; thus, I also record them [as such].
One should regard these afflictions as bandits, for they are able to plunder the various wholesome dharmas of sentient beings;
one should likewise regard these afflictions as a torrential river, for they are able to sweep sentient beings away into the great ocean of suffering within birth and death;
and one should likewise regard these afflictions as fetters and shackles, for they are able to bind sentient beings within the prison of birth and death so that they cannot escape.
Because the six realms are interconnected and the four modes of birth are unceasing, evil karma is inexhaustible and the fruits of suffering do not cease;

one should know that these are all the faults and afflictions of *kleśa*. Next, repent of the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*). Generally speaking, the reason the retributions experienced in the six realms differ should be known to be the work of the power of karma.
Specifically, first repent of the three actions of the body, and second, repent of the four actions of the mouth.
As for the remaining obstacles, they are to be confessed in sequence: the three [physical] actions refer to killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct;
the four verbal actions refer to false speech, divisive speech, harsh speech, and frivolous speech; and the three mental actions refer to covetousness, malice, and wrong views.
These ten branches of the three types of karma have the power to induce retribution in this life; this is clearly stated in the teachings on the ten paths of unwholesome action.
If one does not repent and eliminate [these transgressions], the cycle of rebirth cannot be halted. As stated in the "Ten Stages Chapter" (Daśabhūmika-parivarta):
"The ten unwholesome karmic paths have the superior cause for rebirth in hell, the middling cause for rebirth as an animal, and the inferior cause for rebirth as a hungry ghost.

Among these, the sin of killing can cause sentient beings to fall into the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts; even if they are born among humans, they will obtain two [kinds of retribution]."
The retributions for [the sin of] stealing are twofold: first, a short lifespan; second, much illness. Furthermore, the sin of stealing causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms.
If they are born among humans, they obtain two kinds of retribution: first, poverty; second, being unable to exercise mastery over shared wealth.
The sin of sexual misconduct likewise causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If...
If one is born among humans, two kinds of retributive fruits are obtained: first, one’s wife will not be chaste; second, one will not obtain a retinue according to one’s wishes.
The sin of lying also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, two kinds of retributive fruits are obtained: first, they are constantly slandered; second, they are deceived by others. [The sin of] divisive speech...
The sin of [this] also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, their retinue will be estranged and separated; second, their kinsmen will be wicked and foul-mouthed. The sin of harsh speech also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, they constantly hear evil [words].
Regarding the second type of speech, excessive contention and the sin of frivolous talk also cause sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms;
even if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution: first, no one will believe or accept their words;
second, their speech will not be clear and intelligible. The sin of lustful desire also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; even if they are born among humans, they receive...
There are two kinds of retributive fruits: first, the mind is never satisfied; second, one has many desires and is never satiated.
The transgression of anger also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms. If they are born among humans, they obtain two kinds of retributive fruits:
first, they are constantly sought out by others for their faults; second, they are perpetually tormented and harmed by others.
The sin of wrong view also causes sentient beings to fall into the three evil realms; even if they are born among humans, they receive two kinds of retribution:
first, being born into a family of wrong views; second, having a mind that is deceitful and crooked.
Son of the Buddha, these ten unwholesome paths of action can produce such immeasurable and boundless masses of great suffering. Therefore, the Bodhisattva...
Thus one should reflect: "I shall distance myself from the ten unwholesome paths and take the ten wholesome paths as my garden of Dharma;
I shall delight in dwelling therein and likewise encourage others to dwell therein.
Since retribution is such as this, arising entirely from the influence of karma, if one wishes to avoid the fruits that are brought about, one must first sever the causes that produce them.
Therefore, one must perform repentance. Next, regarding the repentance for karmic retribution, it is said in general:

"When the time for karmic retribution arrives, there is no place—neither in the sky, nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering between the rocks of the mountains—where one can escape and avoid receiving the retribution;
only through the power of repentance can it be eliminated. Why is this so? Because when the five signs of decay appeared for Śakra Devānām-indra, he was filled with fear."
With a heart of utmost urgency, take refuge with sincerity in the Triple Gem; the five signs of decay will vanish, and you shall obtain an extension of your celestial lifespan.
It is the same for Śubhavyūha, with this distinction: first repent for the hells, next repent for the hungry ghosts, and finally repent for the animals.

Regarding the initial analysis of the hells, there are the eight hot and eight cold hells, as well as the neighboring, peripheral, and solitary hells. According to the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, these include Sañjīva (Reviving Hell) and the others.
The six *nāraka*s (hells), followed by the eight hot hells and the six heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), share the same calculation for the length of their lifespan from bottom to top.
Fifty human years constitute one day and night for the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*).
Thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year; the fixed lifespan of that heaven is five hundred [celestial] years.
A hundred years on earth is equivalent to one day and night in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell.
Thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve such months constitute a year; the fixed lifespan there is five hundred years.

It is called "Saṃjīva" because beings die and are revived in equal measure. Within that hell, karmic forces produce two-horned hell-wardens who, with swords and blades, cut the inhabitants into a thousand pieces.
After suffering death in ten thousand pieces, they are again gathered into a single heap and pressed down with iron pincers, crying out, "Alive! Alive!
The offender returns to life as before; thus they are punished and suffer in this manner for a fixed period of five hundred years.
Furthermore, one hundred years in the human realm constitutes one day and night for the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; that heaven likewise [counts] thirty...
Twelve months of the sun constitute one year; their fixed lifespan is one thousand years.
This constitutes one day and night in the Saṃghāta (Crushing) Hell. Thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year;
their fixed lifespan is one thousand years. As for the name "Saṃghāta," it means that the offenders stand in the center while mountains come from all four sides [to crush them].
The sinners are crushed into fine dust and suffer in this manner for a full one thousand years.

Furthermore, two hundred human years constitute one day and night in the Yāma Heaven; that heaven likewise has thirty such days to a month and twelve months to a year, with a fixed lifespan of two thousand years.
This [lifespan] is equal to one day and night in the Ink-Line Hell (Sūtradhāra-naraka).
In the hells, thirty days constitute a month and twelve months a year; their fixed lifespan is two thousand such years.
As for the "black cord," it is like using a black cord to mark straight lines on a wooden figure in the human world;

several lines are drawn upon the bodies of these sinners, which are then split with a saw by clamping them between iron leaves. Furthermore, four hundred years in the human world [equals one day in the next realm].
One day and night in Tuṣita Heaven is equivalent to thirty days in that heaven;
twelve such months constitute a year, and their fixed lifespan is four thousand years. This same duration constitutes one day and night in the Raurava (Howling) Hell;
thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve such months constitute a year, and their fixed lifespan is likewise four thousand years. Furthermore, in the human realm...
Eight hundred years in the Heaven of Delighting in Emanations (*Nirmāṇarati*) constitute one day and night in that heaven;
thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year. Their fixed lifespan is eight thousand years, which is equivalent to one day and night in the Great Howling Hell (*Mahāraurava*).
In that hell, thirty such days make a month, and twelve such months make a year; their fixed lifespan is [eight thousand years].
Eight thousand years in the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Transformations (*Paranirmita-vaśavartin*) is equivalent to one day and night in the human world;
thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve such months constitute a year.
Their fixed lifespan is sixteen thousand years, which corresponds to a single day and night in the Saṃjīva (Reviving) Hell. In that hell, thirty such days likewise constitute a month.
Twelve months constitute a year; the fixed lifespan in [the Saṃjīva hell] is sixteen thousand years.

Furthermore, the lifespan in the Extremely Hot (Pratāpana) Hell is half an intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*). When the human lifespan is eighty-four thousand years and it decreases by one year every hundred years until it reaches ten years, this period is called half an intermediate kalpa; such is the duration of the lifespan in the Extremely Hot Hell.
In my opinion, this refers to taking half of a *kalpa* from the long duration of the hells;
if it were taken from half a *kalpa* of the human realm, then the lifespan limit of this hell would be fewer *kalpas*. Consider this again and again:
the same applies to the subsequent intermediate *kalpa* for the Great Screaming and other hot hells. The lifespan in the Avīci Hell is one [full *kalpa*].
The period of increase and decrease is called one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*).

When the human lifespan increases by one year every hundred years from ten years up to eighty-four thousand years, and then decreases by one year every hundred years from eighty-four thousand years back down to ten years, this is termed one intermediate kalpa;
this is precisely the lifespan in the Avīci Hell. "Avīci" is a Sanskrit term.
This is called the "Uninterrupted" (Avīci) hell; it has five aspects: first, uninterruptedness of action, referring to the punishment of sentient beings;
second, uninterruptedness of retribution, spoken of in terms of the fruit; third, uninterruptedness of suffering, spoken of in terms of agony;
fourth, uninterruptedness of lifespan, meaning that life does not end prematurely; and fifth, uninterruptedness of physical dimension, as the body fills the entire hell, which extends east and west.
It extends twenty thousand yojanas in each direction—north, south, up, and down; its iron gates are a thousand fathoms high and its black walls ten thousand fathoms deep.
The fire above penetrates below, and the fire below penetrates above. Those who commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*) and the ten evil deeds fall into this hell.
However, by relying on the power of Samantabhadra’s Vows and Sincere Repentance, all such karmas may be extinguished. Therefore, the subsequent text says: "In the past..."

By reciting this King of Samantabhadra’s Great Vows, even the most heinous five deeds of immediate retribution committed through the power of a lack of wisdom are swiftly extinguished in a single thought-moment;
recitation itself is confession. Next, regarding the eight cold hells, their lifespans are even longer:
first, in the Arbuda hell, the lifespan is said by the World-Honored One to be beyond calculation.
It is, for example, like a *vāha* of sesame seeds from the kingdom of Magadha—specifically twenty *śīrṣa* of oil-pressing tubs filled with sesame seeds.
If a person were to remove one seed every hundred years until all the twenty *śīrṣa* of sesame seeds were exhausted, that duration would constitute the lifespan in the first hell;
the lifespans in the remaining seven hells increase by double each time. As for the eight cold hells, the first is called *Arbuda*, which means "blister," shaped like a sore or blister.

2. Arbuda (the name is established based on its physical appearance); 3. Nirarbuda; 4. Aṭaṭa; 5. Hahava and 6. Huhuva (these three hells are named based on the sounds of suffering emitted by the inhabitants); 7.
Utpala (named because the bodies of the offenders, touched by intense cold, change color like the blue lotus); 8. Padma; 9.
Mahāpadma (when the bodies of the offenders are touched by the extreme suffering of great cold, they take on a color like that of the red or crimson lotus). [End of the Small Vehicle explanation.]
If one follows the *Mahāyāna-yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* regarding the life spans of the eight cold hells, they are compared to the eight hot hells by successively reducing them by half;
that is, the first cold hell is compared to the first hot hell as being half its duration, and so on until the eighth cold hell is compared to the eighth hot hell as being half its duration.
According to this, the eight cold hells are lighter than the eight hot hells. The three neighboring [hells]...
As for the peripheral hells, outside each of the four gates of the eight hot hells, there are four additional hells.

The first is the Hell of Hot Ashes (*Kukūla*), where ashes and embers reach up to the knees; when a sinner steps down, his feet immediately rot away, but when he lifts his feet, they are restored as before.
Only after many such eons does one finally emerge from this hell. The second is the Hell of Corpses and Excrement (*Kuṇapa*), where corpses and excrement form a mud that reaches... [up to the knees].
In the mud from the knees downward, there are worms called *vṛścika* (scorpions), over a foot long, with white horns, black heads, and mouths with teeth like awls—hard, sharp, and piercing.
When the sinner places his foot down, they devour him entirely; when he lifts his foot, they grow back.
He suffers such torment until his retribution is exhausted, at which point he finally emerges. In the Hell of the Three Sharp Blades, there are blades such as knives and swords.
When one steps down upon the road, it is cut into thousands and tens of thousands of pieces; when one lifts the foot, it is restored as before.

One suffers for many kalpas until the retribution for one's sins is exhausted, at which point one finally emerges from the Four Ash-River Hells. These rivers are filled with boiling, scalding ash-liquid that cooks and boils the sinners until their skin and flesh are completely rotted away.
Furthermore, there are iron beds, iron dogs, iron snakes, and other such creatures that devour them; thus they endure immeasurable suffering.
The retribution is as explained elsewhere: the locations of the four solitary hells (*pratyeka-naraka*) are not fixed;

they may be among mountains, beneath trees, in wildernesses, at city walls, and so forth. According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the lifespans in the neighboring hells (*utsada-naraka*) and the solitary hells are indefinite, varying according to the brevity or length of one's karma.
Next, regarding the hungry ghosts (*preta*), their lightness or gravity is not... [text ends].
There are nine types in total: first, the Torch-mouthed, who constantly emit fierce flaming torches from their mouths;
second, the Needle-throated, whose heads and bellies are like mountains while their throats are like needles; third, the Foul-mouthed, whose mouths smell like a rotting corpse.
These three types are eternally unable to obtain food and are called *niścidana* (the "destitute" hungry ghosts). Fourth, the Goitrous ghosts, who have goiters on their necks.
There is the "Goitered" [ghost], who, due to the suffering of hunger and emptiness, uses his own hands to lacerate [his body] and eat the pus and blood from within;
this is the Five-Needle-Haired Ghost, whose hair is like needles, and when walking against the wind, the hair pierces its body, causing it to bleed as it eats.
Sixth is the "Foul-Haired" Ghost, who, loathing the stench of its hair, plucks it out with its hands and eats the blood; these three types are few in number.

1. Those who obtain food and drink are called *alpabhoga* (few-wealth) ghosts. 2. Those who obtain discarded [food] are called *ucchistabhuj* (scavenger) ghosts; they constantly receive sacrificial offerings. 3.
Those who obtain what is lost are called *pranaṣṭalābha* (gain-from-loss) ghosts; they constantly receive food left behind in streets and alleys.
4. The *bahubhoga* (much-wealth) ghosts are of three kinds: first, *yakṣas*; second, *rākṣasas*; and third, *piśācas*. These constantly obtain food and drink and are thus called "much-wealth" ghosts.
Regarding the hungry ghosts (*preta*), some say that although they obtain food and drink, by the power of their karma it transforms into pus and blood, and they constantly undergo such suffering.
The lifespan of these aforementioned ghosts is calculated as follows: thirty human days constitute one day and night for them;
thirty such days constitute a month, and twelve such months constitute a year. They fully possess a lifespan of five hundred years. This is according to the *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra*.
Regarding the lifespan in the realm of ghosts, it is said that while it is indefinite, the longest lasts for seventy thousand years.
Next, concerning animals—namely those that fly, those that walk, and those that dwell in the air, on land, or in water—their species are vast and numerous.
Among them, those with the greatest merit include the dragon kings, the garuḍas, and others; their lifespans within the animal realm are likewise unequal.
There are extremely long-lived beings whose lifespan lasts for one *kalpa*, as the sutras state; there are dragon kings who dwell in the world for one *kalpa* and are able to sustain the great earth.

Since the retributive suffering of the three aforementioned evil realms is immeasurable, those who have foreknowledge of it ought to avoid them from afar and resolutely seek the roots of goodness, concentrating their minds upon the Path.
If the mind does not abide [in this], it will follow after various unwholesome dharmas.
One should reproach oneself, thinking: "The thoughts of old age, sickness, and death are exceedingly near; the ocean of suffering is deep and has no shore.
Since beginningless time, I have been submerged in the wheel of existence, enduring myriad forms of affliction.

Now, having fortunately obtained a human body and encountered the Buddha-dharma, if I do not cultivate pure karma but instead create further evil causes, I shall fall again into the three miserable realms and undergo all manner of suffering. Thus one should repent.
By holding oneself accountable and gathering the mind so that it is not distracted, one dwells securely in the vast practices and vows of Samantabhadra;

through diligent cultivation, there are no karmic retributions for transgressions from which one does not obtain liberation. Therefore, the subsequent scripture states: "One is able to utterly destroy all evil destinies.

Regarding the four obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) mentioned in the commentary, they are as listed in the *Anuvyañjana-parivarta*: the obstacle of karma (*karmāvaraṇa*), the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), and the obstacle of views (*dṛṣṭyāvaraṇa*).

The two obstacles—the obstacle of karma and the obstacle of retribution—are distinguished according to cause and fruit; within the obstacle of afflictions, they are further distinguished by their sharpness or dullness.
Thus, four [obstacles] are established. Furthermore, the obstacle to the known (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is also termed the obstacle of views (*dṛṣṭyāvaraṇa*).

△ Commentary (Sū): Second, explaining the characteristics. Now, there are two kinds of repentance (*pratikramaṇa*). If one has committed an obstructive offense (*āvaraṇa-āpatti*), one should first perform the ritual repentance according to the teachings.
○ Sub-commentary (Chāo): Explaining the characteristics. The text is divided into two parts: first, stating the meaning; second, explaining the text.

In the first part, there are three sections: 1. Clarifying the ritual repentance of formal acts; 2. Clarifying the repentance of the practice of arising phenomena and principles; 3. Extensively clarifying the application of the inverse and the direct.
Regarding the first point, the "Prohibitions": these are the prohibitions established by the Buddha; violating these prohibitions constitutes an offense by its very nature (*dharmatā*).
Among these, the ten grave offenses are of a natural nature (*prakṛti-sāvadya*), while the others are prohibitions (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*).

According to the Hīnayāna school, the four grave offenses and the eight [offenses] do not admit of repentance—just as one cannot restore a severed head or a shattered stone. It is only for the four categories of offenses from *saṃghāvaśeṣa* downwards that repentance is permitted.

This refers merely to what are called "obstructive offenses" (*pratikṣepaṇa-śikṣāpada*). The *Xiangbu lüshu* (Commentary on the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya) states that in the Mahāyāna, heavy offenses are extinguished for three reasons:

first, the principle is profound and the medicine is wondrous; second, the remedial practice is superior; and third, the fruit is superior. In the Hīnayāna, the principle is shallow, the practice is inferior, and the fruit is not wondrous.
That which is "not wondrous" merely extinguishes light offenses. As for the ritual procedure (*vidhi*), the essential requirement for a Hīnayāna confession is to request a great elder (*mahallaka*).
When confessing before a large assembly of five or more, one must perform these five steps: (1) baring the right shoulder; (2) placing the right knee on the ground;

(3) joining the palms with deep reverence; (4) reciting one’s name and declaring the offense; and (5) prostrating at the feet. When confessing before a small group, the step of prostrating at the feet is omitted.
If it is a *saṃghāvaśeṣa* offense, one must request twenty monks to perform the *mānatva* penance for six nights, providing them with service and support.
When the seven-day period is complete, the Saṃgha performs a *karmavācanā* (formal ritual) to remove the offense, restoring the precepts to their original purity.
For a *bhikṣuṇī*, this period is forty days. If it is a minor offense, one simply serves for one day; there is no necessity to assemble the Saṃgha.

Regarding the Mahāyāna ritual procedures, they are as explained below. [Commentary: If one commits a *prakṛti-sāvadya* (inherent offense), one must further initiate a course of practice (*caryā*). Regarding the initiation of this practice...

There are two types: first, the practice (*śīla*), and second, the principle (*tattva*). 1. Regarding the practice, it is as described in the *Vaipulya-buddhanāma-sūtra* and other texts, which encompass the myriad practices. 2.
Regarding the principle, it is as described in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, such as the contemplation that the nature of sin is empty and does not exist within or without.

*Commentary*: "If one commits a natural transgression (*prakṛti-sāvadya*)... and below, this clarifies the dual repentance of both practice and principle. Within this, there are three parts: first, the simultaneous presentation of practice and principle.
Second, the detailed explanation of the ritual (*vastu*) and the principle (*tattva*); third, the dual conclusion on the ritual and the principle. Within the second [section], there are three parts:

first, citing the *Buddhanāma-sūtra* and other texts to explain the ritual repentance; second, citing the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* to explain the principle repentance; and third, citing both sūtras to clarify the dual repentance of ritual and principle. Now, for the first:
the *Vaipulya-sūtra* (fangděng jīng) instructs that one should first adorn the *maṇḍala* (dàochǎng), applying fragrant mud to the ground and within the inner chamber.
Adorn the circular altar with colored paintings and suspend five-colored banners; burn *kōhai* incense, light lamps, and arrange a high seat.
It is not forbidden even if more than twenty-four images are invited. Prepare various delicacies, exerting oneself with a focused mind, and don new, clean clothing and shoes.
If one lacks new or clean items, washing the old ones will suffice; ensure that when entering or exiting, or putting on and taking off garments, they do not become intermingled with impurities.
Observe the long fast (*upavāsa*) for seven days, bathing three times each day.

On the first day, make offerings to the Sangha according to one’s means, whether large or small, and separately invite one who is well-versed in both the internal and external Vinaya to receive the twenty-four precepts and the *dhāraṇī*.
One should confess one's transgressions before the teacher; the period should be set for seven days, from the eighth to the fifteenth day. This is the procedure.
It cannot be reduced; if one can further extend it, one may do as one pleases according to one's inclination. Once ten days have passed, one must not go beyond this limit.
This layperson must also prepare a single-layered robe (*pāṭa*) with three patches sewn together.

Before the Buddha, he establishes the boundary (*sīmābandha*), circumambulates one hundred and twenty times, and then sits down in contemplation, as described in detail in the sutras. Regarding the *Buddhanāma-sūtra*, its versions are numerous and diverse.

The ritual procedures (*vidhi*) also involve the cultivation of practice, yet they pertain solely to the phenomenal aspect (*vastu*). The names of the Buddhas mostly clarify the cultivation of practice and seldom explain the ritual procedures;
furthermore, these names also encompass the ultimate principle (*tattva*). A sutra states: "Those who wish to repent must first pay reverence to the Triple Gem.

The reason for this is that the Triple Gem is the true friend and field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) for sentient beings; if one can take refuge in and revere them, [their transgressions] will be extinguished.
Immeasurable sins can be transformed into immeasurable merit, enabling the practitioner to leave behind the suffering of birth and death and attain the bliss of liberation.
First, one should arouse seven kinds of mental states as preparatory means: first, shame and remorse; second, fear; third, weary detachment;
fourth, the arousal of the bodhicitta; fifth, equanimity toward enemies and kin; sixth, mindfulness of [the Buddha’s] grace; and seventh, the resolve to repay [that grace].
The seventh [aspect] of the Buddha’s grace is contemplating the emptiness of the nature of offenses.

Having given rise to these seven kinds of minds and others like them, one visualizes the Buddhas and holy sages of the ten directions, joining the palms with raised fists, laying bare one's heart in earnest prayer, feeling shame and remorse, and reforming and clearing away [the offenses] until they are as pure as described in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, such as "both internally and externally" and so forth.
Second, citing the *Vimalakīrti* to explain the principle of repentance; that is, Upāli...
The *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed Upāli, "Go to Vimalakīrti to inquire after his illness.
Upāli said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I am not fit to go there to inquire after his illness. Why is this?
I recall that in the past, there were two bhikṣus who had violated the rules of discipline; feeling ashamed, they did not dare to ask the Buddha, but came instead to question me."
I said at length, "I pray you will resolve my doubts and regrets so that I may be spared this fault," and I immediately explained the Dharma for them according to the rules.
At that time, Vimalakīrti came and said to me, "O Upāli, do not further increase the transgressions of these two bhikṣus;
you should simply eliminate them and not disturb their minds. Why is this? Because the nature of those transgressions does not exist [inherently]."
It does not exist internally, nor externally, nor in between, as the Buddha has taught: "Because the mind is defiled, sentient beings are defiled; because the mind is pure, sentient beings are pure.
The mind likewise does not exist internally, externally, or in between. As it is with the mind, so it is with the stains of transgression;
so it is with all phenomena (*dharma*). They do not transcend suchness (*tathatā*). Upāli, one attains liberation by means of the characteristics of the mind.
"Venerable Upāli, when one is liberated, is there still any defilement? "I say there is not. Vimalakīrti said:
"The mental nature of all sentient beings is likewise free from defilement. It is only conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that is defilement; the absence of conceptual construction is purity.
Inversion is defilement; the absence of inversion is purity. Grasping at a self is defilement; not grasping at a self is purity."
"All dharmas are false perceptions, like a dream, like a mirage, like the moon reflected in water, like an image in a mirror;
they arise from deluded conceptualization. One who knows this is said to uphold the Vinaya; one who knows this is said to be well-versed in it.
Then the two bhikṣus said, "How sublime is his wisdom! This is beyond the reach of Upāli, even though he is a master of the Vinaya."
When [the Buddha] could not explain it further, etc., the doubts and regrets of the two bhikṣus were immediately removed, and they resolved their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, etc.
A commentary by Shi [Daoxuan] of Guanzhong states: "There are two kinds of Vinaya:

first, the Vinaya of the nature-purity of the Dharma-body; second, the Vinaya of the body, speech, and mind of the aggregate-body (*skandha-kāya*). Now, Upāli maintains the [Vinaya of] body and speech."
Regarding the Vinaya that perceives offenses as arising and ceasing, it is for this reason that the Dharma-body is characterized by signlessness, and thus [the text] issues a reprimand.
Tiantai says: "The Dharma of the Bodhisattva has three gates: first, the Gate of Precepts, which relies on the Vinaya-dharma for repentance (as in the ritual procedures mentioned above);

second, the Gate of Merit, which refers to prostrating to the Buddha, reciting sutras, and the *Pratyutpanna* and *Vaipulya* practice halls (as in the aforementioned *Vaipulya Sutra*); third, the Gate of Non-arising."
This causes one to realize that the nature of sin is empty (this is the present section). Question:

If seeing that sin has no inherent nature means that sin is extinguished, then when one sees that merit also has no inherent nature, should merit likewise be extinguished? Answer: No. Sin is contrary to the realization of the absence of inherent nature;

when one realizes the absence of inherent nature, sin is immediately extinguished. Merit, however, accords with the absence of inherent nature; when one realizes the absence of inherent nature... [merit is not extinguished].

When the nature [of phenomena] is perceived, merit is not extinguished. Why? Because the counteragent to sin is the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*), and sin is that which is to be remedied;
therefore, when the absence of intrinsic nature is seen, sin is immediately extinguished. As for the counteragent to merit, it is the absence of intrinsic nature, and merit is that which is produced;
therefore, when the absence of intrinsic nature is seen, merit becomes vast. This is because one is able to produce the vision of what preceded. Thus it is said.
The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states that the merit of giving with a mind of non-abiding is equal to empty space.

△ The *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sukhāvatī-vyūha Sūtra* and the "Chapter on the Secondary Marks" both contain two types of repentance. △ Within the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, it is clarified that diligently paying homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions day and night constitutes ritual repentance (*vastu-pratikramaṇa*).
△ Regarding the contemplation of the mind as being without mind, if one wishes to repent from thoughts arising through inversion:
To repent by sitting upright and contemplating the true nature (*dharmatā*) is the repentance of principle (*li-chān*).

○ In the second fascicle of the *Commentary*, two sutras are cited to clarify both types of repentance. This section has two parts: first, the simultaneous presentation of the two sutras as possessing both types of repentance;

second, the individual citation of textual evidence for each. Within this, there are further two parts: first, citing the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna-sūtra*; second, citing the *Sūtra on Following* [the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*].

This is the first section of the "Good Chapters. This sutra instructs one to perform universal repentance for the six sense organs before the Buddhas of the ten directions and Samantabhadra Bodhisattva during the six periods of day and night;
this is the practice (*śīla*). It subsequently instructs one to contemplate the mind (as explained in the commentary);
this is the principle (*dharma*). Regarding the common practice used today: "The ocean of all karmic obstructions arises from deluded thoughts. If you wish to repent, sit upright..."

"Mindfulness of the true mark (the principle) means that all transgressions are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can eliminate (this clarifies the function of the single repentance of universal illumination).

Therefore, one should with a sincere heart diligently repent for the offenses of the six sense organs (the practice). This is the general verse at the end of this sutra, which elucidates both principle and practice.
△ Regarding the "Chapter on the Secondary Marks," [it concerns] the wholesome karma of body, speech, and mind within the realm of sentient beings.
To repent and eliminate all obstacles is the ritual confession (*sāṃkathyika-pratikramaṇa*).

△ To contemplate that the nature of all karma does not come from the ten directions, but dwells within the mind, arising from inversion and having no fixed abode, is the confession of principle (*tattva-pratikramaṇa*).

○ In the commentary, under the section on "the secondary marks" (*anuvyañjana*), it quotes the "Chapter on the Secondary Marks. This scriptural passage praises the merit of the secondary marks, clarifying that the Buddha is for the sake of bodhi...
At that time, from beneath the soles of his feet, auspicious marks emit light that illuminates worlds as numerous as the atoms within a hundred billion nayutas of Buddha-fields.
Sentient beings in the Avīci hell who encounter this light are reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven, where celestial drums sound to cause them to repent.
This text consists of four sections; the first is to cause them to resolve upon Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi as the foundation for the practice of repentance.
Second, purifying the three karmas constitutes the essence of the act of repentance; third, clarifying the offenses to be extinguished, which are enumerated as the four obstacles previously cited;
fourth, clearly explaining the characteristics of the repentance, which the present commentary cites in its full text as follows:
"With bodies equal in number to all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, with heads equal in number to all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, with..."

With tongues equal in number to the sentient beings within the realms, one uses body, speech, and mind—each equal in number to the sentient beings throughout the entire Dharma-realm—to repent and eliminate all obstacles, faults, and evils.
Since one brings forth these three karmas to perform the confession, this is precisely the practice itself.

However, because it is stated that they are "equal to the entirety of the Dharma-realm," this is a matter of the complete principle. Regarding the commentary on the nature of these various karmas: [the text states] "observe the nature of all karmas."

Regarding the "Repentance of Ultimate Principle," the *Sutra on Successive Events* states: At that time, the sons of the gods were filled with great joy and asked, "How does one repent and eliminate all transgressions and evils?
(Although they had already been taught how to repent, they ask again to clarify that the Repentance of Principle involves the application of the mind.
The Heavenly Drum replied, "The Bodhisattva knows that all karmas do not come from the east, nor do they come from the south..."

[They] come from the west, the north, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir, converging and coming to rest within the mind (this does not mean that a pre-existing entity comes from the ten directions to manifest the meaning of emptiness);
they arise solely from inversion and have no place of abiding (this explains the reason for emptiness).

The Bodhisattva thus clearly perceives with certainty and without doubt (the above constitutes the individual contemplation of the emptiness of karma; karma is the proximate cause for the obstruction of retribution). Hereafter follows the scriptural text.

Regarding the contemplation of the retribution of karma, he said: "O sons of the gods, suppose there were a crystal mirror named 'Able-to-Illuminate,' pure and transparent, equal in measure to the worlds of the ten directions.
Within it, all the mountains, rivers, and all sentient beings within all those lands would appear as reflections. Those various reflections can indeed be described."
[Question: "Does that which comes into the mirror go out from the mirror? [Answer: "No, O sons of the gods. All karmas are likewise.
Although they can produce the fruits and retributions of karma, there is no coming and no going; though they appear, they are non-existent.
Just as a reflection appears in dependence upon a mirror, yet the reflection neither comes nor goes, so too retribution arises from karma—how could it have any [coming or going]?"

Coming and going. △ Ritual Repentance removes the branches; Principle Repentance uproots them. ○ Regarding the commentary’s statement, "Ritual Repentance removes the branches," etc., these three pairs summarize ritual and principle repentance.
Since delusion regarding principle gives rise to afflictions and karma, Principle Repentance serves as the root for removing both;
the subtlety of this is beyond words. However, if one finds it difficult to practice fully, one must first seek out a virtuous friend.
Regarding the "Repentance for Understanding the Principle": if one uproots the root while leaving the branches intact, the branches will eventually wither away gradually;

yet if the root remains even when the branches are exhausted, it will grow back despite being cut a thousand times. Let the wise examine this carefully. If one performs the "Complete Repentance," one must thoroughly master the ten minds of opposition and compliance (*ni-liun shi-xin*). *Commentary*:
From "If one performs the Complete Repentance" onwards, the following three sections explain in detail the application of these minds of opposition and compliance.

"Repentance" refers to what is taught in the fourth fascicle of Tiantai’s *Zhi guan* (Stopping and Contemplation). Within this, there are three parts: first, a general outline; second, a detailed explanation beginning with "First, [repenting]...

and so forth; and third, a comparative analysis of the individual sections. The commentary states that one first repents the ten types of mind that accord with birth and death (*saṃsāra*) as the objects to be remedied:
1. Delusively calculating a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*), giving rise to the view of a body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*); 2. Internally possessing afflictions (*kleśa*)...

1. When encountering external adverse conditions, my mind of affliction increases and flourishes. 2. Since both internal and external factors are present, I cease all virtuous activities and take no pleasure in the goodness of others.
3. I give rein to the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, committing every kind of evil. 4. Although my actions may not be extensive, my evil mind is pervasive throughout.
5. My evil mind continues in succession, uninterrupted day and night. 6. I conceal and deny my faults, unwilling to let others know them.
1. Knowing the eight barbarians to be arrogant and impetuous, they do not fear the evil paths; 2. They are shameless and lack remorse, having no dread for either ordinary beings or sages;
3. They deny cause and effect and act as icchantikas. △ From beginningless time, whether oneself or others, there has been none who has not been thus.
○ In the second section of the *Commentary*, part one clarifies the ten minds that accord with birth and death which are to be remedied; part two clarifies...

This is the first [section], concerning the ten minds that oppose the cycle of birth and death, which can be remedied. First, regarding those who give rise to the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) through the false calculation of a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*):
from time immemorial, being deluded and confused by inversion and intoxicated by afflictions, they falsely calculate a personal self; thus, they give rise to the view of a self-body.
Having already grasped and identified the four great elements as the characteristics of their own bodies, they fail to understand that these are empty and illusory, and not permanent.
First, one gives rise to craving and attachment to moisten [the mind], and because of this, one commits various transgressions.
Second, due to possessing afflictions within and encountering evil friends without, who fan and delude my mind, [these afflictions] increase and flourish all the more.

Third, once these internal and external adverse conditions are present, they can internally extinguish the wholesome mind and externally destroy wholesome deeds, such that one feels no sympathetic joy whatsoever toward the goodness of others. Fourth...
Fifth, one who does not rejoice in the goodness of others delights in evil;

just as a hunter harbors a murderous intent toward all manner of birds and beasts, so too does a miserly person harbor a desire for every worldly resource—though their aims may not be fulfilled, such a mind persists constantly.
Sixth, they obstruct what is before and block what is behind. Seventh, as soon as they perform a single act of virtue, they immediately proclaim it to others.
"Three: 'accumulated years passing' does not mean it was not previously recorded on paper. Eight: 'lu-hu-lu'—*lu* means to plunder or to be coarse; *hu* means to be overbearing;
all these are manifestations of a lack of respect. Nine: 'shameless and without remorse' refers to being heedless of one's own dharma and lightly rejecting the virtuous and good.
This is designated as 'shamelessness' (*āhrīkya*), meaning having no regard for one's own dharma."

That which lightly rejects the virtuous and good, feels no shame regarding faults and evils, and is able to obstruct *hrī* (moral shame) while giving rise to all manner of evils, is therefore named [lack of shame].

That which disregards the world’s veneration of the violent and evil, feels no shame regarding faults and transgressions, and is able to obstruct *apatrāpya* (moral dread) while giving rise to all manner of evils, is called *anapatrāpya* (lack of moral dread);

that is, one who has nothing to regard in the world venerates the violent and evil and feels no shame for their faults and crimes. It is able to obstruct *apatrāpya* and give rise to all manner of evils.
Therefore, this is used as its name. To deny cause and effect is to be an icchantika. "Icchantika" is a Sanskrit term;

in its full form it should be *icchantika*, which here means "one who has severed the roots of goodness. The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* (Treatise on the Ornament of Mahayana) states that there are two types of icchantikas:
first, those limited by time (*kāla-paryanta*), meaning temporary. Because they have severed the roots of goodness, they do not possess even a temporary [state].
Regarding the two types of those who enter parinirvāṇa, there are those who are ultimately icchantikas—those who absolutely lack the nature for entering nirvana.

Having severed their roots of goodness long ago, they dwell in the evil realms; even if they should obtain a human body and encounter virtuous friends, they can only be brought to maturity through the roots of goodness of humans and devas.
These are precisely the sentient beings without the spiritual lineage (*agotra*) within the Five-Nature school.

Second, from "Since beginningless time" onwards, the conclusion clarifies that all births are fully endowed [with these afflictions]. This means that all sentient beings, corresponding to these ten kinds of factors that flow with the stream of birth and death, create evil through delusion;

like insects in a latrine who delight in the latrine without awareness or knowledge, they accumulate and pile up heavy burdens beyond measure—namely, the four grave offenses, the five heinous crimes, and the most extreme evil of the icchantikas—such that their cycle of birth and death is vast and boundless.
Yet there are no boundaries; all ordinary beings are universally like this. Therefore, the Commentary states: "Whether for oneself or for others, none are otherwise.
△ Next, one gives rise to ten kinds of thoughts that oppose the cycle of birth and death, overturning them from the last to the first:
1. Clearly understanding cause and effect; 2. Self-reproach and self-censure; 3. Fear of the evil realms; 4. Not concealing one's flaws and blemishes.
1. Severing the continuity of the mind; 2. Generating the bodhicitta; 3. Cultivating merit to compensate for transgressions; 4. Guarding the True Dharma; 5.
Mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions; 6. Contemplating the emptiness of the nature of offenses.

[Commentary] Second, arising from below to reveal the ten minds that counteract birth and death as the remedies. This has two parts. [Sub-commentary] Second, arising from below: first is the heading. It says: "Now..."
If one wishes to repent, one should counteract this flow of transgressions by employing ten kinds of mental states to overturn and eliminate unwholesome dharmas.
Next, to explain the first point, "Clearly Believing in Cause and Effect": this means that one must first clearly understand that cause and effect exist; they are determinate and real.
Although the seeds of karma may persist for a very long time, they do not perish. Therefore, a sutra says: "Even if one were to fill a hundred kalpas..."
Karma does not perish; when causes and conditions meet, one must personally undergo the retribution. Ultimately, there is no case where what one has done oneself is experienced by another.
One who clearly discerns good and evil will give rise to no doubt. This constitutes profound faith, which overturns and destroys the tenth mind—the mind of an icchantika.
Second, as for self-reproach and self-censure: if one wishes to be negligent, one should reproach oneself.
Base and evil sinners, devoid of shame and lack of modesty, practice the ways of beasts and abandon the pure vision of the heavens;

they commit offenses when I am in private, and therefore feel *hrī* (shame) before me, the Heavenly Being. They commit offenses where others can see them, and therefore feel *apatrāpya* (modesty) before other people.
By overturning this ninth state of mind—lack of shame and lack of modesty—the practitioner becomes one who fears the threefold dread of the evil realms.
One should reflect for oneself that human life is impermanent, passing faster than a flickering candle; once a single breath does not return, one departs forever for a thousand years.
The path to the netherworld is vast and remote, and there are no provisions for the journey. The waves of the sea of suffering are deep—where can a boat or raft find refuge?
The sages reprove us for having nothing to rely upon as our years gradually pass; the power of the wind [of youth] will not linger. How could one sit idly by?
When you are suffering from pain and aching, the *Buddhanāmasūtra* states: "If one does not repent, when the great life is about to end, the evil signs of hell will all appear before one.
At such a time, regret and fear will arrive together; if one has not previously cultivated goodness, what can repentance avail?
At that moment, if you wish to seek even a single prostration or a single act of repentance, how could you possibly obtain it? You and the assembly must [prepare now].
Do not rely on your youth, wealth, power, or influence to indulge in negligence and self-indulgence; once the suffering of death arrives, it cannot be known beforehand.
Neither youth nor robust physical beauty can exempt one from this. When the mind of fear arises, it is like treading upon boiling water or fire;
there is no leisure for attachment to the six sense objects or the five desires. It is like the city of Pāṭaliputra one hundred years after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa.
There was a king named Aśoka (also known as A-yu, which translates as "Sorrowless"). This king ruled during the age of the iron wheel;
he had deep faith in the Buddha-dharma, destroyed all non-Buddhist heretics, and gathered the relics of the Buddha to erect eighty-four thousand precious stūpas throughout Jambudvīpa.
He established grand assemblies to make offerings to more than three hundred thousand arhats and śaikṣas (those still in training).
Twice as many ordinary people as this, immeasurable and incalculable, engaged in various deeds that were beyond description or calculation.
The king had a younger brother named Vitāśoka (which means "Remover of Sorrow") who was deeply attached to false views;
seeing the non-Buddhist brahmins practicing various ascetic penances in the mountain forests, such as "roasting with five fires," he conceived a sense of reverence and admiration for them.
The King asked again, "Brahmin, do you give rise to afflictions? The Brahmin replied, "When I see various defiled objects, the fire of desire arises within me and burns my body and mind.
Upon hearing this, the King’s younger brother felt doubt and thought:
"If even one who practices such asceticism still gives rise to sensual desire, how could a disciple of the Buddha—who constantly cultivates pleasant conduct—ever develop revulsion for desire?"
Vīradeva further stated: "The disciples of Śākyamuni deceived King Aśoka into performing meritorious deeds.
When the king heard this, out of compassion for his younger brother, he devised a stratagem and said to his ministers, "My brother has placed his faith in the non-Buddhists;
you must employ a skillful means to cause him to enter the Buddha-dharma. The ministers replied, "By what method shall we do so?"
The king then said, "I am now going to bathe; enter that bathhouse, but you must remove your celestial crown and garments.
You should adorn my younger brother with my regalia and have him ascend the royal throne.
Following the king's command, once the king had entered the bathhouse, the ministers said to the king's younger brother, "If King Aśoka has no heir..."
"You should become king now; try on the celestial crown, don the celestial robes, and ascend the royal throne.
Having spoken, he immediately had them put them on and caused him to ascend the throne. Once the ministers had caused him to ascend the throne, they went secretly to inform the king.
The king came out and saw his younger brother wearing the crown and seated upon the throne. The king said to his brother, "I have not yet passed away, yet you have already acted [as king]."
The king immediately ordered his execution; the man was dressed in blue garments, with disheveled hair and holding a bell.

When he arrived before the king, the king said to the executioner, "I grant this younger brother of mine his life; you may kill him instead. At that moment, many people took up ritual implements and staffs to surround him.
A minister addressed the king, saying, "This is the king's own younger brother; I pray the king will restrain his anger."
The King Śānta said, "This is my younger brother; for seven days I shall entrust him with the affairs of state and let him act as king.
When the seven days are complete, I shall kill him. He then provided him with various musical performances and female attendants for his service and protection.
All the ministers and citizens went to offer their greetings, while the man destined to carry out the killing stood at the gate holding a sword.
Day after day, King Śveta said, "One day has already passed; in six days I shall die.
This continued until six days had passed and only one day remained. On the completion of the seventh day, the ministers and others led the king’s younger brother to King Aśoka.
The king asked his brother, "For seven days you were king, with a hundred kinds of musical entertainments."
"All shall do as you wish; countless people will come every day to inquire after your health and offer you blessings.
Will you take pleasure in seeing and hearing them? His younger brother replied, "Because I am terrified by the fear of death, I shall not see or hear anything at all.
He then answered with a verse:
For seven days, I neither saw nor heard sounds, nor smelled odors, nor tasted flavors, nor perceived any tactile sensations.
Because my body was adorned with ornaments and surrounded by various court ladies, and because I was preoccupied with the fear of death, I was unaware of these things;
I did not hear the sounds of the singing and dancing of the female musicians, nor did I notice the palace, the bedding, the earth, or any of the precious jewels.
With a joyful mind, he saw an executioner standing at the gate holding a sword and heard the sound of a ringing bell;

this caused him to harbor a dread of death that pierced his heart like a stake, such that he was unaware of the exquisite five sensual pleasures. Once possessed by this fear of the "disease" of death, he could not sleep in peace;
contemplating that death was approaching, he did not realize that the night had already passed.
At that time, King Aśoka said to his younger brother: "For seven days you contemplated the suffering of death with fear;
even though you obtained the most excellent five objects of desire, you did not give rise to attachment.

How could one who has left the household life, contemplating the immeasurable impermanence of birth and death within the twelve sense bases (*āyatana*), give rise to afflictions? Furthermore, contemplate the various stages (*bhūmi*)."
Reflecting upon the suffering of the hells and the mutual slaughter of the various animals, and being oppressed by the manifold sufferings of hunger and thirst among the hungry ghosts,
one wanders in all four directions within the human realm, finding no peace at all. Reflecting upon the suffering of decay and ruin in the heavens—
thus observing that within these five destinies there is no place of happiness, and that these five aggregates are impermanent and suffering.
Emptiness, selflessness, and unreality are like an empty village with no inhabitants; likewise, the five aggregates are all empty and without self.
As the fire of impermanence burns all worlds, the disciples of the Buddha constantly cultivate this contemplation—how then could afflictions arise? Furthermore, he spoke a verse:
For seven days, you contemplated the terrors of birth and death and found no joy; you did not give rise to a mind of greedy attachment.
The disciples of the Buddha observe birth and death day after day; how could they observe it with a sense of joy and give rise to a mind of affliction?
Regarding food, clothing, bedding, and other necessities, they contemplate the Dharma of liberation and do not—

Arising from the state of mind that contemplates the body as an enemy and perceives the three realms of existence as a house on fire, he contemplated by what skillful means one might attain the profound bliss of liberation.
Contemplating the Dharma of liberation, his mind was not attached to the five desires, like a lotus flower in water that remains unstained.
The King, through such skillful means, taught and transformed his younger brother, who consequently—
Changing his mind, he joined his palms and addressed the king, saying: "I now take refuge in the Tathāgata, as well as the Dharma and the Saṅgha.
Then he spoke these verses:
"I now take refuge in the Buddha; the Buddha’s face is like a lotus flower, the refuge of gods and humans. And [the Dharma] free from outflows..."
When the King saw that his younger brother had turned his mind back toward the Triple Gem, he was greatly rejoiced;
with various gentle words, he comforted and established his brother. Thereupon, the brother made offerings to the Triple Gem and listened to the True Dharma.

Having subsequently attained realization, he took leave of the King to go forth as a monk and attained the fruit of Arhatship. It is said that although this younger brother of the King, during the seven days [of the festival], possessed...
Regarding the five desires and various objects of pleasure, because he feared the king, he did not savor them at all but focused solely on the anxiety of death.
Therefore, a practitioner whose provisions of merit are not yet complete must not be attached to the five desires;

fearing the evil realms of the future, one should employ such skillful means as that king who feared [the king] to discipline the mind and advance in the pursuit of the roots of goodness. Thus, it is reversed.
Breaking the eighth [precept], one does not fear the evil realms. Fourth, not concealing flaws: when the roots are exposed, the branches wither;

when the source dries up, the stream runs dry. If one conceals their transgressions, they are an ignoble person. Kāśyapa Dhūta required that one confess before the great assembly, while the Vaipulya sutras require that one confess before a single person.
As for all other methods of practice, one should simply face them with a sincere heart.
Before the Buddha image, one must reform. It is like having an abscess in a hidden part of the body; if one conceals it and fails to treat it, it will lead to death.
By doing so, one overturns and breaks the seventh transgression of concealment. Regarding the fifth, the mind that severs the continuity [of evil]:

if, after having already repented, one commits the act again—just as under royal law, where an initial offense may be pardoned but a repetition is punished more severely—the fault incurred upon first entering the *dōjō* (meditation hall) is such that...
That which is easily extinguished is difficult to undo once it has been committed; having already vomited it out, how could one swallow it back again?
By this, one overturns the sixth evil mind and its continuity, which would otherwise persist without interruption day and night. Regarding the sixfold arousal of the bodhicitta:
"bodhi" refers to the fruit and virtue sought, namely unsurpassed bodhi, while the "mind" is the present capacity for seeking. Because it is aroused—
Because this is the mind that seeks bodhi, it is called "generating the bodhicitta. Alternatively, "bodhi" means awakening—that is, discernment and enlightenment.

It refers to thoroughly understanding the faults and afflictions of all delusions so as not to give rise to negligence, reaching the source of the fundamental mind where the light of wisdom shines inwardly.
Because one gives rise to this mind, it is called "generating the bodhicitta. Formerly, due to...
When one is unaware, an evil mind pervades all objects, giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion;

yet, if one now arouses the mind of awakening (*bodhicitta*) to illuminate them, one realizes that all objects are fundamentally empty, and thus transgressions do not arise. Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"The bodhicitta has great compassion as its essence, is the primary cause for attaining Buddhahood, and is the root of wisdom; it is capable of destroying [ignorance]."

Clarifying karmic retribution and so forth: because in the past I lacked wisdom, I universally afflicted sentient beings; now, possessing wisdom, I shall provide universal relief throughout the realm of empty space and benefit all.
By generating this mind, one overturns and destroys the aforementioned fifth [category]:
the arising of an evil mind in all places. Seventh, regarding the cultivation of merit to compensate for transgressions: formerly, due to the three types of action (karma), I committed various...
Without reckoning days or nights regarding past transgressions, one now exerts oneself with a virtuous body, speech, and mind without ceasing;
for unless one can move mountains, how could one fill up ravines? By this, one overturns and destroys the fourth type of mind: that which is indolent and unrestrained in the three karmas.

Eighth, regarding the "guarding of the True Dharma," this section is divided into two parts: first, explaining what is to be guarded, and second, clarifying that which guards it. As for what is to be guarded:

That which is thus described is the True Dharma (*saddharma*). The True Dharma consists of the teaching (*śāsana*), the principle (*nyāya*), the practice (*pratipatti*), and the fruit (*phala*), all of which are termed the True Dharma. "Teaching" refers to the twelvefold division of the scriptures;
"principle" refers to the suchness of the two kinds of emptiness (*dvividha-śūnyatā-tathatā*) and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*) and three non-natures (*triniḥsvabhāvatā*);

"practice" generally indicates the myriad practices; and "fruit" refers to the fruits of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), namely *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*. As for the transmigrating of sentient beings, it is [the cycle of] birth and death.

Since there is a covering of beginning and end that prevents the protection of the dharmas that will bear fruit in the future, how much more so regarding the principle of the two transformations of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), which are ultimately true and eternal?
For all who practice, it is essential to maintain firm protection; to protect the dharmas that constitute the fruit, one must first protect the practices.

Because the practices that cause the fruit are achieved through cultivation, they must be protected. To wish to protect these practices, one must necessarily protect their underlying teachings and principles. If one is deluded regarding the correct [path]...

The principle of their conduct must be upright, for since that principle is manifested through the teaching, it is necessary to protect the teaching. If the correct principle exists, one may seek it by relying on the teaching;

however, if the teaching is ruined and distorted, there is nothing left to rely upon. Therefore, it must be protected. Below, the capacity to protect is clarified by the two characters "shou" (to guard) and "hu" (to protect).
"Shou" is itself "hu"; because one steadfastly guards the True Dharma, it is called "shouhu" (guarding and protecting). Now, as for the person [who protects]—
The ability to propagate the Dharma depends upon individuals to transmit it; for while the Dharma endures when there are people, it perishes when people are lost.
Therefore, it is necessary to have people to protect it. This protection is twofold: first, internal protection; second, external protection.

"Internal" refers to the monastic community of the noble and holy ones of the Three Vehicles, all of whom are capable of propagating and elucidating the teachings, and all of whom are capable of upholding them. "External" refers to kings, ministers, and others. Thus it is said.
The inner assembly alone is able to propagate the teaching and protect its practice, yet lacks the power to rectify and uphold it;
only when there is the majesty of an external king can the Dharma be protected. As stated in the *Rājanirdeśa-sūtra*, the Buddha told King Prasenajit:
"I do not entrust this sūtra to bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, or upāsikās. Why is this? Because they lack the majestic power of a king."

Because it is able to establish [the Dharma], you all should always receive and uphold this so that those who protect the True Dharma do not destroy their own past roots of goodness nor the goodness of others;

they should neither fail to rejoice in them themselves nor fail to rejoice in others, but should cause people to guard all skillful means for goodness, increasing and expanding them so that they are never severed.
The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* says: "Protecting the True Dharma is [the practice of] gathering."
Receiving the True Dharma is the most supreme; by this, one overturns and destroys the third [fault], which is the lack of sympathetic joy.
Ninth, regarding the mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions: in the past, due to intimacy with evil friends, one believed and accepted their words.

One should now practice the mindfulness of the Buddhas of the ten directions, mindful of their peerless compassion as uninvited friends, mindful of their peerless wisdom, and placing faith in them as Great Guides, wishing not to go against them.
Since the evil conditions of birth and death must be brought into accord with the correct path of Bodhi, one must practice the recollection of the Buddha (nien-fo).
This single gate of recollecting the Buddha is the essential ford for cultivation and the pivotal point for gathering the mind; therefore, I shall briefly clarify the meaning of nien-fo.
As for the term "recollection" (nian), its definition is to maintain clear mindfulness without forgetting; its essence is wisdom (prajñā). That which is now called "recollection" is...

The neighboring [schools] distinguish their names, yet the practice of *nien-fo* (Buddha-recollection) generally comprises four types: first, recollecting by invoking the name; second, recollecting by contemplating the image;

third, recollecting by contemplating the mark; and fourth, recollecting the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*). Regarding the first, recollecting by invoking the name, the *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"Furthermore, there is the One Practice Samādhi; if a son of good family or a daughter of good family cultivates this..."
Regarding samādhi: those who wish to swiftly attain the Bodhi of a Buddha and enter samādhi should dwell in a secluded place, abandon all distracted thoughts, and not grasp at external appearances.
They should bind their minds to a single Buddha, single-mindedly reciting His name. Following the direction of that Buddha, they should sit upright and face forward.
By maintaining an uninterrupted continuity of mindfulness toward that one Buddha, within that very mindfulness they will be able to see the Buddhas of the past, future, and present.
When one contemplates the merit of a single Buddha among all Buddhas, it is immeasurable and boundless; such merit is non-dual from the merit of all Buddhas.
Thus, one fully knows that the Dharma-realm of all Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is characterized by no differentiation.

Ānanda, even a hundred thousand equal portions of dhāraṇī, extensive learning, and eloquence do not equal one such portion [of this merit]. Second is the contemplation of the image, which refers to visualization.
Regarding images of the Tathāgata such as clay sculptures and paintings, as described in the *Mahāratnakūṭa Sūtra* concerning the Buddha’s past causes:

while he was the Bodhisattva Mahāvīrya, upon seeing a bhikṣu painting an image of the Buddha, he resolved his mind on renunciation. Taking this painted cloth image with him, he entered the mountains to contemplate it.
Through contemplating this painted image, he realized it was no different from the Tathāgata himself; he attained the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and achieved universal [wisdom].

In the contemplation of the light samādhi, one visualizes the Buddhas of the ten directions and so forth; within these three types of visualization, there are two aspects: first, the clarity, and second, the marks.
Regarding the marks, if one contemplates any single one among the thirty-two marks, all grave offenses are extinguished, as described in the *Buddhabhāṣita-buddhadhyāna-samudra-sūtra*.
When the Buddha explained the contemplation of the white tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*) to his father, the King, he taught that one should contemplate only the white tuft between the eyebrows.
The marks swirl to the right in graceful curves like the ten-angled moon in autumn;
they are perfectly formed and transparent both inside and out, like a tube of white lapis lazuli, or like a brilliant star in the midst of the dark night.

Whether one’s contemplation is perfected or not, the grave sins of birth and death accumulated over ninety billion nayutas of Ganges-sands of kalpas are extinguished, and one shall always receive his guidance and protection.

Second, regarding the visualization of the entire body: as stated in the *Zuochan Sanmei Jing* (Sūtra on the Samādhi of Seated Meditation), "If one seeks the Buddha-way and enters dhyāna, one should first bind the mind to mindfulness of the Buddha’s birth-body (*janmakāya*).
One must not contemplate earth, water, fire, wind, mountains, trees, grasses, or wood, nor the myriad categories of heaven and earth, nor any other dharmas;
one should contemplate only the Buddha-body abiding in empty space, like the clarity of a great ocean."
There is the King of Golden Mountains, whose marks and signs are perfectly complete, emitting immeasurable pure light within this blue void;
by constantly recollecting the Buddha’s body therein, one will cause all Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time to appear before one's eyes.

If the mind wanders to other objects, one should withdraw it and bring it back to dwell [on the object], thereby eliminating the sins of immeasurable kalpas. This is also the mindfulness of the fourfold true reality (*dharmatā*).
It is called the *dharmakāya* because it refers to contemplating the true nature (*tattvasvabhāva*) of one’s own body and all phenomena. The *Mañjuśrī-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states:
"Neither arising nor ceasing, neither coming nor going, neither name nor mark—this is called the Buddha. It further says:

"Contemplating the true mark of one's own body, one contemplates the Buddha in the same way," and so forth. It also says: "Binding the conditions to the single mark of the *dharmadhātu* is called [the Buddha]."

Regarding the *Ekavyūha-samādhi*, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "One does not recollect the Buddha by means of his physical body (*rūpakāya*) or his marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), because the Buddha-body itself is non-existent and because there is no recollection;
this is what constitutes the recollection of the Buddha. Furthermore, the *Sūtra on the Examination of Karma* states:
