yet possess the characteristics of aggregation and dissolution. O Son of the Buddha, when the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, have completed their buddha-work,
fulfilled their vows, turned the wheel of Dharma, and brought to maturity all those who were to be transformed, there are bodhisattvas who should receive the honorable title.
Having bestowed these individual predictions, the Dharma should be understood as thus entering the unchanging Great Parinirvāṇa.
Regarding "spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*), this is clarified in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*) through ten kinds of spiritual friends. The Sūtra says:
"O Sons of the Buddha, Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas have ten kinds of spiritual friends. What are the ten? They are those who cause one to abide in Bodhi."
A spiritual friend causes the roots of goodness to arise; a spiritual friend causes one to practice all the *pāramitās*;
a spiritual friend causes liberation from all phenomena; a spiritual friend causes the maturation of all sentient beings;
a spiritual friend causes the attainment of definitive eloquence; a spiritual friend causes non-attachment to all worlds. A spiritual friend... [is] well-knowing.
The spiritual friend who causes one to practice throughout all kalpas without weariness; the spiritual friend who causes one to abide in the conduct of Samantabhadra;
the spiritual friend who causes one to enter that which is entered by the wisdom of all Buddhas, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "I exhort them all," it is as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: when our Buddha, the World-Honored One, was on the verge of entering nirvāṇa...
By the Buddha’s spiritual power, a great sound was produced, which, in accordance with the various voices of all beings, proclaimed everywhere: "Today, the Tathāgata,
the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha— out of compassion for sentient beings, protecting and sheltering them, regarding all beings equally as he does Rāhula—
the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One, who serves as their refuge, dwelling, and home, is about to enter parinirvāṇa."
"If there are any among the sentient beings who have doubts, you may now ask them all; this is your final question.
At that time, in the early morning, the World-Honored One emitted various kinds of light from his face.

These lights were of many colors and illuminated the Buddha-world of the trichiliocosm, extending even to the ten directions. Any sentient beings therein who encountered this light [were cleansed of] their karmic defilements and afflictions.

All afflictions were eliminated; when these sentient beings saw and heard this, their hearts were filled with great sorrow, and they simultaneously raised their voices in lamentation and weeping, crying out, "O Compassionate Father! Alas! What suffering!

They beat their heads with their hands, struck their chests, wailed, and sobbed with choked voices, causing the great earth, the mountains, and the oceans to tremble all at once. At that time, all the sentient beings...
They spoke to one another, saying, "Let us each restrain ourselves for now and do not grieve so greatly;

we shall immediately go to the city of Kuśinagara, the birthplace of the Mallas, to where the Tathāgata is staying, and with our heads bowed in prostration, pay him homage and entreat the Tathāgata not to enter parinirvāṇa, but to remain in the world for a kalpa, or at least for slightly less than a kalpa.
Thus they spoke, grasping one another’s hands, and further said: "O World..."
The intermediate space is empty and void; the merit of sentient beings is exhausted, and unwholesome karmas increase.
O Benevolent Ones, you must now go quickly, go quickly! Before long, the Tathāgata will surely enter parinirvāṇa.
At that time, there were forty-eight assemblies, each bringing offerings, who came to the Twin Śāla Trees. At that moment, the auspicious and blessed ground between the Śāla trees was—
The assembly, thirty-two *yojanas* wide, was so densely packed that there was no empty space, and they offered a great sacrifice; yet the Buddha would not accept it.
After the five-colored light from his mouth had emerged and vanished again, the great assembly of devas and humans saw the earth tremble violently.
Seeing the light vanish, the hair on their bodies stood on end, and they all wept piteously with one voice, speaking verses to entreat him.
We prostrate in homage to the Tamer of Men; we now entreat you to remain, for in your absence there will be no protector.
Now that we behold the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, we are submerged in the ocean of suffering, filled with grief and anguish like a calf who has lost its mother.
We are destitute and without refuge, like a sick man in distress who has no physician and eats whatever he pleases.
They do not eat the medicine for the diseases of sentient beings' afflictions; they are constantly harmed by various views and remain far removed from the Physician of the Dharma.
Consuming the poison of false teachings, the Buddha, the World-Honored One, should not abandon them.

Just as when a country has no sovereign and its people all suffer from hunger, we are likewise now deprived of the aggregates and the flavor of the Dharma. Having heard that the Buddha is entering *nirvāṇa*, [we are distressed].
Our minds are utterly bewildered, like the great earth trembling and losing its bearings.
Now that the Great Seer of Dharma-Power has entered *parinirvāṇa*, the sun of the Buddha has fallen to the ground and the waters of the Dharma have all dried up. We shall surely die;
the *Tathāgata*’s *parinirvāṇa* brings such extreme suffering and distress to sentient beings as when the son of an elder recently loses both his father and mother.
If the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa and does not return, neither we nor all sentient beings will have any protection.
From the time the Tathāgata enters parinirvāṇa until all sentient beings [pass away], sorrow, fear, and suffering will gather in our hearts;
how could we not be grieved and distressed now? We feel as if the Tathāgata has abandoned us, casting us aside like discarded refuse.
Tears and spittle are like the light of the rising sun; its brilliance is so radiant that it can both illuminate itself and dispel all darkness.
The light of the Tathāgata’s supernormal powers can likewise eliminate my suffering and afflictions. When he dwells amidst the great assembly, he is like Mount Sumeru.
Furthermore, using various parables, [the interlocutor] earnestly exhorts the Buddha, who then comforts them and preaches the Dharma, for such is the proper way of the Dharma.

Question: Since all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take the benefit of sentient beings as their primary intention, they remain in the world to bring great benefit; therefore, it is necessary to exhort them.
But as for Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, since they cannot benefit others and seek only their own nirvāṇa, why is it necessary to exhort them? Answer: [The text continues: ... [as follows].
Having personally severed the afflictions and realized the emptiness of persons, their sustenance of the Buddha-dharma brings even broader benefit.
Furthermore, among the Śrāvakas who benefit sentient beings: Subhūti and Śāriputra inquire everywhere about the Mahāyāna;
Śāriputra and Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra excel in expounding the sublime principles; Kāśyapa and Ānanda compiled the extant texts of the Tripiṭaka; and Piṇḍola...
Arhats such as Lu and others abide in the maintenance of the True Dharma and are able to benefit many beings; since there is such superior benefit, they must be invited.
Furthermore, those Pratyekabuddhas who benefit beings appear in worlds where no Buddha is present to gather in sentient beings through supernatural powers.

As for those who make offerings, they shall obtain inexhaustible fruits in their present lives or in future bodies. For example, the Devaputra Sunetra once made offerings to a Pratyekabuddha in the past.

The Buddha was born in the palace of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven because he was moved by an ethereal voice that came to inform him; through this, he was able to escape seven more rebirths in the evil realms.
Furthermore, during a twelve-year drought under King Suvarṇavarṇa, when the people had exhausted all their grain stores, the king made an offering of a single meal to a Pratyekabuddha;
by virtue of this cause, his extraordinary vows were fulfilled in this very life, and he was able to benefit all beings to the utmost.

Because the merit of benefiting sentient beings is particularly great, one must offer exhortations and requests. Question: Since the noble ones of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) have severed afflictions, realized suchness, and possess high merit in benefiting others, they too must be exhorted and requested.
Furthermore, who are these spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra), what are their functions, and why should they also be exhorted and requested?
Answer: As stated in the "Chapter on King of Virtue" (*Guṇarājaparivarta*) of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, spiritual friends are as follows: [text continues].
This refers to those among the Buddhas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas who believe in the Vaipulya (Mahāyāna) teachings. For what reason are they called "virtuous friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*)?
A virtuous friend is one who can teach sentient beings to distance themselves from the ten unwholesome actions and practice the ten wholesome actions;
for this reason, they are called virtuous friends. Furthermore, they speak in accordance with the Dharma and act according to what they have spoken. Of themselves...

One who distances themselves from the ten non-virtues and causes others to do likewise, and who practices enlightenment themselves and causes others to practice it, is called a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).
Furthermore, one who practices generosity, ethical discipline, learning, and wisdom themselves and causes others to practice them is called a spiritual friend.

Moreover, one who cannot take pleasure in themselves but constantly acts for the sake of sentient beings, who does not speak of the faults of others and always speaks of virtuous matters, is called a spiritual friend. As it is said: "Like a great..."
Just as a boatman is skilled at ferrying people across, so too are the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;
they deliver all sentient beings from the ocean of birth and death and are thus called "Good Spiritual Friends. Therefore, you must exhort them to inquire [of the Buddhas].

It is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that the Tathāgatas constantly manifest clouds of inexhaustible bodies everywhere to teach and benefit all. Since the Buddhas are already inherently present in the world, why do you further say that they must be requested?
When asked whether the Buddha dwells in the world, the answer is "yes. To explain this through the contrast between the Buddha’s appearance in the world and his parinirvāṇa, there are two intentions:

first, according to the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), and second, according to the capacity of sentient beings (*yathā-vineya*). Regarding the ultimate meaning, there are three aspects, namely the explanation of the three truths within the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*):

First, the truth of reality (*tattva-satya*) in which conditions and nature are identical to emptiness; because it is neither appearing nor passing away, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: [the Buddha] does not appear, nor does he enter parinirvāṇa.
The verse says: "The Tathāgata does not appear in the world, nor is there any parinirvāṇa.

Regarding the conventional truth of the dependent origination of the two dharma-dhātus, he appears in every thought-moment and in every place, and enters nirvāṇa in every thought-moment and in every place.

As stated in the chapter on "Attaining Perfect Enlightenment" within the *Prādurbhāva-parivarta*: "O Son of the Buddha, you should know that within one's own mind, a Buddha is always attaining perfect enlightenment in every thought-moment."
Why is this? It is because all Buddhas and Tathāgatas do not depart from this mind to achieve perfect enlightenment.
Just as it is with one's own mind, so it is with the minds of all sentient beings; within them all, there is likewise a Tathāgata who achieves equal and perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, it is said that the attainment of omniscience and the continuous succession of great compassion for the sake of rescuing and delivering sentient beings manifests in every single thought-moment. Moreover—
It should be known that there is not even the slightest place empty of the Buddha-body. Why?

Because the Tathāgata, having attained perfect enlightenment, reaches no place where he does not manifest; thus he appears in every location. As for "entering extinction," this refers to the aforementioned Buddha-body appearing everywhere;
from the perspective of the conventional meaning of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*), it arises and ceases in every moment.
The simultaneous extinction of the four characteristics is now said to mean that arising is itself extinction; thus, one enters nirvana in every thought-moment and in every place.
First, regarding the reality-body of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) as the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya): it is eternally abiding in the world, or eternally in nirvana.
Being quiescent yet constantly illuminating is "abiding in the world"; being illuminating yet constantly quiescent is "nirvana. Second, regarding the relative [perspective].
"Kai" (the opportune moment) refers to the fact that when the conditions for resonance are met, one appears beneath the Bodhi tree;
when the conditions for resonance are exhausted, one enters parinirvāṇa between the twin śāla trees. Therefore, it is said in the "Chapter on Nirvana" within the "Appearance Chapter":
"O Sons of the Buddha, the Tathāgatas appear in the world in order to cause sentient beings to give rise to joy, and they desire to cause sentient beings to give rise to longing."

Out of regard for those who long for [the Buddha], he manifests *nirvāṇa*; now, since it is necessary to exhort the Bodhisattvas through their practices and vows to request that he remain in the world, this constitutes the second gate of responding to capacities.

Although the Buddha is fundamentally eternally abiding, the reason one speaks of "requesting him to remain in the world" is that sentient beings, due to the defilements of their minds and the evil of their karma, do not see the Tathāgata;
even if their minds were to open and they were to awaken, and thus once again obtain a vision of the Buddha—

Because emotional consciousness and habitual tendencies arise suddenly yet do not remain manifest, those who now offer exhortations should rely solely on wisdom and remain detached from consciousness, constantly practicing the contemplation of the Buddha.
When the mind is pure and wisdom is luminous, one sees the Buddha at all times, and he never enters nirvana.

If, however, the mind stirs even for a moment and afflictions continue in succession, such that the wisdom of contemplation is interrupted, one will not see the Buddha; this is called the Buddha’s passing into extinction.
This is because it is a matter of "deliverance. Thus, in the "Chapter on Nirvāṇa" within the "Appearance Section," it says:

"The Tathāgata eternally abides in the pure Dharma-realm, yet manifests nirvāṇa in accordance with the minds of sentient beings. Son of the Buddha, it is like the rising of the sun, which appears universally throughout the world;
its reflection is not absent from any vessel of clear water. Yet, if a vessel in one place is broken, the reflection does not appear therein."
“Son of the Buddha, what do you think? Is it the fault of the sun that its reflection does not appear?
He replied, “No, it is simply because the vessel is broken; it is not the fault of the sun. “Son of the Buddha, the sun of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is likewise:
it universally appears throughout the Dharma-realm without before or after, and within the vessels of the pure minds of all sentient beings, there is no place where the Buddha does not appear.”
When the vessel of the mind is always pure, one constantly beholds the Buddha-body; if the mind is turbid or the vessel is broken, then one cannot see [the Buddha]. The commentary states:
Because the Dharma-body is formless, there is no vessel that does not manifest its form. Because holy wisdom is without a [discursive] mind, there is no stimulus that it does not respond to.
Form is not "mine"; it arises from the deficiency or fullness of that vessel. Mind is not "mine" to produce; how could it be that [the Buddha] does not universally manifest?
If the vessel of precepts held before and after is broken, the water of meditative concentration has no support; if the vessel of bodhi is broken, how can the water of wisdom remain?

Since there is no clear pearl of faith, the water of the mind becomes turbid; by what means, then, can one see the Buddha? Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Explaining Dependent Origination," within the section clarifying the gate of the Buddha’s appearance in the world, it says:
"It is not that the Buddha-body remains hidden and does not appear, nor is it that [the Buddha] does not exist."
The wise say that even if a Buddha does not appear in the world, one should know that there has never been a world in which a Buddha was not manifest.
This manifestation or non-manifestation depends on the presence or absence of wisdom; it is not due to the coming or going within the treasury of a Buddha’s activities.
Rather, because the One True Dharma-realm is constantly illumined, all Buddhas are eternally present before us. Thus it should be known.
"Please, World-Honored One, purify your mind. This is identical to the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, which states: "If one wishes to obtain a pure land, one must purify one's own mind;
when the mind is pure, the Buddha-land is pure," and so forth. △ This heading refers to the superior [aspect] of the practice, requesting only the Tathāgata.
△ Explanation: From the perspective of the general meaning, those of all three vehicles make this request.
△ Third, the summary of inexhaustibility:
"Thus, until the realm of empty space is exhausted, the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, the karma of sentient beings is exhausted, and the afflictions of sentient beings are exhausted, I..."
This exhortation is inexhaustible, continuing from moment to moment without interruption; the activities of body, speech, and mind are never weary or fatigued.
*The Commentary on the Separate Recitation of the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Vows" from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, Volume Four.
Sub-commentary on the Separate Circulation Commentary to the "Chapter on Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*, Fascicle Five.
Compiled by the Śramaṇa Chengguan of Dachongfu Monastery in Taiyuan Prefecture under Imperial Decree;
the Sub-commentary following the Commentary composed by the Śramaṇa Zongmi of Caotang Monastery at Mount Guifeng.
△ Commentary, Part 8: "Those who Constantly Follow the Buddha" — From here below, these three sections are all dedications of the preceding two;

that is, they represent specific aspects within the category of dedication. ○ Sub-commentary: Regarding the fact that these three sections are all dedications, this has already been clarified in the previous analysis of their names and numbers, including their synthesis and differentiation.
△ Therefore, at the end of the seventh line of the following verses, "dedication" is explicitly indicated.

This is because one wishes to gather these two categories for the purpose of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). △ If explained separately, they constitute the essential substance of the two types of beneficial practices cultivated.
△ Furthermore, they represent a separate explanation of the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) to be dedicated. ○ Regarding the "essential substance of the two types of beneficial practices":

constantly following the Buddha’s example constitutes self-benefit, while always acting in accordance with sentient beings constitutes the benefit of others. Regarding the "separate explanation of the roots of goodness to be dedicated": [this refers to the specific virtues arising from those practices].
This refers to the tenth section, which involves dedicating the merit of these two benefits as well as all blessings toward three destinations.
△ The text consists of three parts: first, stating the title.

Furthermore, "son of good family," the phrase "constantly following and learning from the Buddha" means that its significance is equal to the dedication of all Buddhas. △ This is also a practice for one's own benefit.
○ The Commentary states: "Constantly following and learning from the Buddha" refers to taking as one's object the practices traversed and the deeds performed by the Buddha from cause to fruition.

To draw forth the mind and wisdom toward the objects of focus and train accordingly is called using contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to integrate one’s own body and mind, so that they always abide within such an object.
One must not grasp at fixed characteristics of body and mind, thereby falling into the inverted states of stinginess, greed, anger, the six sense-objects, the five desires, and delusion.
Instead, one should cause the objects of the austerities practiced by the Buddha to be ever-present.
Regarding the contemplation of one's own mind: when encountering various painful matters, one accords with one’s original vow and remains free from resentment or distress;
when encountering various pleasant matters, one is naturally free from attachment, for this is the aspiration of the contemplation of the mind as impermanent.
Thus, the wise should reflect well and strive to study it. "Dedicating the meaning of the commentary equally to all Buddhas" refers to the Ten Dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*).
The third dedication within the middle [section] is also designated as such because it shares the same specific meaning within the dedications;
the seventh dedication, "conforming to all sentient beings," is identical to the ninth dedication below, "constantly conforming to sentient beings."
△ Second, the explanation of the characteristics, in two parts: 1. Studying the Original Teacher; 2. Explaining what is studied. 1. Explaining the causal practice.
Thus, in this Sahā world, the Tathāgata Vairocana, △ from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment, practiced with diligence without ever retreating.
△ He offered up unspeakably unspeakable numbers of his own bodies and lives as alms. △ He flayed his skin to serve as paper.
They split their bones to make pens and draw their blood for ink to transcribe the scriptures until they were piled as high as Mount Sumeru.

△ Because they held the Dharma in such high regard, they did not spare even their own bodies or lives. △ How much less would they begrudge their royal thrones, cities, towns, villages, palaces, gardens, groves, or any other possessions?
△ Nor would they hesitate regarding any other various kinds of difficult practices or ascetic austerities.
Regarding the passage beginning with "The Saha world, Vairocana, etc.":
although the Flower Treasury World (Huazang) is precisely the environmental retribution (*āśraya-vipāka*) for the ten bodies [of the Buddha], the Saha world is not separate from it;
rather, it is the thirteenth of the twenty tiers within the central Fragrant Water Sea. This is intended to clarify that sentient beings within this very impure land may [attain realization].

Furthermore, because one cultivates through the practice of contemplation, and because the Buddha originally did not achieve realization apart from the defiled lands, the realm mentioned is the Sahā world;

thus, the Buddha to whom one returns must be described according to his actual, perfect manifestation. Therefore, the Buddha mentions "light shining everywhere," which is an abbreviated expression based on the Middle Truth of the True Response (the Nirmāṇakāya).
As for the phrase "from the first production of the thought of enlightenment" (*prathamacittotpāda*), "production of the thought" refers to...
This refers to the arousal of the great bodhicitta. The *Necklace of Primary Karma Sutra* (*Yingluo benye jing*) states:

"An ordinary person bound by all fetters has not yet recognized the Three Jewels or the causes and effects of good and evil, nor have they given rise to even a single thought of faith toward the Buddha-dharma.

Yet, from this point on, by abiding within the true teachings of the Buddha’s bodhi and arousing bodhicitta and giving rise to a single thought of faith, at that moment they are called [a Bodhisattva]."
The Bodhisattva Śraddhālakṣaṇa’s Yoga of Consciousness-Only requires the two types of Mahāyāna lineage:
the innate lineage (*prakṛtistha-gotra*) and the acquired lineage (*samudānīta-gotra*). Only through these can one gradually enter the five stages.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* explains the characteristics of generating the resolve (*cittotpāda*) as follows: "If there is a person who says, 'May I become a Buddha in the future and deliver all sentient beings...'"
The suffering and affliction of sentient beings is called the arousal of the bodhicitta. The *Bodhicittotpāda-vihāra-sūtra* asks:

"What is the Bodhisattva’s dwelling of the arousal of the mind? This Bodhisattva beholds the Buddha, the World-Honored One, whose physical form is upright and majestic, whose marks and signs are perfect, whom all people delight to behold, and who is difficult to encounter.
He possesses great majestic power; he may manifest supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) or grant prophecies (*vyākaraṇa*).

Whether receiving a prophecy, hearing instructions and admonitions, seeing sentient beings dwelling in intense suffering, or hearing of the Tathāgata’s vast Buddha-wisdom, one generates the bodhicitta seeking all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*).
These characteristics of generating the mind are of ten kinds:
first, approaching virtuous friends; second, making offerings to the Buddhas; third, cultivating roots of goodness; fourth, aspiring for the supreme [enlightenment].
1. The mind is always gentle and supple regarding the Dharma; 2. one is able to endure suffering when encountering it; 3. compassion and loving-kindness are profound;
4. the deep mind is impartial; 5. one loves and delights in the Mahāyāna; 6. one seeks the wisdom of the Buddha.
These ten matters are all the characteristics of generating the resolve to seek great Bodhi. Furthermore, there are ten minds: first, the mind of faith, because the mind is pure.
There are four kinds of faith for this purpose: first, faith in the root, which means delighting in mindfulness of the *tathatā* (suchness) dharma;

second, faith that the Buddha possesses immeasurable merits, constantly mindful of approaching, making offerings to, and honoring him, thereby initiating roots of goodness and aspiring for all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*);
third, faith that the Dharma has great benefit, constantly mindful of practicing all... [the text continues].
Fourth, because of the practice of the *pāramitās*, one has faith in the Saṅgha as being able to correctly cultivate practices for their own benefit and the benefit of others;

thus, one constantly delights in drawing near to the assembly of bodhisattvas and learning through authentic practice. Second, "advancing the mind" means that having established the aforementioned faith, one causes it to become firm;
therefore, one courageously exerts diligent effort (*vīrya*) in order to distance oneself from all suffering. Thus it is said.
Regarding the three aspects of advancing the mind, the first is mindfulness (*smṛti*). This means that through the power of diligence (*vīrya*), right mindfulness manifests before one.
It consists of the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*): 1. Recollection of the Buddha: this refers to the three bodies (*trikāya*), the seed of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*), and his boundless qualities.

2. Recollection of the Dharma: this refers to the teachings, principles, practices, and fruits, because they are capable of bringing benefit. 3. Recollection of the Saṃgha: this refers to the Bodhisattvas who are in harmony with both principle and phenomena. 4. Recollection of [the precepts].

"Precepts" refers to the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*) of all bodhisattvas. "Recollection of giving" means bestowing upon sentient beings the three kinds of gifts: material wealth, the Dharma, and fearlessness.

"Recollection of the heavens" (the fourth) means recollecting the heaven of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-deva*), which is characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity; this is called the recollection of the heavens.

Fourth, "the mind of wisdom" means that through non-delusory discrimination, one awakens to and discerns the principle of *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only), such that the liberating understanding of wisdom manifests.
Fifth, because one previously correctly contemplated all phenomena, one cultivates correct practice with a concentrated mind. The *Awakening of Faith* states:
"The practitioner ceases all signs of objective realms; this is to accord with the meaning of *śamatha*, which is the concentration of the mind.

Sixth, regarding the mind of precepts (*śīla-citta*), according to the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra*, when a bodhisattva abides in the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-saṃvara-śīla*), this is called the mind of precepts. Seventh...
Eighth is the mind of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*): it refers to dedicating the roots of goodness cultivated by a bodhisattva toward the fruit of great enlightenment;
this is called the mind of dedication. Eighth is the mind of teaching the Dharma (*dharma-deśanā-citta*):

it means that when the Dharma is about to perish in an evil age, one resolves to uphold the True Dharma of the Tathāgata, exerts oneself in practice, and extensively explains it to others, so that the Dharma may spread widely and cause all people to... [understand it].
The ninth is the mind of relinquishment (*tyāga-citta*); because one universally relinquishes body, life, wealth, as well as afflictions and karma, it is called the mind of relinquishment.
The tenth is the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-citta*); because one vows to seek the great enlightenment of the Buddha-fruit, it is called the mind of aspiration.
When these ten minds are fully perfected, one enters the stage of the worthy (*ārya-bhūmi*) and is named the "Abode of the Arising of the Mind" (*cittotpāda-vihāra*). Thus it is said.
"Vigor without retreat" distinguishes [this practice] from laziness and indolence; it refers to being courageous and undaunted, which is termed "vigor" (*vīrya*).

The fact that the myriad practices are not intermingled is designated as "refinement" (*saṃskāra*). This also has three aspects: first, the vigor of donning the armor; second, the vigor of wholesome dharmas;
and third, the vigor of benefiting and bringing happiness to others. These will be explained in detail below. Furthermore, regarding the term "without retreat":
This means that non-retrogression is precisely non-regression. There are four types: first, non-retrogression in faith; second, non-retrogression in realization; third, non-retrogression in practice;

and fourth, non-retrogression in the stage of faith. Regarding the first, non-retrogression in faith: the sixth of the ten faiths is called the "mind of non-retrogression," because one does not retrogress into the paths of externalist schools.

Regarding the second, non-retrogression in position: the seventh of the ten abidings is called the "abiding of non-retrogression," because one does not retrogress into the vehicles of the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha).

Third, non-retrogression through realization refers to the Bodhisattva of the first stage (*bhūmi*), who, having transcended the level of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and realized the noble Dharma, no longer regresses;
this is called non-retrogression through realization because one does not regress to the state of an ordinary being.

Fourth, non-retrogression through practice refers to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), wherein, having attained the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one will certainly become a Buddha and never again regress from all dharmas.
To practice all practices without being moved or swayed by the influence of signs is called "non-retrogression in practice"; thus it says, "from the beginning," and so forth.

Regarding the passage "peeling off one's skin to make paper" and so on, there are two interpretations: first, the interpretation according to the literal characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and second, the interpretation according to contemplative wisdom (*jñāna*).
As for the first, because one must necessarily memorize the sacred teachings when various conditions are lacking, one does not spare even body or life, and thus peels off one's skin.

Even if one were to carve [the teachings] into bone, or upon bamboo, silk, paper, and ink—not to mention the abundance of these materials—one must nonetheless revere the Dharma and subject the body to hardship to manifest a sincere and respectful resolve;
this is why it is so. As the *Sarvapuṇyasamuccaya-samādhi Sūtra* states:
"In the distant past, incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a seer named Jyeṣṭha who dwelt in the mountain forests."

In the midst [of his travels], he saw various immortals constantly practicing a mind of loving-kindness. He further thought: "It is not only through a mind of loving-kindness that one can save sentient beings;
only by accumulating extensive learning can one extinguish the afflictions and false views of sentient beings and give rise to right view.
Having had this thought, he went to cities and villages, seeking everywhere for a teacher who could preach the Dharma. At that time, a celestial Māra came to him.
He said to the rishi, "I now have a single verse spoken by the Buddha.
If you can now flay your skin to serve as paper, draw blood for ink, and split your bone to serve as a pen to transcribe this verse, I shall then recite it for you.
Upon hearing this, the most excellent rishi thought to himself, "Throughout immeasurable hundreds of thousands of kalpas, I have always used my body for nothing at all..."
Having undergone immeasurable suffering from being cut and mangled, he realized it was entirely without benefit; "I shall now sacrifice this non-essential body to obtain the sublime Dharma.
With great joy and exultation, he immediately used a sharp blade to flay his skin for paper, pricked his blood for ink, and split his bones for pens.
Joining his palms toward the heavens, he requested that the Buddha’s verses be proclaimed. When the Māra saw this, he was filled with sorrow and distress.
Becoming emaciated, he then vanished. When the seer saw him, he spoke these words: "For the sake of the Dharma, I now disregard my own body and life;
I shall flay my skin to serve as paper, draw blood for ink, and split my bones for pens.
For the sake of sentient beings, my vow is sincere and not in vain. May those who possess great compassion and can preach the Dharma in other worlds appear before me."
When these words were previously spoken, thirty-two lands to the east of here contained a buddha-field named Universal Stainless.
Within it dwelt a buddha named King of Pure Fame, who suddenly appeared before him, emitting a great radiance that illuminated his most excellent body;
his pain was immediately removed, and he was restored to his former state. The Buddha then extensively expounded the "Collection of All Merit."
Guṇottama attained samādhi and, upon hearing the Dharma, obtained unimpeded eloquence. After the Buddha had finished preaching the Dharma, he returned and no longer appeared.
Having attained eloquence, Guṇottama the Rishi extensively expounded the sublime Dharma for the sake of all sentient beings, causing immeasurable beings to abide in the paths of the Three Vehicles.
A thousand years later, he passed away and was reborn in the presence of the Buddha Viśuddhanāmanarāja.
The Land of Universal Purity attained its buddhahood through reverence for the Dharma. The Buddha told Pure Splendor:

"He who was once Most Victorious is my very self today. Therefore, you should know that if there is anyone who can reverently seek the Dharma, the Buddha will not enter parinirvāṇa for that person, nor will the Dharma perish;
though they may be in a different land, they shall always behold the Buddha face-to-face."
Regarding the phrase "hearing the True Dharma," it refers to [the practice] such as "peeling off one's skin to make paper" and so forth.

As for the explanation through the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*), it means observing this body—whether its skin or its bones—that none of them possess fixed reality; the entire body is utterly empty, devoid of self or what belongs to a self (*anātman-anātmiya*).
Although one perceives with the eyes what appear to be existent forms, they are like a mass of foam, like a bubble, like a mirage, and like a plantain tree. Thus it is said.

Lacking intrinsic nature, they are fundamentally identical to the Dharma-realm; thus, through this step-by-step investigation, the three truths are fully realized as the three contemplations of emptiness, provisionality, and the middle.
When these meanings are articulated, one gives rise to understanding and attains a realization that accords with the perfect capacity [of the practitioner];

this is what is meant by "copying the sutra. The sutra is that which articulates and expresses the meaning for the arising of understanding. If one does not contemplate or investigate, the mind becomes deluded and grasps at appearances. This is [the opposite].
There is no sutra [to the contrary].

up to attaining Great Bodhi under the tree. △ Manifesting various supernatural powers. △ Arising various transformations.

Nirvāṇa. ○ In the commentary on the "Exposition of the Functions of the Fruit," regarding the demonstration of various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), some refer to them as "supernatural feet" (*ṛddhipāda*) or "supernatural realm" (*ṛddhiviṣaya*).

One should properly say "the supernormal power of the realization through the knowledge of the supernatural realm" (*ṛddhiviṣayajñānasākṣātkriyābhijñā*). Others call it the "power of transporting the body" (*kāyavāhinī-ṛddhi*), meaning the lightness of the body.
It is named "sovereignty" (*vaśitā*) because it is unimpeded; alternatively, it is called "spiritual power" (*ṛddhi-pāda*). That which is unfathomable in terms of yin and yang is called "spiritual";
that which moves and acts with immediate wisdom to transport the body is thus termed the "supernormal power of spiritual mastery" (*ṛddhi-vidhi-jñāna-abhijñā*).

As for the phrase "various kinds," it may refer collectively to the six supernormal powers within the state of fruition (*phala*), meaning that these six types of wisdom have no limit to their objective sphere.

Because it is obstructed, it is called "congestion"; because it is unobstructed, it is called "penetration," hence the phrase "various kinds. Regarding the arising of various transformations (*nirmāṇa*):

the conversion of an old substance is called "transformation" (*vikāra*), while that which was non-existent suddenly comes into being is called "manifestation" (*nirmāṇa*). Both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are capable of performing these transformations and manifestations;
this refers to the eighteen transformations (*aṣṭādaśa-vikurvaṇā*). As for what are called the eighteen transformations: the first is "trembling," trembling...

The "Great Earth" refers to the power of the sovereign mastery of the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, which can universally cause trembling— whether shaking a single room, a courtyard, a monastery,
a county, a province, a kingdom, a small thousandfold world system, a middle thousandfold world system, a great thousandfold world system, or even countless worlds—
causing them all to surge up in the east and subside in the west, and so forth. Second, "blazing intensity" refers to...
The clarity of the physical marks also arises from the power of the sovereign mastery of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
whereby they produce fierce flames upon their own bodies until their entire forms are ablaze, emitting various lights— blue, yellow, red, white, and so forth—

just as when the Tathāgata Tiṣya entered the fire-light concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*), which is called "blazing. Third, there is the dissemination [of light] through the sovereign mastery of the meditative concentration of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
He exerts power so that the teachings may be practiced. As the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra says in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*:
"I shall, by means of my supernatural powers (*ṛddhibala*), protect this sutra and cause it to be widely proclaimed and disseminated throughout Jambudvīpa so that it shall never be interrupted.
This is precisely the meaning of Rādhana. Fourth, he manifests various transformed bodies in diverse forms, relying upon meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Fifth, the power of transformation (*pariṇāma*) refers to the manifestation of various bodies to convert all sentient beings;

it means that size is indeterminate. Through the sovereign power of meditative concentration (*samādhi-vaśitā*) possessed by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, they give rise to the supernormal power of resolute conviction (*adhimukti-abhijñā*) to transform the size of their bodies as they wish.
They may transform the great earth into gold, churn the long rivers into ghee and curd, or transform bricks [into gold].
Sixth is the transformation of coming and going:
whether going or coming, mountains, rivers, and stone walls present no obstruction;
from the Brahma Heaven above to the ten directions in all their variety, one arrives wherever the mind directs, just as when Samantabhadra traveled.
Seventh, by means of the power of mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*) of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
they cause Mount Sumeru to enter into a mustard seed, and immeasurable worlds to be contained within a single atom,
and so forth. Eighth, they expand the small to become large, such that a single atom or a single hair-pore pervades the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

Ninth, the entry of all forms into the body, wherein the body internally contains all shapes and images, just as Lady Māyā contained boundless worlds and the assemblies of great bodhisattvas gathered to hear the Dharma;
furthermore, within the body of Samantabhadra, there are infinite Buddhas, and within the pores of each Buddha, there are successive layers of bodhisattvas. Tenth, going to realms of similar kind.
By the power of mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*), one is able to manifest a body within the six realms of existence,
assuming forms identical to those beings and teaching the Dharma through their speech and sounds to transform and guide them.

(11) "Disappearance from what exists" refers to the sudden non-appearance before a great assembly of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas through the power of mastery over meditative concentration, such as when Mañjuśrī vanished from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa.
In response to Maitreya at this assembly, he answered the great multitude; having long since vanished from sight, he had already entered the Dragon Palace.

These twelve manifestations are like appearances arising from non-existence, just as the immeasurable Bodhisattvas who surged forth from the earth at the assembly on Vulture Peak—each Bodhisattva adorned with the marks of a hundred merits.
Thirteenth, their activities are sovereign and unimpeded.
14. Mastery over others refers to the supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) that restrains others;
this means that by the power of mastery over meditative concentration (*samādhi*), Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are able to restrain all erroneous supernatural powers.
15. Ability to bestow eloquence (*pratibhāna*); this means that there is...
Those who with sincere resolve seek wisdom from the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas shall all be granted it;
just as the Venerable Lishi sought Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and obtained a superhuman eloquence of unimpeded discernment.

Sixteenth, they can grant the power of recollection, causing one to know past events—meaning that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas bestow their grace upon sentient beings, enabling them to remember their own past lives.
17. He fully attains knowledge of all events throughout eons of long antiquity;

this is the power to bestow peace and happiness, meaning that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, through the force of their great compassion, extract suffering and grant happiness to those they transform. 18.
He emits great radiance, or emits light that illuminates all worlds, as the Sūtra says: "It illuminates eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction."
It extends even to universally illuminating countless worlds in the ten directions, all of which are attained;
this is because the Buddha’s transformations consist of these eighteen kinds, and it is for this reason that it is said he "arises in various transformations.

Regarding the manifestation of various Buddha-bodies, this refers to the two layers of the ten bodies (*daśakāya*), which integrate the ten bodies of the three worlds; within these ten bodies, there are the body of sentient beings (*sattvakāya*) and the body of the land (*kṣetrakāya*).

The body of karmic retribution, the body of a śrāvaka, the body of a pratyekabuddha, the body of a bodhisattva, the body of a Tathāgata, the dharma-body, the wisdom-body, and the space-body—since all the spiritual friends encountered by Sudhana are not separate from the Buddha-body, they are described as "various.
Furthermore, when discussing the Buddha-body in general, there are many types; some say that the single body is itself the one dharma.

Regarding the *dharmadhātu-kāya*, some speak of two bodies: the true body (*tattva-kāya*), also called the *dharmadhātu-kāya*, and the second, the responsive body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*), also called the birth-body (*janma-kāya*).
Some speak of three bodies: the *dharma*, *saṃbhoga*, and *nirmāṇa* bodies. Some speak of four bodies by dividing the *saṃbhoga* into two:
first, the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*), and second, the other-enjoyment body (*parasambhoga-kāya*). Some speak of five bodies: first, the firm essential nature (*sāra-svabhāva*).
The first is the body of the two-fold merit-accumulation; the second is the body of enjoyment and wisdom; the third is the body that performs transformations;
the fourth is the body of the pure dharma-realm; or it is said there are ten bodies as previously explained, up to the inexhaustible clouds of bodies of the dharma-realm.
If these are condensed, they do not exceed the three aspects of essence, characteristics, and function. Essence is the dharma-body; characteristics are...
The function of the *saṃbhogakāya* is the *nirmāṇakāya*. Although the merits of the Buddha-body are immeasurable, they are subsumed within no more than the three bodies (*trikāya*);

thus, what is called "various" can be understood accordingly. As for the phrase "sometimes dwelling as a Cakravartin King," this refers to the Cakravartin King, who is surrounded by a thousand sons, possesses the seven treasures at his side, and governs the four continents.

His sovereign domain is vast, he extensively propagates the ten wholesome paths of action, his physical marks are perfect, and he is endowed with a hundred merits; his feet tread upon the thousand-spoked wheels. Regarding the seven treasures: first, the wheel-treasure; second, the jewel-treasure;
third, the woman-treasure; fourth, the horse-treasure; fifth, the elephant-treasure; sixth, the minister-treasure who oversees the treasury;
and seventh, the minister-treasure who oversees the military. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "The king has a thousand sons, handsome and heroic, capable of subduing all enemies."
There are others who possess silver wheels, copper wheels, iron wheels, and so forth, known as minor wheel-turning kings (*kṣudra-cakravartin*).

As stated in the *Bodhisattva-alaṃkāra-mūla-karma-sūtra*, the silver-wheel king has five hundred spokes and rules over three continents; the copper-wheel king has one hundred spokes and rules over two continents;
the iron-wheel king has fifty spokes and rules only over the southern continent. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* refers to them as minor wheel-turning kings.
Furthermore, those among the kṣatriyas who are not wheel-turning kings—such as the great lords of small territories and so forth—are all called minor kings.
Alternatively, they may act as such kings within assemblies to transform their retinues, or they may manifest various bodies within those gatherings to preach the Dharma and provide instruction;
thus it says "residing therein" and so forth. Or, regarding the phrase "residing among kṣatriyas, brahmins, and so forth," this is an enumeration.
There are four classes of lineage. The *Xiyuji* (Records of the Western Regions) states:
"As for the distinctions among lineages, there are four streams. First is the Brāhmaṇa, of pure conduct; they preserve the Way, dwell in poverty, and maintain their integrity with purity.
Second is the Kṣatriya, the royal caste; formerly called 'Chali,' which is an abbreviation, later generations corrupted it. For generations they have presided over the throne."

The second is the *kṣatriya*, whose will is characterized by benevolence and forbearance. The third is the *vaiśya*—formerly called *viśa*, which is an error—the merchants who transport goods, exchanging what they have for what they lack and pursuing profit far and near.
The fourth is the *śūdra*—formerly called *śaudra*, which is an error—the farmers who exert their strength in the fields and labor diligently at sowing and reaping.
These four castes differ in their purity and turbidity; as for marriage and taking spouses:
The lineages of close relatives and those who fly or hide follow distinct paths; the branches of the inner and outer clans and their matrimonial alliances do not intermingle.

Once a woman has been wedded, she never undergoes remarriage. As for the remaining miscellaneous surnames, their lineages are truly numerous; they each cluster according to their kind, making it difficult to record them in detail.
The kingship has been passed down through generations solely by the Kṣatriyas; the rest may be understood from the texts. This continues until he manifests his entry into Nirvāṇa.
The character *pan* (槃) subsequently clarifies the benefit of returning to truth and aiding sentient beings.

For example, when our Buddha entered *nirvāṇa*, he used his buddha-power to emit a voice that universally proclaimed: "Today the Tathāgata desires to enter *nirvāṇa*. If there are those with doubts, you may all ask now;
this is my final question. Then, at dawn, he emitted various colored lights from his face, illuminating everywhere.
Those in the world who encountered this light had their karmic defilements extinguished; those who heard the sound raised their voices in lamentation, crying out, "Alas, Compassionate Father!
How bitter! How painful! They beat their heads with their hands and struck their chests in wailing, causing the great earth, mountains, and rivers to tremble.
The assembly of devas and humans all gathered at the Śāla grove to pay homage to the Buddha in grief.
The blood from his entire body ceased and he appeared like a *pārijātaka* flower. At that time, the World-Honored One uttered eight kinds of sounds and addressed the great assembly:
"Do not wail excessively like infants; each of you should restrain yourselves and do not let your minds become disordered.
He then preached the Dharma for them: "I have now manifested inconceivable power through skillful means here to enter Great Nirvāṇa."
I manifest in accordance with worldly dharmas in order to cause sentient beings to know that the body is like lightning; to inspire longing for good births;
and to realize that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) revolve and flow rapidly like a torrential river—such is the nature of the dharma.
You should know that this Great Nirvāṇa is the adamantine treasure-store of all Buddhas, characterized by permanence, bliss, self, and purity, perfect and without deficiency.
It is here that all Buddhas enter parinirvāṇa; it is the final, ultimate, and exhaustive principle from which nothing remains.
Because all Buddhas here relinquish body and life, it is called nirvāṇa. Having thus given this brief instruction, he addressed Ānanda regarding the method for the cremation.
Then, with his golden hand, he drew back his saṃghāṭī robe, revealing his purple-golden [skin].
Rising into the air from the chest of the Golden Lion to the height of seven *tāla* trees, he addressed the great assembly twenty-four times:

"I wish to enter *nirvāṇa*. You should, with deep resolve, behold my vajra-like, indestructible, purple-golden, fearless physical body, which is as difficult to encounter as the *udumbara* flower. The great assembly ought to—"
"With deep resolve look up to me; after my parinirvāṇa, you should practice swiftly and emerge early from the three realms of existence.
Do not again be indolent, distracted, or negligent. Having spoken these words, he entered and emerged from various meditative absorptions (dhyāna) three times to provide instruction.

Then, upon a couch made of the seven precious gems, he lay on his right side with his head to the north, his feet to the south, facing west and with his back to the east, at the very hour of midnight.
Entering the fourth dhyāna, silent and without sound, he entered nirvāṇa.

When the Buddha had passed into nirvāṇa, the two *śāla* trees to the east and west joined together to become a single tree, and the two pairs to the north and south likewise joined to become a single tree;
they hung down and covered the jeweled couch, shielding the body of the Tathāgata. Naturally, the branches, stems, bark, and trunks turned white and spontaneously burst open.
Torn asunder and shattered without remainder, at that time the great earth and all its mountains collapsed and split apart;
the great oceans surged and boiled, the rivers and streams dried up, and the sun and moon lost their light. A black wind raged and blew, scattering sand and dust;

all the trees and vegetation were crushed and fell to the ground, each making a sound as they lamented the Buddha’s entry into *parinirvāṇa*: "The world is now without a protector! Thus did the devas wail.
Their grief and lamentation shook the great trichiliocosm. "Alas! Alas! What can be done? What can be done?
Who would have thought that today the Teacher of Gods and Men, having completed his task, could not be retained? Thereupon Ānanda fainted;
after being comforted and consoled, he was revived by the sprinkling of water. The gods and humans also fainted and wailed loudly, unable to restrain themselves. Each...

Each restrained the other and exhorted one another; thereafter, they each prepared extensive offerings and performed the cremation according to the Dharma, following the rites for a Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*).
They wrapped the body in a thousand layers of fine cloth, drenched it with various fragrant oils, and piled up a great quantity of fragrant wood.
Then, they burned it with fire. Having collected the remains, they erected a stupa to enshrine them, as described in detail in the sutras.

Thus, as long as the realm of space is exhausted, the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, the karma of sentient beings is exhausted, and the afflictions of sentient beings are exhausted, my emulation of this [practice] shall have no end;
it continues from moment to moment without interruption, such that my actions of body, speech, and mind are never-ceasing.

Furthermore, good son, as for the phrase "constantly accord with sentient beings":

This refers to the accomplishment of benefiting others in accordance with the various types of sentient beings' faculties and natures. △ The Commentary (*Shu*) states: This is the practice of benefiting others.
○ The Sub-commentary (*Chao*), fascicle nine, on the "Practice of Constantly Accordance with Sentient Beings," quotes the Buddha as saying: "Learn according to the students.

It explains that "constantly accordance" means that the causal and resultant practices of all Buddhas are worthy of being taken as models and admired; because they accord with ultimate truth, one must apply the mind to emulate and study them.
The wholesome and unwholesome actions of sentient beings do not depart from a deluded mind; being coarse, wild, and contrary to the Way, they cannot serve as a standard for emulation.

For these reasons, they are not said to be "learning. Nevertheless, without destroying conventional designations and without extinguishing conventional appearances—since all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are eternally thus—one universally integrates self and others through great compassion of the same essence.
Therefore, it is said that one "constantly accords with" them. How does one accord?

Yexian Shi [argues that] non-compliance actually clarifies the meaning of compliance: if one perceives sentient beings as definitely existent, this definite existence constitutes an entity distinct from true nature;
thus, there is an obstruction that makes them difficult to transform, and for this reason it is called "non-compliance.

If one perceives sentient beings as definitely non-existent, this definite non-existence is annihilation; annihilation is likewise distinct from true nature and results in an obstruction, which is also not [compliance].

This is the principle of accordance. Now, by the power of the practices and vows of Samantabhadra, one universally perceives that all sentient beings are nothing other than the dependent origination of the true nature (*dharmatā*).

Since they manifest by relying upon this true nature, they possess no self-substance. Yet, because they are said to "manifest," their illusory appearances are vividly present—neither severed nor extinguished.
It is like a face appearing as a reflection in a mirror; one simply says that the face has no self-substance of bone or flesh.
Is it not that the reflection of the face is manifest? To see all sentient beings in this manner is what constitutes "constant accordance.
Therefore, in the "Chapter on Dependent Origination," within the section on entering the realm of the Buddhas and the realm of sentient beings through the practices of Samantabhadra, it says:

"When sentient beings are in their state of quiescence and originally exhausted from the very beginning, this is the realm of the Dharmakāya; when the Dharmakāya follows conditions and arises, this is [the realm of sentient beings]."
The realm of sentient beings is established as eternally non-different from reality because sentient beings, who are neither existent nor non-existent through their present quiescence;
furthermore, the Dharma-body, which is neither existent nor non-existent as it accords with conditions, manifests as eternally non-different from phenomena.
Therefore, when a Bodhisattva enters the realm of sentient beings, they enter the realm of Buddhas; and when they enter the realm of Buddhas, they enter the realm of sentient beings.
Question: Since the principle is thus, why do you further say that sentient beings deviate from the Way and cannot learn it?

Answer: Although sentient beings are in their entirety and wholly true, they do not yet know this; because they deviate from and oppose this principle, their actions are inverted and cannot be emulated or learned.
Therefore, in the *Yuanqi zhang* (Chapter on Dependent Origination), the Buddha is presented from the perspective of the gate of sentient beings.
Furthermore, sentient beings are all within the realms of arising and ceasing, good and evil; this is precisely because their emotional calculations have not been shattered.

Therefore, the Buddhas they perceive likewise conform to those emotional calculations. One should know that among what sentient beings perceive, there has never been a single Buddha who is pure and liberated.
Thus, when consciousness is inverted, the Buddha also appears inverted; when emotions are deluded, the Buddha also appears deluded. This is why it is said [that he does not exist].
[Question: "It may be studied; but if that is so, why must one comply? [Answer:
Suppose there is a virtuous person who possesses integrity, trustworthiness, loyalty, and filial piety, and suddenly dreams of killing his parents and committing various unrighteous acts.
When others hear of this, would they discard him simply because he committed unrighteous acts in a dream? Although he should not be discarded, could one then desire to [punish him] further?
If one were to imitate those dream-events and create what is contrary to the Dharma, both the one who rejects [the teachings] and the one who imitates [them] are equally deluded and insane.
Thus, we know that those who study the practices of deluded sentient minds, or those who exclude sentient beings and claim everything is false, are likewise both deluded and insane.
Therefore, these things must not be studied; they are merely spoken of for the sake of conformity. Nevertheless, although one does not study them, one must nonetheless...
Vast and expansive, with a vacant mind, there is no duality between self and others; one’s own awakened true nature is indistinguishable from that of ordinary beings or sages.

Thus uniting upward with the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and downward with the sentient beings of the six realms—seeing things in this way and applying the mind in this manner is precisely what is called the practice and vow of Samantabhadra.
Therefore, while the preceding section required union with all Buddhas, this section requires union with sentient beings; how wondrous!
Ah! Let those who possess wisdom examine this in detail: that which accords with others' conduct is to follow their own kind and faculties;
that which accomplishes benefit by following the provisional marks of conditions is to observe according to principle so that they may correspond to reality, each being distinct from the other.
As stated in the passage below, it acts as light for the impoverished and causes them to find hidden treasures.

The meaning of these categories is illustrated by the following seven types of taking upon oneself the suffering of sentient beings; among these, the sixth and seventh meanings constitute the practice of benefiting others (*parārtha*).

Therefore, while the preceding section on "following the Buddha's example" was designated as "benefiting oneself" (*svārtha*), one may also consider the former to be wisdom (*prajñā*) and the latter to be compassion (*karuṇā*).

This refers to all sentient beings of every variety and distinction throughout the entirety of the dharma-realm, the realm of empty space, and the oceans of lands in the ten directions.

○ Commentary: First, the beings to be accorded with are indicated; subsequently, the actual process of accordance is clarified. This section is divided into two parts: first, the individual explanation of the scriptural text;
second, the reconciliation of the meaning of the sub-commentary (*shu*). Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the general indication of the location (which is self-evident);

second, the manifestation of the beings to be accorded with. Regarding this second section, there are two parts: first, the general indication that the scriptural term "sentient beings" (*sattva*) is as described in the *Mahābherī-hāraka-sūtra*.
It is said that the provisional designation (*prajñapti*) resulting from the conjunction of all phenomena is called a "sentient being" (*sattva*).

That is to say, the combination of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), the eighteen constituents (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*), and so forth, is conventionally designated as a "person" and termed a "sentient being.
Furthermore, the *Prajñāpradīpa-śāstra* states: "Sentient beings are so called because they are born again and again; thus they are termed a 'multitude' (*gaṇa*)."

The *Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa-parivarta* states: "This dharmakāya is by nature pure, yet when it is entangled by afflictions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and follows along with the world, coming and going within birth and death, it is called a sentient being."

The four modes of birth—oviparous, viviparous, moisture-born, and transformation-born—when further combined with those who possess form and those who are formless, those with perception and those without perception, and those with neither perception nor non-perception, constitute nine categories in total.
The Night Goddess Samantasattvatrāṇojas (Universal Savior of Beings) is the spiritual friend mentioned previously in the context of the ten stages;
her full name should be stated as Samantasattvatrāṇojas-caryāguṇaviśuddhamati-rātridevatā (Night Goddess of Pure Conduct and Virtuous Wisdom Who Universally Saves All Beings).

Abiding at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*) while relying on the stage of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*), he attained the Bodhisattva liberation door of universally manifesting throughout all worlds to discipline sentient beings.
Regarding this, there is a commentary on the nine categories of text which states: "The nine categories briefly have two types of distinctions.
First, the explanation of the four modes of birth clarifies the distinction of the basis, as it is that upon which retribution relies; the remainder..."
The three types of birth—womb, egg, and moisture—are dependent on what? They depend on karma and defilement for their arising.

The *Bhūmivastu* (Dìchí lùn) simply states "karmic defilement," which accords with the meaning of the verse in the *Lokadhātu-paṭala* of the *Abhidharmakośa*: "With a perverted mind, one approaches the realm of desire; Moisture-born and transformation-born beings are defiled by odors and locations; Devas have their heads upward;
the three [other] horizontal births and hell-dwellers have their heads downward. The treatise says: In this manner, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) proceeds to its destination.
Having first given rise to perverted thoughts, one rushes toward the realm of desire. By the power of karma, although the eye-faculty has arisen, it can see from afar;
thus, when seeing the parents engaged in union at the place of birth, one gives rise to perverted thoughts. If male, one takes the mother as an object and gives rise to male desire;
if female, one takes the father as an object and gives rise to female desire. Conversely, regarding these two objects, both give rise to a mind of hatred.

If one is born by moisture (saṃsvedaja), one is born through attachment to fragrance; that is, smelling from afar the scent of the place of birth, one immediately conceives a defiled attachment and goes there to undergo birth.
According to what is appropriate to one's karma, the fragrance may be pure or foul. If one is born by transformation (upapāduka), one is born through attachment to the location;
that is, seeing from afar the place where one is to be born, one immediately conceives a defiled attachment and goes there to undergo birth. According to [one's karma]...
According to the places to which karma leads, there are pure and impure realms. Furthermore, the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of gods ascends head-first, like one rising from a seat;
those of humans, ghosts, and animals move horizontally, just as humans do on earth; and the intermediate state of hell-beings falls head-downward with feet upward into their realm.
As for the other five classes [of beings], they differ in terms of coarseness and subtlety. This clarifies the characteristics of retribution below.
Regarding the two realms, those with form are coarse and those without form are subtle. Within those with form, those with perception (*saṃjñā*) are coarse and those without perception are subtle.
As for the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" realm, within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), only its subtlety is mentioned in contrast to the coarseness of the others;
by way of this principle, it should be stated that "perception and non-perception" are coarse, while "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" is subtle.

Because the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*) is subtle, this refers to its meaning; however, although the scriptural text lists many types, they are subsumed within no more than nine categories, which is why the commentary merely points to these nine.
That previous explanation only correlated them with their bases and their relative coarseness or subtlety, without correlating them with the five destinies (*pañcagati*);
here, we further clarify that among those born by transformation (*upapāduka*), there are devas and hell-beings, while hungry ghosts (*preta*) possess both [transformation and womb-birth].

Transformed beings and animals each possess all four modes of birth. Among ghosts, those born from wombs and those produced by transformation include the earth-walking rākṣasas, yakṣas, and the children of the Mother of Ghosts (*piśācī*), all of whom are born from the womb;
the rest are transformed beings. Those who possess all four modes are as follows: the egg-born are like Viśākhā’s mother, who gave birth to thirty-two sons from an egg;
the womb-born are like ordinary humans; the moisture-born are like the woman Nanda, who was born from an *āmra* tree.
Those born from moisture are the Aṃrapālī women; their transformation is like that of humans at the beginning of a kalpa.

Regarding those who descend from the second dhyāna to be born among humans and possess all four modes of birth: this is because dragons and garuḍas each have all four types of birth. Thus, the *Saddharmasmṛtyupasthāna Sūtra* states:
"The transformation-born garuḍa can eat dragons of the four modes of birth, in order: moisture-born, womb-born, egg-born, and transformation-born."
They are able to consume those born from eggs, those born from wombs, and so forth; among the remaining birds, all are born from eggs, and among the remaining beasts, all are born from wombs.

Whether on land, in flight through the air, in water, or on dry ground, there are minute, wriggling creatures—whether born by transformation (*aupapāduka*), from moisture (*saṃsvedaja*), from eggs (*aṇḍaja*), or from wombs (*jarāyuja*)—whose various categories cannot be fully distinguished.

Furthermore, the *Saṃyukta-abhidharma-hṛdaya-śāstra* states: "Birth encompasses the destinies (*gati*), but the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is not included within the destinies; birth [therein] is by way of transformation."

Question: Since the mode of birth by transformation (*upapāduka*) is not included within the [other] destinies (*gati*), why is it not placed at the beginning? Answer: There are two reasons: first, an explanation based on the object (*viṣaya*); second, an explanation based on the mind (*citta*). Regarding the explanation based on the object: that which possesses the most conditions is placed at the beginning. For instance, egg-birth (*aṇḍaja*) necessarily possesses all four—womb, moisture, and transformation; womb-birth (*jarāyuja*) possesses moisture and transformation; moisture-birth (*saṃsvedaja*) possesses only transformation; and transformation-birth possesses only transformation. Thus, because it possesses the most conditions, it is placed at the end. Regarding the explanation based on the mind: the mode of birth by transformation is produced solely by the power of karma, whereas the other three modes of birth are produced by both karma and afflictions (*kleśa*). Therefore, because it is produced solely by the power of karma, it is placed at the end. Furthermore, among the four modes of birth, transformation-birth is the most subtle, while the others are progressively coarser. Because it is the most subtle, it is placed at the end. Consequently, the order of the four modes of birth is established according to the principle of descending coarseness. This concludes the explanation of the four modes of birth. Next, the explanation of the five destinies follows. Regarding the five destinies, there are three types: first, the definition of the term; second, the determination of their number; third, the refutation of objections. First, regarding the definition of the term: "destiny" (*gati*) means "going" (*gamana*). It refers to the various places where sentient beings go, such as hell, hungry ghosts, animals, humans, and gods. Alternatively, it refers to the various states of existence (*bhava*) to which sentient beings proceed. Therefore, it is called a "destiny. Second, regarding the determination of their number: why are there exactly five destinies? Answer: There are five destinies because they are established based on the distinction between the wholesome and the unwholesome.
