First, regarding the sequence of arising: each stage arises alone and does not coexist with the others; that is, each preceding stage possesses the subsequent stages, while each subsequent stage does not possess the preceding ones.

This is why they are arranged in this order. Second, explaining the sequence in terms of the mind: from the root to the branches constitutes the order. Ignorance (avidyā) refers to the birth of sentient beings from eggs;

"ignorance" here denotes the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), specifically the first of the three subtle states of mind, namely the initial phase of karmic activity (*karmalakṣaṇa*). This is the beginning.
The thought that arises is undifferentiated between subject and object, a chaotic state like an egg; because it is the fundamental basis, it is explained first.

Ignorance (avidyā) initiates karma and resides within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), acting as the embryo. The flow of craving (tṛṣṇā) moistens it, enabling the taking of birth, which constitutes the "moisture" [birth].
As for transformation-birth (upapāduka), there is sudden existence where none previously existed, which constitutes the "transformation. This refers to those with form.
Those belonging to the two lower realms all possess the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), which refers to the five contaminated sense-faculties (*āsrava-indriya*).

Those who are "formless" (*arūpin*) belong to the four spheres of emptiness (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.), where the body consists solely of the four aggregates (*skandha*) and lacks the five sense-faculties of the form-aggregate. Those who "possess ideation" (*saṃjñin*) include all beings except for those in the Heaven of No-Ideation (*asaṃjñisattva*) and the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);
all others are subsumed herein. Those who are "without ideation" (*asaṃjñin*) refer specifically to the Heaven of No-Ideation; they do not exist elsewhere.

That which is "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" refers to the Heaven of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*). If one assigns the nine categories to the three realms, then the category of "apparitional birth" (*upapāduka*) pervades all three realms;
the three [other] types of birth exist only in the desire realm; and the category of "possessing form" (*rūpin*) pervades the lower two realms.

As for "possessing perception" (*saṃjñin*), it encompasses all three realms but does not pervade the other two heavens [the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception and the Heaven of No-Thought]; therefore, "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*) refers to one specific heaven within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), and is not [present] elsewhere.

The notion of "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" refers to one class of devas within the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Fearing that those with power might insist on a specific interpretation, I have recorded it in full;
had I not mentioned it, I would have worried about an omission in its utility.
△ Second, the main explanation of conformity (*anuloma*).
In all such matters, I act in accordance with them. I perform various services and offer various forms of worship.
I revere them as I would my own parents, as I would my teachers and elders, and even as I would Arhats and Tathāgatas, without any difference.
For those suffering from illness, I act as a skilled physician; for those who have lost their way, I show them the correct path.
In the midst of the dark night, he acts as a light; for those who are impoverished, he causes them to obtain hidden treasures.
Thus, the Bodhisattva equally benefits all sentient beings.
Regarding "turning in accordance": it is called "turning" because one gives rise to contemplative wisdom in accordance with each and every sentient being as described above.
As for the phrase "like revering one's parents," this is as explained in the *Bhūmi-citta-darśana-sūtra* (The Sutra on Contemplating the Mind-Ground of Past Lives):

the father possesses the grace of compassion and the mother possesses the grace of pity; the grace of their nurturing extends throughout all under heaven, and the virtue of their怜愍 (compassionate pity) is vast.
In this world, nothing is greater than the mountains; yet the kindness of a compassionate mother exceeds Mount Sumeru.
In the weightiness of the world, the great earth comes first; yet the kindness of a compassionate mother surpasses even that.
If one turns one's back on such kindness and fails to be compliant, causing resentment toward one’s parents, an evil son shall immediately fall accordingly into the miseries of the world.
The signs of resentment caused by fierce winds are even more severe than that; yet,

to offer hundreds of thousands of kinds of supreme and exquisite offerings to a hundred seers possessing the five supernatural powers, a hundred practitioners of pure conduct, and a hundred virtuous friends,
is not comparable to offering even a small amount of goods to one's parents— when their merits are weighed, they cannot be compared, as was the case with Viśvantara.
The Prince himself cut flesh from his own body to make offerings to his parents as he practiced the path of a Bodhisattva;
the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also states that by making offerings to one's parents, one obtains immeasurable merit, as explained at length in the sūtras. It says:

"Just as one serves one's teachers and elders, so too are those who give birth to us our parents and those who bring us to completion our friends. The birth of my Dharma-body is entirely due to my teachers and elders," and so on, up to the instruction.
The term *arhat*—which, when translated from Sanskrit into the language of Tang (Chinese), possesses several meanings—is here taken in three senses.

Master Paramārtha explains that *arhat* means "non-arising" (*anutpāda*), because one no longer undergoes the retribution of birth and death within the afflictions of the triple world; hence it is called "non-arising."

The first is called "one who should be taught" (*śaikṣa*); this means that having completed one's own training and being capable of teaching others based on what one has realized oneself, one is thus named "one who should be taught.

The third is called "one worthy of offerings" (*arhat*); as the *Sudarsana-vinaya* states, such a person is fully endowed with wisdom and the abandonment [of defilements], serving as a supreme field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) capable of receiving material offerings and generating great benefit; for these reasons, they are called "worthy of offerings. Because they possess these meanings, [they are so designated].
This is what is meant by "constantly accords with. It is similar to this:
although it is known that the Tathāgata does so, it is solely through the power of Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices that one’s contemplative practice pervades the entire Dharma-realm.

Among the various kinds of sentient beings mentioned above, in every thought-moment, one acts in this way; and among those various sentient beings, whoever possesses the capacity for understanding will personally receive the benefits described above.
"Equality" refers to the universal contemplation and universal benefit that accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
△ The commentary has two parts: the inquiry and the explanation. First, causing the Buddhas to rejoice.
First, the inquiry: "For what reason?"
The commentary asks: If one should merely follow the Buddhas, why is it necessary to follow sentient beings? The sub-commentary provides two explanations: 1.
If a bodhisattva can accord with sentient beings, this constitutes acceding with and making offerings to all Buddhas.
2. If one honors and serves sentient beings, this constitutes honoring and serving the Tathāgatas. 3. If one causes sentient beings to give rise to joy...
"Joy causes all Tathāgatas to rejoice.
The commentary explains the meaning as follows: "If one accords with sentient beings, one accords with the Buddha; if one does not accord with sentient beings, the Buddha does not rejoice.

Regarding the phrase in the *Chao* (Sub-commentary), "To accord with sentient beings is to accord with the Buddha," since this text is brief, it is further explained by means of the *Haiyin* (Ocean Seal) Samādhi.
This analogy is used to clarify that just as in a pure, tranquil sea of fragrant water, Mount Sumeru, the sun and moon,
the four continents, various sentient beings, various lands, dwellings, and houses all appear within it—
if one grasps these images as being actual living beings or substantial worlds, this contradicts the nature of the reflection; it is not merely a contradiction of the image itself.

This would also contradict the nature of the ocean; one must certainly know that each and every image possesses the ten qualities of the ocean, such as having a salty and moist substance and not harboring corpses.
The thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that the ocean has ten qualities to illustrate the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
First, it becomes progressively deeper, just as the great vows produced in the first stage become increasingly profound.
1) Therefore, it does not receive corpses, because, like the second stage (*dvitīyā bhūmi*), it does not receive the corpses of those who have broken their precepts;
2) other waters enter into it and sink away, which is called being like the third stage (*tṛtīyā bhūmi*) because it is free from worldly conventional designations (*prajñapti*);

3) it is everywhere of one single taste, because, like the fourth stage (*caturthī bhūmi*), it is of one single taste with the virtues of the Buddha; 4) it possesses immeasurable treasures, because, like the fifth stage (*pañcamī bhūmi*), it gives rise to them.
1. Because it is a treasure of skillful means and supernormal powers (*upāya-abhijñā*), it is like the first ground, which cannot be fathomed by others;

2. Because it observes the profound principle of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it is like the second ground; 3. Because it is vast and immeasurable due to the well-observed, expansive wisdom of awakening, it is like the third ground;

4. Because it manifests vast and magnificent adornments, it is like the fourth ground; 5. Because the great body dwells therein, it is like the fifth ground; 6. Because the tides do not overstep their bounds, it is like the sixth ground.
Being limited to the profound understanding and practice of the ninth stage, one does not exceed its bounds;
therefore, the "ten universal receptions of great rain" refers to the tenth stage, which can receive the great rain of the Dharma-light of all Tathāgatas without ever being satiated.

Only then is it called "conforming to the image" (*xiang*); since it conforms to the image, it is first named "conforming to the ocean. The ocean is the Tathāgata, and the image is the multitude [of beings].
Since other meanings arising [from this] are clearly visible, the "Appearance Chapter" states:
"O Son of the Buddha, it is like the great ocean, which can universally reflect the forms and bodies of all sentient beings within the four continents;
for this reason, it is collectively called the 'great ocean. The Bodhi of all Buddhas is likewise: it universally manifests within the minds of all sentient beings."
Because the faculty of mindfulness, desire, and inclination do not manifest as anything [separate], the Sūtra says:
"To accord with birth is to accord with the Buddha," and so forth, up to "revering, serving, and rejoicing. Therefore, it is called the Bodhi of all Buddhas.
△ Commentary II: Increasing Great Compassion II.
1. Inquiry: "For what reason?

The intent of this inquiry in the commentary is: since the state of ordinary beings and that of the Buddhas are vastly separated, how can one accord with the joy of all Buddhas? △ 2. Explanation of the Intent.

It is said that the Buddha takes great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as his essential nature; if one does not accord with the arising [of this compassion], it would not conform to the essence of a Buddha.
*Commentary:* Regarding "taking great compassion as the essential nature": from cause to fruit, there is nothing that the Buddhas do not perform for the sake of sentient beings.
Only when Great Compassion and Prajñā (Wisdom) constantly assist one another can it be called "non-abiding nirvāṇa" (*apratisthita-nirvāṇa*); therefore, compassion is the essence.
△ Section 3: The Exegesis. Part 1: The Teaching by Dharma.
Because the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, take great compassion as their essence, they give rise to great compassion based upon sentient beings;
from great compassion, the bodhicitta arises; and from the bodhicitta, they achieve equal and perfect enlightenment.

The *Sū* (Commentary) immediately indicates the Great Compassion of the same essence. The *Chāo* (Sub-commentary) states: "Because of [sentient beings]... until attaining equal and perfect enlightenment.
This means that because Great Compassion seeks to transform sentient beings, one must study the wisdom of transforming beings. Once this wisdom is perfected, one is naturally called a Buddha;
thus, the Bodhicitta must necessarily possess Great Compassion, Great Vows, and Great Wisdom. Therefore, it is said:
All Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, take great compassion as their very essence.
This means that within the gate of Samantabhadra’s universal transformation and guidance, he universally understands all things, encompassing them without exception; this is termed "Great Vision.

Seeing that sentient beings constantly dwell in birth and death, cycling through the five destinies, creating various causes of evil and undergoing manifold sufferings, the Tathāgata feels deep pity for them.
Because it adds a profound sense of compassion and pity, it is called "compassion" (*karuṇā*). The compassion of the mundane world cannot be called "great";
only the supramundane compassion is called "great. Within the supramundane, the compassion of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) is not called "great";
only the compassion of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is called "great. This is because this great compassion is the foremost of all practices; therefore [it is so named].

The *Tattvārtha-ṣaṭpāramitā-sūtra* states: The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Maitreya, "When practicing the pāramitā of dhyāna, one should cultivate immeasurable great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
This great compassion serves as the leader for all virtuous deeds; it is like the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*), which precedes the inhalation and exhalation of breath."
Just as the seven treasures of a Wheel-Turning King are preceded by [the sovereignty of] the wheel, so too are the myriad practices of the Mahāyāna preceded by great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
For example, if an elder has but one son, his parents’ affection for him penetrates to the very marrow of their bones;

the great compassion of a Bodhisattva is likewise, dwelling in a state of supreme love toward all sentient beings, like that of a parent toward an only child. Furthermore, this great compassion is able to act as a guide.
Because it brings to completion all factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*); because this great compassion can awaken the untaught, spontaneous wisdom (*anācārya-svayaṃbhū-jñāna*);

and because this great compassion can eliminate all the feverish afflictions of one's own mind and accord with sentient beings for their benefit—for these reasons, the Tathāgata has this as his essence. This is the initial indication within the scriptural text.
The commentary states that "great compassion of the same essence" (*samatā-mahākaruṇā*) is fully illustrated by both the dharma and the analogy, as previously cited:
just as the myriad phenomena within the ocean share the same essence as the ocean, so too do sentient beings within the Buddha’s bodhi share the same essence as bodhi.

△ The *Samantamukha-parivarta* (Chapter on the Manifestation) says: "When the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he universally saw all sentient beings attaining perfect enlightenment... and so forth.
He universally perceives that all sentient beings entering nirvana are of one and the same nature. △ The Commentary (*Shu*) states:
Because he realizes that all sentient beings are devoid of inherent nature, his great compassion continues uninterrupted as he rescues and protects them all.

○ The Sub-commentary (*Chao*), citing the scriptural evidence for the second point, quotes the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-prabhāsa-parivarta* (Chapter on the Manifestation): "Reaching all" is a concise citation; the full text says, "Accomplishing the Correct [Awakening]."
When awakening, one universally perceives within one's own body [the sequence of equality], as cited in the commentary;
this is stated as being "within one's own body" because it takes the Buddha as the gateway. If one takes sentient beings as the gateway, then the Buddha is realized within sentient beings.
Thus, the *Samantabhadra-caryā-prasthāna* (Chapter on the Manifestation) states below that "Bodhisattvas should know that their own minds are constantly present in every thought-moment."
There is a Buddha who has attained perfect enlightenment. Why is this? Because all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not depart from this mind when they attain perfect enlightenment.
Just as it is with one's own mind, so it is with the minds of all sentient beings;
in them all, the Tathāgata has attained equal and perfect enlightenment, vast and pervasive, without ceasing. This passage is further cited here to correspond with what was stated previously.
The intent of this section is to clarify the principle of the mutual interpenetration of the Buddha and sentient beings; therefore, it is fully set forth here.
△ The commentary clarifies this through two metaphors.
For example, in the midst of a vast wilderness of sand and gravel, there is a great king of trees; if its roots receive water, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits [will flourish].
All are lush and flourishing.
The vast distance of birth and death, utterly severed and devoid of any support, is called a wilderness; the failure to produce roots of goodness is likened to a desert of sand and gravel.
The Dharma of the Buddha’s Bodhi is like a great king of trees, while wisdom and meditative concentration are like its branches and leaves.

The Bodhisattva takes the trainings as the soil and illustrates them with flowers; the Buddhas realize this and designate it as the fruit, while all sentient beings serve as its roots and great compassion serves as its water.
△ The Commentary states: "Water nourishes the tree's roots, causing the leaves and fruit to flourish;

through compassionate concern for the myriad classes of beings, one establishes the causes and conditions for the fruit of Buddhahood. △ The text is thus complete. ○ The Sub-commentary says: "For example," and so forth.

Regarding "The Fully Equipped One" asks: How does the Scripture explain the analogy of the "vast wilderness" (*kāntāra*) within the Dharma? [Answer: Birth and death are severed and remote, having no place of reliance; this is called the "vast wilderness.
How is it that "sandy deserts" (*maru*) are used as a metaphor for the non-arising of roots of goodness?
[Answer: This refers to the sandy deserts. How is it that there are "trees within the vast wilderness and sandy deserts"? [Answer: The Buddha’s *bodhi*-Dharma is like a great...
The Buddha-King said: "The 'Dharma of the Tree' specifically refers to the essence of the original awakening (*prakṛti-āśraya-jñāna*) of all sentient beings.
This means that although the true nature follows various delusive conditions to form all defiled phenomena, it is obscured by afflictions and thus lacks the power and function of a Buddha’s bodhi.
It is compared to a tree in a desert; though this tree has not yet produced flowers or fruit,"
Yet, although the sentient beings within the tree-body do not yet possess the functional power of a Buddha’s bodhi, their fundamental awakening (mūla-avabodha) is ever-present.
Question: If the sentient beings grow and develop within the tree, how are wisdom and meditative concentration (dhyāna-samādhi) cultivated within the process of awakening?
The analogy of branches and leaves is as follows: from the tree grow branches, and from the branches grow leaves; likewise, the Dharma arises from [the root].

Original enlightenment arises from initial enlightenment; since initial enlightenment is wisdom, it is like the branches. Since the mind first arises, yet the mind has no mark of beginning, it is in dark union with the One Suchness.
Since this One Suchness is concentration, it is like the leaves: concentration is accomplished by means of wisdom, such that wisdom comes first and concentration follows.
This is according to what is taught in the True Teaching (Mahāyāna); as the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* says: "Wisdom..."
This is the pure land of this Bodhisattva; when this Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings of right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*) will come to be born in that land.

This differs from the provisional vehicles of the Lesser Teachings, which first establish concentration and only thereafter develop wisdom. Because entry into the Path proceeds by means of wisdom, it is said that one achieves the principle of concentration through wisdom.
In reality, however, concentration and wisdom are cultivated simultaneously, without priority or sequence. This is because concentration can pull out those who are sunken [in delusion].

Stagnant wisdom can suppress restlessness, while penetrating wisdom can provide decisive discernment; these two dharmas support one another to sustain the myriad practices, constituting the most essential and ultimate point.
Therefore, the "Chapter on the Questions of Maitreya" states: "For example, when a powerful king leads the land, all subjects look up to him in reverence;
concentration and wisdom are likewise. Although they are the most wondrous things upon which a bodhisattva relies, [they must function together]."
One must first suddenly reach the fundamental source before the concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) can arise;

furthermore, one must employ concentration and wisdom within the myriad practices (*samskāra*) before one can realize the fruit (*phala*). Question: The tree has branches and leaves to illustrate concentration and wisdom;

what do the flowers that subsequently grow upon these branches and leaves illustrate? Commentary: The Bodhisattva relies on learning to illustrate this; the flowers represent relying upon concentration.

"Wisdom is that which cultivates the flowers of the myriad practices. This means that when Bodhisattvas are fully endowed with both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*), they penetrate the fundamental source and accord with principle to benefit sentient beings;
thus, they must perform the myriad practices. Therefore, based upon their concentration and wisdom, they bring forth the flowers of the myriad practices.
Question: When a tree has flowers, there will inevitably follow fruit. Now that the flowers of the myriad practices have blossomed, what serves as [the fruit]?

The *Foguo shu* (Commentary on the Fruit) states that the Buddhas, having realized this, designate it as the "fruit. This is illustrated by the metaphor that only when flowers have ripened can they produce fruit;
likewise, within the Dharma, only when the myriad practices (*saṃskāra*) are perfected can one realize entry and become a Venerable One of Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). Question:
In the preceding text, it was said that if the king of great trees receives water at its roots, its branches, leaves, flowers, and fruits will all flourish. As stated above...
The explanation of the correspondence between the metaphors of the tree, its roots, branches, flowers, and fruits is now complete.
What, then, is the root of the tree? What is the water? The Commentary states: All sentient beings constitute the root of the tree, and great compassion constitutes its water.
This means that although all sentient beings each possess the root of the Bodhi-tree, they are unable to cause it to sprout.
Those who are born have their roots constantly buried within the coarse and harsh sands of the afflictions of birth and death;
since the nature of sand is dry and lacks the power of nourishment, how could it cause the tree roots to sprout and flourish?
For this reason, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas employ various skillful means to lead all sentient beings to distance themselves from coarse and evil afflictions.

By dwelling within the most excellent field of merit—the Triple Gem amidst the sands of affliction—one can extensively raise the dense clouds of compassion and universally rain down the nectar-like Dharma rain;
only then can the roots of the Bodhi tree be nourished, allowing it to gradually flourish and ripen into the great fruit.
Question: Why is the root of the tree used as a metaphor for sentient beings, while great compassion is likened to [the rain]? Answer: [Because]...
Just as it is not yet clear what function water serves in nourishing the roots of trees, what superior capacity does the compassionate gathering-in of living beings possess?

The commentary states that water nourishes the tree roots so that flowers and fruits flourish; likewise, the compassionate mindfulness of all classes of beings is the cause for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood.
By saying "the cause for attaining the fruit of Buddhahood," the intended meaning is that compassion is the cause of the fruit of Buddhahood. As it is said:
Just as water nourishes the roots of a tree, serving as the cause for its flowers and fruit, the preceding sutra states: "Based on great compassion, one gives rise to the bodhicitta;
based on the bodhicitta, one achieves equal and perfect enlightenment. Regarding this "cause":

if one speaks of the compassionate vows generated during the stage of a causal practitioner (*hetu-bhūmi*), it universally serves as the cause for the fruition for both oneself and others, as it possesses the two benefits. If, however, [it refers] to the Buddha...
Regarding the gate of not abandoning the cause even when the fruit has been attained: the Bodhisattva serves only as a cause for others;
why is this? Because their own fruit is already fulfilled, they act solely for the benefit of others.

If one proceeds from the metaphor to the Dharma and investigates it in detail, one must first clearly perceive that when watering a tree in the wilderness, one must first distinguish the trunk of the tree and then pour water at its roots. One must first distinguish [the parts].
If one realizes the awakened essence within birth and death, compassion arises from that awakened mind;
yet if one does not see the tree, though one waters it throughout the vast wilderness, it only increases one's fatigue and ultimately will not produce flowers or fruit.

Likewise, if one does not awaken to the awakened essence, though one gives rise to compassion throughout birth and death, it only increases attachment and views, and ultimately one will not realize Bodhi.
One may see the roots of trees that, though not watered, still produce flowers and fruit; or one may realize the essence of awakening yet fail to cultivate it, thus failing to realize Bodhi.
Strive diligently for awakening, lest you labor in vain and merely exhaust your body;
exert yourself in practice, lest you deny cause and effect. Contemplate this text, which is perfectly subtle and wondrous, with deep reflection.

all sentient beings are its roots, while the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are its flowers and fruits. By benefiting sentient beings with the water of great compassion, one is able to bring it to fruition.
The flowers and fruits of the wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

The general meaning of the Sūtra states that for one to be perfected in the fullness of wisdom, it is necessary that self and other are not different, and that self and object are identical, just as one sees them as such.
Since all sentient beings are manifested from my awakened mind, benefiting others is itself benefiting myself;
as my wisdom is brought to fulfillment and perfection, he restates the preceding words to establish the logical momentum of the argument, saying:

The meaning of these two scriptural passages becomes even more manifest. Although the preceding explanation of the passage on "identical essence" already fully clarifies this principle, because it was necessary to bring forth the specific intent of this current section of the scripture, the words must be used again.
As for "Anuttara," this is translated as "Unsurpassed. As for "Tri," this is translated as "Right," established as a name in opposition to "False. As for "Miao," this...
The term "cloud" (*megha*) signifies equality; furthermore, the mention of "three" also signifies the sense of being perfectly complete. The term "bodhi" is translated here as "awakening" (*jue*);

it should be understood as applying across the preceding four instances, namely: *anuttara-bodhi* (unsurpassed awakening), *samyak-saṃbodhi* (perfectly complete awakening), *abhisambodhi* (manifest awakening), and *samyag-bodhi* (right awakening).

These terms are used with specific distinctions: "right awakening" (*samyag-bodhi*) distinguishes [the Buddha's realization] from that of ordinary worldlings and non-Buddhists, whose awakening is erroneous.

It is called "Equal Enlightenment" (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) because it distinguishes [the Buddha] from the noble ones of the two vehicles, who have realized only the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*).

Furthermore, it is called "Right Enlightenment" (*samyag-bodhi*) to distinguish [him] from the noble ones of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), whose realization of the two kinds of emptiness is partial rather than perfectly complete.

The initial term "Unsurpassed Enlightenment" (*anuttara-bodhi*) is used in its most eminent sense and refers specifically to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); however, if discussed according to their general characteristics, all three bodies (*trikāya*) are included.
Because they have come together for the sake of unsurpassed enlightenment and are endowed with the aforementioned four meanings, they obtain the title *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Second, that the contemplation and observation of the meaning of the Dharma involves this mind arising moment by moment; this too is the state of sentient beings, and it must necessarily [be transformed through]...

The nine rounds of the practice of perfect interfusion lead from the mundane toward the supramundane; the ten rounds follow the principle of phenomena toward the phenomena accomplished through that principle.
Among these ten, the first three concern sentient beings, the next three and the ninth concern Bodhi, the seventh and eighth concern the Reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the tenth pervades all three.
Although these are opened out into ten, they are also subsumed into two: namely, those with characteristics (*sanimitta*) and those free from characteristics (*animitta*).
The arising of bodhicitta is with characteristics (*sanimitta*) while the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is without characteristics (*animitta*);

or, sentient beings are with characteristics while bodhicitta is without characteristics, and the limit of reality is neither with nor without characteristics. Although there are many ways to open and close these categories, one cannot be missing from this pair.

As the *Jingming juepin* (Chapter on the Enlightenment of Radiance) states: "If one generates a mind of dedication toward all-knowledge, it is 'with characteristics'; if one perceives the mind [itself], it is 'without characteristics'."

"Non-arising" means being free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); "obtaining great renown" refers to dedication (*pariṇāmanā*). If one lacks following characteristics, one falls into the stage of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*);

if one lacks freedom from characteristics, one falls into the stage of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). Following characteristics guards against the two vehicles; freedom from characteristics guards against afflictions (*kleśa*).
According to the "Ten Dedications" chapter (*Daśapariṇāmanā-parivarta*), there are ten names: first, "Protecting Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from Sentient Beings."

Regarding dedication through signs: this bodhisattva practices the six pāramitās and the four immeasurable minds, and by means of these roots of goodness, causes all sentient beings to completely eliminate the sufferings of the three evil realms.

Constantly observing all sentient beings with eyes of compassion, they dedicate these roots of goodness toward the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) of awakening, yet their own minds remain free from [attachment].

That which is thus described is called the dedication "Rescuing and Protecting Sentient Beings while Remaining Free from the Notion of Sentient Beings. Second is the indestructible dedication (*akṣaya-pariṇāmanā*):

this refers to when a bodhisattva attains indestructible faith in all Buddha-dharmas, penetrates deeply into the true meaning, accumulates a treasury of merit, and practices great giving with a mind that is never destroyed; this is called the indestructible dedication. Third is the... [equal dedication].
The dedication of all Buddhas refers to this Bodhisattva’s learning of the dedications of all Buddhas of the past, future, and present;
seeing beautiful or ugly forms with a mind free from hatred or attachment, their faculties become pure.
Because they attain such a dedication as that of the Buddhas, it is called "the dedication equal to all Buddhas. Fourth is the dedication reaching all places, which means:

This Bodhisattva cultivates all roots of goodness so that the power of the merit of these roots reaches the abodes of all Tathāgatas of the three periods of time as well as their great assemblies, serving as an adornment.
Within a single thought-moment, they fill boundless worlds, pervading everything just as the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) does; this is called the dedication reaching all places.

Fifth is the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit, which means that this bodhisattva attains the power of the roots of goodness of the inexhaustible Dharma and turns toward the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge);
because the mind is as pure as space and as immovable as the great earth, it is called the dedication of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.
Sixth is the dedication of the firm roots of goodness that accord with the great fruit.
This Bodhisattva skillfully transforms sentient beings through the four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) and the four immeasurable minds (*apramāṇa*), remaining firm and non-retrogressive.
By dedicating these roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) to seek the Great Fruit, it is called the "Firm Dedication.
Seventh is the dedication that accords with all sentient beings through the seven equal minds; this Bodhisattva’s growth of roots of goodness becomes immeasurable and boundless.
Closing the gates to the evil realms and attaining mastery over the mind, one constantly seeks to practice giving through these roots of goodness.
For example, it is like a person who comes to beg throughout all future kalpas; the Bodhisattva bestows gifts with a mind of equanimity, never feeling weary or exhausted.
This is called the dedication that accords with all sentient beings through a mind of equality. (8) Suchness.
As for dedication (*pariṇāmanā*): this bodhisattva, having accomplished mindfulness and wisdom, dwells immovably and causes all sentient beings to likewise dwell securely in all dharmas of merit.
Thus, with a mind that has no basis, he dedicates these roots of goodness to accord with the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*) for the benefit of all sentient beings;
this is called dedication according to the characteristic of True Suchness.
Ninth, the dedication that is unbound and unattached: this bodhisattva does not abandon any roots of goodness;
with palms joined in reverence, they prostrate to all Buddhas and entreat them to turn the wheel of Dharma.

With this mind that is unbound and unattached, they dedicate [the merit] toward the fruit of great Bodhi. This is called the dedication that is unbound and unattached. Tenth, the [dedication of] the ten dharma realms...
As for "the dedication of all," this Bodhisattva is fully endowed with compassion and is able to bestow extensive gifts to benefit sentient beings without ever resting;
by means of these roots of goodness, they dedicate them toward seeking the infinite Buddha-fields of the Dharma-realm.
This is called the "Inexhaustible Dedication of the Dharma-realm. These ten dedications, in general, follow the great ocean of boundless practices.
The vow is to take the accomplishment of the qualities and functions of Samantabhadra’s Dharma-realm as its goal.

The commentary states that "removing narrow and inferior obstacles to accomplish vast goodness" reveals the benefit and the intended purpose. A mind that does not dedicate [merit] is narrow and inferior;
because even a hair’s breadth of goodness is made to pervade the entire Dharma-realm through the mind of dedication, it is called "vast," like an echo.
Entering the corner, it is heard from afar.
△ The second [section] of the commentary, explaining the characteristics, has two parts. First, clarifying the roots of goodness to be dedicated:
from the initial prostration up to all merits resulting from compliance.
This refers to the preceding nine gates. △ The Commentary (Sū) has two parts: first, the general explanation; second, the specific clarification of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*).

Herein, the specific clarification of dedication toward sentient beings so that they may achieve Bodhi—that is, dedicating toward Bodhi until the end of the Dharma-realm—is identical in meaning to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

this scriptural passage is explicit. The phrase "causing them to attain," etc., expresses the intent of the scripture as containing three [aspects].

Regarding the sentient beings who are the objects of dedication, one must vow that they will certainly attain Bodhi. The section beginning with "exhausting the dharma-realm" assigns [the dedication] to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

The text of the *Shu* (Commentary) is also clear. △ The reason why these three are essential is that all Bodhisattvas necessarily transform downward through great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and seek upward through great wisdom (*mahājñāna*), while remaining free from the marks of sentient beings and *bodhi*.

○ The *Chao* (Sub-commentary) subsequently provides the reasons for these three essentials; therein are three points: first, possessing both compassion and wisdom while being free from marks; second, their mutual... [text continues].

Because they support one another, the three [categories] are distinguished into ten classes: because they transform those of superior, middling, and inferior capacities, they are directed toward sentient beings;
because they seek upward, they are directed toward Bodhi; and because they are free from these two characteristics, they are directed toward the Reality Limit (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Furthermore, since a bodhisattva’s roots of goodness are necessarily accomplished through sentient beings, they are the "portion" of sentient beings; therefore, they are directed back toward them. Since these roots of goodness are necessarily Bodhi, they are directed toward it.
Because it involves the method of differentiation, it also tends toward those two; because one must necessarily be free from signs, it tends toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
△ The Commentary further states: These three necessarily support one another; one possesses all three, and all three together constitute one.

That is to say, to realize the true nature (*dharmatā*), one must tend toward sentient beings in order to transform them, thereby accomplishing one's own benefit (*svārtha*) by severing hindrances and realizing the truth; thus, it also tends toward Bodhi.
To accelerate the realization of Bodhi, one must possess all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*) and sever the two obstacles (*āvaraṇa*) before finally reaching the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

△ Commentary: The remaining two cases should be understood by analogy. ○ Sub-commentary: Furthermore, the following sections demonstrate mutual support. Regarding the phrase "realizing the truth" (*zhengshi*), this refers to realizing emptiness apart from form;
however, as this is not the true limit of reality, it is transformed into self-realization (*svasaṃsiddhi*) for the sake of maturing others. This also leads toward Bodhi.

"Attaining" (ti) means that one attains the wisdom of *bodhi* and thereby reaches the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); thus, they mutually support one another in succession. Regarding the other two [terms], they should be understood accordingly:
the two [of "attaining" and "entering"] are for the sake of saving sentient beings; one must head toward the limit of reality, for only by being sovereign over delusions can one transform others.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* says: "If one is bound oneself, it is impossible to untie the bonds of others. One must likewise [head toward the limit of reality].

Since Bodhi must possess wisdom in order to extensively benefit others, the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "If one wishes to deliver sentient beings, one cannot do so apart from the wisdom of unobstructed liberation.
Third, for the sake of attaining Bodhi, one dedicates [merit] toward sentient beings;

yet, because one does not realize the fruit by being directed solely toward sentient beings, one also dedicates it toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). However, if one were to realize the limit of reality, how could one attain Bodhi? △
The Commentary further selects [these categories] by analogy, briefly outlining ten meanings:

namely, because it relies upon the three dharmas, extinguishes the three paths, purifies the three aggregates, manifests the three Buddha-natures, accomplishes the Three Jewels, assembles the three bodies, possesses the three virtues, attains the three types of bodhi, realizes the three nirvāṇas, and dwells securely within the three kinds of secret treasuries. △ Regarding the "three dharmas" mentioned in the Commentary:

This refers to the three aspects of essence, characteristic, and function, which are also the three types of *prajñā*. △ The Commentary states: "Those who turn toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) rely on the dharma of essence;
