Second, first the headings and enumeration, followed by the citation and explanation. Within the explanation, there are two parts: first, the harmonious interpretation of the first gate;

second, the extension of this principle to reveal the remaining nine. In the first part, there are two sections: first the heading, then the explanation. Regarding the initial heading, the commentary states: "The three dharmas" refers to essence, characteristic, and function;
these are also the three *prajñās*. As for the "three *prajñās*," they are: the *prajñā* of true nature, the *prajñā* of contemplative observation, and... [the *prajñā* of practice].

Prajñā, the means of accomplishing Prajñā, and Prajñā itself—these three are among the five types of Prajñā. Among them, "true nature" (tathatā) is the *dharmatā-prajñā* (the Prajñā of ultimate reality);

"contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) is the *pratyavekṣaṇā-prajñā* (the Prajñā of discerning observation); and "means of accomplishment," which subsumes the objects, retinues, and words, is the *sambhāra-prajñā* (the Prajñā of equipment).

When expanded, these become five; when condensed, they become three. The subsequent commentary on the *Śāstra* states: "From 'toward the limit of reality' (*bhūtakoṭi*) onwards, it can be understood. This second example clarifies [the point].

Regarding the statement that "the sequence of the remaining nine [categories] and the remaining three dharmas is to be understood by analogy," this means one should follow the first three and apply them to the *bhūtakoṭi* (reality-limit), *bodhi* (enlightenment), and sentient beings.
Specifically, the second [category] states "because it extinguishes the three paths": only by seeing the *bhūtakoṭi* can one extinguish suffering;
by illuminating the emptiness of afflictions, one attains *bodhi*, and transforms the karma of bondage and fetters into the karma of benefiting sentient beings, and so forth.

The three purities and three clusters refer to: [the purity of restraint] because it is directed toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); [the purity of gathering wholesome dharmas] because it widely encompasses all virtues while being directed toward bodhi;

and [the purity of benefiting sentient beings] because it is directed toward sentient beings, which is precisely the benefit of sentient beings. The fourfold manifestation of the three Buddha-natures refers to: the true cause (*hetu-hetu*) because it is directed toward the limit of reality;
the revealing cause (*jñāna-hetu*) because it is directed toward bodhi; and the conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) because it is directed toward sentient beings.

Regarding the formation of the Three Jewels based on the five [aspects]: by turning toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one forms the Jewel of the Dharma; by turning toward Bodhi, one forms the Jewel of the Buddha;

and by turning toward sentient beings, one forms the Jewel of the Sangha of identical essence. Regarding the six assemblies as the three bodies (*trikāya*): this refers to the Dharma, Sambhoga, and Nirmāṇa bodies. Regarding the possession of the three virtues:

by turning toward the limit of reality, one forms the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇaguṇa*); by turning toward Bodhi, one forms the virtue of wisdom (*jñānaguṇa*); and by turning toward sentient beings, one forms...

Regarding the eighth, attaining the three types of *sambodhi* through the grace [of the Buddha]: this refers to attaining the *bodhi* of true reality (*bhūtanimitta*) by turning toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*);

attaining the *bodhi* of true wisdom (*bhūtaprajñā*) by turning toward *bodhi*; and attaining the *bodhi* of skillful means (*upāya*) by turning toward sentient beings, because one manifests the attainment of Buddhahood beneath the Bodhi tree.

Regarding the ninth, realizing the three types of *nirvāṇa*: these are the *nirvāṇa* of intrinsic purity (*prakṛti-viśuddha*), the *nirvāṇa* of perfected purity (*pariśuddha*), and the *nirvāṇa* of ultimate peace (*anupadhiśeṣa*).
This refers to the extinction of the fire when the fuel of conditioned existence has been exhausted, which is pure nirvāṇa. Regarding the ten ways of abiding in the three secret treasuries:
by turning toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one abides in the Dharmakāya Buddha; because the Dharma constitutes the body, it is as pure as space.
By turning toward bodhi, one is able to accomplish prajñā; because bodhi is luminously discerning, it clearly illuminates the ultimate. By turning toward...

Sentient beings are able to achieve liberation; being themselves free from bondage, they cause others to be released from their bonds. Manifesting according to the capacities of beings, this is also the unimpeded liberation.
Furthermore, within these ten [liberations], taking one as the primary focus, they unfold sequentially and depend upon one another.

△ The commentary has two parts: first, the elimination of suffering and the accomplishment of virtue, all of which are dedicated to all sentient beings throughout the entirety of the dharma-realm and the space-realm.

△ May sentient beings always attain peace and happiness, free from all illness and suffering. △ May any desire to practice unwholesome dharmas fail to be accomplished. △ Regarding the wholesome [dharmas] they cultivate...
All karmic actions are swiftly accomplished. △ Closing the gates to all evil realms. △ Revealing the correct path to humans, devas, and nirvana. Commentary:
May they be freed from suffering, accomplish goodness, and even attain nirvana. ○ Sub-commentary: All are dedicated toward the attainment of nirvana.
Regarding the phrase "the true path and so forth," since the entire dharma-realm is simultaneously the object of one's vows, it extends horizontally throughout the ten directions.
Regarding the phrase "always attaining and so forth," it reaches vertically through the three periods of time.
△ Commentary 2: Taking on Suffering for the Sake of Generating the Bodhicitta.
If all sentient beings, because they have accumulated various evil karmas, experience all manner of extremely heavy karmic fruits of suffering, △ I shall take them all upon myself.
△ May those sentient beings all attain liberation. △ Ultimately achieving [Buddhahood]...
[He] aspires to supreme enlightenment. △ Commentary:
Since suffering arises from karma, how can one possibly take its place? △ Commentary: Briefly, there are seven points. △ Commentary:

First, regarding the cultivation of the compassionate intention, it is not necessarily possible for one who remains within the realm of ordinary beings. △ Commentary: Second, the practice of various ascetic austerities.
Later, when one can serve as a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for sentient beings, this is called "substitution" (*dai*). Commentary 3:

When one retains afflictions (*kleśa*) to moisten rebirth and undergoes a body of suffering in existence for the sake of others, preaching the Dharma so that they do not commit evil—thereby causing the cause to perish and the fruit to be lost—this is called "substitution.

Commentary 4: If one sees sentient beings committing the deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) and that they are about to undergo great suffering, there is no difference [between their suffering and one's own].
Skillful means necessarily require that one’s own life be ended so as to fall into hell, thereby liberating the other from suffering;

this is precisely what is meant by "substitution. △ Commentary 5: From the moment of first generating the bodhicitta, one constantly dwells in the evil realms, even becoming a great fish during times of famine;

this is precisely what is meant by "substitution. △ Commentary 6: Great vows and suffering are both identical to true nature (*dharmatā*); now, by means of that which is identical to the true, [one effects liberation].
The Great Vow secretly reaches the very essence of suffering. △ The Commentary (*Sūtra*) states: "The seven dharma-realms constitute the body;

self and others are not different. When sentient beings suffer, that is precisely the Bodhisattva. ○ The Sub-commentary (*Chao*) states: "If all... [In the section on] generating the mind to vicariously undergo suffering, there are two parts: first, the direct clarification;
second, the interrogation and explanation regarding suffering, which contains three sub-sections: first, the interrogation; second, the brief overview; [and so forth].

Regarding the second point, the "Brief Analysis of the Three Upper and Seven Lower [Categories]," it says: "First, the arousal of compassion," and so forth. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 49, states:
"A bodhisattva cultivates the intention of compassion (*anukampā*) and the non-intention [of aversion] toward worldly beings;
for the sake of benefiting sentient beings in the evil destinies, he vows to dwell in those evil paths as if they were his own home, wishing to take their suffering upon himself in their stead."
Because of the power of this compassionate vow, those evil karmas never manifest again;
all the heavy residues (*dauṣṭhulya*) belonging to the category of afflictions within all the miserable realms are eliminated from their own bases, as they enter the first stage (*bhūmi*).
As the *Sūtra on the Equal and Supreme Dedication* states: "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva sees sentient beings committing..."
Due to the weight of their evil karma, those who undergo various heavy sufferings are obstructed such that they do not see the Buddha, do not hear the Dharma, and do not recognize the Saṃgha;
they then form this thought: "I shall, within those various evil realms, undergo all manner of suffering on behalf of all sentient beings so as to bring them liberation.
When Bodhisattvas undergo such bitter suffering in this way, they become even more diligent and do not abandon their resolve.
They do not avoid, they are not startled, they are not terrified, they do not retreat, and they are not cowardly; they feel no weariness or fatigue. Why is this?
Because they resolutely desire to shoulder the burden of all sentient beings according to their vows, so as to bring them to liberation. Furthermore, they form this thought:
"The practice I cultivate is intended to cause all sentient beings to attain the unsurpassed King of Wisdom; it is not for my own sake."
And yet one seeks liberation. Why? Because my vow is to deliver all sentient beings;

I have resolved upon bodhicitta not for the sake of seeking the Unsurpassed Way for myself alone, nor for the sake of seeking the realms of the five desires or the various pleasures within the three realms of existence while practicing the bodhisattva path. Why? Because there is no worldly pleasure that is not...

Regarding the second point, "practicing various ascetic penances for the sake of suffering": since the Bodhisattva originally performs ascetic practices to seek the Dharma for the benefit of sentient beings, this is already termed "substitution";

furthermore, because by virtue of these practices one attains superior and wondrous threefold karma (trikarma), which serves as a predominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) for others, it is therefore termed "substitution.
Regarding the third point, "retaining afflictions to moisten birth and receiving a body of suffering in existence": this refers to retaining the seeds of affliction.
"Moistening birth" refers to causing one to receive a body subject to the suffering of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*).

Among the two obstructions, those that arise from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) have their active manifestations (*samudācāra*) suppressed prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), and their seeds (*bīja*) are severed at the first moment of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*). Regarding the innate [obstructions], the obstruction to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) is severed portion by portion according to each stage;

as for the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), they can be spontaneously severed from the first stage onward, yet because [the Bodhisattva] intentionally retains them, they are not severed. "Moistening" [thereby] persists.

Because they take birth for the sake of gathering and transforming [sentient beings], because they do not fall into the two vehicles, because they seek to sever the cognitive obstacles (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and because they seek to attain great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
As the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) of the Liang dynasty states: "One retains the afflictions until the afflictions are exhausted, thereby realizing the Buddha’s omniscience.

However, ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) use manifest afflictions to moisten karma and undergo rebirth; the noble ones (*ārya*) do not do so, but rather retain the seeds of the afflictions to use them for the purpose of taking birth.
Because one gives rise to superior practice by employing wisdom to govern [the body], faults and afflictions do not arise. It is like using the power of mantras to govern a venomous snake;

it neither causes death nor allows faults to arise, thereby accomplishing a superior function. Regarding the two types of bodies—the *paricchinna* (segmented) and the *pariṇāma* (transformed)—there are differences across the five teachings.
In the Hīnayāna, there is only the segmented body, which persists until the ultimate stage, at which point even the Buddha [attains the transformed body].
In the same way, this is real and not a transformation [body] in the Initial Teaching (Śrāvakayāna). From the seventh bhūmi onwards, there is still the body of分段 (*bheda-śarīra*, segmented);

from the eighth bhūmi upwards, there is the body of變易 (*pariṇāma-śarīra*, transformation). In the Final Teaching (Mahāyāna), however, all seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are permanently severed from the first bhūmi.

A small portion of both discriminative and innate [afflictions], as well as within the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), are also [severed]; from one portion of the bhūmis upwards, one receives the transformation body. Question: If...
Question: Why do those who do not retain their afflictions (*kleśa*) employ the great compassion of "acting in concert" (*samānārthatā*) to gather in sentient beings?

Answer: In the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-yāna*), because the wisdom of vows is inferior, one retains afflictions to assist those vows. In the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-yāna*), because the bodhisattva’s wisdom of vows is superior, one partially retains them to undergo birth.

In the Sudden Teaching (*tathatā-yāna*), since the stages of practice cannot be described, the physical basis for rebirth is likewise indeterminate. In the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-yāna*), while the transformation of support (*parāvṛtti*) is not discussed, it is nonetheless partially retained.
From the stage of *dāna* up to the tenth ground, prior to the *vimala-samādhi*, one attains the "fleshly eye" (*māṃsa-cakṣus*) that perceives universally;
therefore, it is known that this refers to the *paricchinna* (segmented) body. Furthermore, it is because Sudhana, with his segmented body, exhausted the causal stages. Question:
Why is the *pariṇāmanika* (transformative) body not mentioned here? Answer: Because this teaching does not differentiate between the coarse and subtle aspects of birth and death.

The characteristics [of these realms] are collectively treated as a single limit based on their defects and afflictions. If one’s faith is fulfilled and accords with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), that limit is suddenly overturned;

thus, the segmented [birth-and-death] becomes free of obstruction. Furthermore, because it is not easy to transform the coarse into the subtle, this is not mentioned here. Therefore, the *Huan-yuan guan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source) states:
"Sentient beings grasp and cling to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which shift and flow from moment to moment; this is called suffering. This is the teaching of the Bodhisattvas."

To cause one to realize that the aggregates (*skandha*) are empty and quiescent, and that karma arises from delusion, and to never for a moment abandon the two gates of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, so that when the cause is extinguished the fruit perishes and suffering has no basis to arise—merely ensuring that one does not enter the three miserable realms (*apāya*) is what is called "universally taking the place of others in undergoing suffering.
Fourth, regarding the phrase "if one sees," the eleventh fascicle of the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra) from the Liang dynasty states: "If a Bodhisattva, by such a method..."

The *Vyākhyā* states: A Bodhisattva is able to know such matters; if there is a person whose mind intends to commit an evil deed such as an *ānantarya* [immediate] offense, the Bodhisattva thoroughly understands that mind and has no other expedient means [than to act].

Thus, by performing the ten deeds including killing and so forth with a mind free from defilement or turbidity, one generates immeasurable merit and wisdom, and swiftly attains the supreme fruit of unsurpassed *bodhi*.
One might think: "I can cause him to abandon these evil deeds by merely taking his life;

furthermore, I know that if he gives up his life, he will certainly be reborn in a happy realm, whereas if he does not give up his life, he will surely commit this karma and suffer for a long time. The Bodhisattva reflects:
"I must fall into hell; let me undergo this retribution of suffering on his behalf, so that this person may experience only a small portion of it in the present life."
Because one undergoes great happiness in future lives by enduring slight suffering, it is like a skilled physician who first applies a mild treatment to cure a serious illness;
the same applies to the commission of theft, sexual misconduct, and so forth. Furthermore, the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Repaying Kindness) states:

"A bodhisattva knows kindness and repays kindness by cultivating great skillful means to benefit sentient beings; one should recognize that these are taught as skillful means manifested according to what is appropriate."
After the parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata King Fearless of the Past, during the period of the True Dharma, there was the son of a Brahmin who was intelligent and wise.
He had received and upheld the five precepts and maintained the True Dharma.

On account of some business, he traveled to another country with a company of five hundred companions. When they reached a perilous road ahead, five hundred bands of bandits intended to plunder the traveling party; among them was one [who...]
A man who had previously been on friendly terms with the brahmin’s son came to inform him beforehand: "At the first watch of the night, the thieves will rise up;
you must leave secretly so as not to let your companions know.
Having heard this, the brahmin’s son was like a person choking, unable to swallow and unable to spit it out; he wished to tell his companions, yet he feared that they would harm him.
"If I remain silent, my companions will fall into the evil realms; yet if I do not speak, the bandits will harm my companions and fall into the evil realms.
Having reflected thus, he immediately took up a knife and severed the life of the bandit. "The retribution of the three evil realms is what is fitting for me," he thought.
All his companions said, "You are a superior man; why have you committed such an evil deed? The son of the Brahmin then related the preceding events in detail.
The same applies to the bandits who accompany the arousal of the bodhicitta. Fifth, "by means of the initial [vow]" and so forth:

because from the very beginning a Bodhisattva cultivates the correct vow to undergo suffering for the sake of sentient beings until reaching the ultimate stage, that vow becomes sovereign, such that they constantly dwell in the evil destinies to rescue suffering beings—like Kṣitigarbha Bodhisattva and King Saṃdarśanarāja—and even manifest as a body during times of famine.

They become large fish, all of which belong to that same class; or they emit light that illuminates everything, with their spiritual powers adding grace in the unseen realm—such instances are not limited to one type.

*Commentary:* Among the seven meanings above, the first consists solely of the intention (*āśaya*); the next two serve as conditions (*pratyaya*); the next two involve actual substitution (*pratideśanā*); and the last two involve contemplation according to principle (*yoniśomanasikāra*).
*Sub-commentary:* However, it is only when there is a karmic connection (*sahakāri-pratyaya*) that one is able to perform such substitution. *Excerpts:* The seven meanings mentioned above.

The third section below provides a detailed analysis. It states that "it is only by virtue of having a karmic connection (*sambandha*) that [the Bodhisattva] can substitute [for others]. This anticipates and addresses a potential objection:
"If one relies on the two meanings of the fourth and fifth [stages], one should be able to universally substitute for all;

why, then, do sentient beings still undergo suffering? In response, it says: "It is only through the presence of a karmic connection that one is able to substitute. According to the *Dajingchao* (Notes on the Mahāyāna Sūtra), there are two further points regarding this.
Because karma is either determinate or indeterminate, that which is indeterminate can be substituted.

Furthermore, if undergoing suffering is beneficial, the Bodhisattva causes [the being] to undergo it so that they may ultimately attain liberation. This is like parents instructing their child by entrusting them to a strict teacher for training;
such a profound intention is not something that ordinary or inferior beings can understand.
△ Third, the commentary concludes on inexhaustibility:

"When the realm of empty space is exhausted, when the realm of sentient beings is exhausted, when the karma of sentient beings is exhausted, and when the afflictions of sentient beings are exhausted—only then will this dedication of mine be exhausted.
Moment by moment it continues in succession without interruption."
To sever the karmic actions of body, speech, and mind without weariness or fatigue.
△ Commentary 4: Concluding the benefits so that they may be known.
"Good son, these are the ten great vows of a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, fully and perfectly accomplished. △ If..."
All bodhisattvas who accord with and enter into this great vow will be able to bring all sentient beings to maturity;
they will be able to accord with *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
and they will be able to fulfill the ocean of practices and vows of Samantabhadra Bodhisattva. Therefore, son of good family, you should understand this meaning in this way.
△ Commentary (Sū): Part Two: Manifesting the Superior Virtue of the Sūtra; Sub-part One: Comparing the Virtue of Hearing the Sūtra.
"If there be good sons or good daughters...
[The *Chao* (Excerpts) states under the second section, "Manifesting the Superior Virtue of the Sūtra": the terms "good sons or good daughters" are used as a collective designation.]

To speak of them in terms of the categories of discipline (*vinaya*), there are nine; to speak of them in terms of the types of persons, there are seven: namely, three for men and four for women. Regarding the three for men:

among householders, there is one, which is the male lay follower (*upāsaka*) who observes the five precepts; among those who have left the home life, there are two, namely the *bhikṣu* and the *śrāmaṇera*. Regarding the four for women:
among householders, there is one, which is the female lay follower (*upāsikā*) who observes the five precepts; as for those who have left the home life...
There are three [categories]: namely, bhikṣuṇīs, śikṣamāṇās, and śrāmaṇerīs; thus there are seven.
To these are further added two other types—men and women who have not received the precepts—making nine in total.
These nine categories encompass all virtuous men and women, both those outside and within the kalpa.
△ [This is] to fill all worlds throughout the ten directions— numbering as many atoms as there are in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields—
with the most exquisite seven treasures and the supreme peace and happiness of devas and humans.
The *Shu* (Commentary) states that regarding the "seven treasures," the *Zhendi ji* (Record of True Meanings) explains that there are one hundred and eight types of precious substances in total;
yet, speaking of the most excellent, these are fully subsumed within the seven treasures: first, gold; second, silver; third, coral;
fourth, red pearls—produced by red insects or being red in substance themselves; fifth, maṇi jewels, which are wish-fulfilling gems; sixth... [the text continues].

The *śaṅkha* (conch-shell) is a substance like stone, with an intermingling of blue and white; the *musāragalva* (cat's-eye) differs slightly from that described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, as can be known.
△ Bestowing [gifts] upon all sentient beings throughout all those worlds. △ Making offerings to all those...
The merit obtained by the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the worlds through a continuous succession of eons as numerous as the atoms within that many Buddha-fields—
compared to the merit of anyone who hears this *Vow King Sūtra* but once,
the former does not equal even a hundredth part, nor a thousandth part, nor even a fraction of it, up to an *upaniṣad*.
It does not even equal a fraction of a *pāṇiśata*.

△ [The Commentary] has two parts: first, revealing the virtues of the other practices; second, specifically clarifying the merits of the practice of Dharma. First, a general explanation of the merits of the practice of Dharma:
"Furthermore, there may be someone who, with deep faith, upholds, recites, and even transcribes this great vow."
A single four-line verse.
This commentary generally elucidates the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*), which comprises ten types in total: first, copying; second, making offerings;
third, giving it away; fourth, listening; fifth, reading aloud; sixth, receiving and upholding; seventh, explaining to others; eighth, reciting; ninth, reflecting; and tenth, practicing.
Practice. △ Commentary: Now there are only four [practices], namely: first, receiving and upholding; second, reading; third, reciting; and fourth, copying.
Combined with the previously mentioned listening and hearing, these constitute five practices. Even as few as two characters encompass all that remains. ○ Sub-commentary:
Regarding "a single four-line verse," in Sanskrit it is called *pāda*, properly *pada*; this is translated here as "line" (*jù*). According to the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*...

There are five types of treatises (*śāstra*); here, we take a phrase from among the five internal sense bases (*adhyātma-āyatana*), namely eight characters as a single phrase, which corresponds here to a line of five or four characters.
As for "verse" (*gāthā*), it is a Sanskrit term translated here as "stanza" (*yǒng*). A stanza consists of four lines; this refers to the minimum number, not exceeding that.
A "four-line verse" (*catuspāda*) refers to a group of words that fully expresses a meaning; because a single meaning is complete within it, it is called a four-line verse.

Each such verse conveys a distinct sense. Here, the intended meaning is that if a person upholds even a single four-line verse of this sutra, they will be able to eliminate the karma of the five immediate retributions (*pañcānantarya-karma*) and so forth. First, the ten kinds of dharma-practice are explained in general.
Regarding the practice of the Dharma (*dharmacaryā*), there are ten kinds in total, as listed by name in the commentary: 1. **Transcribing**:

There are those who, out of reverence for the Dharma, constantly transcribe the sūtras themselves. 2. **Making Offerings**: There are those who constantly offer incense and flowers to the scriptures and the Dharma. 3. **Distributing**:
There are those who, having personally mastered the art of transcription, bestow it upon others so that they may recite and read the texts.
Or, one may personally reflect and dedicate this merit to others: (4) those who constantly listen to the teachings at Dharma assemblies;
(5) those who constantly peruse the teachings, reading them according to the text;
(6) those who receive and uphold the scriptures, never forgetting them; (7) those who explain...
1. Those who demonstrate: there are those who, having personally attained the flavor of the meaning, constantly expound and skillfully reveal it to others.
2. Those who recite: there are those who memorize the words and phrases and constantly chant them themselves a thousand or ten thousand times. 3. Those who contemplate:
there are those who, having heard the teaching, contemplate its principles and give rise to the wisdom of realization. 4. Those who practice: there are those who... [The text ends here.]
To personally realize the teachings and practice according to the Dharma is also called the "Ten Dharma-Masters.

Among these, one is the "Master of Persons" because they are able to explain the principles and meanings; the remaining nine are the "Dharma as Master. Regarding these ten modes of Dharma practice, the *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā* states:
"Transcribing, making offerings, giving to others, listening, reading, receiving, upholding, [explaining, reciting, and contemplating]."
To explain, recite, contemplate, and practice refers, in general terms, to the expedient means for upholding the Mahāyāna teachings and entering into the principle.
In the fourth section, the "Distinction of Teachings," within the *Huayan Samādhi Contemplation Gate* composed by the Great Master Xianshou, a hypothetical question is raised:
"Is it essential for sentient beings practicing cultivation to uphold the holy teachings?"
Is it necessary to abandon the teachings? Answer: There are ten categories. First, there are sentient beings who, lacking discernment, arbitrarily discard the sacred words;
their own minds are deluded, and they further follow false friends to practice in violation of the teachings, employing craftiness and deception to mislead others—these are evil persons.
Second, there are also sentient beings who likewise turn their backs on the sacred teachings, yet do so with a sincere and straightforward mind.

First, those who, seeking liberation, diligently practice asceticism but ultimately derive no benefit; these two types of people alike abandon the holy teachings and do not rely on their underlying principles.
Third, those who merely recite the sacred words without understanding their meaning and intent, relying on the holy teachings to seek fame and profit;
they contradict what they themselves recite and are thus called "evil persons. Fourth, those who merely pursue the literal phrasing and do not understand...
Regarding the principles of meaning (artha), those who merely recite and chant with a straightforward mind, though free from artifice and deceit, derive no benefit from them.
These two aforementioned types of persons both fail to relinquish the teachings yet fail to attain their true meaning; as such, the four preceding approaches are all untenable.

Fifth, those who recite the holy words and possess a partial understanding of view, conduct, and practice, but read many phrases while engaging in little cultivation. Sixth, those who are extensive...

1. Seeking the sacred teachings; 2. Universal knowledge through understanding and practice; 3. Gradually abbreviating the sacred words; 4. Grasping the intended meaning; 5. Single-minded cultivation; 6.
Receiving and upholding the meaning once attained, such that one relies solely on practice without further seeking the words; 7.

Seeking the teachings to realize their ultimate purport—that all phenomena are without exception in accord with the nature of reality—and thus neither clinging to nor abandoning the teachings, for these very words and teachings are themselves in accord with the nature of reality.
Ninth, regarding the practice according to the provisional teachings: one constantly upholds the teaching that accords with the nature of reality, neither abandoning nor clinging to it;
one perpetually contemplates the principle beyond words, neither discarding nor stagnating in it. These five preceding gates have not yet reached ultimate perfection. Tenth:

having sought the teaching and attained the true principle, one is unimpeded regarding both teaching and principle; one perpetually contemplates the principle without being hindered by the teaching, and constantly upholds the teaching without being hindered by the principle.
This principle is precisely the point where both principle and teaching are merged into a single contemplation; only then can it be called ultimate.
Regarding these ten gates above, the first four are entirely not to be followed in sequence. The subsequent five gates proceed from shallow to deep according to the capacity for awakening and entry;
however, these are merely expedient means for transforming the ordinary person into a sage and have not yet reached the ultimate. Only the tenth gate is truly [the ultimate].
Furthermore, the Great Master Xianshou stated that in upholding Mahāyāna sūtras, one must understand five matters.
First, one must clarify the text, which has five aspects: (1) being well-versed in the divisions, their beginnings and endings, and their mutual connections and sequential conjunctions;

and (2) ensuring the expression of the meaning is complete, without addition or omission. Second, one must understand the subject matter, which also has five aspects: (1) the place where the teaching was given...
The ritual for requesting the Teacher and his assembly, as well as understanding the meaning of what is taught in the perfect sound, also consists of five parts:

first, briefly indicating the essential outline; second, explaining in detail to remove doubts; third, using analogies to facilitate understanding; fourth, citing examples to establish the proof; and fifth, pointing out the benefits to encourage study. Furthermore, there are five ways to grasp its meaning:

causing [beings] to resolve upon the Great Mind (*mahācitta*), contemplating the true reality (*tattva*), subduing the afflictions (*kleśa*), practicing loving-kindness (*maitrī*), and... [the final term is missing from the source].
Compassionately rescuing all beings, one diligently cultivates the ten thousand practices (*sāhasra-saṃskāra*). Regarding the five ways of conforming to these practices, there are five types:
first, regarding the dharmic practice within the four preceding gates, it abides in both body and mind without ever ceasing for even a moment;

second, traversing the four preceding gates to give rise to the superior mind—namely, giving rise to the thought of its being difficult to encounter regarding the aforementioned verbal teachings, and giving rise to a mind of reverence regarding the aforementioned phenomenal signs, while maintaining mindfulness.
The Buddha is difficult to encounter; one laments one’s own meager merit from the past.
One gives rise to a heart of love and joy toward the preceding principles and meaning, with sorrow and joy mingling together. Third, upholding the True Dharma:

this refers to transcribing and circulating the preceding written teachings, painting images to manifest the assembly of the Buddha-dharma, and succinctly summarizing the essential meaning to provide detailed guidance for practitioners. Fourth, increasing one's own practice.
This refers to associating with virtuous friends and engaging in focused contemplation, which constitutes five practices that achieve unimpeded action:

because one has attained the meaning, the expression is transcended, and thus it cannot be clung to; yet because the transcendence of expression is due to the teaching, it cannot be abandoned. Therefore, regarding the teaching, one gives rise to the practice of neither clinging nor abandoning.
Although these are now opened up as ten dharma-practices, they are merely the various conditions that provide the necessary support for the primary and auxiliary factors of realization.
Taken together, these are called "receiving and upholding" (*śīla-dhāraṇa*) and "cultivating through practice. Those who rely entirely upon this can take it as the perfect cause;

by practicing with diligent perseverance without regression, they shall all realize the fruit of fulfillment. From its introduction to the Great Tang, there have been many practitioners who followed the Dharma and cultivated their studies, resulting in spiritual communications and auspicious omens in great numbers.
These are fully recorded in the five fascicles of the *Huayan zhuan* (Biographies of the Avataṃsaka) and the two fascicles of the *Zuǎnlíng jì* (Records of Spiritually Manifested Miracles).
To summarize what has been said: it refers to the transcription of scriptures in five colors.
Specifically, Wang Yanming and Wang Yuanxi of the Later Wei dynasty—men of brilliant intelligence and vast learning—once used incense and gold to transcribe one hundred copies of the scriptures.

Each copy was composed of five types of incense and placed within a casket made of the seven treasures. They maintained a pure fast day and night while performing their devotions, at which time the scriptures emitted a divine radiance.
The five colors illuminated the courtyard and halls, witnessed by all who saw them; those who were thereby inspired to resolve their minds for enlightenment were beyond counting.

The *zhū* fragrance spread in all directions, and his monastic virtue was perfect and wondrous. He unified the essential teachings and reached the ultimate cultivation. He maintained a single pure garden where he planted *zhū* trees with fresh blossoms, interspersed with fragrant herbs.
Whenever he was about to bathe, he would enter the garden and irrigate the plants with scented water. Three years had passed since the *zhū* trees were first planted.
The fragrance spread in all directions; later, when paper was used to transcribe the sutra, as soon as several lines were written, each character emitted radiance.

Second, regarding the auspicious omen of the offering bird: the monk Facheng constructed a Huayan Hall at Gaigu, where he painted the transformation tableaux of the seven locations and nine assemblies and transcribed this sutra, making offerings with single-minded devotion. From time to time, auspicious birds appeared.

The physical form was impermanent; holding flowers in his mouth, he entered the room and circumambulated to make offerings. Three times he offered water from his cupped palms, yet it still saved living beings.

The monk Miqiataluo, a person who had attained the third fruit [of Arhatship] from the Kingdom of Siṃhala, once encountered various monks reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Xitaiyuan Temple. Suddenly, his expression changed and he said, "I did not know this."
In that place as well, there was this sutra; with palms joined in reverence and filled with joy, they praised it, saying: "The merit of this Mahāvaipulya Sūtra is inconceivable.
According to tradition from the Western Regions, there were those who, while praising this sutra, sprinkled water upon their palms;
even those insects and ants touched by that water who then passed away were all reborn in the heavens—how much more so for those who receive, uphold, recite, contemplate, and meditate upon it!
The Bodhisattva Vajra of the Wisdom of All-Knowledge said: "Examine the merit of these four types of hearing;
it is equal to the merit accumulated through the practices of one with all-knowledge. Fifth, regarding reading and reciting: Miaoran of Sui dynasty Chanding Monastery practiced walking upon the void.
The monk Huiewu of the same monastery held the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and lived in seclusion together with a monk who held the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* on a cliff in Zhongnan Mountain.
While dwelling in the trees and seeking food, each was devoted to his own practice. Later, a person invited them both for a vegetarian feast. The two men yielded to one another;
the host said, "I invite Hua-yan Wu-shang," and he immediately followed him. It was actually a mountain deity. A thousand arhats all deferred to him, requesting that he take the seat of honor.
When the meal was finished, the deity called for a youth to serve him, and as soon as the youth entered, Wu-shang obtained the deity's secret oral instructions.
Tong returned to retrieve his scriptures; he bid farewell to his *nirvāṇa-saṃghāṭī* robe and departed, treading through the air with a transcendent air, so that no one knew where he had gone.

Sixth, regarding the upholding [of the teachings]: Sengbian was as radiant as if facing the actual realm [of the Buddha]. He studied under Dharma Master Xu and studied the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for a long time without attaining realization.
For three years, he practiced with single-minded devotion in a pure chamber, until he dreamed of Samantabhadra instructing him. Upon awakening, he understood the entire text thoroughly.
He was as clearly illuminated as if looking into a mirror. Seventh, regarding the "Flower and Fan" (Chinese and Sanskrit) correspondence:

during the Song dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra, a native of India, brought the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* to this land. Over seven hundred people requested him to lecture on it, but they regretted that he was not yet proficient in the Chinese language.
They prayed with devotion and sincerity, whereupon he dreamed of a person holding a sword and carrying a... [fragmentary text].

The person who had beheaded himself was An-t'i (Bhadra); he came to master the Tang language after reciting it several dozen times, hence the phrase "mastering the rhymes" (*tōng yùn*), which is followed by both humans and devas.
During the Wei dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Ratnamati, a native of Central India, arrived in this land and also mastered the Chinese language;
he lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Shortly thereafter, a man suddenly appeared holding a ceremonial tablet.

His appearance was like that of a celestial official. When the Emperor ordered him to invite the Master to lecture on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the presiding lecturer, the *vinaya* master, and those responsible for the Buddhist chants were all required to accompany him.
Ratnamati asked, "May I wait until the lectures are finished before departing? The envoy replied, "So be it.
Upon the conclusion of the lectures, he suddenly passed away upon the Dharma seat along with the presiding lecturer and others; everyone sighed in admiration.
A divine light entered the monastery; the Dharma Master Fazang, whose courtesy name was Xuanshu, at the age of seventeen, took leave of his parents to seek the Dharma on Mount Taibai.
Later, when he returned home to visit his ailing mother, he encountered Master Yan lecturing on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* at Yunhua Monastery.
At midnight, he suddenly saw a divine light illuminating the courtyard and buildings, knowing that there was a person of extraordinary character there. When dawn broke, he went to visit Master Yan.
The Master (Heshang) then served him with reverence and deeply penetrated the essential meaning of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*.
This was truly because the wondrousness of a single phrase encompasses all meanings without exception, and the power of a single verse can shatter the hells. He was a man from Jingzhao surnamed Wang;
his personal name is unknown. After he died, he was led by two men to hell, where he saw a monk who said, "This is Dizang. The Master then commanded—
He recited a verse, saying: "If one wishes to thoroughly understand all Buddhas of the three periods of time, one should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm:
everything is created solely by the mind. Thereupon, he attained liberation. Wherever his voice reached, those who were suffering were all freed from their pain.
One day, he revived and remembered this verse; he recounted it to both monastics and laypeople, whereupon the virtuous ones sought out the scriptures and its source.
It was learned that these were the verses of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* from the Yāma Heaven.

Regarding the recitation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, every time Fán Xuánzhì of Āndìng Commandery recited it according to the instructions of Master Shùn, he frequently obtained śarīra from within his mouth;
over the course of time, there were several hundred grains in total. This coincided with the occasion when the divine monk Lǜshī of Jīngzhào appeared.
At the beginning of the Zhenguan era, a monk stayed at an inn by the Baqiao Bridge in a separate room from the innkeeper.
He drank wine and ate meat. A Vinaya Master, whose observance of the precepts was pure and rigorous, grew indignant and rebuked him.

After the monk had finished eating, he rinsed his mouth with ash-water and recited the Avataṃsaka Sūtra; in a short while, he completed one fascicle, and before the fifth watch was over, he had finished the entire work.

The Vinaya Master entered the room and wept with grief as he offered his repentance and apologies; when dawn arrived, they parted ways. He did not disclose his name, nor was it known where he had gone.
Jiushiwei then attained realization of the non-arising of phenomena. He composed verses of praise that ascended into the void, thereby attaining liberation.
Later, at Foguang Temple on Mount Tai, he established a vihara and recited the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, following the scripture to manifest the Buddha-nature.
Guangguan again sought Mañjuśrī and was able to see him. [Mañjuśrī] asked, "Why do you pay homage to me? You should instead repent and reproach yourself.
Later, through his own seeking, he realized non-arising (*anutpāda*). He then desired to pay extensive homage to all Buddhas to verify these causes and conditions.

In response, the Buddhas manifested themselves and spoke this verse for him: "The Dharma of the Buddhas is quiescent and profoundly deep; Only now, after practicing through vast eons, have you attained it."
If one can open and understand this Dharma-eye, all Buddhas will rejoice in it. Again, he asked: "How can the dharma of quiescent extinction be taught to others?
The Buddha then vanished from sight, and only a voice was heard, saying: "The wisdom of skillful means serves as a lamp to illuminate the realm of the mind;
yet, if one seeks to investigate the true reality of dharmas, nothing at all is seen. (10) Cultivation.
The Sea God heard him and sent down a torrential rain. Sengdaoying was a native of Bozhou; when he reached the age of twelve, his parents arranged a marriage for him.
For five years they lived together, yet he remained entirely free from worldly affairs.

Later, while listening to a lecture on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, he left the household life and entered Baiti Temple on Mount Taihang to practice *śamatha-vipaśyanā*. At that time, there was a severe drought, and he lectured exclusively on the *Avataṃsaka*.
Yan Gan said that two youths were sea deities who had come to listen to his lecture on the sutra; he then caused it to rain, and in an instant, a torrential downpour ensued.
When Tiantong went to meet him, the great waters overflowed. During the Sui dynasty, Linggan lectured on the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* while residing at Xingshan Monastery;
he constantly practiced the contemplations of Tuṣita Heaven and the *Avataṃsaka*. On the day of his death, a celestial youth came to him.
He welcomed [the monk] but did not follow him as he departed, saying, "My aspiration lies in the Flower Treasury World (*Huazang*).

Soon thereafter, he saw a vast expanse of water filled with lotus flowers, whereupon he joyfully exclaimed, "This is indeed the fulfillment of my vow! He then took leave of his fellow resident, the novice Tongzhen;
having finished their parting, he suddenly passed away.

△ It can swiftly eliminate the five deeds of immediate retribution. △ All physical and mental ailments of the world, various forms of suffering and affliction, and even all evil karma as numerous as the atoms within a Buddha-field, shall all be eradicated.
The *Chao* states: Regarding the "five acts of immediate retribution" (*pañcānantarya-karma*), the Sanskrit is *pañcānantaryāṇi*.
In the vernacular (Gāndhārī), it is called *pañcānantariya*; alternatively, it is called *avīci*, or *abhi-ku*.
Translated [into Chinese], it is rendered as "no-selection" (*wuzé*) or "immediate" (*wújiàn*). It possesses four meanings, or perhaps five: first, "immediacy of rebirth" (*upapatty-anantara*).
Second, there is no interval in lifespan, because there is no premature death; third, there is no interval in physical stature, because the body is fully developed;
fourth, there is no interval in the experience of suffering, because there is no intermediate state (*antarābhava*) as a place of transition;

fifth, there is no interval in the retribution received, because it is certain to follow in the very next birth. Because these five conditions are present, they are called "uninterrupted" (*ānantarya*); thus, by performing even a single such deed, one immediately incurs [retribution].

The five mentioned here as retributions refer to the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya-karma*): namely, killing one’s father, harming one’s mother, shedding the blood of a Buddha, killing an Arhat, and causing a schism in the Saṃgha.

If one commits even a single one of these five, one incurs a heinous crime and falls into the Avīci Hell, where one undergoes uninterrupted suffering for one intermediate kalpa; therefore, they are called the five actions of immediate retribution. Furthermore, this...

Regarding the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), there is a distinction between minor and major varieties. The five heinous crimes mentioned above are still considered minor; however, in the Buddha’s *Candragarbha-sūtra* and other texts, they are termed major heinous crimes.

Thus, the eighth fascicle of that sūtra states: "If one merely sheds the blood of a single Buddha, one incurs the crime of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*) such that its consequences cannot even be calculated, leading to rebirth in the Avīci Hell;
how much more so for one who sheds the blood of ten thousand koṭis of Buddhas? Ultimately, there is no escape.

Some say that if one causes affliction, reviles, beats, or binds those who have shaved their heads and donned even a single thread of the *kāṣāya*—whether they have not received the precepts or have broken them—the offense incurred is greater than that; how much more so for one who upholds the precepts?

Therefore, it is called "the great [offense]. As stated in the verse below, this refers to the five most heinous *ānantarya* offenses as well as the four grave transgressions (*catur-uttara-pārājika*).
It is called "near" because its transgression is likewise grave; thus it is termed "near.
Except for the power of the majesty of the *Samantabhadra-praṇidhāna-rāja* and the *dhāraṇī* methods, nothing can eliminate it.
Regarding all illnesses of body and mind in the world, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, there are two kinds: first, physical illness; second, mental illness. As for the body...
There are five types of illness: first, those caused by water; second, those caused by wind; third, those caused by heat;

fourth, miscellaneous illnesses; and fifth, adventitious illnesses. There are four kinds of adventitious illnesses: first, performing tasks beyond one's capacity; second, falling due to forgetfulness or error;
third, injury from blades, staves, tiles, or stones; and fourth, possession by malevolent spirits. Furthermore, there are also illnesses of the mind.
There are four kinds: first, elation; second, fear; third, sorrow; and fourth, delusion.
Furthermore, son of good family, there are generally three kinds of physical and mental illness: first, retribution for karma;
second, not being able to remain far removed from adversaries; and third, the transition of the seasons. Such are the names of these various causes and conditions.

Regarding the causes and conditions for the discrimination of sensation: the names of various diseases such as wind-disorders (*vāta*), and so forth, include mental distress, lung congestion, upward gasping, coughing and retching, heart palpitations, and diarrhea—these are what is meant by the discrimination of the sensation of disease.
Furthermore, the "various kinds of suffering and affliction" mentioned here are of two types.
The first refers directly to the various sufferings and afflictions of all diseases;
the second encompasses all other sufferings and afflictions, namely all matters of oppression and the like.
△ All demonic armies, yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, bhūtas, and so forth.
All evil ghosts and spirits who drink blood and eat flesh will completely depart. At times, they may even resolve to draw near and provide protection.
This commentary briefly explains the merits; it states that merely being freed from evil is itself a present retribution.

In the sub-commentary (*Chao*), regarding the section on "ghosts and devils secretly providing protection," there are two points: first, it clarifies the departure of ghosts and devils; second, it reveals their protective resolve.

Regarding the initial mention of "Māra": in Sanskrit it is fully called *māra*, which here means "the slayer. He is the slayer because he destroys the life-force of wisdom of those who practice the Path;
thus, he is the very root of birth and death. Briefly stated, there are four types: first, the *kleśa-māra* (affliction demon), which is the cause of birth and death;

second, the *devaputra-māra* (heavenly demon), which is the condition for birth and death; third, the *skandha-māra* (aggregate demon); and fourth, the *maraṇa-māra* (death demon). These constitute birth and death.

Regarding the "fruits of death," what is here called the "army of Māra" refers to the celestial Māras; "army" means a multitude, referring to the various spirits and deities below who constitute the hosts of Māra’s army.
As for the *yakṣas*, this is translated as "fierce and swift," meaning they are rapid and agile.
The *rākṣasas* are a class of ghosts that consume flesh and blood; there is a city of *rākṣasas* in the ocean into which people may fall.
They frequently suffer from being devoured. *Kumbhāṇḍa* means "Guardian of the Palace Deity" (*shǒugōngshén*) and is also called "Gourd Ghost" (*dōngguāguǐ*), because their scrotum resembles a gourd.
*Piśāca* refers to ghosts that devour vital essence; among the *preta* (hungry ghosts), this class is slightly superior.
*Bhūta* means "Large-Body Ghost" (*dàshēnguǐ*) and is also called "Self-Arising Ghost" (*zìshēngguǐ*); these are of this same category.
Those born from parents are called yakṣas; those who are self-born are called bhūtas.
The phrase "drinking blood and so forth" collectively enumerates all such classes. "All are completely removed" is the concluding summary of their removal.

Furthermore, "also being a present retribution" refers to the present-life retribution (dṛṣṭadharmavedanīya) in contrast to the subsequent-life retribution (upapadyavedanīya) and the later-life retribution (aparaparyāyavedanīya), thereby completing the three types.
△ Commentary [Section 2]: Partially citing one practice to extensively reveal all virtues. [Subsection 1]:
Citing one practice. Therefore, if a person recites this vow—here, the commentary cites one example to represent the rest.

△ Commentary 2: An extensive discussion of the qualities [reveals] that although many superior qualities are possessed, they do not exceed the five fruits. ○ Sub-commentary: Regarding the statement that they do not exceed the five fruits, the *Abhidharmakośa* clarifies the characteristics as follows:
"The ripening (*vipāka*) is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), belonging to sentient beings (*sattvākhya*), and produced by determinate (*vyākṛta*) karma;

however, because it is exclusively non-obscured indeterminate (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*), it does not extend to other [types of indeterminate states]. It is called 'produced by determinate [karma] of sentient beings' because it is induced by causes that are wholesome or unwholesome."
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "All unwholesome dharmas result in the maturation of fruits (*vipākaphala*) within the evil destinies;

wholesome contaminated (*sāsrava*) dharmas result in the maturation of fruits within the good destinies. It further explains that the "outflowing fruit" (*niṣyandaphala*) resembles its own cause, being similar to its own kind, while also including the cause itself.
Moreover, the thirty-eighth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "Because one practices the unwholesome, one takes pleasure in abiding in the unwholesome."
Because unwholesome dharmas increase when one is habituated to wholesome dharmas, one dwells happily in wholesome dharmas;
thus, wholesome dharmas increase as their outflowing fruit (*niṣyanda-phala*), or as a subsequent result that follows from a prior action. This has two meanings;

the latter meaning—that the fruit resembles the cause—is precisely this point. For example, [the result of] killing is a short lifespan, and so forth; this refers to the former meaning, namely, the subsequent result of—

Retribution is like one who delighted in killing in a previous life now still delighting in killing; this is the meaning. Disconnection (*visamyoga*) refers to the exhaustion of all fetters through wisdom;

it is called the fruit of disconnection because it is manifested by that disconnection which is the cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*). "Wisdom" means discernment (*pravicaya*); "exhaustion" means cessation (*nirodha*).
This is because it is manifested by the disconnection that is the cessation through deliberation. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "By means of the Path..."

The cessation of afflictions is called the fruit of disjunction (*visamyoga-phala*). Furthermore, because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) eliminate various afflictions through the mundane path (*laukika-mārga*) without reaching ultimate completion, it is not the fruit of disjunction.
If a result arises by the power of that [cause], it is called the fruit of human effort (*puruṣakāra-phala*).

If a phenomenon arises by the power of that [cause], such as when an impure meditative absorption (*sāsrava-samādhi*) of a higher stage arises due to the power of the preparatory application (*prayoga*) of a lower stage, yet remains distinct [from that cause].
That which is bound [to arise] is called "non-arising"; because it is realized through the power of the Path, it may also be termed the "non-arising fruit of human effort" (*puruṣakāra-phala*).
Excluding preceding conditioned phenomena, there is the "dominant fruit" (*adhipati-phala*) of conditioned phenomena;

that is to say, when a conditioned phenomenon arises, the fact that other phenomena do not obstruct it constitutes its dominant fruit. Thus, the dominant fruit consists only of conditioned phenomena, excluding those conditioned phenomena that have already arisen.
Dharmas that are not dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*) refer to cases where the fruit is either simultaneous with or subsequent to its cause;

since it is impossible for a preceding fruit to have a subsequent cause, these are excluded by the term "except. Aside from these cases of precedence and succession, all other conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are dominant fruits, as the treatise states:
"the fruit of dominance" (*adhipatiphala*). Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi* states: "If visual consciousness and so forth are the dominant fruits of the eye faculty..."
Up to and including the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), these are the dominant fruits (*adhipatiphala*) of the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*).

That the constituent parts of a sentient being are neither dispersed nor destroyed is the dominant fruit of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). The commentary explains: the various faculties, such as the eye and so forth, do not obstruct the arising of consciousness;

that the constituent parts of the body are not destroyed or dispersed, thereby preventing the interruption of the life-faculty—all of this is termed a "dominant fruit" from the perspective of the meaning of non-obstruction. Note: *adhipatiphala* is translated here as "dominant fruit. The term "仔" (zi) at the end of the passage indicates the conclusion of the section.

Question: What is the distinction between *puruṣakāra-phala* (the fruit of human effort) and *adhipati-phala* (the dominant fruit)? Answer: *Puruṣakāra-phala* applies exclusively to the agent (*kartṛ*), whereas *adhipati-phala* extends to all others.
For example, the tools employed by a craftsman to produce a work receive the names of both *puruṣakāra-phala* and *adhipati-phala* with respect to the craftsman who employs them.

However, with respect to other things that are neither the craftsman nor the instruments of production, they do not receive the name of *puruṣakāra-phala*, because they are not the human effort (*puruṣakāra*) of the agent. Nevertheless, as for those mentioned above...

This is cited from the "Chapter on the Roots" (*Mūlavastu*) of the *Abhidharmakośa*, where it is established that these five fruits are produced by means of six causes; however, this is not what is required here.
We simply recite the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna*, whereby these five fruits are spontaneously possessed through a single cause.

This is like the various schools which share the same causes but differ in their fruits—just as within the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, one practices the same five kinds of ten wholesome actions, yet the resulting fruits are each distinct.
There are cases where the causes differ but the fruits are the same, such as this cause and the six causes; that both causes and fruits may differ can be understood through reflection.

The perfection of merit alone constitutes one mark; this is called the common cause, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, "Lion’s Roar" Chapter.
Thus, each of the thirty-two marks has its own specific cause, as that sūtra says:
"If there is a bodhisattva mahāsattva whose observance of the precepts is unshakable, whose mind of giving is immovable, and who dwells securely in truthful speech like Mount Sumeru..."
By these karmic conditions, Śāriputra, one obtains the mark of having soles as level as the bottom of a casket.

If one provides and supports parents, teachers, elders, and even animals with wealth acquired in accordance with the Dharma, by these karmic conditions one obtains the mark of the thousand-spoked wheel on the soles of the feet.
If one refrains from killing and stealing, and always gives rise to joy toward parents, teachers, and elders...
Through these karmic conditions, one attains three marks: first, fingers that are slender and long; second, heels that are broad and long; and third, a body that is square and straight.
If one practices the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*) to gather sentient beings, one attains webbed fingers like those of the king of white geese.
If one personally washes, wipes, holds, or massages the hands and feet of one’s parents, teachers, elders, or when they are ill, one attains [the mark of] hands and feet [with webbed fingers].
Being supple, observing the precepts, hearing the Dharma, and practicing giving without weariness, one attains two marks: first, the ankles are full and prominent;
second, the body hairs curl upward. By listening to the Dharma with single-minded devotion and expounding the true teaching, one attains the mark of calves like those of a deer-king.
By not giving rise to thoughts of harm toward sentient beings, being moderate in food and drink, always delighting in giving, and tending to the sick, [one attains further marks].
He attains a body of perfect symmetry like a nyagrodha tree, with hands reaching past his knees, a crown protrusion (*uṣṇīṣa*) on his head, and an invisible crown;
he provides protection for those who see him in fear, gives clothing to those who are naked and barefoot,
attains the mark of the horse’s concealed organ (*kośagatavastiguhyatā*), draws near to the wise, stays far away from fools, delights in skillful inquiry and response, and sweeps clean.
By practicing wholesome conduct on the road, one obtains skin that is fine and soft, with body hairs curling to the right.
If one gives clothing, food and drink, bedding, medicine, incense, flowers, and lamps to others, one obtains a golden-colored body that is constantly illuminated by light.
When practicing generosity, if one can relinquish what is most cherished without stinginess, and does not discriminate between a field of merit and a non-field of merit, one attains this.
The seven parts of his body are full; when giving alms, his mind does not give rise to doubt, whereby he obtains a soft and supple voice.
If he seeks wealth in accordance with the Dharma to use for giving, he obtains flat and full clavicles. His upper body is like that of a lion, and his arms and elbows are long and slender.
Having distanced himself from divisive speech, harsh words, and anger, he obtains forty teeth that are white, even, and closely set toward all sentient beings.
By practicing great compassion, one obtains the mark of two fangs; by constantly making this vow to give whatever is requested to those who come seeking, one obtains the mark of a lion’s jaw;
by giving all manner of food according to their needs, one obtains the mark of the supreme flavor among flavors;

by personally practicing the ten wholesome paths while simultaneously transforming others, one obtains the mark of a broad and long tongue; and by not praising the faults of others nor slandering them, [one attains further marks].
By attaining the true Dharma, one gains the Brahma-voice; by viewing those who are hostile with a mind of joy, one obtains eyes of deep blue;
by not concealing the virtues of others and praising their goodness, one obtains the mark of the white tuft between the eyebrows.

Thus, each of these must be cultivated individually before the thirty-two marks can be fully perfected; yet now, through the single cause of the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra, they can be manifested.
These are the thirty-two marks.

△ Commentary: Fifth, the fruit of dissociation (*visamyoga-phala*).
He is able to liberate himself from all afflictions (*kleśa*), just as a lion king subdues the herd of beasts.
△ He is worthy of receiving offerings from all sentient beings.
[Commentary: Because the eightfold noble path, which is the fruit of detachment (*visamyoga-phala*), extinguishes the afflictions. ○ The Sub-commentary (*Śāstra*) says "all afflictions..."
"Afflictions" (*kleśa*) refers to the root and secondary afflictions. There are six roots: first, greed; second, hatred; third, ignorance; fourth, pride; fifth, doubt;
and sixth, wrong view. When these are expanded, they become ten. Wrong view is divided into five: first, the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*);

second, the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*); third, false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*); fourth, the grasping at views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*); and fifth, the grasping at precepts and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*). Thus, they are expanded into ten.

That is to say, the six superknowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) arise simultaneously with twenty-one types of discrimination that give rise to delusion; therefore, they are called "root afflictions" (*mūlakleśa*).

Second, there are twenty-one secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*): (1) anger (*krodha*), (2) resentment (*upanāha*), (3) vexation (*pradāśa*), (4) concealment (*mrakṣa*), (5) deception (*māyā*), (6) guile (*śāṭhya*), (7) arrogance (*mada*), (8) harmfulness (*vihiṃsā*), (9) envy (*īrṣyā*), (10) avarice (*mātsarya*), (11) lack of shame (*āhrīkya*), and (12) lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). [The thirteenth...]

Lack of faith (14), laziness (15), heedlessness (16), lethargy (17), restlessness (18), loss of mindfulness (19), lack of clear comprehension (20), and distraction (21)—among these, the ten beginning with anger are called the "minor derivative" (anuvṛtti) afflictions;

the two, lack of shame and lack of dread, are called the "medium derivative" afflictions; and the eight beginning with lack of faith are called the "major derivative" (mahā-anuvṛtti) afflictions, because they follow [the primary afflictions].

They are called secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*) because they arise through the power of the root afflictions (*mūlakleśa*). They also include both those that are innate (*sahaja*) and those that are conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*).
Those that are conceptually constructed have coarse and superficial modes of activity; they are eliminated upon entering the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*).

Those that are innately arisen have subtle modes of activity; they are only exhausted upon reaching the final fruit (*phala*). Because this refers to all afflictions in general, it says "all. This is like the lion king and so forth.
When the lion, the king of beasts, roars, all other animals crouch in hiding; the majestic power of this vow and practice is likewise so.
Through these vows and practices, right mindfulness becomes manifest, and until the attainment of Buddhahood, all evils are forever severed;
therefore, it is said to be "like [the lion]," and so forth. The "Noble Eightfold Path" refers to the Eightfold Right Path, namely: right view... [and so on].
The eight factors are right view, right thought, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.
To discern the principle without error is called right view; to deliberate upon the right meaning is named right thought; untainted verbal karma is named right speech;
untainted bodily karma is named right action; and for body and speech to be without error constitutes right livelihood, which accords with reality.
Diligently applying effort is called right effort; following the Dharma and recording the mind is called right mindfulness; and untainted samādhi is called right concentration.
Among these eight factors, right view is both the Path and a constituent part of the Path, while the remaining seven dharmas are only constituents and not the Path itself.

The reason they are collectively referred to as the "Right Path" is twofold: first, because their understanding serves to overturn the eight wrong paths; and second, because their essence constitutes the Noble Path.

Furthermore, at the moment of death, during the final instant, all the faculties of such a person shall completely disintegrate;
all kinsmen and relatives shall completely abandon them; and all power and authority shall completely recede, including that of ministers and high officials.

*Commentary on the Pure Land*: In the section explaining the text regarding the fruit of the Pure Land, there are two parts: first, revealing the power of the Dharma; second, specifically clarifying the supreme fruit.

Within the first part, the meaning of the sutra text is divided into three sections: first, the final loss of worldly fruits; second, this vow of non-separation; [and third, the attainment of the fruit].
Regarding the subsequent rebirth in the Pure Land, here is the first part: as explained generally in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, at the time of death there are many circumstances;
for those with heavy karmic conditions for evil, there is the suffering of the "vital points" (*marmaccheda*).

When even a very small joint within the body is severed, death ensues; this is the suffering of the vital points. It occurs when any one of the elements—earth, water, fire, or wind—increases or decreases.
Just as when the edge of a sharp blade touches the *marmans*, intense painful sensations arise therefrom, and before long, life comes to an end;
furthermore, among humans there are many kinds of signs of death:

either being struck by another's poison, or losing one's voice due to a wind-disorder (*vāta*), or being seized by spirits or deities, or suffering the difficulty of childbirth while pregnant, or being overwhelmed by a great flood.
Whether drifting and drowning, or burned by wild fires, or mangled by fierce beasts,
or executed for no fault, or struck by lightning and thunderbolts, or perishing on the battlefield, or facing execution under royal law,
or slain by the blades of enemies— such various ways of ending one's life are beyond enumeration; even when the lifespan of the gods in the heavens is about to end, these five omens first appear.
Five minor signs of decline appeared: first, his robes emitted an improper sound; second, his own bodily radiance suddenly became dim and inferior;
third, while bathing, the water clung to his body; fourth, his naturally restless mind now became stagnant upon a single object;
fifth, his eyes, which were originally tranquil and still, now blinked repeatedly. These five signs appeared.
One's death is certain beyond doubt. Furthermore, there are five kinds of signs of great decline: first, one’s clothing becomes stained with dust and grime;
second, one’s flower garlands wither and fade; third, sweat breaks out from both armpits; fourth, a foul odor enters the body;
fifth, one finds no pleasure in one’s own seat. When these five signs appear, death is inevitable. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* describes the signs of a person’s death as follows: "The two eyes..."
The tongue turns white, the nose becomes black, the ears tilt, the tendons of the neck stand out, and the lower lip hangs down;
furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that failing to give rise to a mind of reverence toward physicians and conceiving a thorn-like resentment toward one's kinsmen and friends are signs of death.
As the *Ratnakūṭa Sūtra* says, at the final moment of relinquishing one’s life, the mind is extremely clear.
When all good and evil manifest before one, fear and joy arise in the mind, and one immediately proceeds toward them;
this is a general description of all signs of death. Now, the person who recites and maintains [this dharma] shall not be oppressed by such evil signs as these:
(2) the dissolution of the sense faculties, (3) the abandonment by relatives, and (4) the decline of power.
The loss of the five [obstacles] and the fact that all things do not follow the literal text can be understood through these manifest indications.

thus it is named Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*), or alternatively, Peaceful Bliss (*Anurakṣita*), or also Nurturing Peace (*Anurakṣa*). That is to say:
The land upon which Amitābha Buddha relies is a realm where the ground is resplendent with the seven treasures and the ponds possess the eight virtues;
when the wind stirs the trees, their sounds resonate in unison with celestial music, and as the clear waves surge, their rhythms harmonize with the Dharma-sounds.
Therefore, the Buddhas who guide the six directions praise it with their golden mouths, and the Tathāgatas of the three periods direct their hearts toward its protection.

Regarding the statement "Amitābha Buddha" mentioned at the beginning of the introduction:
this is translated as "Immeasurable Life. He is named Amitābha for two reasons: first, because his radiance is immeasurable; second, because his lifespan is immeasurable.
Thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* (Amitābha Sūtra) says: "For what reason is that Buddha titled Amitābha? Because that Buddha’s radiance is immeasurable and boundless."
He illumines the lands of the ten directions without obstruction; therefore, he is named Amitābha.
That Buddha’s lifespan, as well as that of his people, lasts for immeasurable, boundless asaṃkhyeya kalpas; therefore, he is named Amitāyus.
Because in former lives, during the stage of causes, his great vows, his radiance, and his lifespan were all immeasurable, he is so named. Thus, he is Great and Infinite.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "If, when I attain Buddhahood, my radiance were limited such that it did not illuminate even hundreds of thousands of billions of nayutas of Buddha-lands, may I not attain perfect enlightenment. It further states:

Lín said: "As for Amitābha, his body is sixty trillion nayuta Ganges-sands of yojanas in extent—immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable.

his radiance has no limit, the number of his retinue is unknown, and his feet do not tread the ground."

Throughout the ten directions, his voice pervades all without speaking, yet all classes of beings hear him. With Avalokiteśvara attending on his left and Mahāsthāmaprāpta on his right, this land is characterized by the ten wholesome deeds and free from the three evil realms.
By reciting his name even once, one extinguishes the calamities and sins of eighty billion kalpas;
by prostrating before his image once, one attains the marks and signs of a Buddha. Whether raising a hand or bowing the head, every act brings benefit.
Furthermore, regarding Mañjuśrī, there are four translations for his name. *Zhengfahua* (Saddharmapuṇḍarīka) translates it as Pǔshǒu (Universal Chief).

There is a sutra that names him Rǔshǒu (Gentle Chief), which correctly renders it as Miaode (Wondrous Virtue) or Miaojixiang (Wondrous Auspiciousness). This is because at the time of his birth, ten kinds of miraculous omens occurred:
first, light filled the chamber; second, ambrosia overflowed the courtyard; third, the earth surged forth with the seven treasures; fourth... [and so on].
The gods opened the hidden treasure; five hens gave birth to phoenix chicks; six pigs gave birth to dragon piglets; seven mares produced qilin; eight oxen gave birth to white-zhai;
the granaries were filled with golden grain; and ten elephants were born with six tusks. Because of these auspicious omens, he was named Mañjuśrī.
Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that in the past, during the time of the Buddha Ratnagarbha, he was known as Araṇemin.
The third son of King [Amitābha], named Indrasena, made a vow before the Buddha to attain a wondrous and pure land.
The Buddha said, "Since you have yourself made the vow to attain a wondrous and pure land, I now name you Mañjuśrī;
this signifies that auspicious matters concerning the pure land have long been present. Now, assisting the Buddha in guiding and transforming beings, you shall manifest birth in Śrāvastī."

In the village of Rājagṛha, there was the son of the Brahmin Brahmadeva named Gandhamādana (translated as "Fragrant Mountain"), whose virtue was wondrous and who manifested universally throughout the ten directions.
As the Honored One of the Path, he was the teacher of all Buddhas; in the past, he delivered five hundred rishis and concealed his radiance on the Snowy Peaks.
Now, together with ten thousand bodhisattvas, he dwells at Mount Liangshan. This is as extensively described in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtras and other texts. May Samantabhadra [grant his grace].

"Intellectual liberation" (jñāna-vimukti) is so named because one attains mastery in contemplating and penetrating the realm where phenomena and principle are unimpeded, and furthermore, because one possesses unimpeded mastery in observing the capacities of sentient beings and proceeding to rescue them.

Moreover, when Bodhisattvas reach the eighth stage (bhūmi), they attain the ten masteries: first, mastery over life (*āyur-vaśitā*), because they can abide for an inexpressible number of eons; second, mastery over mind (*citta-vaśitā*)... [knowledge]... *Note:
