According to the *Maitrīcittahetupratyaya-sūtra*, in the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) eons ago, there was a world named "Victorious" (*Jaya*).
In the world of the Buddha Puṣpaprabha, whose name was Maitreya, all were constantly taught and transformed by means of the four immeasurable states of mind rooted in loving-kindness.
At that time, there was a brahmin named Sarvajñānaprabha who possessed sixty-four arts and was widely learned and profoundly insightful.
Upon hearing the Buddha preach the sutra, he immediately gave rise to a spirit of challenge; yet, unable to refute or subdue him, he instead conceived faith and made this vow:
"I vow that by upholding this sutra, I shall certainly attain Buddhahood and be named Maitreya.

Furthermore, in the past, together with Śākyamuni, he had resolved upon Bodhicitta in the presence of Puṣya Buddha and constantly practiced the concentration of loving-kindness; from that time until now, he has always been known as Maitreya.
Maitreya is also named Ajita, which means "Invincible. Because his roots of great kindness and compassion are invincible, he was born as the son of the prime minister of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī;

It is said that in the Land of Fragrant Mountains, he will adorn the Pure Land to deliver sentient beings, and he shall manifest his descent even before Śākyamuni begins his path.

at the time of the three assemblies under the Dragon Flower tree, he shall grant them all deliverance. Now, manifesting his residence in Tuṣita Heaven to guide those in Jambudvīpa, his profound compassion and heavy kindness can never be repaid throughout eternal kalpas.

The Treasury Adorned with the Wisdom of Unforgetting Mindfulness Regarding All Objects of Perception. Question:
Is it necessarily the case that one who is born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss will behold Amitābha Buddha and the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara?

Furthermore, since the body of Samantabhadra is the very body of the pure *dharmadhātu*, there is no impediment to beholding the essence of all Buddhas. As for Mañjuśrī and Maitreya, they reside here in this Sahā world...
The Venerable [Vasubandhu] now says that going there and being able to see [the Buddha] are either the same or different. How so? The answer is that there are two meanings.
First, they are identical in substance but differ in name; for example, when the *Āyus-sūtra* speaks of the time, it is said that in the West there is also an Amitāyus Buddha, and so forth.
Because they are praised together, we know that this is merely a case where the names are the same while the substances are distinct. Second, it is said that they are the same and not different. Why?
Just as Mañjuśrī is the father and mother of the Buddha-way, manifesting through great skillful means to assist the Buddha in propagating the transformation throughout the entire Dharma-realm,
appearing in various bodies to benefit and bring joy to all classes of beings—
just as Maitreya spoke to Sudhana regarding Mañjuśrī’s most supreme great vows, which no other bodhisattvas, even those numbering in the hundreds of thousands of nayutas, can equal.
Furthermore, it is said that Mañjuśrī’s conduct is vast, immeasurable, and boundless;
his vows are limitless, continuing without interruption, and he is always able to give rise to all the most supreme merits of bodhisattvas.
He constantly serves as the teacher for immeasurable bodhisattvas, causing them to diligently practice and deeply realize and enter [the truth]. Throughout the ten directions...
He constantly turns the wheel of Dharma to teach and bring all sentient beings to maturity;
he constantly serves as a Dharma teacher in all worlds throughout the ten directions; and he is always praised within the great assemblies of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of all Buddhas.
As Maitreya Bodhisattva says in the Great Sūtra: "He has achieved [perfection]."
Because all modes of conduct lead everywhere, one attains mastery over all places of birth. Furthermore, it is said:
"My body is born universally throughout the entire Dharma-realm and among all sentient beings.

This reveals the distinct characteristics of the path, manifesting various sounds, various names and titles, various inclinations, and various dignified demeanors, in order to accord with the world and to teach, transform, and subdue beings.

He manifests his body through various forms and various majestic virtues that fill the Dharma-realm— manifesting in ways revealed by such immeasurable means as showing sentient beings pure rebirths, conforming to and entering into the profound inclinations of all sentient beings, and being transformed by the great vows of all Bodhisattvas—
in order to bring to maturity those who were his companions in the past.
For those who have regressed from the bodhi-mind, he manifests here in this Jambudvīpa;
furthermore, for the sake of maturing the fellow-practitioners among the gods in Tuṣita Heaven, he causes them to know that the prosperity of the gods must inevitably decline.
Desiring to manifest the auspicious signs of his descent into birth, he teaches and matures those left behind by Śākyamuni Tathāgata, causing them to become like lotuses.
Because all have attained awakening and because they pass away from this place to be born in the Tuṣita Heaven and so forth, we know that they are the same and not different.
Alternatively, it would not be problematic to say they are identical in essence yet distinct in person.

As for the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), it includes all other newly enlightened and long-established sages, as well as the various bodhisattvas who have constantly attended [the Buddha]. Thus, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* says: its...

The section on "Exhorting All Beings to Receive and Uphold [the Teaching]" is divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the divisions; second, the detailed explanation. These three sections are clear and can be understood as they appear in the commentary.
Regarding the repeated citation of virtues within the Sūtra, where it says "all shall attain rebirth" and so forth:

from this place proceeding to that [Pure Land] is termed "going. According to the *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra*, those who attain rebirth are categorized in total as follows: [The text continues with the categories of rebirth.]
There are nine grades; according to one's grade and according to one's karmic conduct, one attains rebirth there. Regarding these nine grades:
first, the highest grade of the highest birth involves the arousal of three kinds of minds, namely the bodhicitta and so forth. Furthermore, there are three practices:
first, a mind of loving-kindness that refrains from killing and maintains all precepts and practices; second, the recitation and study of Mahāyāna Vaipulya sūtras.
Third, by practicing the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*), dedicating merit, and making vows— whether for one day or up to seven days—
the Honored One of Longevity, together with two bodhisattvas, innumerable transformation buddhas, and a great assembly of śrāvakas,

will hold a *vajra*-pedestal and arrive before the practitioner to welcome them by extending their hands. Upon being born in that land, one immediately realizes non-arising (*anutpāda*), and in an instant, reaches the ten directions.
Regarding the realms, there are three grades of rebirth: the first is the "Superior Grade of Superior Rebirth," and the second is the "Superior Grade of Middle Rebirth.
This refers to one who is not startled or shaken by the ultimate truth (paramārtha), who has deep faith in cause and effect, and does not slander the Mahāyāna.

When the Honored One of Longevity and two Bodhisattvas arrive before the practitioner, carrying a purple-golden platform, they simultaneously extend their hands along with a thousand transformation Buddhas. In a single thought-moment, the practitioner is born upon that great jewel-flower.
Having stayed overnight, they immediately enter the seven-day period and attain non-retrogressive Bodhi, flying to the ten directions;
this is called "Birth by Superior Grade II. Birth by Superior Grade III also involves faith without slander, merely giving rise to the great Bodhicitta;
at the time of death, they see the Buddha and two Bodhisattvas holding golden lotus flowers, with five hundred transformation Buddhas simultaneously extending their hands to receive them.

After one day and one night, the lotus flower opens; by the seventh day, one is able to see the Buddha. After twenty-one days, one travels through the ten directions and receives a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) from the Buddha.
This is called the "Lower Birth of the Superior Grade" among the four grades of birth.

Those who do not commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*), observe the five precepts or the eight precepts, and see the Buddha at the time of death, receiving his praise and being encouraged to leave the household life, shall attain liberation from the masses.

Upon suffering, one immediately sits upon a lotus pedestal; before the head has even been raised, one is born in the Pure Land, where the lotus flower soon opens and one attains the fruit of Arhatship—this is called the "Middle Grade, Upper Birth.

As for the "Middle Grade, Middle Birth," if one upholds the eight precepts for at least one day and night, or the śrāmaṇera precepts, or the full precepts with flawless deportment, one will see the Buddha at the moment of death who comes to console them.

This is illustrated by the analogy of one who, seven days after being reborn, the flower blooms and they attain the fruit of a stream-enterer (*srotāpanna*). Among the six grades of birth, this refers to the lower-middle grade.

Having been filial and supportive toward one’s parents and practicing benevolence in the world, one encounters others and speaks to them of the merits of the Buddha-land and the forty-eight vows of the Bhikṣu Dharmākara.
Although one does not see the Buddha, at the end of life one is reborn; seven days later the flower blooms, and one likewise attains the fruit of a stream-enterer.

Regarding the seventh fruit, those of inferior capacity who are born in the higher grade, although they do not slander the sutras, are like these many foolish people who commit evil deeds without shame or remorse;

yet, at the time of death, upon hearing praise for the twelve divisions of the Mahayana sutras and being further consoled by the appearance of transformation Buddhas as they recite the Buddha’s name, they immediately attain rebirth there.
After seven times seven days, their lotuses bloom, they behold the sages, and they hear the most profound Dharma.

Those of the eighth grade, middle-superior level, who have violated the various precepts, stolen the property of the Sangha, and preached the Dharma impurely, lacking shame and remorse, and whose bodies are adorned with all manner of evils—
when their lives come to an end, the fires of hell arrive together with them; yet, if they encounter a virtuous friend who explains for them the Tathāgata’s ten powers,
majestic virtue, radiant light, and supernormal powers, as well as his morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation, [they may attain rebirth].

Having known and seen this, the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas were extinguished; the fire was transformed into a cool breeze, and a Buddha appeared to welcome them.
In a single thought-moment they were reborn there, where the lotus blossomed after six kalpas, and they conceived the unsurpassed resolve for the Way.

Even those of the lowest of the low grade—those who have committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds, possessing all manner of unwholesome karma and destined to fall into the evil realms to suffer endless pain—at the very moment of their death...

Even if one is ultimately oppressed by suffering and has no leisure to recite the Buddha’s name, if one merely invokes the Name so that the sound does not cease and completes ten recitations, then after the end of life, one will see a golden lotus flower and be reborn in a single thought-moment.

After twelve kalpas, the flower will open and one will hear the true nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*). Having extinguished all transgressions, one gives rise to the aspiration for the Unsurpassed Way; this is the rebirth of the ninth grade.
To be reborn there, each individual must possess various kinds of merit;

furthermore, within the Great Canon, there are over a hundred texts—whether sutras or treatises—that explain the cultivation of those causes, all of which state that one must diligently accumulate them to attain rebirth there.
Now, however, by merely reciting a single line of a sutra for even a single kṣaṇa, one may attain rebirth and receive a prediction of enlightenment from the Buddha.
This is truly marvelous! The *Shu* (Commentary) states that "abundant" (*fēng*) means "much. *Shū* refers to the pivot or bolt, that is, the critical juncture;
the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the term "Teacher of Gods and Humans" (*devamanuṣyaśāstṛ*): "Gods" (*deva*) refers to those in the heavenly realms where days are long and nights are short; therefore they are called gods.

He is the Teacher of Gods and Humans.

△ Dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) and the vow (*praṇidhāna*) are largely the same with minor differences.
The difference is that dedication requires the presence of roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) to be dedicated, whereas a vow can be made even without such roots. As for their general similarity:
the stage of the ten dedications takes great vows as its essence, because both general and specific vows are dedicated therein. △ This present [practice] is precisely the dedication of great vows. ○
Regarding the dedication at the end of the three verses: it consists of thirty verses beginning with "When I was practicing for the sake of Bodhi.
Within this, there are three parts: first, a general correlation with the prose commentary; second, a specific correlation with the First Ground; and third, an explanation of the main text.
As for the first, the commentary notes that these are also *gāthās*. In Sanskrit, they are called *geya*, which means "repeated verse," referring to verses that recapitulate the prose.
The term *gāthā*, as mentioned in the preceding verses and so forth, is translated from Sanskrit as "recitation" (*fèngsòng*).

This refers to independent verses of praise that do not follow or summarize preceding prose; however, if these ten vows were expressed in verse following the preceding dedication, they would be *geya*.

This is not entirely uniform; the general vows and the specific vows are distinct.

For instance, the fulfillment of the Buddha’s bodhi according to one's wish constitutes the general vow, while within that, the differentiation between self-benefit and benefit for others constitutes the specific vows.
As for these being the dedication of great vows, since the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*) are themselves the dedication of great vows, we know that the great vows are the dedication.
This is his great vow. △ The text of the commentary contains ten vows that are entirely identical to those of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*), though their sequence differs.

In that [first stage], the sequence is: 1. the vow of making offerings; 2. the vow of upholding; 3. the vow of turning the wheel of Dharma; 4. the practice of the two benefits; 5. the maturation of sentient beings;
6. serving [the Buddhas]; 7. purifying the land; 8. not being separated [from the Buddhas]; 9. benefiting [sentient beings]; 10. [the vow of] ... [the tenth is omitted in the source].

The attainment of perfect enlightenment follows the sequence of the sutra. In the sub-commentary (*chao*), regarding the ten vows below, there is a second section that harmonizes them with the first stage (*bhūmi*).

This refers to the first of the three sections—namely, the "Section on the Excellence of Vows"—within the fourth part, the "Section on the Measurement of Superior Virtues," where Vajragarbha Bodhisattva explains the ten vows of the first stage to Vimukticandra Bodhisattva. Now, based upon this...
In the preceding commentary, the text explains [the subject] by means of five pairs and ten gates. First, regarding the pair of "essence" (*tattva*) and "name" (*nāman*):

"name" is a general term, while "vow" (*praṇidhāna*) carries the specific meaning of aspiration. There are ten specific names; according to the sutras and the *She lun* (Mahāyānasaṃgraha) translated during the Liang dynasty, these names are identical to those here, though their sequence differs.
Now, following that sequence, they are first listed and subsequently explained based on the present text.

Regarding the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the various *Saṃgrahaṇī* treatises, although their names differ slightly, their meaning is entirely the same. As for its essential nature (*svabhāva*), it consists precisely of the three:

faith (*śraddhā*), aspiration (*chanda*), and resolute conviction (*adhimukti*). If one takes its basis (*āśraya*)—namely, compassion and wisdom guiding one another—then its essence is subsequently attained wisdom (*prsthalabdha-jñāna*).

Regarding the two types of cultivation and realization, for the practitioner: the first seven [stages] are the beginning of cultivation; the next two are the maturation of cultivation; and the final [stage] is the completion.

First, regarding cultivation and realization: "Realization" refers to the simultaneous realization of the three practices upon entering the first bhūmi from the stage prior to the bhūmis (pṛthagjana-bhūmi). Regarding the correspondence between the stages and the practitioner:

the first two stages concern self-benefit; the next five concern the benefit of others; the eighth concerns the fulfillment of self-benefit; and the ninth concerns the fulfillment of the benefit of others. As for the twelfth, it is the fruit of benefit.
If discussed generally, all ten stages involve both types of benefit; this general discussion refers to what is attained in the first bhūmi.

Furthermore, because that [passage] is the text concerning the First Ground (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), it is thus correlated [with this]. If one considers the ten vows within this context, they are a perfect fusion of beginning and end, not restricted to fixed stages.
Fourth, the correspondence of cause and fruit: the first nine seek the cause, while the last one seeks the fruit.
Fifth, the correspondence of the perfect fusion of the intent of establishment: as for why only ten are taught, it is because they encompass the two types of adornment (*dvividha-saṃbhāra*).

Because the practices and stages of the causes and effects of the two benefits are all-encompassing, and because they signify inexhaustibility, it is said that "each and every one encompasses incalculable [asamkhyeya] vows.
This "perfect interfusion" (*yuanrong*) occurs because they accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*); within a single vow, all vows are complete.
Thus, one enters into layers of profundity, as is commonly analyzed through the six aspects of perfect interfusion (*liu xiang yuanrong*), which is precisely what is addressed in this passage.

Therefore, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu stated that there are six characteristics: the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), the identical characteristic (*tulya-lakṣaṇa*), the different characteristic (*bhinnalakṣaṇa*), the characteristic of formation (*siddhi-lakṣaṇa*), and the characteristic of disintegration (*bhaṅga-lakṣaṇa*).
The "general" refers to the fundamental dharma, because from the very first dharma, there is nothing that is not subsumed within it.

The "specific" refers to the other nine dharmas, which depend individually upon the fundamental [dharma] to fulfill that fundamental. The "identical" refers to these dharmas being called by the same name, "dharmas. The "different" refers to their distinctness.

"Arising" (*utpāda*) refers to the increase of characteristics, for all phenomena gradually increase. "Formation" (*siddhi*) refers to a concise explanation; it is a synthesis formed by gathering nine conditions into one.
"Destruction" (*bhaṅga*) refers to a detailed explanation; it divides the one into nine. Outside of these nine, there is no single entity;
these nine causes and conditions each abide in their own specific characteristics and do not mutually form one another. It is like beams and pillars that together form a single house as a whole.
Thus, when unified, the various conditions are distinct; when identical, they do not mutually contradict one another; when different, the various conditions are not the same.

When established, the various conditions accomplish the fruit; when disintegrated, each abides in its own dharma. Generally speaking, every single phenomenon is the perfect fusion of the six aspects (*ṣaḍlakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, the Third Patriarch of the Avataṃsaka, National Teacher Kangzang, pointed to gold for Empress Wu Zetian.
The Master Siṃha explains the perfect fusion of the six aspects as in his *Jinshizi Zhang* (Treatise on the Golden Lion). That scriptural text has two distinct sections:

first, the direct manifestation of the ten vows to reveal one’s own diligent practice; second, the elucidation of the ten "exhaustive phrases" (*daśa-paryanta-padāni*) to be shared with sentient beings.

Within the first section, there are four parts: first, a general heading; second, a detailed enumeration; third, a summary; and fourth, the inclusion of attendant members. Regarding the first [of these], the stage...
The Sūtra says: "O Son of the Buddha, when a Bodhisattva dwells in this Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), they are able to accomplish such great vows, such great courage, and such great activities.
The Commentary explains: The term "able to accomplish" encompasses the latter three phrases.

The first phrase refers to the initial formation of the formal resolve (*samādāna*). The second phrase refers to the application of skillful means to initiate practice, meaning that one brings each and every vow to fulfillment.
Because all the skillful means employed therein are courageous, the latter phrase expresses the vow that the practice of the path will be accomplished;

that is to say, by being able to make offerings to the Buddha, one is thereby able to make offerings [to all beings]. The remaining nine cases should be understood by analogy. This vow is itself the practice, and because it accords with the vow, it is called "vow-practice" (*praṇidhāna-caryā*);
it is not like the empty formal aspirations of ordinary people. Therefore, it is stated in general terms that "one is able to accomplish. The general term encompasses the specific instances.
Each of the ten vows possesses these three [aspects]. Regarding the separate enumeration of the ten vows, within each individual vow there are four parts:
first, the four characters that serve as a general heading to initiate the vow;

the phrase "furthermore, he makes a great vow" (又發大願) appears in nine of the vows, but is absent from the first vow on "Making Offerings" because it is included in the preceding heading. Second, the manifestation of the vow.

The aspects of the ten vows are distinct from one another; however, while they differ in wording from this sutra, their meaning is identical. Below, I shall cite them according to the text and provide a harmonious explanation.
Third, to manifest the power of the virtues of the vows: all ten vows are described as being vast, pervading the Dharma-realm, and ultimately like empty space.

thus, one should say "making offerings without cessation" and so forth, as it does not resemble the third section where both word and meaning are identical. Regarding the first and last sections, the wording is general while the meaning is specific;

Third, the summary states: "The Son of the Buddha, dwelling on this Stage of Joy, makes such great vows," and so forth;
these three phrases are identical to the introductory text. Fourth, regarding the gathering of retinues:
"With these ten vows as the foremost, he fulfills one million *asaṃkhyeya* great vows. However, this sutra contains only the practices from the second of these specific vows.
Regarding the three sections on the characteristics of the text and its meaning, one must understand that the vows in that sutra are largely the same as these, differing only slightly;
therefore, I have briefly indicated and explained them without wearying over minor variations.
Next, "according to the sutra" means explaining the original text according to the sequence of this sutra, while following the convenience of the meaning to correspond with that sutra.
△ Commentary, Part Two: Specific Formulation of Great Vows, Section Eleven: The Vow of Receiving and Upholding.
When I practice for the sake of Bodhi, may I attain the memory of past lives (*jātismara*) in all realms of existence;

may I always be able to leave the household life and cultivate pure precepts—untainted, unbroken, unblemished, and without leakage—among devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and even humans and non-humans.

△ Now, the first phrase of the current text subsumes *bodhi*. △ The next phrase maintains the Buddha-dharma. △ The following two phrases protect the Buddhist teachings;
because practicing the precepts constitutes protective conduct. △ The meaning of "breaking" and "piercing" has already been seen in the preceding section on "Sublime Abiding.

○ In the first fascicle of the *Commentary*, the two verses beginning with "I am... clarify the vow of receiving and maintaining [the teachings], which corresponds to the second [section] of that [text].

Because the *Yuan* (Vow) is broad, the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra-śāstra* states: "Reaching all Buddha-dharmas. These four phrases are a complete transcription of the passage concerning their aspects of practice (*ākāra*).

All subsequent instances follow this pattern. While these four phrases apply to both self-benefit and the benefit of others, if they are discussed in terms of being able to receive and uphold [the teachings], etc., [they are categorized as such].

"Receiving" (*pratigraha*) means to experience; "gathering" (*saṃgraha*) means to belong to; "protecting" (*rakṣā*) means to guard; and "maintaining" (*dhāraṇa*) means to sustain. Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* says:
"Gathering and receiving the true Dharma, and protecting and maintaining the true Dharma. If we speak in terms of what is received and maintained, there are four aspects:

first, the teaching; second, the fruit; third, the practice; and fourth, the principle. Regarding the third—protecting the teaching and judging it as the dharma of practice—the treatise states: "That is to say, cultivation..."
When practicing the teachings, because there are various obstacles and difficulties, one must provide protection and rescue;

thus, although the phrases such as "able to receive" are mentioned interchangeably in the text, their meaning actually applies to all. To say that one "constantly leaves home to cultivate pure precepts," "home" refers to a household, taking the sense of confinement and bondage;
being free from the fetters of affliction is called "leaving home. Furthermore, those who remain at home are constrained...
The narrowness [of the household life] is like a prison, while the vastness of renunciation is like space. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:

"Though a peacock may have colorful plumage adorning its body, it cannot fly as far as the wild goose or the crane; likewise, though one at home may possess the pleasures of the five desires, these do not equal the profound merit of renunciation.
Also, in the *Cittabhūmi-parivarta-sūtra*, the Buddha spoke to Jñānaprabha the Elder...
Regarding the question of the relative superiority or inferiority of the two types—those who have left the home life and those who remain at home—the Buddha said:
"A bodhisattva who has left the home life is immeasurably and boundlessly superior to one who remains at home; they cannot be compared. Why is this?
Because a bodhisattva who has left the home life uses the power of right wisdom to minutely observe all the various faults inherent in the household life, namely, all worldly things."
One accumulates wealth within one's home without knowing contentment, just as the great ocean receives all rivers, large and small, yet never knows satisfaction.
Furthermore, it is said that those living in the household state constantly give rise to delusive thoughts and cling to external objects;
unable to realize the truth, they are mired in the intoxication of ignorance and, being inverted, remain perpetually unsettled whenever they encounter sensory objects.

Evil thoughts arise easily while the virtuous mind is difficult to produce; through the conditions of deluded conceptualization, various afflictions arise, and by means of these afflictions, one creates wholesome and unwholesome karma.
Depending on this wholesome and unwholesome karma, one experiences the fruits of the five destinies. In this way, birth and death continue without end.
A renunciant Bodhisattva who can contemplate in this manner and cultivate weary detachment toward the world is called a true renunciant. (Verse)
It is said that a renunciant bodhisattva surpasses a householder by a measure of calculation and a measure of comparison;

the householder’s confinement is like a prison, making it extremely difficult to seek liberation. Renunciation is as vast and open as space, characterized by sovereignty, non-action, and freedom from attachment.
Furthermore, it is said that if any man or woman, for one day and one night, renounces...
Having received the precepts at home for two million kalpas, one does not follow the evil paths; by virtue of these causes and conditions, one vows to always attain them.

Regarding the meaning of "breaking and piercing" as it appears in the section on "Sublime Abiding," this refers to the fourth spiritual friend of Sudhana, the bhikṣu Subhūti (also known as Supratiṣṭhita in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtras). This spiritual friend represents the third stage, that of "Cultivation."
In this chapter on "Abiding," twenty kinds of precepts are taught; the commentary correlates these with the twenty Brahma-conducts (*brahmacarya*) of the "Dedication" chapter.
Among them, the twelfth, the "precept without deficiency or leakage" (*avaikalya-śīla*), is correlated with the second, "Brahma-conduct without deficiency";
and the twentieth, the "stainless precept" (*vimala-śīla*), is correlated with the first, "unbroken Brahma-conduct. Regarding that, the commentary states: "If one breaks [it]..."
The fourfold and tenfold precepts are like a broken vessel that can no longer be used because they are the most gross and heavy;
therefore, this sutra speaks of "stainless," which refers to stainless precepts, and "unbroken," which refers to unbroken *brahmacarya*.
Although the word "pierced" (*chuan*) is added while the word "deficient" (*que*) is absent, the meanings of "pierced" and "deficient" do not differ.
Therefore, pointing to that [passage] to explain this meaning is also identical to the parable in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* of the rākṣasī of craving and views begging for a life-preserving float.

All śrāvakas within the realms are the voice of the Tathāgata.

Diligently cultivating the pure pāramitās, constantly never forgetting the bodhicitta, and eliminating obstructive defilements without remainder.

All other sublime practices are fully accomplished; one attains liberation amidst all afflictions, karma, demonic realms, and worldly paths, just as a lotus is unsullied by water and like the sun and moon that do not abide in the sky.
The commentary states that "all sublime practices are accomplished therein" is the general statement (*sūtra*).
This refers to the vast and immeasurable various mundane and supramundane practices, as well as the application of skillful means (*upāya*). [The *Yichao* (Commentary) states:
"The second section, 'diligently cultivating' and below, concerns the practice of the two benefits; the vow is the fourth of those. The commentary notes that this is the general statement.
The text states "all," which is a general term. It is not explained according to the sequential order because it follows the convenience of the meaning;
much of what follows below is modeled after this section. Regarding the phrase "vast, immeasurable, up to various practices," that sutra says:
"May all bodhisattva practices be vast, immeasurable, indestructible, and unmixed. The commentary explains: "Vast..."
"Immeasurable" refers to the practice of worldly activity—the clear wisdom of conventional knowledge that extends broadly from the first stage through the sixth stage.
"Great" refers to the seventh stage; "immeasurable" refers to the eighth stage and above.
It is non-worldly practice because it is not mixed with worldly, out-flowing (*āsrava*) dharmas; it is indestructible because it is darkly identical with true nature (*dharmatā*). (Commentary)

Furthermore, regarding those who practice skillful means (*upāya*), within that walking meditation (*caṃkrama*) there are four stages: the aspect of practice, the essence of practice, the activity of practice, and the practice of skillful means.
Within the practice of skillful means, one employs the six aspects in perfect fusion so that a single practice embodies all practices as skillful means.

As the Sūtra says: "It encompasses all the *pāramitās*, purifies all the stages (*bhūmi*), and integrates their general characteristics, specific characteristics, identical characteristics, and different characteristics."

All bodhisattva practices—characterized by differentiation, formation, and destruction—are explained according to reality, teaching and transforming all beings so that they may accept and practice them, thereby causing their minds to grow.
The statement "now, all sublime practices are accomplished" contains this same intent;
thus, it refers to the "skillful means of practice. The remaining three [aspects] should be correlated with this, as can be seen in the commentary (*shu*).
△ Commentary: The remaining phrases distinguish the substance of the practice (*caryā-tattva*) of the first phrase as the ten *pāramitās*, which are purified by the removal of obscurations.

This is now identified as their "substance" (*tattva*), clarifying these ten *pāramitās*.
The meaning of "Honey" (*madhu*) will be briefly analyzed through three sections: first, the explanation of the name; second, the clarification of its essential nature;

and third, questions and answers concerning its breadth and brevity. Within the first section, there are two parts: first, the explanation of the general name, and second, the explanation of the specific names.
Regarding the first: "Ten" is a number. "Pāramitā" is translated here as "Reaching the Other Shore. Taking birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as this shore, [the afflictions are the current].
Delusive thoughts constitute the middle current, while the state of true emptiness is the further shore. Thus, the *Ben* commentary states:

"Due to the absence of correct wisdom, one dwells on the shore of birth and death, drowning in the flow of afflictions; giving rise to delusions and creating karma, one cycles through saṃsāra without end.

However, if one causes the cultivation of formless wisdom to illuminate the emptiness of the five aggregates, this is called leaving this shore; when delusive thoughts are forever stilled, this is crossing over."
The realization of the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) within the middle stream is likewise reaching the other shore.

Furthermore, according to the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, the presently arising suffering and its origin constitute this shore, while the non-arising of suffering and its origin constitutes the river; awakening (bodhi) and nirvāṇa constitute the other shore, and the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) serve as the boat and raft.
The provisional person composed of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) of the practitioner is that which is to be ferried across. Moreover, there is [this] in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
There are three meanings: first, taking birth-and-death as this shore and bodhi as the other shore;
all Tathāgatas cross the great river of the four currents from this shore of birth-and-death to reach the other shore of bodhi—this is explained in terms of the fruit (*phala*).
Second, taking that which has marks (*sanimitta*) as this shore and that which is markless (*animitta*) as the other shore—this is explained in terms of the mind (*citta*). Third...
Taking the six obscurations as this shore and the six perfections as the other shore—this is an explanation in terms of practice.
