"The assembly of beings gathered by Ratnakūṭa is the Buddha-land of the Bodhisattva. Why is this? It continues:
"A Bodhisattva takes up a Buddha-land according to the beings they transform," and so on, up to: "Generosity is the Bodhisattva... [and so forth].
First, when a Bodhisattva of a Pure Land attains Buddhahood, all sentient beings who are capable of renunciation come to be born in that land.

Second, the precepts are the pure land of a Bodhisattva; when the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood, sentient beings who practice the ten paths of wholesome action and fulfill their vows come to be born in that land.
Third, patience is the pure land of a Bodhisattva; when the Bodhisattva attains Buddhahood...
Third, beings adorned with the thirty-two marks will come to be born in that land; this is the pure land of the bodhisattva’s diligence.
When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, beings who have diligently cultivated all meritorious virtues will come to be born in that land.
Fourth, meditative concentration is the pure land of the bodhisattva. When the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, those whose minds are gathered and undisturbed [will come to be born in that land].
Fifth, sentient beings who come to be born in that land possess wisdom; this is the pure buddha-land of a bodhisattva.

Sixth, when the bodhisattva attains buddhahood, sentient beings who abide in right concentration (samyak-samādhi) come to be born in that land. △ Commentary: Second, regarding the basis and its cause, there are further two aspects:

first, the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) and pure consciousness serve as the basis for the land; second, the subsequently attained wisdom (prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna) and penetrating insight constitute the land itself.

[The Mirror-like Wisdom as the Basis] In the *Jiaochao*, it is stated that the pure consciousness of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*) serves as the basis for the land. Generally speaking, there are four kinds of Buddha-wisdom:
first, the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom; second, the Wisdom of Equality; third, the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; and fourth, the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done.
Question: Why is it called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom? Answer: It is named after a metaphor. This means that the nature of this wisdom is intrinsically pure.
Because its perfect luminosity is able to reflect and illuminate all phenomena, it is named the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

This includes the various distinct categories of mental activities of all sentient beings, the images of bodhisattvas, the images of the Buddhas of the three periods of time, and even the images of the five destinies;
whether as phenomena (*dharma*) or principles (*dharmin*), there is no among the myriad virtues—conditioned or unconditioned—that is not [reflected therein].
Because all things are clearly reflected within it, it is named the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*); this is just like a great round mirror that can illuminate all phenomena.
Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "The mental complex associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is the support for the pure, perfect virtues of both actualities and seeds;
it can manifest and produce the reflections of bodies, lands, and wisdom, continuing without interval or interruption until the end of time."

The future limit (*anāgata-koṭi*) is like a great round mirror manifesting all forms and images; this admits of two grammatical explanations: *karmadhāraya* (attributive compound) and *tatpuruṣa* with the possessive suffix (*matup*), meaning "that which possesses the names of others.
Regarding the wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*): "equal" (*sama*) means uniform; "equality" (*samatā*) means evenness.
This refers to the state where, when perceiving all objects, one is equal toward oneself and others, because the seventh consciousness, while in the causal stage, clings [to a self].

I previously held the view that dharmas have high and low, giving rise to inequality; now that they have become untainted (*anāsrava*), these two attachments have been eliminated, and self and other are equal.
This is what is meant by "attaining its name based on its object. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states:
"The mental state associated with the wisdom of equality observes all phenomena such that oneself and all sentient beings are entirely [equal]."
Regarding "equality" and "wonderful discerning wisdom" (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*): its divine activity is unimpeded and manifold, hence it is called "wonderful.
It takes as its objects the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, hence it is called "discernment. Its decisive judgment is unobstructed, hence it is called "wisdom.
Because this mental state manifests supernormal powers, clearly reflects all things, and brings benefit and happiness through preaching the Dharma, it is named the "wonderful discerning wisdom."
It is precisely from its function that it receives its name; thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"The mental state associated with the wisdom of wondrous observation (*pratyavekṣaṇājñāna*) refers to this mental state which skillfully contemplates the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena, proceeding without obstruction.
Within great assemblies, it can manifest infinite varieties of activity, attaining mastery over them all, raining down the great rain of Dharma, and severing [doubts]..."

It cuts through all nets of doubt and causes all sentient beings to obtain benefit and happiness. Regarding the wisdom of accomplished action (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*), it is also called the wisdom that accomplishes tasks (*kṛtya-sampādaka-jñāna*);

this means it is named "wisdom of accomplished action" because it can successfully carry out the tasks of benefiting and bringing happiness to sentient beings, being designated according to its object and its function.
Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* states: "The wisdom of accomplished action..."

Regarding the category of the corresponding mind: it refers to this mental state which, for the sake of benefiting and bringing happiness to all sentient beings, manifests various transformations throughout the ten directions through the three types of action (trikarma), thereby accomplishing the tasks required by the power of its original vows.

These four wisdoms are possessed exclusively by the Buddha; they are formed by the transformation of the eight consciousnesses—specifically, by transforming the eighth consciousness, one achieves the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna).
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is the transformation of the seventh consciousness; the Wisdom of Equality is the transformation of the sixth consciousness;

the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation is the transformation of the five sensory consciousnesses; and the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done is the transformation of the same [five]. Question: Since there are eight consciousnesses, how do they transform into these four wisdoms?

Answer: In principle, they actually transform into eight wisdoms; however, because the names for the first five are identical [to those of the five sense organs], they are simply [grouped together as one].

Establishing four aspects also incurs no fault; all have the meaning of definitive discernment (*niścaya*) as their essence. Taken collectively, they take wisdom (*prajñā*)—which apprehends specific objects—and its simultaneous concomitants, the twenty-one mental factors (*caitasika*), as their substance.
Question: The eight consciousnesses are mind-kings (*citta-rāja*), whereas wisdom is a mental factor (*caitasika*).
How can it be that the mind-king is transformed into a mental factor? Answer: As for "transformation," it refers only to the transformation within the mental factors.

Wisdom (prajñā) perfected is the essence of gnosis (jñāna), not that of the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛtti-vijñāna). This means that in the causal stage, consciousness is predominant and gnosis is subordinate;

thus, when one speaks of the eight consciousnesses, all mental factors (caitta) are subsumed therein. When one reaches the resultant stage, however, gnosis is predominant and consciousness is subordinate;
thus, when one speaks of the four gnoses (catur-jñāna), they collectively subsume the eight consciousnesses, as each has transformed its own respective aspect of consciousness.

Regarding the wisdom that corresponds [to this]: if one asks, "If the first seven consciousnesses possess corresponding wisdom during the causal stage, it can be said that they transform into the eighth at the resultant stage;
however, since there is no such wisdom in the eighth consciousness during the causal stage, how can it transform at the resultant stage? The answer is:

although the eighth consciousness lacks the correspondence of tainted wisdom during the causal stage, at the resultant stage, it arises as an active manifestation from the seeds of untainted mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśajñāna*).
There is also no fault here, for the *Śāstra* states: "The pure consciousness of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) serves as the basis for the land;
the mirror-like wisdom is the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*mahādarśa-jñāna*) among the four wisdoms. For this reason, the four wisdoms have been briefly explained.

Regarding the statement in this *Śāstra* that "the pure consciousness of the mirror-like wisdom serves as the basis for the land," the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* says: "[It is] associated with the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom."
The mental complex refers to this mental state which is free from all conceptualization; its objects and modes of activity are subtle and difficult to perceive.
It does not forget nor is it deluded regarding any objective aspect. Its nature and characteristics are pure, free from all obstructive defilements, and it is purely radiant and perfectly luminous.

As the support for both seeds and manifest states, it can manifest and generate the reflected images of bodies, lands, and wisdom, continuing without interval or interruption until the end of the future.
Regarding the phrase "like a great round mirror manifesting various forms and images," the statement "free from all conceptualization" follows the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, which says:
"Free from the grasping of 'I' and 'mine,' and free from all conceptualizations of the apprehended and the apprehender;

that which is subtle and difficult to know refers to the fact that both the object and its mode of activity (*ākāra*) are unfathomable. Regarding the phrase "subtle and never-forgotten," it means [it is] constant.
Because of this, the Tathāgata achieves the quality of non-forgetfulness (*asaṃpramoṣa-dharma*). Because of this, he is not deluded and is not obscured regarding the meaning [of phenomena].
For this reason, the Tathāgata is named "Omniscient One" (*sarvajña*) and "One Possessing the Nature and Characteristics of Sublime Wisdom in All Its Aspects" (*sarvākāra-prajñā*).

Being pure in nature and characteristics, his self-nature is luminously enhanced; thus he is named "Pure in Nature and Characteristics," "Utterly Pure," and "Perfectly Radiant. There is none [who surpasses him].

The term "various" (*miśra*) refers to being free from faults; "pure" (*viśuddha*) means complete (*paripūrṇa*). Furthermore, "pure" (*kevala*) distinguishes it from the inferior outflow-free states within the causal stage; "pure" distinguishes it from all contaminated states;

and "complete" (*paripūrṇa*) distinguishes it from the qualities of those in the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) among the two vehicles. As for its function as the support for both the manifest and seed states:
it serves as the basis for the manifest qualities such as the "pure and complete," and it gives rise to these qualities. Thus, it is "pure" in the same sense as the pure and complete [qualities].
Because the seeds of equality act as the sustaining function that maintains the seeds, they are able to manifest and produce the reflections of the body,
the land, and wisdom; that is, they are able to manifest the reflections of the three wisdoms— the body, the land, and wisdom— continuously and without interruption until the end of the future,
because they manifest reflections at all times and in all places, never ceasing, and manifesting them within a single body.
Regarding the statement that "all reflections are like the manifestation of various forms and images in a great round mirror," the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* says:
"In the Tathāgata’s round mirror, the reflections of all images appear; based upon the mirror of Buddha-wisdom, the objects of all sense-bases appear as the reflections of various images.
Because these manifestations are all equal, it is used as a metaphor. What is now referred to as the "basis of the land" refers precisely to the purity of the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

Consciousness (*vijñāna*) serves as the basis for the manifest virtues (*saṃmukhībhūta-guṇa*). Based on this, if we provisionally explain the two lands—the Enjoyment Land (*saṃbhoga-kāya*) and the Transformation Land (*nirmāṇa-kāya*)—by subsuming the objects within the mind, they take [consciousness] as their support.
However, if one subsumes the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) back into the nature (*dharmatā*), then True Suchness (*tathatā*) must be taken as the support.

Regarding the phrase "subsequent wisdom, penetrating wisdom, and so forth," "subsequent wisdom" refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); it is used here to distinguish [it from non-conceptual wisdom].

Fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*) is such because it is realized solely through internal realization; therefore, if the body and the land manifest, these are both subsequently attained wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).
However, this is a general explanation regarding the basis of the three lands:

although the seeds of the body and the land reside within the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), the manifestation of the body and the manifestation of the land must depend on the various forms of wisdom acting as the catalysts to trigger the self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*).
The "earth" refers to the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*); the "enjoyment-realm for others" attained subsequent to it is the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*);

and the "transformation-realm" attained subsequently is the wisdom of accomplishment (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). These exist solely as subsequent wisdoms because they are each activated by subsequent wisdom to cause the pure consciousness of the mirror-like wisdom to manifest from its internal seeds.
As for the term "supernatural wisdom," this refers to the wisdom of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*); it is based upon these powers.

Because wisdom manifests both body and land, these serve as the basis for the body and land; thus, the Buddha-ground is described as *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) according to its primary and secondary aspects.
In the *Biefo di lun* (Treatise on the Distinct Buddha Grounds), it is said that all three lands manifest from the mirror-like wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

In the *Weishi lun* (Treatise on Consciousness-Only), the various wisdoms are presented differently; however, if one synthesizes these accounts, they do not contradict one another. △ Commentary: Both of these [teachings] are...
The realm of all Buddhas. △ Furthermore, "realm" (*viṣaya*) refers to the purity of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-viśuddhi*), such as the seven treasures and so forth.
△ The eighth phrase subsumes the three purities. △ Specifically, the two characters "like an illusion" (*māyopama*) refer to the purity of the fruit (*phala-viśuddhi*);
this fruit also has two aspects. △ First, the "fruit that is produced" is the purity of characteristics; it is abbreviated as "realm," but when expanded, it is...
The reflection appears among the attendants behind. △ Second, the manifestation of the fruit is called "like an illusion" because it manifests according to the occasion.
△ Fifth, the power of liberation refers to the purity of enjoyment; that is, enjoying the pure land, being free from faults and perfected in virtues, such as attaining samādhi through fragrant food.
Here, the liberation from afflictions is precisely the power of the Path that is free from faults.

This capacity is itself the perfection of virtue. *Commentary:* Regarding the passage "By using fragrant food, one attains samādhi," etc., this refers to the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, Chapter on the Fragrant Accumulation (*Gandhavyūha*).
When the time for the midday meal was approaching, Śāriputra thought about food.

Vimalakīrti then commanded a manifested bodhisattva to go to the Land of Universal Fragrance to the abode of the Tathāgata Fragrant Accumulation, and to bring back some of the remains of the Buddha’s own meal.
Vimalakīrti addressed Śāriputra, saying... [and so forth]. After the great assembly had finished eating, they proceeded to the "Chapter on the Conduct of Bodhisattvas.
Vimalakīrti, Mañjuśrī, and the entire great assembly together went to the place where the Buddha was. Ānanda, having smelled the fragrance from the pores of the bodhisattvas, questioned the Buddha.
The Buddha said to Ānanda: "All those who have taken food from the Land of Universal Fragrance..."
The pores all emit such fragrances as these. Ānanda asked Vimalakīrti, "How long will this fragrance remain?
Vimalakīrti replied, "If a śrāvaka who has not yet entered the stage of certainty eats this food, it will only be digested after they have entered that stage;

likewise for those who have attained the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) or are in their final birth before Buddhahood (ekajāti-pratibaddha). Commentary: "Entering the stage of certainty" means attaining...
The "patience regarding non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and so forth are precisely the *samādhi*. △ The *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* therefore states: "Accomplishing the pure path.
△ Sixth, in the Sanskrit original, this phrase lacks the words "and majestic power" (*prabhāva*), but includes the word "retinue" (*parivāra*).

This is because [the land] is adorned by sentient beings dwelling there, pure persons, and jewels. ○ In the *Commentary* (*Chao*), the word "majestic" (*wei*) is absent, while the word "retinue" (*juanshu*) is present.
This sentence should be stated as follows: "Like an illusion, by the power of the retinue of liberation, it is judged to be the purity of sentient beings within the dwelling place.
The commentary states: "The seventh, the purity of characteristics (lakṣaṇaviśuddhi), has already been explained as before.

Regarding the phrase in the sub-commentary, "The purity of characteristics has already been explained as before," this refers to the two characters "object-condition" (*ālambana*) within the third phrase, "purity of causes," which constitute the purity of characteristics.
△ Commentary 9: The Vow of Service.

Within a single hair-tip atom, I shall manifest the adornments of the three periods of time; I shall enter deeply into all the hair-tips of the dust-motes of the lands of the ten directions and purify them.
May all future lamps that illuminate the world attain enlightenment, turn the Dharma wheel, and awaken [beings].
I shall go to and draw near all those who manifest the ultimate Buddha-work of entering *nirvāṇa* within the realms of sentient beings.
[This is] because of the vow to go to all Buddha-lands to constantly see the Buddhas, always serve them with reverence, and listen to and receive the Dharma.

[Commentary on the] Ninth Section: The two verses beginning with "In a single hair-pore" concern the vow of service; they correspond to the sixth [vow] of that [section]. [End of] Section One of the Commentary.

The eight phrases constitute the general [principle], while the remainder are all specific [applications]. ○ In the *Commentary*, the eighth phrase is taken as the general [principle] because "going to visit and drawing near" precisely constitutes the act of serving.
△ In the *Sub-commentary*, the first verse refers to the locus of service.
△ The first two phrases universally represent the meaning of reality (*tattva*): they mutually interpenetrate like a net of Indra (*indrajāla*). ○ In the *Commentary*, [this is called] "reality."

Regarding the "characteristics of meaning" (*arthalakṣaṇa*), that sutra presents three kinds of characteristics: first, all characteristics; second, the characteristic of true reality (*tattvārthalakṣaṇa*);
and third, immeasurable characteristics. The present [section] concerns the second. That sutra states: "Like the distinctions within Indra’s net. The commentary explains:
"The lands are of the same substance, not maintaining their own individual natures, but interpenetrating one another; therefore, it is called 'true reality. [Commentary: Regarding this...
The phrase "the adornment of the lands of the three periods of time" refers to the fact that there are distinctions in the essential characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the pure lands of all appearances.

*Commentary:* Regarding the passage from "among these" to "because of the distinctions," this takes the quality of "not abiding in its own nature" from the preceding two phrases and designates it as the "pure land of all appearances.
That sutra states: "Vast and immeasurable, coarse and subtle, disorderedly situated and uprightly situated..."
Regarding "abiding," "entering," "practicing," and "departing," the commentary on the latter three phrases states: "Entering" means gathering others into oneself;
"departing" means pervading among others; and "practicing" means coming and going without remaining still.

△ The third phrase in the *Sūtra Commentary* (Shù) refers to the characteristic of immeasurability, meaning that the preceding two characteristics pervade the ten directions. ○ The third phrase in the *Sub-commentary* (Chāo) likewise refers to the characteristic of immeasurability.

That sutra states that in the ten directions there are immeasurable and diverse worlds of different kinds. It further cites the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, which says: "The number of world-systems in space exceeds the number of atoms in all the great trichiliocosms; yet, due solely to the power of karma, they do not obstruct one another. If this is so even when they are stacked vertically one upon another, how much more so when they extend horizontally in all directions.

△ Commentary on the Fourth [Section] The fourth section concerns the nature of the Buddha-lands. Regarding the phrase "immeasurable and diverse," it refers to the fact that the lands of the Buddhas are not uniform. Some are pure and adorned with jewels; some are impure and filled with suffering; some are vast and expansive; others are minute and subtle. These differences arise from the diverse karmic conditions of sentient beings and the various vows made by the Buddhas.

As for the passage concerning the *Bodhisattvapiṭaka-sūtra*, it uses the analogy of atoms to illustrate the infinite density of worlds within the void. The point is that while the physical dimensions of these worlds are inconceivable, their existence is sustained by the invisible force of karma, allowing them to coexist without spatial obstruction. This principle applies both to the vertical stacking of worlds and, by extension, to their horizontal pervasiveness across the ten directions. Thus, the text demonstrates that the dharmadhātu is infinitely layered and boundless.

Regarding the phrase "the power of discernment (*kauśalya*) is able to know and see," the *Dìjīng* (Sūtra on the Stages) states: "Wisdom is entirely clear and manifests as direct knowledge and vision;
clarity constitutes wisdom, for it is not an object of consciousness (*vijñāna*). The *Chāo* (Commentary) explains that "able to know and see" is divided into two sections:
first, the "known," which refers to the three aforementioned types of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); second, the "knower," which refers to these two phrases cited here.
The commentary explains that the characteristic of the true meaning can only be known through wisdom, whereas all other characteristics can be seen with the physical eye.
△ The Sanskrit text says: "I have deeply entered the adorned lands. △ There are two kinds of "deep entry": first, deep entry by means of wisdom;
second, deep entry by means of the body. △ Entering those adorned lands to serve the Tathāgatas does not refer to the [external] adornments.
[This] purifies them. △ If the character "刹" (kṣetra) were added below the character "而" (er), there would be no logical contradiction. ○ According to the *Chao* (Commentary):
If the character "刹" were added above the character "而," this sentence should read: "I shall deeply enter and thoroughly purify all lands."

△ The first phrase of the fifth section [of the commentary] refers to all Buddhas who are served. △ The sixth and seventh phrases refer to the eight phases [of the Buddha's life] at the time of such service.
△ In the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra*, only the distinct characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) are listed; this sūtra lacks them.
△ Commentary Ten: The Vow to Attain Perfect Enlightenment.
The power of swift and all-pervading spiritual penetrations; The power of universal entry through the Gate of the Mahāyāna; The power of universally cultivating merit through wisdom and conduct;
The power of great compassion that universally covers with majestic spirit; The power of supreme merit that universally purifies and adorns; The wisdom that is unattached and independent.
The power of wisdom; the power of concentration and the skillful means of wisdom; the power of universally accumulating all majestic strengths;
the power of purifying all wholesome karmas; the power of destroying and extinguishing all afflictions; the power of subduing all māras;
and the power of fulfilling all practices of Samantabhadra.
The Commentary states: "I vow that all sentient beings, together with me, shall simultaneously attain unsurpassed Bodhi and eternally perform the deeds of a Buddha.
The text contains twelve powers (*bala*). The first nine clarify their functional activity (*karmayoga*), while the final three conclude by showing how the cause achieves the result.
Within the former section, there are nine phrases containing seven activities; in the first six phrases, the word "power" (*bala*) stands in the middle. *Chao* (Excerpts), Fascicle Ten.

The three verses beginning with "Swiftly and pervasively" constitute the vow for attaining perfect enlightenment; this is also the tenth [vow]. The text is divided into two parts: first, the presentation and explanation of the name of the vow;
second, the sequential commentary on the text. Within the latter, there are two sections: first, the presentation of the subject matter; second, the sequential explanation.

Within the second section, there are two parts: first, clarifying the activity and function; second, concluding with the fulfillment of the cause and the attainment of the fruit. Regarding the first of these:

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the general indication and preliminary analysis; second, the detailed explanation following the text. Regarding the first, the commentary states that there are seven activities, based on two sections in that sutra:
first, the essence of attaining enlightenment, which is the perfection of one's own nature (*svabhāva*), as the sutra says:
"In all worlds, one attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*"; second, the activity of operation, which is the movement [of compassion].
In the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, there are seven activities; this current commentary relies entirely upon that [text], differing only in the order of presentation.

Therefore, it is said that "there are its seven activities. Although the sequence is different, there is no need to reconcile them. The word "power" (*bala*) is placed in the middle because it follows the convenience of the meaning;
thus, the scriptural text has been rearranged for the sake of explanation to make it clear, as in the beginning, one should say: "the power of supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*) is swift."
The meaning of "pervasive" (*zōubiàn*) is that by means of spiritual power (*ṛddhi*), one attains the power of rapid pervasion;

since the character for "power" (*lì*) is in the middle [of the term], its meaning is easily seen, and the following five phrases should be understood accordingly. *Commentary*: The first phrase refers to the karma of mastery (*vaśitā-karman*), because one universally pervades everywhere by means of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

*Sub-commentary*: Regarding the "karma of mastery," that sutra states: "By means of the supernormal knowledge of the Dharma (*dharmajñāna-abhijñā*) and the supernormal power of the bases of psychic power (*ṛddhipāda-abhijñā*)."
The sovereign transformations of illusory power fill the entire *dharmadhātu*. △ The commentary’s second line indicates the activity of perfect enlightenment.
△ Without departing from the space of a single hair-tip, one attains the path through the eight phases in all places; therefore, it is called the "Universal Gate" (*samantamukha*).
○ The sub-commentary states that regarding the indication of the activity of perfect enlightenment up to the attainment of the path through the eight phases, that sutra says: "Without departing..."

Upon the tip of a single hair, at every location of all hair-tips, there are manifested the entire sequence of all Buddhas—from their initial birth, renunciation, proceeding to the site of enlightenment, attaining perfect awakening, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering nirvana—within the various gates of manifestation.
Although many of these eight phases are frequently displayed, they differ slightly in name and order while being largely identical in meaning; or, in some cases, [the Buddha] ascends alone.
The eight marks are: first, ascending to heaven; second, descending into the mother’s womb; third, initial birth; fourth, leaving home; fifth, defeating Māra; sixth, attaining perfect enlightenment;
seventh, turning the wheel of Dharma; and eighth, entering nirvāṇa. These are as explained in the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra*. Regarding the first, the mark of ascending to heaven:
all Buddhas, when they are about to manifest birth, preach the Dharma, and benefit sentient beings, must first...
Going to the Tuṣita Heaven, for a lifespan of four thousand years therein, he performs ten kinds of sovereign deeds:

first, he teaches the Dharma of wearying detachment to the sons of gods of the desire realm; second, he teaches the entry into and emergence from the various dhyānas, liberations, and samādhis to the gods of the form realm;
third, he enters a samādhi named "Adornment of Radiance" that constantly illuminates the three thousandfold world system.
He preached the Dharma spontaneously, and upon hearing it, sentient beings were reborn in Tuṣita Heaven where they diligently applied their minds toward awakening.

This continued until the tenth discourse, wherein he taught the immeasurable and boundless Dharma-gate of illusion-like phenomena throughout the worlds of the ten directions, manifesting various forms and activities to bring joy to beings according to their capacities.
Furthermore, in order to bring to maturity those gods who shared the same spiritual path as him, he caused them to...
Hearing the Dharma and generating the bodhicitta is the sign of ascending to heaven. Second, regarding the descent into the mother’s womb:

when the four thousand years were complete and he was about to descend to be born, he manifested ten kinds of events. First, from beneath his feet, he emitted the light of "Peaceful Adornment" which shone everywhere;
those in the evil realms who encountered it attained peace, and all knew that the Bodhisattva was about to depart from the palace. Second, the *ūrṇā* mark...

From his center, he emitted the "Awakening Universal Illumination" light, which universally illuminated the bodhisattvas who had practiced together with him in past lives, causing them to know of his descent into birth and each to offer worship;

First, regarding his birth: first I shall distinguish the time of his birth, and afterwards clarify his childhood, as described in the *Mahāvyūha-sūtra*.
When the Bodhisattva was in the womb for a full ten months, he was about to be born...

"I now wish to go to the Lumbinī Garden, where the season is fragrant springtime and the trees and forests are in full bloom, fit for wandering and enjoyment. I pray the King will make the necessary preparations. Upon hearing this, the King [gave his command].
He immediately granted him a magnificent and exquisite jeweled palanquin for use throughout the park, providing all necessary enjoyments according to his needs;
he was praised by songs of the *nāgas* and devas, guarded by the fourfold army, and accompanied by many court ladies as they arrived at the park.
There they saw the *pārijāta* tree, lush and in full bloom, adorned with various jewels and fragrant with wondrous scents, surrounded by hundreds of thousands of celestial musical performances.
Immediately, he circled [the tree] and, grasping an eastern branch with his right hand, yawned and stretched;
supported by the gods of the desire realm and held up by Brahmā and Śakra, he was born peacefully from his right side, as described in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
He took seven steps in each of the ten directions, and with every step, lotuses sprang forth, emitting light that shone everywhere while the earth shook in six ways, as he proclaimed: "I am..."
He was the most honored among all beings; Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas all came to serve him personally.

Furthermore, he manifested a smile that emitted hundreds of thousands of rays of light, and upon completing these deeds, he returned to his palace. His father, the king, was filled with joy and appointed many court ladies to attend and serve him.
Later, during his youth, as described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*, he again manifested the practice of learning writing, accounting, calculation, and numeracy.
In matters of vocal arts, medical science, hygiene, mantras, seals, and other games of skill, he excelled beyond others, as described in the *Prakaraṇapāda*.
His father, the King, ordered him to study writing, arithmetic, and so forth under Āśvalāyana;

In his athletic feats, there was none who could equal him; together with the minister Dhanus (Zhizhang), he underwent each of these trials and excelled beyond all others, as described in detail in the *Lalitavistara Sūtra* and other texts.

△ Commentary: Part One—Universally Identical with Samantabhadra.
All Tathāgatas have an eldest son, whose name is the Honored One Samantabhadra. △ I now dedicate all my roots of goodness.

The buddha-fields are likewise so. △ Thus, my wisdom is named Samantabhadra’s Vow; may I and he be equal in all respects. △ Commentary:
This refers specifically to being equal to Samantabhadra. The reason for this equality is that [the vow] is the practice of Samantabhadra and is called the Dharma-realm.

If this represents the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), since it represents the Dharma-realm, there is nothing that arises among the myriad things that exceeds it. As a verse says:

In the "Contemplation of the Holy Ones," the teachings of the two holy ones and the three layers are first clarified. The first layer represents Samantabhadra as the Dharma-realm of that which is believed in, which is precisely the Tathāgatagarbha capable of giving rise [to all phenomena].
This is the Dharma-realm of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), not a direct pointing to the One True Dharma-realm (*ekavyūha-dharmadhātu*).
This is because the True Dharma-realm serves merely as the fundamental basis; it is from within this True Realm that all phenomena are able to arise.
From the perspective of its meaning, Samantabhadra is that which can illuminate the Dharma-realm; from the perspective of its meaning, Mañjuśrī is that which is illuminated.
Because the Dharma-realm as the object of faith still carries the duality of subject and object, it also belongs to the second level of dependent origination.

As for the "convergence of principle and wisdom," this refers to returning to the single true Dharma-realm by interpreting conditions through the lens of ultimate reality. Thus, although the characteristics of all phenomena manifest in a thousand differences and ten thousand distinctions, there is nothing that does not [ultimately accord with this].
Because he arises subsequent to the generation of Samantabhadra, we know that the primary generator is fundamentally of the nature of the *dharmadhātu* (True Realm).
Since his body is identical [to that realm], his arising is non-arising. Thus, the following verse states:
"Pervading the *dharmadhātu*, he is the Lord of the World, without beginning and without end. This verse is from the *Vajrayoginīcūḍāmaṇi-tantra*.
That which is pervaded is the single True Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*); that which is able to pervade is Samantabhadra;

the world is all dependently arisen phenomena (*pratītyasamutpanna-dharma*); the "Lord" is the primordial progenitor; and "having no beginning or end" means being entirely identical with the True Realm.
The *Śāstra* merely says "equal," meaning not only that the immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* vows are like the Dharma-realm, but [that they are also equal to it].

The *Śrīguṇaratnasaṃcayagāthā* (Chapter on the Virtuous King) states:
"A bodhisattva mahāsattva contemplates that there is no difference between a vicious elephant and an evil spiritual friend (*pāpamitra*). Why? Because both destroy the body.

Yet, while the bodhisattva mahāsattva feels no fear toward the vicious elephant and the like, they give rise to a mind of dread toward the evil spiritual friend. Why? Because these vicious elephants and the like..."
An evil friend can destroy only the body but cannot destroy the mind;

however, because an evil friend destroys both, he is like an evil elephant and the like, which destroys only a single body, whereas an evil friend destroys immeasurable bodies of merit and immeasurable wholesome minds.
Evil elephants and the like can only destroy an impure and stinking body, whereas an evil friend can destroy a pure body.
Furthermore, while pure minds are like elephants that can destroy the physical body, evil associates (*pāpamitra*) destroy the *dharmakāya*.
Those killed by elephants and the like do not necessarily fall into the three evil destinies, whereas those killed by evil friends will certainly go to the three evil destinies.
Thus, while elephants and the like are merely enemies to the body, evil associates are enemies to the wholesome Dharma. For this reason:
A Bodhisattva should always remain far removed from evil associates.
What is called "Immeasurable Light" is the name of Amitābha Buddha. "Immeasurable" means transcending all numerical quantities;
that is to say, each individual ray of light has its own retinue, and each retinue possesses various colors that cannot be measured. The *Sixteen Contemplations Sūtra* states:
The Buddha of Immeasurable Life possesses eighty-four thousand marks; each mark has eighty-four thousand secondary signs (anuvyañjana);
each secondary sign, in turn, has eighty-four thousand rays of light;

and each ray of light shines universally throughout the worlds of the ten directions, never abandoning those sentient beings who mindfully recite his name. Furthermore, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
The light of that Buddha shines immeasurably throughout the lands of the ten directions without any obstruction; therefore, he is named Amitābha.
All of this is brought about by the great vows made within that land. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"If, when I attain Buddhahood, my light were limited such that it did not reach even hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas [of worlds]..."
Those who calculate the number of Buddha-fields do not grasp at bodhi; yet among the practices and transformations of all Buddhas, none precedes light.
It can turn the ignorant into the wise, extract suffering and bestow joy, and transform beings without words. For this reason, it is what they seek and pray for.
Therefore, that Buddha has another name called "Boundless Light" and so forth, which refers to the twelve lights—twelve in total.
Light is immeasurable, boundless, unobstructed, and without counterpart; it is the king of flames, pure, joyful, and inconceivable in its wisdom.
It is uninterrupted, beyond praise, and surpasses the two luminosities of the sun and moon as its natural outflow (*nisyanda-phala*).

As for the person who has well-attained this supreme lifespan, it refers to the limit of the duration of a single lifetime of maturation (*vipāka*) induced by the power of prior karma, which may be short or long.

That which is long is called "life-span. Regarding this life-span, if one follows the interpretation of the Sarvāstivāda school of the Hīnayāna, it is said that life, warmth, and consciousness are a triadic conjunction;
among these three, the substance of life and warmth is provisional. The life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) exists as a distinct, substantial entity apart from matter and mind.
If one follows the Mahāyāna school, the life-faculty is established upon the seeds of the eighth consciousness, rather than being taken as a present manifestation.
"Functioning" (*pravṛtti*) refers to seeds; they are the primary capacity to produce manifest activity and furthermore can maintain it.
Because this is taken from the perspective of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), it specifically refers to seeds. Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states:

"However, based on the seeds that directly produce this consciousness, which are maintained by the specific functional capacities induced by karma, the 'life-faculty' (*jīvitendriya*) is provisionally established. The phrase "based on those that directly produce" serves to exclude [other factors].

The seeds of karma are not direct causes; rather, they are established based on the seeds of names and phrases (*nāma-pada*) within the threefold division of the fundamental consciousness (*mūla-vijñāna*), which arise from direct causes.
They are not established based on the seeds of the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of the karma that produces [the result].

This is because the seeds of karma, being remote, lack the power to act as a direct cause for the production [of the result] or to maintain its continuity; therefore, they do not constitute the essence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*). As for the term "arising" (*utpāda*):

"Excluding other seeds that are causes and conditions for the non-arising of active manifestations" means that those which have not yet produced an active manifestation do not constitute the essence of the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*);
this excludes other consciousnesses. "Consciousness" excludes the seeds of the five associated mental factors (*caitta-dharma*).

"Seeds" exclude the active manifestation of this consciousness, because the active manifestation is inferior to the seed; for although the active manifestation can indeed maintain the seed, [the seed is superior].
However, because it cannot produce seeds, the life-faculty (jīvitendriya) is not established based upon actualized phenomena (pravṛtti).
Furthermore, this seed possesses two functions: first, the general function, which serves as the capacity to produce actualized phenomena;
this function is real and permeates all seeds, for every seed possesses this capacity, and thus it is called "general. Second, the specific [function]...
A distinct function serves as the capacity to maintain matter and mind so that they do not cease;

because this maintenance exists only here, it is termed a "distinct function. If the life-faculty (*jīvitendriya*) were established solely upon this distinct function—being unique and not shared with others—then its substance would be merely nominal.
This is why it is established here based exclusively on a distinct function. Within this context:
The intended meaning is this: those who practice according to the *Samantabhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna* dwell for a duration of life determined by their prior karma;
throughout the entirety of that single lifetime, they cultivate sublime practices and do not waste time. This is called "superior lifespan.

By contrast, it is implied that those who indulge in the three unwholesome karmas commit every kind of evil; being unfit for taming, even if they were to remain in the world, [their life would be of no value].

In the interim of reporting one’s fate, as kalpas pass, evil causes become ever more extensive and the fruits of suffering are inexhaustible; thus, when goodness diminishes and evil increases, it is not a superior lifespan.
As the *Dharmapada* says: "A human life of a hundred years in which greed and avarice increase ever more—this is not equal to a single day of renouncing wealth and sensual desire.
A human life of a hundred years in which one delights in not upholding the precepts—this is not equal to a single day of purity."
A person who guards the precepts with their mind for a hundred years, yet is full of anger and lacks forbearance, is not worth a single day of one who harbors joy and is free from ill-will.
A person who lives for a hundred years, yet is indolent and lacks diligence, is not worth a single day of one who exerts both body and mind.

A person who lives for a hundred years, yet is clumsy in governing body and mind, is not worth a single day of one who is skillful and adept in their conduct. A person who lives for a hundred years, yet constantly harbors...
To be timid and weak for a hundred years is not as good as possessing the power of courageous wisdom for a single day;

to live for a hundred years without giving rise to a single virtuous aspiration is not as good as practicing the Four Great Vows for a single day; to live for a hundred years without producing a single moment of wisdom is not as good as having an intelligent and sharp nature of wisdom for a single day.

The commentary states: though one may indulge in excess for a hundred years, the transgressions will grow ever deeper; yet by practicing and maintaining discipline for even a single day, [the merit is immeasurable].
The reason they do not attain such great benefit is as stated above. △ The second section of the commentary consists of two verses on the ultimate fruit:

"Swiftly proceeding to the King of Great Bodhi Trees, having sat upon it, he subdues the hosts of Māras, attains Equal and Perfect Enlightenment, turns the Wheel of Dharma, and universally benefits all sentient beings."

Regarding the "ultimate fruit" at the end of the *Chao* (Commentary): "Swiftly proceeding to the King of Bodhi Trees," etc., means that when all Buddhas manifest their transformation bodies and approach the attainment of perfect enlightenment, they all sit beneath the Bodhi tree.

For example, during Śākyamuni’s causal stage before he became a Buddha, after six years of ascetic practice, he realized that this was not the ultimate path; he then reflected that all past Buddhas...
Having gone to the Bodhi tree, he subdued the hosts of Māra and attained equal and perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).

He then departed from that place and went to the banks of the Nairañjanā River, intending to shave his hair and bathe. At that time, there was a village headman named Senāpati from the village of Uruvilvā, who had ten daughters;
these girls had previously been providing sesame and wheat as offerings to the five Bhadravargīyas.
The Bodhisattva’s youngest son was named Sujāta;
during the time of the Bodhisattva’s ascetic practices, he constantly provided food and drink as offerings to eight hundred brahmins, vowing to assist the Bodhisattva in swiftly attaining Bodhi.
Realizing that self-starvation was not the true path, the Bodhisattva obtained a *kāṣāya* robe from Prince Vigatābhāsa. Upon reaching...
At dawn, as he entered the village to beg for alms, the deity of that settlement addressed Sujātā:
"O Sujātā, a person of pure conduct is about to come to this village to beg for food. Since you wish to make an offering to him, you should prepare it with haste.
Upon hearing this, Sujātā was filled with great joy; she took the milk of ten cows, made it extremely refined and pure, and boiled it into a gruel, intending to offer it.
When the foster-mother of the Bodhisattva realized this, auspicious signs immediately appeared upon the gruel.
Suja was greatly amazed, and a seer said to her, "If anyone eats this gruel, they will surely attain perfect enlightenment.
He then prepared a magnificent seat and instructed her to invite the Brahmins as she usually did; however, when she looked in the four directions, she saw none of them. Only...
Seeing that the Bodhisattva had returned, he went back to report to Sujātā, saying: "This is the most excellent one; I was originally intended for him, so you should invite him quickly.
Having accepted the invitation, the Bodhisattva proceeded immediately to her seat. Sujātā, filled with joy, took a golden bowl, filled it with milk-rice, and presented it to the Bodhisattva.
The Bodhisattva reflected: "Once I have eaten this congee, I shall certainly realize supreme enlightenment."
To whom shall the bowl be given? Sujāta addressed him, saying, "Please accept it as you wish.
Having accepted it, the Bodhisattva went to the Nairañjanā River, placed the bowl on the bank, shaved his hair, and bathed. The devas scattered fragrant flowers everywhere upon the river.
Having finished bathing, he collected the water and returned to offer it to the heavens. Sujāta gathered the hair and erected a stūpa, fully prepared with incense and flowers.
Having offered worship, he sat in contemplation on the Shore; as he sat, he took his meal. The Naga Queen brought forth a seat and emerged to offer it to the Bodhisattva.
Having sat down, he took the milk-rice; his body was restored to its former state. He placed the bowl in the river, where the Dragon King collected it for worship.
Śakra, having transformed himself into a Garuda, seized it and returned to heaven, where he erected a stupa to offer worship. Thus the Sūtra speaks of our Buddha.
When the World-Honored One approached the Bodhi tree, immeasurable bodhisattvas and hosts of devas each adorned the Bodhi tree;
some were a hundred thousand *yojanas* in height and composed entirely of flowers, some of pure sandalwood,
some of pure silks and brocades, some of pure jewels, and others made of the seven precious substances— such was their reckoning.
There were eighty-four thousand trees, and beneath each one was spread a lion throne according to its respective color and kind;

these thrones were adorned either with pure flowers, or incense, or jewels—whether singular or composite—and each was consecrated with the vow that the Bodhisattva would sit beneath the tree and attain unexcelled enlightenment.
At that time, the Bodhisattva bathed his body and partook of food.
With his physical strength fully restored by the milk-rice, he set out for the site of the Bodhi tree—the ground of sixteen merits—in order to subdue all demonic adversaries.
Walking with the marks of a Great Man toward the four directions, he caused the great earth to tremble and produced a great sound.
Light radiated from his feet, and wherever he stepped, lotus flowers sprang up; he proceeded with perfect mindfulness.
As he walked while gazing directly at that Bodhi tree, immeasurable winds and rains of majestic deportment arose;
from the Nairañjanā River, wind-gods and rain-gods came to the Bodhi tree, sweeping and sprinkling everywhere until it was entirely pure and adorned.
Furthermore, they rained down immeasurable, most excellent fragrant flowers, which completely covered the ground and all the large and small trees within the three-thousandfold world system.
All the great and small mountains bent low toward the Bodhi tree;
the gods of the desire realm scattered flowers, each flower measuring one *krośa* in size, forming a pedestal for it.
Furthermore, a broad road appeared, with railings made of the seven treasures on both sides, as high as seven *tāla* trees, adorned with banners of various jewels.
Everywhere it was magnificently adorned, and he further manifested seven-jeweled *tāla* trees draped with golden cords;
from these cords hung precious bells, interspersed with bright pearls and lapis lazuli.

Between every two trees stood a pool of the seven jewels, its bottom strewn with golden sand and filled with fragrant water, while four types of flowers perfumed the air and jeweled staircases surrounded them on all four sides in complete splendor.
Kalaviṅka birds and others emitted harmonious and elegant sounds; eighty-four thousand celestial maidens sprinkled various fragrant waters upon the road.

Furthermore, superior types of celestial flowers were scattered about, and beneath each tree there was a wonderful terrace made of various jewels, upon which were eighty-four thousand celestial maidens, all holding [offerings].

Precious vessels filled with various exquisite incenses were presented; furthermore, five thousand celestial maidens performed heavenly music, singing, dancing, and offering hymns of praise, producing harmonious and elegant sounds.
The Bodhisattva’s body universally emitted light that illuminated all Buddha-fields.
Additionally, immeasurable hundreds of thousands of devas played heavenly music in the void while raining down various celestial flowers.
Furthermore, flowers rained down, as did immeasurable hundreds of thousands of exquisite celestial garments.

There were also immeasurable elephants, horses, oxen, and other creatures surrounding the Bodhisattva, letting out roars whose sounds were harmonious and pleasant. Immeasurable flocks of birds soared about him, emitting melodious and elegant notes.
As the Bodhisattva proceeded toward the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), there were such immeasurable occurrences as these.

With auspicious signs of rare excellence, causing all sentient beings throughout boundless realms to attain peace and happiness and be freed from suffering and affliction, the Bodhisattva then emitted a great radiance that illuminated boundless realms; those who encountered this light had all their suffering and affliction removed.
The Naga King Kali spoke verses in praise, and the Naga Queen, surrounded by golden light, made offerings. Thus it was.
Having arrived beneath the tree, he again reflected to himself: "Upon what kind of seat did the Buddhas of the past sit to realize supreme enlightenment?
He recalled that all those Buddhas had sat upon pure grass. At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, transformed himself into a grass-cutter and stood beside the Bodhisattva holding grass.
The Bodhisattva asked him gently, "What is your name? Who are you? He replied:
"I am named Śrīkūṭa; my heart is filled with joy, for I shall now certainly realize unsurpassed bodhi.
Then, with a wondrous voice, he begged for the grass. The people were moved to joy and offered it to him.
Having accepted it, the Bodhisattva spread it out with his own hands and sat down in the full lotus posture, making this great vow: "If I do not attain Buddhahood, I shall never rise from this seat."

Regarding the phrase "sitting and so forth," this refers to the manifestation of subduing Māra. Once the Bodhisattva had sat down, he reflected that Pāpīyān of the desire realm was the most honored and supreme;
he should be summoned here and subdued. He immediately emitted light from his white tuft of hair, which illuminated the three thousandfold world system.
Upon encountering it, Pāpīyān dreamed of thirty-two inauspicious omens, and upon waking, his heart was struck with alarm.

He addressed his ministers and aides, saying, "I have heard a voice from the sky declaring that Prince Siddhārtha, having perfected his ascetic practices, will surely attain *bodhi* and empty my realm; how shall I subdue him?

His ministers and his thousand sons all offered counsel against this, but Pāpīyān became even more enraged and immediately summoned his daughters to go before the Bodhisattva, each displaying her seductive charms and desires.
When his pure conduct was thus violated, the Bodhisattva felt compassion and spoke verses to transform them, so that all the celestial maidens would recognize the faults of desire.
He further replied to them: "You possess merit and have now attained birth in the heavens; yet you do not contemplate impermanence and instead create various illusions and delusions.
You shall surely fall into the evil realms, and it will be extremely difficult to escape. At that time, the maidens scattered heavenly flowers over him.
The Bodhisattva Dakṣiṇāvarta returned to the heavens and related the circumstances in detail to Pāpīyas. He exhorted Pāpīyas, saying, "I pray that you do not cause further trouble.
At that time, a son of the Māra division named Śāstṛ addressed his father the King, saying, "The Bodhisattva is pure and transcends the three realms;
his supernormal powers and spiritual might are such that no one can withstand him, including the devas, nāgas, and spirits."
They all praised him together, saying, "He certainly cannot be defeated or humbled by Your Majesty; there is no need to commit evil and bring calamity upon yourself.
Pāpīyān did not accept this and went away to dismiss them himself, but they would not obey.

The Wheel-turning King dwelt alone in the mountains, desiring the Buddha-way, yet he merely exhausted his own body in vain. The Bodhisattva said to him, "I am sitting here now, having resolved to attain Bodhi."
"The moon falling to earth and Mount Sumeru collapsing—could such things truly happen? My resolve shall not waver!
Pāpīyān roared with a voice like thunder, summoning the yakṣas and leading his own followers. Of base, evil, and hideous form, they were of hundreds of thousands of different species;
some spread black clouds with thunder and lightning, some rained down sand and stones, some hoisted great mountains, or [spoke] from their mouths...
Some spat out venomous snakes, while others emitted fierce flames from their bodies; they drew their bows, brandished swords, danced with spears, and whirled pikes.

These immeasurable billions of demonic armies caused great terror, yet through the Bodhisattva’s power of loving-kindness and meditative concentration, the sand, stones, arrows, and arrowheads were all transformed into flowers.
The wicked dragons who spat poison all turned their venom into fragrant scents. Even when Māra, the Evil One, seized a sword intending to harm him, his own sons [could not prevent it].
Embracing him, they admonished him so that he would not incur sin or blame;
the Bodhi-tree deity and immeasurable hosts of devas spoke words of censure against him while praising the virtues of the Bodhisattva. At that time, the Bodhisattva said to Māra:
"I shall now sever your enmity here, extinguish your evil karma, and eliminate your jealousy; you should turn your mind back and give rise to great joy."
"By means of a small amount of merit, I have now obtained this celestial body; yet for immeasurable kalpas I have cultivated the noble path—what evidence do you, Māra, have for your words?
The Bodhisattva then pointed to the earth with his right hand and spoke this verse: "On what do all things depend to grow?
The great earth can act as an impartial witness. Therefore, she should provide me with testimony. You.
Now, at the time of this teaching according to reality, the Earth Goddess emerged from the ground holding a flower garland as an offering and said:
"I can bear witness that the Bodhisattva, having practiced for many eons in the past, has now attained enlightenment to repay his former causal deeds.
Furthermore, this ground of mine is the Vajra-navel; while all other directions may turn, this place does not move. Having spoken these words, she remained there.
The great trichiliocosm shook in six ways and emitted a great sound characterized by eighteen aspects.
When the hosts of Māra saw this, their bodies and minds became frantic and disordered; they fled in chaotic confusion.
Pāpīyān was terrified and fainted, collapsing instantly upon the ground. A terrestrial deity sprinkled water on him and said, "Depart quickly! There is an army here."
"When they come wishing to harm you, the hosts of Māra retreat, disperse, and flee"—this concludes the section on the signs of subduing Māra.

As for "attaining equal and perfect enlightenment," this refers to the signs of attaining the Way (*bodhi*), which has already been explained within the section on the application of the fruits of training.
△ Section Three: Three Verses Concluding with Exhortation to Receive and Maintain. Part One: Concluding the Previous Practices.
If a person reads, recites, receives, maintains, and expounds these vows of Samantabhadra, [they shall attain the fruit].
△ Second, the commentary further clarifies the supreme benefits:
"The karmic fruition can only be realized by a Buddha; one will certainly attain the path of supreme Bodhi.

If a person recites this *Samantabhadra-praṇidhāna*, I declare that even a small portion of their roots of goodness will, in a single thought-moment, be entirely perfected and fulfilled, bringing all sentient beings to purification."
Pure Vow.
△ Commentary III: Concluding the Dedication.
May these supreme practices of mine, Samantabhadra, and all boundless, excellent merits be dedicated universally, so that all sentient beings submerged in suffering may be saved.
One will be born and swiftly proceed to the Buddha-field of Amitābha.
△ [Commentary] Part Two: Concluding the Explanation and Praising its Excellence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Samantabhadra, before the Tathāgata, spoke these vast vows of Samantabhadra.
The King’s Verses on Purity were concluded. △ Sudhana the youth leaped for joy beyond measure.
△ All the Bodhisattvas were filled with great delight. △ The Tathāgata praised them, saying: "Excellent, excellent!"
The Commentary states that the praise for "skillful" refers to the arising of the meaning;

when this assembly entered meditative absorption, the Buddha had not yet spoken, so the ancient masters collectively established [this teaching] to allow the multitude to realize it instantaneously. The Sub-commentary explains:

"When this assembly entered meditative absorption, the Buddha had not yet spoken" means that at the beginning of the assembly, as soon as the World-Honored One entered the *Siṃhavijṛmbhita-samādhi*, he caused the Jetavana Grove to suddenly become vast and expansive, manifesting [the Pure Land].
The various matters of adornment were developed by Samantabhadra and praised by Mañjuśrī, whereupon the great assembly attained sudden realization.
Subsequently, Mañjuśrī went out to the east of Puṇḍravardhana to instruct Sudhana, leading him through a succession of teachers in his quest for the Way until the end of the chapter.
Since there is no place in the Buddha’s own discourse where he speaks of this, the phrase "the Tathāgata spoke in praise" refers to Arthavarman.
△ Commentary, Part Two: The Section on Circulation, Part One: Indicating the Dharma Taught.
At that time, when the World-Honored One was expounding this supreme dharma-gate of the inconceivable realm of liberation to the assembly of noble Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas.

The commentary previously explained that what was spoken by Samantabhadra already constitutes the established meaning; now, stating that it was "spoken by the Buddha" likewise constitutes the established meaning.

This intention is intended to encompass everything in its entirety, and therein there are two points: △ First, in this particular assembly, although the Buddha serves as the presiding host, even though the various spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) are present, because the general encompasses the specific, these too belong to what was spoken by the Buddha.
△ Second, it universally encompasses all nine assemblies, for in each of them, [the Bodhisattvas] do not give rise to the thought of awakening (bodhicitta).
The King of Trees (Dharmakṣema) preached it all at once, pervading every place. *Commentary:* Regarding the statement that "this single assembly...
also belongs to the Buddha’s teaching," it means that from the first assembly onward, the Bodhisattvas serve as the primary interlocutors; this is intended to signify something.

Specifically, the first assembly has Samantabhadra as its primary figure, serving as a general representation of the nine assemblies. It signifies the essence of the two fruits—the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* (the body of reality) and his *saṃbhogakāya* (the enjoyment body).

1. This Dharma-realm Samantabhadra is the lord because he presides over the dharma-realm; 2. Mañjuśrī is the lord because he presides over the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*); light is emitted from beneath his feet. 3.
Dharmamati is the lord because the ten abodes (*vihāra*) are the stage of understanding; light is emitted from the toes of his feet. 4.
Guṇakūṭa is the lord because the ten practices (*caryā*) are as dense and towering as a forest; light is emitted from the insteps of his feet. 5. Vajradhvaja...
1. Because the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī acts as the presiding lord for the sake of returning merit toward transcendence, light is emitted from his two knees. 2.
Because the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha acts as the presiding lord for entering the stages (*bhūmi*) to be able to produce inexhaustible merit, light is emitted from between his eyebrows. 3.

Because the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra acts as the presiding lord for the fulfillment of the stages such that he returns to be identical with the *dharmadhātu*, and because within a single assembly there are distinct symbolic indications according to each chapter, there is the "Remaining Bodhi" (the Bodhisattva of Remainder).

8. Those such as Samantabhadra and Samantamati are the primary speakers; they preside over the Dharma and advance the cultivation of wisdom, for wisdom can induce practice, and Samantabhadra presides over practice.
9. Only at the beginning of this assembly does the Buddha himself preside as the host, signifying the entry into the fruit through the cause;
for if one does not harmonize with the Buddha-mind, there is no way to enter realization. Therefore, it says "the Buddha."

As the presiding host of these assemblies, all the spiritual friends are manifestations of the remaining categories within the Buddha’s ten bodies; thus, they collectively encompass the specific instances.

Furthermore, even the primary speakers of the first eight assemblies are the Bodhisattva body among the Buddha’s ten bodies. Therefore, at the beginning of each assembly, the Buddha is first designated.
Those of shallow understanding do not comprehend this meaning and claim that the *Avataṃsaka* is for the most part not [the Buddha's teaching].
To say that what the Buddha himself spoke was not yet the most sublime is entirely mere street talk.

The commentary’s second section, which encompasses all nine assemblies, extends to the "simultaneous sudden teaching," meaning that without rising from the Bodhi tree, he ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and the other three heavens;
in all cases, he ascended without rising, as stated in the "Ascent to Mount Sumeru" chapter: "At that time, the World-Honored One..."
The Honored One does not depart from beneath every Bodhi tree when he ascends Mount Sumeru toward the palace of Śakra.
As the Bodhisattva Dharmamati said in verse: "O Son of the Buddha, you should observe the Tathāgata’s power of mastery:
in every Jambudvīpa it is said that the Buddha is therein; yet we now see the Buddha dwelling upon the summit of Sumeru, and so it is throughout the ten directions."
However, since the sovereign power of the Tathāgata is such that all three heavens are likewise so, four propositions are established:
first, not arising from any bodhi tree, yet ascending to one heaven, as in the preceding scriptural passage; second, not arising from one place, yet ascending to all places;
third, not arising from one place, yet ascending to one place; fourth, not arising from all places, yet...
Regarding the two sets of four phrases for "ascending to all places," take the text concerning the conclusion as an example: "The same applies to all ten directions.
Taking the previous case of one Jambudvīpa corresponding to all the Trāyastriṃśa heavens as the same applies here constitutes the fourth phrase;

taking one Jambudvīpa corresponding to all the Trāyastriṃśa heavens [in each direction] constitutes the second phrase; and the third phrase is as follows: [taking all Jambudvīpas corresponding to one Trāyastriṃśa heaven].
Because it is easy to understand, there is no further textual elaboration. The meaning must necessarily be that this is so;

thus, the Dharma-realm Bodhi tree universally ascends throughout the Dharma-realm in seven locations—this refers to the fourth phrase. Question: Since movement and stillness are contradictory and going and staying are vastly different, and you have already stated that they are not separate, how can you say "ascends"?
Answer: Indeed, the Buddha’s attainment of Bodhi-wisdom is such that there is nowhere its essence does not pervade.

He does not abide in non-reliance, non-dwelling, non-going, or non-coming; yet, through the spontaneous response of his very essence, this response follows the essence as it universally pervades all conditions.
Thus, there are those who perceive him dwelling or ascending at various times—some perceive him on the Bodhi tree in Jambudvīpa, while others perceive him ascending to the celestial palaces.
It is not that the Buddha at the Bodhi tree moves elsewhere to ascend to the celestial palaces.

It is said that one does not leave the tree of awakening to ascend to the palace of Śakra; thus, the *Dharmaprajñā* states: "O Son of the Buddha, you should observe," and so forth. These words and principles have scriptural authority. To further clarify this through analogy: it is like the bright moon, whose reflections flow everywhere in accordance with conditions. Suppose there is a single moon over a clear river, and three boats are observing it together. One boat remains stationary while the other two move north and south. For the one moving south, the moon appears to move north. (The same applies to the one moving north. Thus, although the moon is one, its reflections appear as many according to the conditions of the observers.
