Those traveling a thousand *li* south see the moon moving south; those who have moored their boats and are traveling north for a thousand *li* see the moon as stationary.

This means that this single moon does not leave the center of the stream to travel toward the south or north. Suppose a hundred or a thousand people were to observe it together from the eight directions, each at a different location;
then a hundred or a thousand moons would appear to follow each person's movement. Those with discerning awareness understand this principle.

△ Commentary: Previously, it was seen that Samantabhadra, at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa), subsumed the derivative within the fundamental and encompassed the derivative with the fundamental, all for the sake of the Buddha’s teaching.
○ Sub-commentary: Regarding the passage from "previously seen Samantabhadra" to "the Buddha’s teaching":

although the first assembly began at the site of enlightenment as the place where the Way was realized, the Buddha did not depart from the Bodhi tree to be in the Jeta Grove; rather, it was Mañjuśrī [who was there].
Emerging from the Buddha’s assembly and proceeding as far as the eastern gate of Puṇyavatī to meet Sudhana represents the progression from the root to the branches.

Sudhana’s successive journey southward in search of spiritual friends constitutes the "branches. From the point where he is introduced to those who have attained the stages (*bhūmi*) onward, there is generally no further mention of directions;
finally, when he meets Samantabhadra within the Bodhimaṇḍa, this represents the return of the branches to the root.
Therefore, it is said that "taking the root to encompass the branches" constitutes the entirety of what was taught by the Buddha.
△ Section Two: The Assembly Receiving and Upholding at Two Times. Part One: Listing the Capable Holders of the Teaching. Sub-part One: The Assembly of Bodhisattvas.
With Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva as their leader, there were all the great bodhisattvas; with Maitreya Bodhisattva as their leader, there were the six thousand bhikṣus who had been brought to maturity;

and with Vimalasamantabhadra Bodhisattva as their leader, there were all the great bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, those who are in their final birth before buddhahood and abide in the stage of consecration.
And there were all the assemblies of bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, numbering as many as the atoms within the oceans of all lands, who had gathered from various worlds throughout the ten directions.
The commentary contains four categories; the first two categories mostly pertain to this assembly, while the third concerns the meaning of Samantabhadra.
Generally speaking, "following" (sui) encompasses all nine assemblies; the fourth assembly, where various worlds gather from afar, also applies to both meanings.

Furthermore, this refers to the newly gathered multitude who have come from afar, as these two apply to the gatherings of all nine assemblies, though there is no such textual record in the Sanskrit original.
Regarding the *Chao* (Commentary), the six thousand bhikṣus who were brought to maturity are none other than Mañjuśrī.
Taking his leave of the Buddha, he departed for the south.

Śāriputra also took his leave of the Buddha and led his own assembly of six thousand bhikṣus, with the bhikṣu Sāgarabuddhi as their leader. On the way, Śāriputra exhorted them to take refuge in Mañjuśrī.
Mañjuśrī, turning like an elephant king, gazed upon the bhikṣus and spoke to them of ten kinds of non-... [the text continues].
The mind free from weariness consists of: the mind that accumulates all roots of goodness without weariness;
the mind that sees all Buddhas, serves, and makes offerings to them without weariness; the mind that seeks all Buddha-dharmas without weariness;
the mind that practices all perfections without weariness; and the mind that accomplishes all bodhisattva samādhis without weariness.
Entering successively into all minds of the three periods of time without weariness; universally adorning and purifying the Buddha-fields of the ten directions without weariness;
teaching, transforming, and subduing all sentient beings without weariness;
and practicing throughout all eons to accomplish the mind of a bodhisattva without weariness, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to fulfillment.

The accomplishment of the *pāramitās* equal in number to the atoms of all Buddha-fields, and the successive attainment of the ten powers of a Tathāgata in order to mature all realms of sentient beings—this is the mind that never tires in accomplishing all the powers of a Tathāgata.
Because the bhikṣus have attained the universal illumination of the Dharma-realm, the Preface to the Great Commentary says: "The Elephant King turns in circles six times."

A thousand paths are accomplished beneath a single word; therefore, these are listed here. Regarding the term *bhikṣu*: the new translation is *biqiu* (苾蒭), which in the language of Tang means "possessing purity" (*viśuddha*).
In India there is a plant called *bhikṣu*, which possesses five virtues; by way of analogy, the disciples of the Buddha possess five kinds of virtues.
First, their essential nature is supple, just as the *bhikṣu* plant is subdued; they restrain the three karmas.
Subduing afflictions so they do not arise, being gentle and speaking kindly without offending others;

these two extend their influence laterally and spread abroad—this illustrates how a bhikṣu must transmit the Buddha’s teachings, exhorting and transforming all beings, leading one another in succession and transforming each other, just as one lamp lights hundreds of thousands of lamps.
Third, the fragrance rises far and wide; those who perceive this fragrance rejoice.
The joy of body and mind is like this: when the fragrance of a bhikṣu’s precepts wafts abroad, all who hear it give rise to joy and conceive the aspiration for the Way.
As for the four types of touch that bring peace and comfort to the body, even those with ailments are entirely healed when brushed by these blades of grass;
this is used as an analogy for how a bhikṣu severs his own afflictions to seek unsurpassed bodhi, while outwardly transforming others through teaching.
May all sentient beings cause the severing of evil and the extinction of afflictions and delusions, abiding securely in wholesome qualities.
Fifth, they shall never turn their backs on the light of the sun, just as the heliotrope flower always turns toward the sun;

this illustrates how a bhikṣu, throughout the four modes of conduct—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—always faces the Tathāgata and never conditions upon external objects or false views. These are the five virtues. Furthermore, there are another five.
The meanings are as follows: First, "Terrifier of Māras," referring to when he first left the household life, the palaces of Māra shook;

this is said in reference to those who leave home with a pure mind. Second, "Bhikṣu" (Almsman), meaning that above, he begs the Dharma from all Buddhas to sustain his life of wisdom, and below, he begs food and clothing from donors to maintain his physical body, seeking unsurpassed Bodhi. Third, "Pure Upholder of Precepts."
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* state that upholding the precepts is called "pure" when it possesses six meanings: first, abiding in pure ethical discipline (*śīla*);
second, possessing the Prātimokṣa vows that can personally prevent wrongdoing; third, being complete in the three thousand modes of deportment and eighty thousand subtle practices;
fourth, being complete in conduct by avoiding the five places where one should not go—namely, [the homes of] virgins and widows; and fifth... [text truncated].
Sixth, because the five types of people—the female liquor-seller, the butcher, and their evil associates—give rise to great fear regarding even minute transgressions, the World-Honored One said:
"Do not slight a small offense, thinking it will bring no calamity; though a drop of water is minute, it gradually fills a large vessel. To be cautious is truly sublime.
These are the six points concerning the necessity of relying on a superior teacher when receiving [the precepts], so as not to manifest false views. Thus are the six meanings.

This is called "pure observance of the precepts. Fourth is "pure livelihood," which means being free from the four types of wrong livelihood and the five types of wrong livelihood. Regarding the four types of wrong livelihood:

first, "eating by looking downward" (*adhomukha-bhikṣā*), which refers to planting trees, cultivating fields, and breaking up the soil; second, "eating by looking upward" (*ūrdhvamukha-bhikṣā*), which refers to seeking food and clothing by observing the stars and celestial phenomena;

third, "eating by looking across" (*tiryagmukha-bhikṣā*), which refers to engaging in the flow of goods and expenditures throughout the four directions; [and fourth, eating by looking around, which refers to seeking gain through flattery and deception].

Furthermore, there are those who engage in matchmaking; these four types constitute "feeding on the mouth" (oral livelihood). This refers to seeking food and clothing through incantations, divination, calculating one's fortune and destiny, and resolving doubts by using threats against others.
Regarding the five wrong modes of livelihood (*pañca-kuśīdāhārāḥ*): first, falsely manifesting something extraordinary for the sake of gain and offerings;
second, speaking of one’s own virtues for the sake of gain and offerings; third, interpreting signs and portents of good and bad fortune for the sake of gain and offerings... [and so forth].
1. Preaching in order to incite fear for the sake of seeking food and clothing; 2. Praising oneself as having attained offerings for the sake of gain and profit, thereby agitating people's hearts;
3. For the sake of gain and profit, extensively establishing disciples and manifesting a majestic presence with a loud voice to cause others to feel dread and agitation, seeking wealth;
4. If one can remain free from these four and five types of deviant gains that provide for the body, such acquisitions are called pure.
One is called a bhikṣu by virtue of receiving the alms-food; fifth is "Destroying Evil," which means being able to subdue the four māras.

As for all the great bodhisattvas of the Bhadrakalpa, they should now be called "Worthy and Good" (Sabhadraka) during this *vāsakalpa*, which is the reason they receive that name as explained in the Mahākaruṇā-sūtra:
when this trichiliocosm was first about to be formed, there was a great body of water.
The Śuddhāvāsakāyika devas, observing this great body of water, saw a thousand exquisite lotuses, each with a thousand petals, golden in color and radiating golden light.
Knowing that there were one thousand noble persons who would attain Buddhahood within the same kalpa, they named it the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Kalpa).
It remains within the twenty intermediate kalpas; we are now in the ninth, while Maitreya will appear in the tenth kalpa.
The attainment of Buddhahood is as explained in other passages. Regarding the term "one birth remaining before Buddhahood" (*ekajātipratibaddha*):

it means that there is only one more birth to be experienced among humans, which is called "one birth"; being destined to succeed the preceding Buddha in his position is called "the stage of succession.

This refers to the attainment of the Way through the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body). According to the interpretation of Cien alone, there are three stages for the "one birth remaining before Buddhahood": first, [the stage of...]

Regarding the three types of bodies—the body bound by one more birth (*ekajātipratibaddha*), the final body (*caramabhavika*), and the body seated at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍastha*)—if one is born above, one is "bound by one more birth," meaning there is only one further birth remaining before liberation.
If one is born below, it is restricted to the latter two types of bodies.
For example, when Śākyamuni was first born, he took seven steps in each of the four directions: east, west, south, and north. It is said that [this refers to] the latter two types of bodies.
A verse says: "My births in the womb are exhausted; this is my very last body. I have attained the exhaustion of outflows (āsrava-kṣaya);

I shall extensively deliver sentient beings. This is what is called the "final body" (*paścima-deha*). Later, when sitting beneath the Bodhi tree, it is called the "body sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa-āsana-deha*).
Once Buddhahood is realized, it is no longer subsumed under these three stages and is called the "Buddha-body" (*buddha-deha*). This is the transformation [body].
Before attaining Buddhahood, there are three types of bodies: the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*), the other-enjoyment body (*parasambhogakāya*), and the birth-body (*janmakāya*).
As described in Maitreya’s commentary, even before attaining Buddhahood, these three types of birth-bodies exist.

Furthermore, bodhisattvas possess five kinds of skillful means of birth for the purpose of gathering, transforming, guiding, and benefiting all classes of beings. The first is the birth that eliminates calamities (*upadrava-vinodana-janman*). By...
May the power of mastery over aspirations act as a great fish to rescue those who are hungry and destitute; may it act as a great king of physicians to save those afflicted by disease;
may it act as a great master of skillful means to harmonize strife and contention; may it act as a great king to pacify suffering in accordance with the Dharma;
and may it act as a great celestial deity, fire, water, a chariot, a boat, and various other things to bring relief.
To eliminate calamities and afflictions, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* states: "Sometimes he manifests as the sun, the moon, the devas, or Brahmā, the Lord of the World;
sometimes he manifests as earth or water, or again as fire or wind. During kalpas of disease, he manifests his body as medicinal herbs;
during kalpas of famine, he manifests his body as food and drink; and during kalpas of warfare, he gives rise to compassion for their sake."
The two types of compassion and so forth arise according to their respective categories; through the power of mastery over vows, they take birth among the evil destinies such as the animal realm.
Therein, they do not themselves commit the evils practiced by others, yet they practice the virtues that others do not.
Just as one who enters various taverns can maintain their resolve, or one who enters brothels demonstrates the faults of desire and preaches the True Dharma for them.

1. Eliminating those three faults; 2. Birth with great power, which is most excellent in terms of innate disposition, lifespan, physical form, lineage, and wealth, and is able to sever the faults of sentient beings such as contempt; 3.
Birth of superior excellence, which receives the fruit of the ten kings and exercises sovereign guidance according to what is appropriate for birth; 4. Most supreme birth—this birth.

Regarding the provisions: having brought them to ultimate perfection, like Śākyamuni and others, one is born into the family of a great kṣatriya royal house and is able to manifest equal enlightenment and perform the various deeds of a Buddha.
As for what is now called "one birth remaining" (ekajātipratibaddha), among the five types of births, it subsumes the latter four;
once one has descended to be born below and dwells in the final body, this is included within the fifth birth—this constitutes the first [point].

Regarding the statement that one is born in the position of the successor (*upapatti-paścima*) and dwells in the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), this is also called the "stage of receiving the office.
The thirty-ninth fascicle of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* states that the mind at the completion of the tenth stage is called the "stage of receiving the office.

When a bodhisattva reaches the end of this stage, they attain ten million *asaṃkhyeya* samādhis; the final of these samādhis is named "Receiving All-Knowledge Victory" (*sarvajñatā-pratilambha-viśeṣa*).
While dwelling in this samādhi, a great precious lotus flower suddenly appeared; its breadth was immeasurable,
equal to hundreds of thousands of triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems, adorned with various exquisite jewels interspersed throughout,
surpassing all worldly realms, and produced by supramundane roots of goodness as numerous as atoms.
With lotuses as their retinue, at that time the Bodhisattva sat upon this lotus seat; his physical form and its proportions were perfectly harmonious.
Immeasurable Bodhisattvas served as his retinue, each sitting upon the remaining lotuses, surrounding him on all sides.
Each one attained a million samādhis and gazed with single-minded devotion toward the Great Bodhisattva.
When this Great Bodhisattva sits upon the flower throne, his radiance and voice pervade the entire Dharma-realm;
all worlds tremble, the evil realms find rest, and the lands become adorned and pure.
Bodhisattvas of the same practice all assemble there, and the music of devas and humans sounds forth simultaneously, so that all sentient beings attain peace and happiness.

From beneath his two feet, he emitted hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* rays of light that universally illuminated all the great hells of the ten directions, extinguishing the suffering of sentient beings;
from his two kneecaps, he emitted light that extinguished the suffering of animals;

from his navel, he emitted light that illuminated the realm of Jambudvīpa, extinguishing the suffering of hungry ghosts; and from his two flanks, he emitted light that extinguished the suffering of humans.

From his two hands, he emits light that universally illumines the palaces of the devas and the palaces of the asuras; from between his two eyebrows, he emits light that universally illumines the śrāvakas;

from the back of his neck, he emits light that universally illumines the pratyekabuddhas; from his mouth, he emits light that illumines bodhisattvas from those who have first resolved upon enlightenment up to those on the ninth stage;
from the space between his brows, he emits light that universally illumines the bodhisattvas of the tenth stage, causing all the palaces of Māra to be completely [overwhelmed].
None of them manifested their crowns; instead, they emitted light from their heads that universally illuminated the assemblies at the sites of enlightenment of all Buddhas.
They circled [the Buddha] ten times to the right, remained suspended in mid-air, and formed a network of light called "Blazing Radiance," initiating various kinds of offerings to worship the Buddha.
This was beyond the reach of other bodhisattvas, from those who have first resolved upon enlightenment up to those on the ninth stage.
If one were to compare other forms of making offerings to this, they would not equal even a fraction of it by way of calculation or analogy.
If there are sentient beings who see such a thing, they shall all attain non-retrogression from bodhi.
Having performed this offering through this great radiance, [the light] again circumambulated each of the Buddha-assembly sites in the ten directions ten times, and then...

At that time, as they enter beneath the feet of all the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know that a certain Bodhisattva in a certain world is practicing the vast conduct and has reached the stage of receiving the position of consecration;

even the assembly of Bodhisattvas up to the ninth stage surround him with reverence and observe him with right observation. At that moment, each of those Bodhisattvas immediately attains ten thousand [qualities].

All the Bodhisattvas who have received their offices throughout the ten directions emit from within the mark of virtue on their vajra-adorned chests a great light called "Able to Destroy the Enemies of Māra.
Having universally illumined the ten directions and manifested spiritual transformations, this light enters the mark of virtue on the chest of this Bodhisattva.
Once the light has entered, it causes the power of this Bodhisattva’s wisdom—
At that time, the power [of this bodhisattva] increased a hundred thousandfold.
Then, from the space between the eyebrows of all Buddhas of the ten directions, there issued forth pure light, with countless rays of light as its retinue;

named "Augmenting All-Knowledge and Supernatural Powers," it universally illumined the Dharma-realm, performed Buddha-works, and then came to this assembly of bodhisattvas, encircling them on all sides.
Having manifested these various adornments surrounding him, [the light] entered from the crown of the Great Bodhisattva’s head;
the radiance of his retinue likewise each entered the crowns of these bodhisattvas.

At the moment of entry, this bodhisattva attained ten million samādhis never before attained, and was called one who had "already received the position of consecration" (abhiṣeka) and entered the Buddha-state.
The commentary states: Regarding those who have gathered from afar, this refers to the assembly of five hundred bodhisattvas and śrāvakas listed here;
because the World-Honored One entered meditative absorption and manifested signs, whereupon the bodhisattvas of the ten directions gathered like clouds, they are called the "new assembly.
As for "endowed with the spheres" and "possessing the ten powers," these refer to their inclusion within the ranks of the Buddhas.
△ Commentary [Section] Two: The Assembly of Śrāvakas.
With the Greatly Wise Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, and others as their leaders, there were the various great śrāvakas.
This commentary restricts its scope solely to this specific assembly. ○ The Sub-commentary (Chao) states: "The Greatly Wise Śāriputra and others" refers to Śāriputra’s original...
His name was Śāriputra, also called Śāradvatīputra; he was named after his mother, Śārikā.
His clan name was Kauṇḍinya, and he was known as Upatiṣya, the son of the master Tiṣya from Rājagṛha.
At only eight years of age, his fame resounded throughout the four quarters. He had been a friend since childhood with Mahāmaudgalyāyana. As for his physical appearance...
Śaila was short in stature and of humble means; the non-Buddhist teacher Śreṇika knew that he had not yet reached the ultimate goal and expected him to attain liberation in the future.
Later, Śaila encountered Aśvajit, heard the Dharma, and attained the first fruit [of the path]. Together with his two hundred and fifty disciples, he went forth under the Buddha.
Half a month later, he attained the fruit of arhatship (*aśaikṣa*). The third *Āgama* states: "Among my śrāvakas, I declare him to be the foremost."
The bhikṣu Śāriputra possessed inexhaustible wisdom. As stated in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*, fascicle 23:
"Śāriputra is the second Dharma King. This is described in detail in the fourth fascicle of the *Madhyama Āgama* (the *Zìguǒ jīng*) and the ninth fascicle of the *Xīyù Jì*, among other sources.
Regarding Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the new [translation] renders it Mahā-Maudgalyāyana.
The disciple Maudgalyāyana’s clan name was Mahāprajñā, which in the fourth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* is translated as Mahā-mudga (Great Bean-Eater).
He was a descendant of the immortal Mudgala, also known as Kolita or Kautika.
He was a great Brahmin of the Kauṇḍinya clan from the city of Kuśinagara in Rājagṛha. Later, he was moved by the verses spoken by Śāriputra.

Having realized the Way and gone forth under the Buddha, seven days later he attained the fruit of Arhatship (*aśaikṣa-phala*). He constantly stood to the left of the Buddha, while Śāriputra was on the right;
they were known as the "Two Worthy Disciples. The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Among my śrāvakas, this bhikṣu is foremost in supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vidhi*);
with his body light and agile, he flies to the ten directions. This is recorded by Mount Nan as being concerning Maudgalyāyana.

There are six individuals who share this same name; the term "Great" (Mahā-) is used here to distinguish him from the others and avoid confusion, as detailed in the *Buddhacarita* (Chapter 48), the ninth [chapter], the *Xiyuji*, and other sources.
Regarding the "great śrāvakas": "voice" (*śabda*) refers to the voice of the Buddha’s teachings;
those who hear this voice and awaken to the Path are called *śrāvakas*. This term applies generally to the Mahāyāna as well, for they too are called "voices."

It is called "Hearing" because it causes all beings to hear through the sound of the Buddha-way. Furthermore, there are six meanings for why it is called "Great": first, the greatness of wisdom, as it exhausts the state of non-arising;
second, the greatness of abandonment, as it exhausts both the views and the cultivation [of afflictions]; third, the greatness of marks, as it consists of the majestic deportment of a Buddha;

fourth, the greatness of benefit, as it is worthy of offerings from the world; fifth, the greatness of function, as it possesses the supernormal powers and clear insights; sixth, the greatness of prediction, as it concerns the future...
Because they become Buddhas.

△ The third section of the Commentary concerns the miscellaneous classes of beings, including all humans and devas, as well as the various world-protectors: devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, and so forth.
The great assembly of all beings, including the *rākṣasas*, *kiṃnaras*, *mahoragas*, humans, non-humans, and so forth.
The *Chao* states that "devas, nāgas, and others" refers collectively to the eight classes of beings. Regarding the first class, the devas, there are four types:
first, the celestial devas, who are called "sons of heaven" (*devaputra*) because they possess merit; these various devas have their merit diminished by one part.
Together with the present Heavenly Son, these are the two types of "Heavenly Births" (deva-jāti) known throughout the world.

From the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there are sentient beings within the "Three Pure Heavens" (*śuddhāvāsa*). Those who attain the fruits of sainthood (*āryaphala*) specifically among human beings are called "Pure Heavens" (*śuddhadeva*), as they possess the sense of mastery (*vaśitva*).
These are the four types of "Pure Birth Heavens," referring to all those within the twenty-eight heavens.
The "sage" refers to this very person. Regarding what is now called "heaven," among the four types [of heavens], it mostly takes the second, which is birth in heaven.
There are four kinds of nāgas: first, celestial nāgas who uphold the celestial palaces so that they do not fall;
second, human nāgas who raise clouds and bring rain in the human realm; third, earth nāgas who can sustain the mountains, rivers, and the great earth; and fourth, royal nāgas who act as guardians.

Regarding the protection of the king’s treasuries and so forth, there are further four kinds: first, the *qiulóng* (horned dragon), which has horns; second, the *yinglóng* (hawk-dragon), which has wings;
third, the *lilóng* (black dragon), which has a pearl; and fourth, the *jiaolóng* (eel-dragon), which has scales.
Furthermore, a dragon must be free from five kinds of obstacles before it can send down rain: first, the obstacle of the fire element (*tejas*).
1. The two winds increase in intensity and blow the clouds apart. 2. The asuras gather the clouds and draw them into the ocean. 3.
The wind-lords and rain-masters become heedless and indolent. 4. Sentient beings commit various evil deeds, causing the dragons and devas to resent and rebuke them, so that the rain does not fall.
5. Among these five, if even one obstacle occurs, the rain will not fall. Regarding the three yakṣas, the new translation says:
*Yakṣa* is translated here as "light-footed ghost" (*qingjie gui*). Tripitaka Master Xuanzang translates it as "fierce and evil deity" (*baoye shen*) or also as "valiant and robust deity.
The females are called *yakṣiṇī*, meaning "the awe-inspiring," who dwell upon the earth and feed upon living beings. The males are called *yakṣa*;
they possess wings and can fly through the air, feeding exclusively on infants. They reside in the lower heavens and guard the gates of the celestial cities. (Section Four: The Dryads)
*Gandharva* is correctly transliterated as *Khandava*, which means "one who travels seeking fragrance" (*xunxiangxing*) or "fragrance-eating deity" (*shixiang shen*).
This refers to a being who consumes odors, plays music, and seeks alms; when the body of Śakra, Lord of Devas, manifests a particular sign, they go to perform music for him.
In India, a class of musicians is called *khandava*, meaning those who do not engage in productive labor but instead seek food through fragrance.
Regarding the "Five Asuras" sought through the music of the *qi*:

the ancient translation was "Gods Who Do Not Drink Alcohol," meaning that because the seawater is salty and bitter, wine cannot be brewed from it; for this reason, they are called "Gods Who Do Not Drink Alcohol.
The new translation is *Asura*, which here means "Non-Gods," so called because they lack the true virtues of gods. Sixth, the *Garuḍa*.
*Lo* (羅) here is translated as "Golden-Winged Bird" (*garuḍa*); more precisely, it is *kalavinka*, which is translated as "Wondrous-Winged Bird.
Its body has four colors: golden, silver, lapis lazuli, and crystal.
Because its wings and feathers are adorned with these four kinds of precious colors, it is called the Wondrous-Winged Bird. It possesses the four modes of birth, as has already been explained above.
The seven *kiṃnara*—properly called *kiṃnara* (Sanskrit) and translated as "song deities"—are of four types;
in the *Lotus Sūtra*, they are referred to as the "assembly of those who sing pure songs and elegant music. These musical deities are by nature animals, yet their forms resemble humans;
they have upright countenances and a single horn upon their heads, such that when people see them, they are filled with doubt and cannot determine whether they are human or not.

These animals are also called "doubting persons. Eighth, the *mahoragas*—properly *mahoragas*, translated as "large-bellied"—where *mahu* means "large" and *loka* means "belly," referring to species such as pythons and frogs.
These eight classes each contain immeasurable numbers; they are all present in this assembly. Ask them about this.
When asked by what cause they were able to reach the assembly of the Buddha, Master Cien replied:

"It is due to the Buddha’s great compassion, which extensively draws in all sentient beings so that they may all hasten toward him, hoping for the rain of Dharma to moisten their sprouts and seeking the medicine of wisdom to eliminate their manifold sufferings.
They are like those returning to a compassionate father or approaching a King of Physicians; it is solely through his impartial compassion."
His grace extends to all that moves and all that is stationary. "The moving" refers to those with sentience; "the stationary" refers to those without sentience, such as plants and trees.
Wherever the Tathāgata traverses, sentient beings who encounter him immediately attain transcendence, while insentient things—such as withered wood—regain life, sprouting flowers and bearing fruit.
△ Commentary II: General Manifestation of Upholding.
"Having heard what the Buddha spoke, they all rejoiced greatly, believed and accepted it, and practiced accordingly.

This commentary generally manifests the act of upholding as it applies to all the assemblies mentioned previously; however, this specific circulation [of the teaching] primarily pertains to the ninth assembly.
The nine assemblies are consistent with the underlying principle; why must this essential [text] alone encompass all nine?

Furthermore, according to previous precedents, following the preaching of the Dharma, there is still a lack of the manifestation of auspicious signs and the section on "Proof of Accomplishment" (*siddhi*). However, based on the Sanskrit original, it is sufficient that it possesses both beginning and end.

*Commentary*: Regarding the passage from "Hearing what the Buddha has spoken" to "faithfully accepting and practicing," the *Compassionate Benefit Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra* (*Cien Yuanjue shu*) cites this.
The *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states that there are three kinds of meaning for which one rejoices and practices with devotion:

first, the purity of the speaker, because they are not defiled by attachment to fame or profit; second, the purity of what is spoken, because of knowing the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) as it truly is;
and third, the purity of attaining the fruit, which refers to the benefit of the teaching. Furthermore, once the exposition of the matter was complete, the assembly...
Those who have gained benefit from hearing the Dharma accumulate goodness within their hearts; those who receive guidance act according to the words they have heard.
Thus, each student receives the teaching and practices it, circulating that which was previously unheard. As for the commentary’s question, "Why is it necessary to include these [passages]?

many ancient masters have said that because the transmission of the sutras was not yet complete, there was no circulation [of this portion]. This statement implicitly points forward to the present text, which serves as a supplement to the nine [previously circulated chapters].

Because it is not employed in this assembly, it is asked, "Why must it be so? As for the phrase "still lacking the manifestation of auspicious signs" and so forth, these are present at the conclusion of every assembly;
thus one knows that each has its own distinct circulation.
△ The commentary on the four verses expresses the intent and dedicates the merit.
My Buddha, in the past, throughout an ocean of great kalpas, practiced austerities for the sake of sentient beings. △ He realized this inconceivable gate of liberation.
△ How fortunate that I have been able to hear and extol it! △ By virtue of this supreme cause, may all merits be dedicated to the imperial succession.

In Chang’an, the Imperial Way flourishes; the four debts of gratitude and the hundred officials, △ as well as all sentient beings, △ together realize the Mysterious Gate and align with the Ocean of Wisdom.
○ The fourth section of the *Chao* (Excerpts), the Text for Rejoicing and Dedication, contains two verses: the first verse rejoices in the encounter and offers praise; the latter...
In the verses that present the benefits and dedication [of merit], the first three lines describe the inconceivable realization, while the final line celebrates hearing and praises the exposition.
Within the former [the description of realization], the first two lines indicate the Buddha’s compassionate vows, and the final line reveals the inconceivability of the realization.

Within the first of these, the upper line indicates the long duration of the practices and vows, while the lower line explicitly clarifies those practices and vows; within that [lower line], the upper [sub-division]...
The first four characters formally introduce the practice; the following three characters indicate the purpose of that practice; and the final phrase reveals the inconceivable realization.

Regarding the term "inconceivable" and so forth, this refers to the realm of the inconceivable liberation into which one enters. "Gate" (or "door") refers to the means of entry, namely the practices and vows of Samantabhadra.
This constitutes the formal presentation of what is being praised at the beginning of the subsequent verses.
The first four characters indicate the roots of goodness to be dedicated; the following three characters and so forth formally apply that dedication.

Within this, the initial portion is the dedication to sentient beings, and the final phrase is the dedication to the other two places. Regarding the initial section, it first clarifies the repayment of the four debts of gratitude;

the last three characters clarify the inclusion of all conscious beings. Within the four debts of gratitude, the first specifically elucidates the debt to the sovereign, as explained in the commentary.

"First, one dedicates [merit] upward for the precious reign and so forth; second, one universally extends it to the four debts of gratitude: first, the debt to the sovereign; second, the debt to the Three Jewels;

third, the debt to one's parents; and fourth, the debt to all sentient beings. As the ancients said, 'the debt to the donor'—since each of these aforementioned entities possesses great kindness and virtue, one dedicates [merit] upward to repay them.
This is explained in detail as set forth in the *Bodhicittotpāda-sūtra* (The Sūtra on the Contemplation of the Mind-Ground) and the *Jātaka* tales."

"Those who are the hundred lords" is a general reference to the ministers and officials who together receive the sovereign's grace. "As for those that contain life" (*han-sheng*) is an alternative name for sentient beings (*yǒu-qíng*), and in total there are ten types:
first, those born by transformation (*lei-shēng*); second, those born from the skin (*fū-shēng*); third, those born in groups (*qún-shēng*); fourth, those who harbor life (*huái-shēng*);
fifth, the azure masses (*cāng-shēng*); sixth, those who give birth (*zhòng-shēng*); seventh, those that contain life (*hán-shēng*); eighth, those that differ... [the text continues].

The ninth is called "arising" (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the tenth is called "sentient beings" (*sattva*); these are now one and the same number. As for the final phrase returning to the other two locations:
the two characters "Mysterious Gate" (*xuánmén*) refer to *tathatā-bhūtakoṭi*, and the two characters "Ocean of Wisdom" (*zhìhǎi*) refer to unsurpassed *bodhi*.
I vow that the four debts of gratitude and those in the three realms of existence may together realize this Way. Within this, the term "all living beings" (*hánshēng*) and so forth [is included].
To turn toward sentient beings is to practice according to signs, which is the level of the ocean of wisdom; to turn toward Bodhi is to practice free from signs, which is the profound gateway.
Turning toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) means that the limit of reality is neither following signs nor departing from them.

To practice according to signs is great compassion that transforms those below; to practice free from signs is great wisdom that seeks the goal above. Thus, these two practices—following signs and departing from signs—are mutually indispensable.

The first is untenable. Why? Because of the mutual dependence of the primary characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the secondary characteristic (*anulakṣaṇa*). If the secondary characteristic were lacking when separated from the primary characteristic, it would become contaminated (*sāsrava*).

If the primary characteristic were lacking when separated from the secondary characteristic, one would fall into a biased emptiness (*ekānta-śūnyatā*). Since the secondary characteristic is attained through the primary characteristic, one contemplates emptiness while the myriad practices (*sarva-caryā*) boil forth;
since the primary characteristic is attained through the secondary characteristic, one traverses existence (*saṃsāra*) while the single path remains pure. Such are these two practices.
Only when there is no deficiency can one contemplate emptiness; being unimpeded by existence, one engages with existence, and being unimpeded by emptiness, one penetrates emptiness.
The reason for this is that phenomena are identical to principle, and form is identical to emptiness. Principle is manifested through phenomena, and phenomena rely upon principle to be empty.

When principle is empty, everything encountered is entirely the Real; when phenomena are manifested, there is nothing that is not Buddha. Furthermore, emptiness is identical to form, yet within the myriad distinctions of phenomena, [the truth remains].
All phenomena are true suchness; form is itself emptiness, and within this single mark of suchness, there is nothing that is not quiescent.

If one understands in this way, there is not a single mind that is not realized, and in every thought-moment the Way is perfected; there is not a single phenomenon that is not true, and every particle of dust is a Buddha-land.

This is precisely what is elucidated by the Perfect Teaching (Yuanzong). Therefore, this teaching is perfectly sublime without anything that is not subtle, and vast without anything that is not all-pervasive.
Profound yet further deep, universal yet all-pervasive, it stands in stark contrast to the practices of the various provisional vehicles of the mundane and the small;

it constitutes the practice of Samantabhadra’s perfect interfusion that accords with the nature of reality. This is truly because the capacities of sentient beings differ and their dispositions are not the same;
for those of the highest wisdom, it is impossible to provide adequate analogies.
A Separate Commentary on the "Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra" from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra of the Buddha*, Fascicle Six.
